articles.title: Toward Reproducible Research with LLMs: Guidance for Documentation, Reporting, and Transparency
articles.authors: Ryan Watkins; Vicky W. Lee
articles.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into scientific research workflows across many disciplines, creating new opportunities for literature review, research design, data analysis, simulation, coding, automation, and other forms of scientific inquiry. Their growing use also creates challenges for transparency and reproducibility, particularly because LLM outputs are nondeterministic, model capabilities change rapidly, and research workflows may involve multiple models, agents, tools, and computational environments. This guide proposes a framework and checklist for systematically documenting and reporting the use of LLMs as scientific instruments. Grounded in the principle that documentation requirements should be proportional to the methodological role of the LLM and its potential impact on research findings, the framework distinguishes among varying levels of human agency, methodological impact, and corresponding documentation needs. We provide guidance for determining what aspects of a LLM-enabled research workflow should be documented, how thoroughly they should be reported, and how those requirements change as the methodological role of AI increases. We further distinguish between documentation collected throughout the research process and information reported in manuscripts and supplementary materials. Rather than treating reproducibility as requiring identical LLM outputs, we emphasize sufficient methodological transparency to enable others to understand, evaluate, and, where desirable and feasible, reproduce or systematically test the research workflow and its results. The proposed guidance is intended to support researchers, reviewers, editors, and disciplinary communities as norms for transparent and reproducible LLM use continue to evolve.

articles.title: Data and Code Availability in Sports Science: A Registered Report
articles.authors: Simon Nolte; Daniel Memmert; Robert Rein
articles.abstract: Sharing scientific raw data and analysis code facilitates cumulative scientific work and enables assessments of reproducibility and robustness. In sports science, preliminary evidence suggests that data and code availability may be low, but previous studies have been based on small cross-sectional samples. To provide a larger audit of the literature, we will document data and code sharing in all original articles published in Q1 sport science journals over the past ten years. We will calculate the percentages of reported as well as actual public availability of data and code and investigate whether general time trends exist. Data and code sharing policies of the analyzed journals will be surveyed to examine associations between policy changes and sharing rates. We provide a resource with all articles in the sample that have shared data and/or code for reuse. The findings of this study can be used to inform future data and code sharing policies in sport science.

articles.title: The Marker Drift Problem: Measuring LLM-Assisted Writing with Unstable Lexical Indicators
articles.authors: Serhii Nazarovets
articles.abstract: Lexical markers are increasingly used to estimate the prevalence of large language model (LLM)-assisted writing across large publication corpora. However, longitudinal applications of this approach rely on an important assumption: that the relationship between these markers and LLM use remains sufficiently stable over time. Recent research suggests that once publicly identified, individual markers may lose their diagnostic value due to adaptation by users and the evolution of language models. Furthermore, lexical markers may reflect not only LLM use, but also linguistic competence, AI-assisted editing, and broader forms of stylistic convergence. This paper introduces the Marker Drift Problem to describe a methodological challenge in which indicators change alongside the phenomenon they are intended to measure. Marker drift raises questions about temporal comparability, as observed changes in marker prevalence may reflect changes in LLM use, changes in the indicators themselves, or both. Without attention to the temporal stability and construct validity of lexical indicators, increasingly precise estimates of LLM-assisted writing may be based on unstable measurement instruments.

articles_hidden.title: A Knowledge Graph Framework for Systematic Collaboration Intelligence in Biomedical Research Portfolios
articles_hidden.authors: Baris YAPICI; Vanessa Lage-Rupprecht; Martin Hofmann-Apitius
articles_hidden.abstract:
Collaboration discovery in large publicly funded research portfolios depends on fragmented information distributed across project records, deliverables, and personal networks. We present a knowledge graph framework that makes collaboration-relevant structure in funding portfolios systematically observable and queryable. Starting from public funding records, the graph is enriched with disambiguated organisations, linked publications, researcher identifiers, and data assets recovered from project documents via large language models.

Applied to 235 biomedical research projects from the Innovative Health Initiative, the resulting portfolio graph reveals both dense organisational connectivity and distinct thematic structure. We show that structural pathways and thematic alignment provide complementary signals for collaboration brokerage. We evaluate lexical, graph-structural, and embedding-based scoring configurations against a structural pseudo-benchmark and show that hybrid approaches outperform individual channels. Document-level extraction recovers hundreds of hidden data assets absent from structured metadata, and a cross-portfolio comparison with the German Research Foundation highlights structural differences between public-private and academic-led funding models. Our work demonstrates that a portfolio graph built from public records can support systematic brokerage of data collaboration and research interest at scale, with implications for research information management and science-of-science indicator design.

articles_hidden.title: Automatic Prompt Optimization for Policy Documents Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Hanif Sajid
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, I leverage three automatic prompt optimization (APO) algorithms to search for optimal prompts that enable large language models to classify policy documents accurately, without requiring task-specific training data. I evaluate the performance of these optimized prompts using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini model, comparing them against prompts created by domain experts as a baseline. Experimental results show that all three algorithms significantly outperform the baseline. Among the algorithms, APE, which induces simple prompts from input-output example pairs, significantly outperforms GRIPS and performs comparably to ProTeGi. Additionally, ProTeGi demonstrates similar performance to GRIPS. However, neither the optimized prompts nor the human-designed ones achieve a research-grade performance (defined as an F1-score of 70%) with the GPT-4o-mini model. To reach research-grade performance in policy document classification using APO methods, future work could explore the use of more powerful models, hybrid APO systems, cross-model evaluations, and inference-time enhancements.

articles.title: From Unstructured Text to Causal Inference: Addressing Proxy Measurement Error and Omitted Variable Bias
articles.authors: Soojin Park; Luke Rabelhofer; Su Yeon Kim; Chioun Lee
articles.abstract: Unstructured text offers a rich source of nuanced information that is often difficult to capture with structured survey measures. However, Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools result in labels prone to measurement error, which can cause significant bias and invalid statistical inference. Although several studies have proposed methods to address measurement error in text-extracted measures, these solutions often rely on the ``no omitted confounders'' assumption, which is rarely met in observational settings. Addressing measurement error in isolation from omitted variable bias is often insufficient for valid causal conclusions. Therefore, this study aims to provide a rigorous and credible foundation for drawing causal conclusions from unstructured text in observational settings. To do this, we derive nonparametric and parametric bias formulas for cases in which 1) we ignore both omitted confounders and measurement error and 2) we correct measurement error in a treatment proxy while ignoring omitted confounders. Based on these bias formulas, we develop a framework for estimating Average Treatment Effects using a text-derived treatment that addresses the dual challenges of measurement error and omitted confounders. We illustrate our proposed methods using unstructured data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study to examine the effect of social interaction on cardiovascular health.

articles.title: Covariance Estimation Matters for Multidimensional Normative Modeling: A Demonstration with Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder
articles.authors: Brian Zaboski; Christopher Pittenger
articles.abstract: Normative models characterize individuals relative to a reference distribution, but choices used to estimate that distribution may change who appears most atypical. We examined how covariance estimation affects Mahalanobis-based deviation scores when reference measures concentrate at their minimum. Study 1 compared minimum covariance determinant (MCD), Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage, and sample covariance across 11 simulated conditions varying distributional shape, floor prevalence, and contamination, with reference samples of 62–5,000. Estimates and distances were evaluated against benchmarks derived from the generating distributions. All three estimators approached the target covariance under multivariate normality. MCD had the lowest covariance bias in the Gaussian contamination conditions. In uncontaminated floor conditions, its bias persisted at the examined prevalences of .25 or greater, while both alternatives approached the target. Study 2 examined 263 adults with obsessive–compulsive disorder and 62 screened controls. MCD excluded 24 controls whose profiles were consistent with ordinary reference variation. Ledoit–Wolf deviation scores correlated with quality of life (r = −.53). Across five scoring specifications, however, deviation added little explained variance beyond depression and obsessive–compulsive severity (ΔR² ≤ .003). Default MCD and Ledoit–Wolf shared only 17 of the 27 patients in their respective highest-deviation deciles. These findings show that stability of a group-level conclusion does not establish stability of individual characterization. Covariance estimation should be evaluated in relation to the reference distribution and intended use, including sensitivity of individual scores and rankings.

articles.title: Mathematical modelling of interactive tapping reveals tap intervals as strongest predictor of subsequent tap timing
articles.authors: Shane Mannion; Ivana Konvalinka
articles.abstract:
Successful interpersonal rhythmic coordination requires people to continuously adapt both the
timing and tempo of their actions to one another. Classical error-correction models distinguish these
processes as phase and period correction, typically modeling them as responses to instantaneous and
cumulative asynchrony, respectively. These models were developed mostly for sensorimotor synchro-
nisation to an external pacing signal, rather than interactive interpersonal coordination where both
partners adapt. It thus remains unknown which temporal information people actually use to adapt
their behaviour to one another. We show, using a bounded generalised least-squares framework and
joint finger-tapping data obtained from both bidirectional (reciprocal) and unidirectional (leader-
follower) interactions, that the previous inter-tap interval (ITI) of a partner is a better predictor for
an individual’s next ITI than either cumulative or instantaneous asynchrony. We argue that this
predictor is not only the strongest from a modelling perspective, but also the most parsimonious
from a theoretical point of view. Our results support these claims and show that the partner’s
previous ITI provides a less endogenous predictor of adaptation, addressing a long-standing issue in
models of tapping behaviour.

articles.title: Development of the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses Scale
articles.authors: Kohsuke Yamamoto; Mami Kato; Ryo Eguchi
articles.abstract: Alcohol-related subjective experiences are associated with drinking behavior and alcohol use disorders (AUD) risk. However, existing measures access limited domains, such as alcohol expectancies, emotional reactions, or physiological effects, hindering multidimensional assessment of subjective alcohol experiences. This study developed and validated the Alcohol-Linked Typical Experienced Responses (ALTER) Scale, positive/negative and psychological/physiological responses to alcohol consumption among Japanese adults. Habitual drinkers provided free descriptions of alcohol-related experiences, which, together with findings from previous studies, informed the development of candidate items. Study 1’s exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a five-factor structure: Communication Facilitation, Negative Emotional Arousal, Cognitive Decline, Relaxation Responses, and Physiological Responses. The scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and one-month test–retest reliability (Study 2). Study 3 supported construct validity through associations with drinking motives, personality, interoceptive awareness, and problematic drinking, assessed using the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Individuals with higher problematic drinking tendencies reported stronger rewarding and aversive psychological responses, whereas physiological responses did not differ significantly. These findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and construct validity of the ALTER Scale as a multidimensional measure of recalled subjective alcohol experiences, providing a framework for examining individual differences in alcohol responses and AUD-related risk.

articles.title: Usage of Digital Technology and Its linkage with the Development of Life Skills, Mental Health, and Psychological Hardiness among university students
articles.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles.abstract:
Background: The pervasive use of digital technology among Indian university students has raised concerns about its implications for life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness. While moderate use may enhance learning, excessive use is associated with adverse psychological outcomes.
Objective: This study examines (a) prevalence of digital technology usage, (b) differences in life skills, mental health, and psychological hardiness across levels of digital technology usage, and (c) interlinkages among these variables.
Methods: The study adopted a two-phase design. In Phase-1, a Self-constructed Digital Technology Usage Scale was developed and standardized on 1,000 university students from Delhi-NCR. In Phase-2, data were collected from an independent sample of 600 postgraduate university students (300 professional, 300 non-professional) from government and private universities in Delhi, using stratified random sampling (Gender x Stream x University Type). Tools used: (1) Life Skills Assessment Scale (Nair et al., 2010), (2) Mental Health Inventory (Jagdish & Srivastava, 1983), and (3) Psychological Hardiness Scale (Singh, 2008).Analysis: Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, One-way ANOVA, and Multiple Regression were performed using SPSS v26.
Results: Moderate users (2-5 hrs/day) showed significantly higher life skills (M=198.60), mental health (M=158.2) and psychological hardiness (M=105.80) compared to low (<2 hrs) and high (>5 hrs) users (F=8.73 to 10.21, p<.01). Mental health (β=.38) and hardiness (β=.32) significantly predicted life skills.
Keywords: Digital Technology Usage, Life Skills, Mental Health, Psychological Hardiness, University Students

articles.title: Psychological Functions of Prayer: Findings from a Series of Experiments Comparing Prayer to Self-Talk
articles.authors: Aaron D. Cherniak; Pehr Granqvist; Mario Mikulincer
articles.abstract: Research on spiritual/religious practices has paid insufficient attention to the meaning-making frameworks distinguishing them from secular analogs. In three preregistered experiments, we tested whether increasing the salience of prayer among Jews affected felt security and positive and negative affect (Study 1), prosocial emotions (Study 2), and transcendence (Study 3) more than self-talk or routine-activity primes, and whether religiosity and attachment to God moderated these effects. Participants (n = 277, 209, 241) completed spirituality/religiosity measures and were randomized to reflect on prayer or one of two secular controls before completing outcome measures. Prayer increased felt security and empathic concern beyond both controls, whereas prayer and self-talk raised positive affect similarly above the routine activity; negative affect and personal distress were unaffected. Prayer also produced greater transcendence than the routine control, but not significantly more than self-talk. These effects were largely independent of religiosity, but avoidant attachment to God moderated prayer's effects on negative affect (Study 1) and transcendence (Study 3) in opposite directions. Prayer's benefits thus appear to reflect its relational, God-directed character rather than its self-regulatory function alone, though the specificity varies by outcome, with implications for how theories of religious ritual and spiritually integrated interventions conceptualize its active ingredients.

articles.title: ¡Mira! How Latina Mothers use imperatives to guide children’s participation during play
articles.authors: Reinaldo Cabrera Pérez; Gustavo Carlo; Elizabeth D. Peña
articles.abstract: Maternal imperatives are often treated as a unitary form of directiveness despite serving distinct communicative functions. We examined how Spanish-speaking Latina mothers used imperatives during toy play and whether use varied by site and child gender. Forty-eight mother–child dyads from Mexico (n = 25) and the United States (n = 23) participated in semi-structured play interactions. Maternal imperatives were coded as encouragement, redirection, repetition, or scaffolding. Across 1,430 tokens, scaffolding was most frequent (36.4%), followed by encouragement (25.8%), redirection (23.6%), and repetition (14.3%). Lexical choice was strongly associated with communicative function, indicating systematic form–function patterning. Imperative use was largely similar across sites and child gender, although exploratory analyses identified greater repetition in the United States. Findings show that imperative frequency alone provides an incomplete account of maternal directiveness and underscore the importance of considering the interactional functions of direct linguistic forms.

articles.title: Phoneme overlap analysis of the visual benefit for speech-in-noise perception
articles.authors: John Magnotti; Yue Zhang; Lin Zhu; Yingjia Yu; Michael Beauchamp
articles.abstract:
Seeing the face of the talker improves the intelligibility of speech-in-noise, termed the visual
benefit. The visual benefit is usually measured at the whole-word level, with responses classified
as "correct" or "incorrect". An alternative method measures visual benefit using the phoneme
overlap between stimulus and response. In 55 participants presented with auditory and
audiovisual words, phoneme-overlap analysis estimated 289 different visual benefit values,
compared with only three different values for whole-word analysis. Phoneme-overlap detected a
positive visual benefit in 67% of word-participant pairs, in contrast to 32% for whole-word
analysis. Individual words varied greatly in their phoneme-overlap visual benefit, from 1% to
72%. Variability across words was accurately predicted (r = 0.78) by the phoneme composition
of the word and the visual benefit for untested words could be predicted with a median error of
9%. Measuring the visual benefit for individual phonemes revealed similarly high variability
(1% to 70%) with six phonemes (W, F, V, TH, P, AW) exhibiting visual benefit more than one
standard deviation above the mean. The increased sensitivity of phoneme-overlap analysis
relative to conventional whole-word analysis may provide a useful tool for investigating
audiovisual speech perception in clinical, neuroscience and computer science contexts.

articles.title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed-Methods Cultural Consensus Study
articles.authors: Saida Heshmati; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Carmen Goicoechea; Andrew Villamil; Catalina LeeAnn Oselio; Saina Salamati; Corey Abramson; Martín Sánchez-Jankowski
articles.abstract: Love can emerge through moments and interactions in our daily lives, varying across different cultural contexts. Using a sequential mixed-method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; Romney et al., 1986), we examined the shared agreement on which daily life experiences evoke loving feelings in Spanish culture across two studies. In Study 1, we conducted semi-structured interviews (n = 54), two-person group interviews (n = 6), and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40) to explore how love manifests across different relationships in daily life in Spain. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified recurring experiences, centering around explicit affection, instrumental support and dependable care, quality time, and thoughtful, attentive actions. This analysis informed the development of the 61-item Felt Love Questionnaire for Spain (FLQ-Spain), which collects everyday experiences with the potential to make people feel loved within the Spanish context. In Study 2, we administered the FLQ-Spain to a representative sample of Spaniards (N = 502) to assess how likely these experiences are to elicit loving feelings in the Spanish culture. Results from cognitive psychometric analysis revealed a shared agreement in the responses. ‘Highly likely’ loving eliciting experiences were characterized by support and dependability, sharing quality time, and explicit expressions of love—and particularly so within close ties such as family, partners, and friends. Results also showed that controlling or possessive behaviors from romantic partners or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. This investigation contributes to the understanding of the shared beliefs in love in everyday life based on the perspectives of Spanish culture.

articles.title: Form Composition: The Generative Structural Engine of Metaphors in Human Cognition
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Drawing on Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, this paper explores the origins of non-literal meaning in human cognition and proposes a generative structural engine based on each concept’s central form, a unitary structure embedded within every concept we learn, which encodes a compressed subset of each concept’s information and gives that information default influence in cognition. Recent work has found evidence for form composition, a default bias to interpret complex expressions in terms of each concept’s central form. The present paper tests the hypothesis that form composition operates across domain boundaries in a way that immediately generates potential metaphorical meanings. Across four experiments, participants judged interpretations of metaphors as possible if those interpretations involved form-encoded properties, even when the metaphors and the concepts involved were novel. In contrast, they rejected metaphors involving non-form properties as impossible. These findings suggest that form composition enables the spontaneous generation of non-literal meaning. Rather than being a derivative part of composition, metaphor may therefore emerge directly from the underlying structure of concepts and how they naturally combine. The findings have implications for concept learning and other forms of linguistic creativity. They also suggest why humans may possess a persistent bias toward reductive thinking across domains.

articles.title: Newborn infants show neural sensitivity to changes in auditorily presented numerical information
articles.authors: Kaisa Lohvansuu; Jarmo Hamalainen; Tiina Parviainen; Hanna-Maija Lapinkero; Daniel Ansari; Bert De Smedt; Minna Torppa; Tuire Koponen
articles.abstract: Human infants are assumed to be born with an innate understanding of quantities—a number sense— that enables them to detect non-symbolic number differences, for example, between sets of objects. This early ability has been found to be a predictor of later math skills. The assumption of innateness is based largely on studies in infants at 6 months of age or older and using visual stimuli with large numerosities, or in studies lacking statistical power. Using EEG, we studied pre-attentive discrimination for auditorily presented non-verbal numerical and non-numerical magnitudes of sleeping newborns (N = 104) to investigate whether the newborn auditory system is discriminating the number of sequentially presented sounds. The results showed that the 2-part repeated standard sound was discriminated from 3-part deviating sound and from 1-part deviating sound. As also the responses to 3-part sound differed from the responses of the same stimulus presented alone as a control, these results suggest that the difference between 2-part repeated sound and 3-part deviant sound is not merely due to physical features of the stimuli but reflects processing of numerosity. These results suggest that newborn infants are able to pre-attentively process at least some differences in the number of stimuli supporting the view of innateness of numerical magnitude discrimination. As the earlier evidence for innateness in newborns is limited, our study utilising small numerosities and auditory modality instead of vision—given the confounds in visual paradigms—offers complementary results on the innate brain processing on numerical information.

articles.title: Better data, better policy: Distinguishing income poverty and financial stress may promote better temporal decision-making
articles.authors: Eike Kofi Buabang; Sarah Ashcroft-Jones; Kai Ruggeri
articles.abstract: The poverty trap is a cycle in which financial hardship is reinforced through short-sighted choices. To design effective policy, it is important to identify who is at risk of falling into it. Yet different measures of poverty may not identify the same people as at risk. This study tested whether subjective financial stress is associated with intertemporal choice over and above income poverty, and whether financial literacy moderates these effects. Across seven countries (N = 1,497; Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain, the UK, and the US), financial stress was associated with more present-oriented choices in five of seven countries on a temporal discounting task and in five of seven countries on a windfall allocation task. By contrast, income poverty showed no reliable association, and financial literacy did not consistently moderate either relationship. These findings suggest that identifying who is at risk of the poverty trap requires capturing lived financial reality, not just income brackets, and that financial education may offer little to individuals whose short-sighted choices reflect constraint rather than comprehension. Policy makers are encouraged to review how poverty is defined for targeting purposes, and to prioritise policies that expand financial resources over those that assume the problem is a lack of knowledge or planning.

articles.title: The ontogenesis of socio-affective touch perception: Assessing valence and inferring social relationships from observed tactile interactions.
articles.authors: Louise P Kirsch; Monica Nkele; Adeline Depierreux; Olivier Mascaro
articles.abstract:
Social touch is a powerful communication channel conveying social dispositions and affiliative relationships across the primate lineage. Yet, how social inferences from observed socio-affective touch develop remains poorly understood. Three complementary experiments with 217 children aged 3 to 6 and 144 adults address this gap.
Experiment 1 tested the ability to assess the valence of observed tactile interactions. By age 3, children accurately evaluated a range of positive and negative touch interactions, integrating multiple cues, including the recipient of the touch (object vs. person) and stroke speed—consistent with key properties of skin afferents that process touch. Valence evaluation of observed touch thus emerges early.
Experiments 2a-2b examined children's and adults' ability to infer social bonds from observed touch. Participants watched two actresses: one stroked a character, while the other performed a matched neutral gesture (no touch, or touch at very fast speed). From around age 4, children consistently judged the stroking actress as more likely to be affiliated with the touched character—but only with that specific character, not with a different one. Adults, by contrast, generalized this inference, expecting affiliation between the stroking actress and characters beyond the one she had touched.
These findings reveal a developmental progression in processing observed social touch, from valence detection, to relationship-specific inference, to generalized trait attribution. Thus, observed-touch processing relies not on one unified ability but on a multilevel system with distinct developmental timelines—underscoring touch's central role in social cognition and the need for further research bridging these domains.

articles.title: Perceived punitive consequences and adolescent violent crime: The moderating role of socio-legal legitimacy in a Brazilian birth cohort
articles.authors: Andreas Bauer; Justice Tankebe; Thaís Martins-Silva; Alicia Matijasevich; Aluísio J. D. Barros; Iná Santos; Luciana Tovo Rodrigues; Joseph Murray
articles.abstract: Research on legitimacy and crime is dominated by cross-sectional evidence from high-income countries. Furthermore, less is known about how legitimacy and deterrence jointly shape adolescent violence in fragile institutional contexts. Using longitudinal data from the 2004 Pelotas Birth Cohort Study in Brazil (n = 1,510), a population-based, prospective longitudinal study, we examine whether perceived punitive consequences and three legitimacy dimensions — regarding the police, the law, and the social system — are associated with violent crime at ages 15 and 18. Higher perceived punitive consequences and more positive perceptions of legitimacy across all domains were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 15, whereas only police legitimacy and perceived punitive consequences were associated with lower odds of violent crime at age 18. Legitimacy of the law and of the social system moderated the association between perceived punitive consequences and violent crime at age 15, with negative associations strongest among adolescents who viewed institutions as less legitimate. These findings suggest that legitimacy is multidimensional and that both normative and instrumental processes jointly shape adolescent violence in high-violence contexts.

articles.title: Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis: The PIMMA Framework
articles.authors: Matteo Manente; Livio Finos; Gianmarco Altoè; Filippo Gambarota
articles.abstract: Meta-analyses, like primary studies, are affected by researcher degrees of freedom: researchers must decide which studies to include, how to compute effect sizes, and which statistical models to use. Different reasonable choices can lead to different results, making multiverse meta-analysis a useful tool for assessing robustness across alternative specifications. However, multiverse meta-analysis also introduces a multiple-testing problem. Current inferential approaches mainly provide a global test, which can establish that at least one specification differs from the null but cannot identify which individual specifications do so while accounting for multiplicity across the full multiverse. We introduce Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis (PIMMA), which allows inference on individual specifications while controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) and accounting for their dependence. In practical terms, PIMMA shows which results remain statistically significant after accounting for multiplicity across all reasonable analytical choices. In simulations, the specification-level test adequately controlled Type I error, with power comparable to robust variance estimation in scenarios where both methods maintained appropriate Type I error control. In an application to meta-analyses of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy efficacy for adult depression, 297 of 336 unique meta-analytic analyses remained significant after step-down max-T adjustment for multiple testing, accounting for dependence among analyses. PIMMA therefore extends multiverse meta-analysis from a global assessment of whether any effect is present to specification-level inference, allowing researchers to evaluate robustness across specifications and identify which individual results remain significant under appropriate error control.

articles.title: Gesturing at the Boundary: Can Concurrent Beat Gestures Bias Speech Segmentation?
articles.authors: Huandi Chen; Hans Rutger Bosker
articles.abstract: Beat gestures, rhythmic hand movements that reliably co-occur with prosodically prominent syllables, are one of the most common types of gestures in everyday conversations. Given their coupling to speech prosody, they can influence stress perception and facilitate lexical access. Still, little is known about their contribution to speech segmentation. Recent work has shown that beat gestures conveying distinct rhythms in a precursor (i.e., distal context) can bias the segmentation of subsequently presented acoustically ambiguous speech (Bosker, 2026). However, whether a single beat gesture co-occurring with the ambiguous speech (i.e., proximal context) can similarly shift boundary placement remains unknown. Across two experiments, participants segmented acoustically ambiguous four-syllable sequences (e.g., cry sister nip vs. crisis turnip) while a beat gesture was aligned to either the second or third syllable. Unexpectedly, no reliable effect of gesture placement on segmentation was observed. These findings suggest that isolated beat gestures may not function as reliable independent cues to speech segmentation. Instead, their influence may depend on the broader audiovisual and rhythmic context.

articles.title: Adaptive multi-frequency oscillator modeling of coordination recovery during rhythm switching in four-person drumming groups
articles.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Alexander Pantelis Demos; Marc Leman; Marcelo Wanderley; Caroline Palmer; Pieter-Jan Maes
articles.abstract: Musical ensemble coordination requires groups to maintain shared timing while adapting to perturbations and changing rhythmic constraints. We developed an adaptive multi-frequency oscillator model of how human quartets recover coordination during switches between binary and ternary meters. The model combines nonlinear harmonic phase coupling, coupling-driven frequency adaptation, and target-directed frequency relaxation within a four-oscillator network, allowing individual tempo adaptation while preserving subgroup-specific coupling within and between dyads. An individual spontaneous production rate dependent resonance term did not reliably improve the model’s prediction for quartet outcomes and was omitted from subsequent analyses. Model parameters were optimized by minimizing discrepancies between empirical and simulated inter-onset intervals, pairwise asynchronies, and cluster-phase dynamics. Simulations reproduced transient destabilization after perturbation cues followed by recovery towards a new coordinated state. Mixed-effects analyses showed that the model fits empirical quartets better than surrogate quartets, indicating sensitivity to genuine human coordination structure and generalization to held-out test data. Optimized parameters revealed condition-specific mechanisms: within-dyad coupling was lower overall in Complex polyrhythms and Binary meter, whereas between-dyad coupling was also lower in Complex rhythms, with a reduction for Ternary meter dyads. Frequency relaxation rates were higher in Complex polyrhythms than Simple isochronous rhythms and in Binary than Ternary meter, suggesting faster target-directed frequency relaxation during polyrhythmic coordination. Stability analyses revealed bounded regions of period and phase synchronization, including Arnold tongue-like entrainment regions shaped by coupling strength, relaxation asymmetry, meter ratio, and the specified harmonic basis. Together, these findings suggest that quartet synchronization depends on a balance between differentiated interpersonal coupling, adaptive frequency regulation, and preservation of distinct rhythmic roles. The model provides an interpretable dynamical framework for understanding how human groups recover and reorganize coordinated behavior under changing rhythmic demands.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Sharing:   Reconsidering the Role of Traditional Femininity/masculinity
articles.authors: X. Jia; Annet Kleiboer; Karen Holtmaat; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: A substantial body of research indicates that men, on average, share emotions less readily than women. The current research examined the extent to which gender differences in traditional femininity and traditional masculinity account for this relationship. In Study 1, 1,500 Dutch adults (938 women and 562 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (Distress Disclosure Index, DDI; Kahn & Hessling, 2001), gender self-concept (Dutch Gender self-concept Questionnaire, NSIV; Willemsen & Fischer, 1996), and self-stigma towards help-seeking (Self-Stigma of Seeking Help Scale, SSOSH; Vogel et al., 2006). In Study 2, 1,645 Dutch adults (979 women and 666 men) completed measurements of emotional sharing (DDI), gender self-concept (Bem Sex Role Inventory, BSRI; Bem, 1981), and help-seeking intentions (General Help Seeking Questionnaire, GHSQ; Wilson et al., 2005). Gender differences in emotional sharing were consistently partially explained by traditional femininity, but not by traditional masculinity. The same pattern emerged for help-seeking self-stigma (Study 1) and intentions (Study 2). These findings contradict widespread beliefs that traditional masculinity keeps men from disclosing their emotional vulnerabilities and seeking mental healthcare. More generally, the present findings highlight gender self-concept as a valuable theoretical concept in understanding the psychology of emotional sharing.

articles.title: Using Virtual Reality (VR) to Facilitate Context Reinstatement in Eyewitness Interviewing: Effects on Memory Performance and Retrieval Experience
articles.authors: Britt Heuker of Hoek; Noortje Sanders; Peter W. de Vries; Iris van Sintemaartensdijk; Lynn Weiher; Steven James Watson
articles.abstract: Using Virtual Reality to recreate environmental cues present during encoding to generate virtual context reinstatement (VCR) may be a promising tool to enhance eyewitness memory. However, VCR’s effectiveness relative to mental (MCR) and physical (PCR) context reinstatement remains unclear, as do mechanisms underlying its potential effects. The present study employed a between-participants experimental design to compare the effectiveness of VCR with PCR and MCR for supporting eyewitness recall while examining the role of cognitive load, stress, rapport, and neurodiversity in retrieval across reinstatement methods. Participants (N = 52) directly observed a mock crime and completed a delayed recall task (2-7 days) under one of three reinstatement conditions (MCR, PCR, VCR). Results provided preliminary evidence that VCR is as effective as traditional methods. Cognitive load was negatively associated with correct recall, suggesting retrieval demands play an important role in eyewitness recall irrespective of reinstatement modality. Qualitative findings further suggested that retrieval success depends on active engagement with reinstatement cues and the management of cognitive demands during recall, including attentional control and retrieval monitoring. Together, these findings provide preliminary support for VCR as a suitable alternative when PCR is not feasible and emphasizes the role of cognitive load in eyewitness memory retrieval.

articles.title: Exploring the Role of Transportation and Narrative Persuasion in Historical Virtual Reality from a Democratic Education Perspective
articles.authors: Lea Frentzel-Beyme; Hannah Decker; Nicole Krämer
articles.abstract: Virtual  reality  (VR)  is  increasingly  used  in  history  education  to  enable  immersive  engagement  with  the  past.  Although  these  applications  may  stimulate  interest  and  emotional  involvement, concerns have been raised about their potential to hinder critical reflection and foster  uncritical  acceptance  of  story-consistent  beliefs.  Drawing  on  the  transportation-imagery  model,  the  present  study  (N  =  106)  investigates  the  correlations  between  transportation  (i.e.,  narrative  immersion)  in  the  history-related  VR  application  Anne  Frank  House  VR  and  users’  emotional  responses,  knowledge,  and  story-consistent  political  beliefs.  Special  attention  is  paid  to  the  role  of  users’  political  orientation.  The  results  indicate  that  transportation is positively correlated with emotional responses and story-consistent beliefs (e.g., support for refugees) but not with factual or perceived knowledge. These findings point to the persuasive potential and educational opportunities offered by VR for history education. Although VR may not convey knowledge, it may foster engagement with socially and politically relevant topics.

articles.title: School and Classroom Heterogeneity and Psychosocial Student Outcomes: Mapping an Emerging Interdisciplinary Research Field
articles.authors: Claudia Neuendorf; Svenja Hascher; Chenru Hou; Camilla Rjosk
articles.abstract: Schools and classrooms are developmental contexts that have major impacts on the lives of children and adolescents. Therefore, research in psychology and other disciplines has identified classroom composition as a crucial factor for the psychosocial development of students. Recent developments in multiple disciplines have increased the attention paid to classroom heterogeneity as a contextual factor. This systematic review is the first to integrate findings across a broad range of psychosocial outcomes, multiple heterogeneity dimensions, and diverse research disciplines. In addition to reviewing theoretical approaches from different fields and compiling evidence on the impact of school and classroom heterogeneity on psychosocial outcomes, we examined the current state of integration into a multidisciplinary emerging field and evaluated the maturity of this research field on the basis of all available evidence. We conclude that the field has already begun to integrate and that studies are building on theory and evidence from multiple disciplines of origin, whereas methodological variety between fields is still evident. Regarding the field’s overall maturity, we contend that the field is still immature and stuck in the phase of translating the concept(s) of heterogeneity into valid operationalizations that align with the various theoretical perspectives.

articles.title: Attention Fragmentation: Toward a Formal Construct Definition, a Differentiated Nomological Network, and a Research Agenda for Scale Development
articles.authors: Diksha Sharma; Pooja Tyagi
articles.abstract: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar & Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

articles.title: Discussing Racial Demographic Change Online: Constructive Discourse Is Prevalent, Rewarded, and Propagated
articles.authors: Jonathan Doriscar; Anika Wilsnack; Tessa Charlesworth
articles.abstract: Racial demographic change is transforming the United States away from a White majority, a shift that can make concerns about group status especially salient. Public responses increasingly unfold in online video comment spaces, which are often perceived as ubiquitously hostile and toxic. Using 14 years of YouTube and TikTok comments (N = 101,103) responding to 106 high-engagement videos, we operationalize two discourse-feature indices: destructive features (e.g., toxicity and identity attacks) and constructive features (e.g., compassion and curiosity). We find that constructive features were: (1) 2.6x more prevalent than destructive features; (2) associated with YouTube engagement, where each unit increase corresponded to 3x more likes and 5x more replies; and (3) propagated in reply chains, with constructive parent comments followed by more constructive replies. Constructiveness is distinct from mere positive sentiment, politeness, agreement, or stance on diversity, and is a widely-prevalent discourse style for climate change. Hostile online content is not what is produced, rewarded, or propagated in the majority of content.

articles.title: When the self is on display: How narcissism shapes facial and emotional responses to social feedback during personal storytelling
articles.authors: Matias Piispanen; Jarno Tuominen; Ville Johannes Harjunen; Emmi Koskinen; Mariel Wuolio; Elizabeth Krusemark; Pärttyli Rinne; Mikko Sams; Anssi Peräkylä; Juha Salmitaival
articles.abstract: Personal storytelling exposes identity-relevant aspects of the self to social evaluation. Narcissism provides a characteristic example of elevated sensitivity to interpersonal evaluation and need for social validation. We examined responses to face-affirming and face-threatening feedback on personal narratives in grandiose and vulnerable narcissism to clarify individual differences in managing such exposure. In line with our hypothesis, data from 177 participants showed that higher narcissistic traits predict heightened nonverbal responses and altered self-reported emotional responses. Machine-learning analysis of video data revealed increased activation of the lip corner puller (AU12) in individuals higher in grandiose narcissism, reflecting enhanced outward signalling through greater smiling in response to both positive and negative feedback. Self-reports indicated heightened pride in grandiose narcissism, whereas vulnerable narcissism was associated with more negative subjective experiences, including lower pride, valence, and dominance, which were not reflected in facial expressions. Our findings shed light on how narcissistic traits may shape the use of facial expressions as strategic tools for impression management under social evaluation.

articles.title: Understanding Public Trust in AI-Based Clinical Psychological Decision-Making: A Qualitative Study
articles.authors: Yangqiong Lei; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied within healthcare and has the potential to support clinical decision-making and improve the efficiency of healthcare delivery. However, concerns surrounding the use of AI in healthcare may influence public trust in AI-generated diagnoses and treatment decisions. These concerns may be particularly important within clinical psychological settings, where decisions can involve sensitive personal information and significant implications for patients.
Methods: This qualitative study explored factors influencing public trust in AI-based decision-making within a clinical psychological context. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' perceptions of AI and the factors that may influence their willingness to trust AI-generated decisions. Interview data were analysed using deductive thematic analysis. Particular attention was given to perceptions of transparency, system design, bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility. Participants' perspectives on AI functioning as an assistant to a healthcare professional compared with AI operating as an independent decision-making tool were also explored.
Results: Several factors were identified as influencing trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making, including transparency, system design, perceived bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility for AI-generated decisions. Participants also distinguished between AI used as an assistant to healthcare professionals and AI operating independently, indicating that the perceived role and level of human involvement may influence trust in AI decisions. The findings additionally highlighted the importance of public understanding of both AI and healthcare when considering the acceptance of AI-based clinical decision-making.
Conclusions: Public trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making appears to be influenced by a combination of technological, ethical, legal, and human factors. Transparency, perceived bias, privacy protections, appropriate regulation, and clarity regarding responsibility may be important considerations in the development and implementation of AI within clinical psychological settings. The findings also indicate a potential need for greater public education and literacy regarding both AI and healthcare. Clear ethical and legal frameworks may further support public confidence in the responsible use of AI in clinical decision-making.

articles.title: Scene and Heard: Spatial layout and verbal labels support young infants’ categorization of places
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Agata Bochynska; Daniel D. Dilks; Moira Rose Dillon; LDM@NYU
articles.abstract: Human infants are limited in their self-guided navigation. Can they nevertheless learn about the places they’ll go? Three experiments examined pre-crawling 6-month-old infants’ (N = 96; 45 girls and 51 boys) ability to categorize places using a novelty-preference looking-time paradigm. During familiarization, infants saw videos presenting forward and backward motion through places from the same category: either fields, which have an open spatial layout; or canyons, which have a closed spatial layout. At test, they saw two videos side by side in silence: a new place from the familiar category and a place from a novel category. When each place was labeled with the same novel noun during familiarization in Experiment 1, infants looked longer at the novel place category at test, suggesting their sensitivity to places’ distinct spatial layouts and an ability to learn place categories. When the places’ spatial layouts were scrambled in Experiment 2, infants attended more to the places’ low-level features, disrupting their place categorization. When the places were presented in silence in Experiment 3, infants showed no evidence of place categorization. These results reveal infants’ sensitivity to category-relevant place information, especially with verbal labels, and their ability to learn place categories prior to self-guided exploration.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles.title: Knowledge: The Real Durable Skill What the Skills Conversation Lost, and How Employers, Educators, and the Workforce Field Can Put It Back
articles.authors: Caleb Braxton Bragg
articles.abstract: Employers say they want durable skills: communication, critical thinking, teamwork, leadership. The label comes from an analysis of 82 million job postings that sorts what workers bring into two bins, technical skills that perish and durable skills that travel. This whitepaper argues the bins are backwards. The durable skills employers name are knowledge in use, organized bodies of domain information deployed on a task, and they look free-floating only because the measurement tradition that could see knowledge was abandoned. Job analysis kept knowledge, skills, and abilities as distinct constructs and showed that job knowledge is the path from ability to performance. Competency modeling replaced task-anchored constructs with behavioral labels, and the posting taxonomies that generate today’s durable-skills evidence fold knowledge into skill by definition. What remains of a job after that instrument is applied is “critical thinking.” The paper engages the transfer literature directly, offers re-planting as what actually carries across jobs, and argues that durability is appetite for knowledge rather than independence from it. It closes with three practical moves for employers and educators, a testable prediction about employer calibration, and three distinctions to replace perishable and durable.

articles.title: The prose penalty in AI-assisted authorship
articles.authors: Faisal Feroz; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Jim Albert Charlton Everett; Sebastian Porsdam Mann; Brian D. Earp
articles.abstract: Generative AI based on large language models (LLMs) is increasingly used in academic, journalistic, and other professional and online writing, yet its implications for human authorship remain contested. We asked whether assignment of authorship credit depends on which task within the larger writing process a writer delegates to an AI assistant; whether any observed credit penalty is unique to AI; and whether credit can be restored through personalization: using an AI trained on one’s own previous writing. Across two preregistered studies (N = 878 US participants), observers evaluated a writer who either wrote unaided or delegated brainstorming, outlining, drafting, editing/revising, fact-checking, or all five tasks to an LLM or human assistant. In Study 1, although delegating a single task reduced authorship credit on average, the largest penalty by far applied to delegated drafting of prose, regardless of whether the helper was human or AI. Only the perceived originality needed for each task was independently associated with differences in credit assignment; perceived effort and skill were not. Perceived writing quality was also lower with LLM than human assistance, despite evaluated passages being randomly drawn from the same pool. In Study 2, using an LLM personalized on the writer’s own prior work increased both authorship credit and perceived writing quality relative to using a standard LLM. These findings show that authorship judgments depended principally on whether the writer produced the prose, regardless of helper type; that credit tracks judgments of originality, rather than effort or skill; and that the “prose penalty” on authorship attributions in AI-assisted writing can be partially reduced through personalization.

articles.title: Facing Trust: How Anthropomorphism and Individual Differences Shape Perceptions of Robot Faces
articles.authors: Lian Fingal; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Trust is essential to the development and maintenance of human relationships, and perceptions of trust based on the face alone can occur in as little as 100ms. Humans also tend to make trust estimations of robots based on their physical design, and these assessments can lead to successful acceptance of the robot or result in rejection. As robots are being designed to integrate into our daily lives, examining the factors that contribute to robot trustworthiness is a crucial component to understanding Human-Robot Interactions (HRI). Anthropomorphism is the attribution of human-likeness to objects, and it is suggested that imbuing robots with human characteristics can facilitate perceptions of trustworthiness. This study investigated the association of anthropomorphism with perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces and whether there is a potentially predictive role of the tendency to anthropomorphise that would mediate trustworthiness perceptions. 43 participants rated their impressions of 30 robot images on trustworthiness and human-likeness. Participants also completed the individual differences in anthropomorphism questionnaire (IDAQ; Waytz et al., 2010). We hypothesised that anthropomorphic ratings on the Godspeed Anthropomorphism questionnaire (Bartneck, Kulić, et al., 2009) would be associated with perceptions of trustworthiness on a single item measure of trustworthiness. We did not find support for this hypothesis (r(41) = .041, p = .795, N = 43). We hypothesised that individual differences in the tendency to anthropomorphise would be associated with human-likeness of robot faces. We found that IDAQ scores were not associated with anthropomorphism (Estimate = .219, S.E. = .286, C.R. = .766, p = .444). Finally, we hypothesised that individual differences would mediate the relationship between anthropomorphism and  perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces. We found that there was no significant relationship between IDAQ scores and trustworthiness perceptions (Estimate = -.005, S.E. = .135, C.R. = -.039, p = .969). These findings suggest that participants accessed prior negative knowledge about robots and applied them to the robot images in this study. Additionally, the results suggest that trust affordances cannot be detected simply in the physical features of a robot. Limitations include the experimental design, especially the one-item measure of trustworthiness and the lack of contextual cues.

articles.title: Pop-Culture Psychopathy: How Media Exposure Affects Laypersons’ Recognition of Clinical Psychopathic Traits
articles.authors: Robyn Marshall; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Entertainment media has proven to be an essential source of information about mental disorders and crucial in educating the public about these conditions. Consequently, how the media portrays the mentally ill is very important, yet they continue to be depicted alongside images of violence and crime. Psychopathy has been portrayed as a disorder of deceit, manipulation and charm despite research continually confirming otherwise. The inaccurate portrayals of psychopathy have far-reaching consequences, most alarmingly in the criminal justice system. These ‘psychopaths’ work alongside stigmatisation, categorisation theories and social learning and cultivation theories to encourage false beliefs about the disorder. This study uses a quantitative approach, collecting responses to a questionnaire through social media, to investigate the influence of inaccurate media depictions on the layperson’s ability to diagnose psychopathy accurately. The study compares psychopathy to participants’ ability to diagnose antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia. The author then looks for a relationship between participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy, their confidence in their knowledge about psychopathy and their interaction with media depictions of psychopaths before finally investigating the influence of several demographic characteristics. A non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA revealed that participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy is significantly worse than their ability to recognise the other conditions in vignettes. A multiple linear regression analysis revealed that a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy increased as their confidence increased and decreased as their media diversity score increased, however only the relationship between ability to identify and confidence was significant. Finally, multiple ANOVAs revealed that age and previous psychological knowledge had a significant impact on a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy accurately.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: The Form Composition Hypothesis: When Concepts Combine, Their Central Forms Are Privileged
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Human cognition involves the rapid combining of concepts to generate complex meaning, as in natural language. However, conceptual combination leads to a Massive Ambiguity Problem: since vast amounts of information are stored within each concept, even simple combinations can have many potential meanings. This paper introduces the Form Composition Hypothesis, a proposal within Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure. On Form Theory, every concept has a central form, a structure with a special cross-domain format for storing a compressed subset of each concept’s conceptual information, which then gives that information default influence within human cognition. The Form Composition Hypothesis proposes that when concepts are combined, the human mind uses this cross-domain format to limit the initial set of possible meanings. Across four sets of experiments, participants consistently prioritized form interpretations over non-form interpretations for familiar sentences, novel sentences, and sentences involving both familiar and novel concepts. Importantly, they judged non-form interpretations to be impossible in context-free tasks, providing evidence that non-form interpretations may require additional processing, and they spontaneously generated form interpretations in open-ended tasks. It is argued that form composition acts as a generative, structural constraint on conceptual combination, providing the structural conditions for linguistic creativity. The framework also has implications for communication and reasoning errors, concept learning, generative language models, and the human tendency toward reductive reasoning.

articles.title: Carrying the Hidden Stone: Mapping "The Sisyphean Quad" in Pre- and Posttrauma Discourses and Its Application
articles.authors: Swarnendu Karmakar
articles.abstract: This article introduces the Sisyphean Quad, a framework conceptualizing trauma as recursive and multidimensional across psychological, social, ethical, and existential domains. The model identifies four interlocking constructs: Sisyphean Burden (enduring moral, emotional, existential weight), Sisyphean Curve (cyclical fluctuations, nonlinear progression, unpredictable rhythms), Sisyphean Reflex (automatic survival responses, defense mechanisms, ingrained coping patterns bypassing awareness), and Sisyphean Paradox (tension between coping and preservation of identity). The recursive tightness of these constructs is captured by the Tono Factor (τ), approximated empirically by the Tono Index (τ^) via the Tono Scale (rating recurrence frequency, reflex rigidity, distress intensity, and recovery latency). To apply the model, this article also introduces the Triangular Model of Sisyphean Discussion integrates logotherapy for meaning; psychoanalysis for Burden, Curve, and Reflex; and Cognitive–Behavioral Pattern Interruption for resolution restructure of the paradox and future occurrence. Analyzing trauma across neurological, cognitive, behavioral, existential, cultural, and narrative layers, the article develops an ontologically stacked, interdisciplinary model, the first of its kind. Clinically, the Quad distinguishes maladaptive recurrence from meaningful return, guiding therapeutic dialogue when clients feel trapped in repeating patterns; reducing τ (and τ^) becomes the goal of intervention, loosening the cycle without erasing it. This theoretical and metatheoretical contribution introduces the Sisyphean Quad as a first universal account of trauma’s recursive architecture, where recurrence becomes not a failure but a gentle invitation to reenter life with renewed meaning and coherence.

articles.title: Fear, Conformity, and Phantom Majorities
articles.authors: Cory J Clark
articles.abstract:
In many ways, modern human brains are not adapted to modern environments, and our social worlds are one of the most significant evolutionary mismatches. Humans evolved in small-scale interdependent tribes, where information about local peer networks was observable or obtainable through mutual acquaintances. In such environments, people would have relatively good information about the prevalence of certain beliefs (a numerator) and a clear sense of their network size (a denominator), and thus could assess the relative popularity of different views and values. This assessment of majority views would help humans navigate their social worlds, allowing them to conform to popular beliefs and values or at least avoid visible violations of those beliefs and values. Given the small size of these environments, if dozens or hundreds of people appeared to support a particular perspective–and especially if one did not share that perspective–that perspective would be socially important and warrant consideration.
In modern environments, and particularly on social media, we routinely encounter views endorsed (via likes and reshares) by dozens, hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of people, where those seemingly popular views might represent <1% of the people who saw and thus could have endorsed the content. Human psychology is not adapted to intuit that thousands of people might be a socially insignificant percentage of people. I refer to these illusory crowds as “phantom majorities”: psychologically imposing masses of people that are experienced as far more representative of a population (and thus far more socially powerful) than they are in reality. In this short essay, I contend that (1) outgroup phantom majorities have contributed to exaggerated negative perceptions of outgroups and reactive extremism, and (2) ingroup phantom majorities have contributed to self-censorship, preference falsification, and mistargeted viewpoint conformity. Because both ingroup and outgroup phantom majorities can polarize, they may also contribute to self-fulfilling prophecies whereby seemingly popular fringe views become more popular, increasing their prevalence on social media and feeding back through the cycle.

articles.title: Revisiting Gino, Ayal, et al.’s (2009) Contagion and Differentiation in Unethical Behavior: A Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Esra Aslan
articles.abstract: Individual behavior is often shaped by observing others’ actions. The seminal Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) study found that individuals behave more dishonestly after witnessing blatant dishonesty by an ingroup member than by an outgroup member. However, because there was no group-irrelevant baseline condition, it remains unclear whether ingroup contagion, outgroup differentiation, or both drive the effect. Furthermore, using natural groups of university students leaves it unclear whether distinct properties of natural groups are necessary, or if mere categorization into arbitrary groups suffices. In this registered report, we tested Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) general hypothesis that exposure to ingroup dishonesty norms increases individual dishonest behavior more than exposure to outgroup dishonesty norms. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of their Experiment 1 with 3,323 U.S. Americans using both minimal and natural groups. Participants were exposed to standardized information about others' dishonest behavior, where we systematically varied the group identities of dishonest others. Then, they completed an incentivized coin-flip task where participants could double their earnings by lying. Despite manipulation checks suggesting that participants processed norm information and strongly identified with natural groups, the pre-registered ingroup-outgroup hypotheses were not supported. Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence for null effects across comparisons (BF₀₁ = 3.15-14.71). The core ingroup-versus-outgroup prediction received particularly strong null evidence (BF₀₁ > 14). We conclude that exposure to ingroup versus outgroup dishonesty norms, delivered through descriptive statistics in online settings, might not differentially affect individual dishonest behavior, revealing a boundary condition of the original finding.

articles.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles.title: A World-Model Theory of Trait Anxiety
articles.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Joel G. Thomas; Noa Yadid; Dafna Yavetz
articles.abstract: Computational psychiatry has sought the mechanisms of anxiety in domain-general biases in learning and planning, and found small, inconsistent effects. We argue this is because trait anxiety is not a bias in how a person learns any task but a property of the person's world model, namely the beliefs they hold about threat, control, and the self in particular domains, and the strategies that bring those beliefs to bear on a situation. We formalize a world model as comprising causal knowledge, an intrinsic reward function, available actions, and internal strategies, and build a minimal generative model in which each has a concrete role in explaining common trait anxiety behaviors. Most importantly, the model inverts the usual place of generalization. Instead of asking whether a task's findings generalize to real-world conditions, it models how far a person's real-world beliefs generalize to the task, and treats the computational parameters of learning and planning that a task measures as contingent on that generalization. Simulations demonstrate how, within tasks similar-enough to the domains of core anxious beliefs, avoidance behavior and anxious thought can arise in qualitatively distinct ways by virtue of world model components. We review prior attempts to relate trait anxiety to computations of learning and planning using our model, and argue that, to advance the field, future studies should personalize cognitive tasks based on threat-related world model content.

articles.title: A triadic model of bilingual shared reading:  Contributions of the book, parent, and child in shaping dual language use
articles.authors: Marissa Castellana; Christine Potter; Viridiana L. Benitez
articles.abstract: This study proposes and tests a triadic model of shared reading in bilingual contexts. Sixty-two Spanish-English bilingual parents (92% mothers, 88% Latino) and children (M=3.86 years, 51.6% male) read an English-only Monolingual book and bilingual Codeswitching book with Spanish words embedded in English text. Both parents and children produced more Spanish and codeswitching when sharing Codeswitching vs. Monolingual books, and dyads’ Spanish use was positively correlated while reading both books. These findings reveal that books, parents, and children all make meaningful contributions to the learning opportunities available during shared reading, consistent with the proposed triadic model. This framework can inform a deeper understanding of shared reading interactions that include diverse language experiences and environments.

articles.title: Expressions of Self-Censorship
articles.authors: Jabin Binnendyk; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract:
Self-censorship poses a considerable threat to public discourse as it can undermine key
democratic processes, such as the wisdom of crowds. While existing conceptualizations of self-
censorship use the lens of avoidance (i.e., withholding of one's opinion), we argue people express
self-censorship in several manners: avoidance, aversion to provocation, epistemic uncertainty,
and conformity. Across seven studies (N = 4,447), we developed and validated the Expressions
of Self-Censorship scale (ESC), a 16-item measure. Confirmatory factor analyses supported a
four-factor structure, suggesting that individuals differ not only in the extent to which they self-
censor but also in how they do so. We then examined the predictive validity of the ESC scale in
two novel contexts: i) willingness to share (publicly and anonymously) and edit a controversial
opinion (N = 555) and ii) discussing an active unionization campaign among other graduate and
professional students at a major U.S. university (N = 146). Across both contexts, the ESC
predicted self-censorship-related behaviors, including willingness to share opinions, whether and
how they edited their controversial opinion, and comfort discussing each of these topics across
different audiences. Further, we found that each of the expressions of self-censorship were
associated with distinct patterns of behaviors, supporting our claim that self-censorship is not
only the absence of voicing an opinion, but can also be the presence of an ingenuine opinion. At
