the societal level, this work highlights the importance of understanding both the information
within public discourse along with those opinions that are modified or withheld.

articles.title: Disentangling between- and within-person effects of HIV PrEP and treatment attitudes on condom use and bacterial STIs among sexual minority men
articles.authors: Trevor Adam Hart; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Yangqing Deng; Syed Noor; David M. Moore; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Daniel Grace; Nathan Lachowsky; Joseph Cox; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling
articles.abstract: HIV treatment attitudes and HIV PrEP are associated with sexual behavior that elevates the risk for bacterial STIs (B-STIs) among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Using a longitudinal multi-site study (Engage Cohort Study, 2017-2024), we modelled direct and indirect within- and between-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on condomless anal sex (CAS) and incident B-STIs among 1863 HIV-negative GBM. We modelled up to four years of follow-up visits using multi-level mediation analysis, with CAS as a mediating variable between HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs. We found direct within-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs, such that participants were more likely to report incident B-STIs at time points if they reported using PrEP and being more optimistic about HIV treatments; there were no indirect within-person effects through CAS. In contrast, we found both direct and indirect between-person effects. Specifically, participants who reported more PrEP use or who were more optimistic about HIV treatments over the course of the study were more likely to report incident B-STIs. Further, these effects were partially mediated by CAS. Given that we found within-person PrEP use is associated with increased CAS and STIs, and the general increase in adoption of PrEP over time, there is a need to expand biomedical intervention programs for B-STIs prophylaxis by integrating them with social and informational interventions about B-STIs risks, especially for GBM who use HIV PrEP.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Trust Talk Is Scoped and Unlexicalized: How People Express Trust in AI, and What Standard Instruments Cannot See
articles.authors: Muhammad Ali Shahidy; USHA LAKSHMANAN
articles.abstract:
Trust-in-automation research has recognized since the mid-1990s that trust can attach to a system's particular functions rather than to the system as an undifferentiated whole, and Lee and See (2004) explicitly recommend maximizing this functional specificity to prevent misuse and
disuse. Widely used self-report trust instruments nonetheless ask respondents to rate "the system" as a single referent; no item in any instrument examined here lets a respondent name the task or capability their rating concerns. This paper reports Phase 1 of a project measuring how far naturalistic discourse about trust in AI diverges from that instrument design. A prevalence sample of 20,000 items was drawn without trust-relevance filtering from a corpus of 12,497,945 items across 17 AI-focused subreddits, December 2022 through January 2026. Among 2,924
trust-relevant items, 96.97% (95% Wilson CI [96.27%, 97.52%]) expressed a trust or distrust evaluation without using trust-specific vocabulary. The same items were coded for whether their evaluation attached to AI as an undifferentiated category or to a specific object; as directly measured, 84% were object-scoped, a figure corrected to approximately 92% after hand verification identified a one-directional coding error in the global label. A keyword-based approximation of the explicitness codebook achieved only κ = 0.464 against the same gold standard, with roughly two-thirds of its positive calls false. The two findings are reported as separable: implicitness in trust vocabulary is documented directly, and scoping is offered as an explanation for it, not as something the data alone demonstrate. If trust evaluations are formed at the level of a specific object in roughly nine cases in ten, and conveyed using trust-specific vocabulary in barely three cases in a hundred, general single-item trust instruments are summarizing a considerably more differentiated attitude structure than the number they return.

articles.title: Some Things Do Last Forever: The Stability Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Humans develop fixed beliefs, even though the world is constantly changing. Drawing on Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, this paper proposes a generative hypothesis about a crucial source of these fixed beliefs: they are triggered when information is encoded as part of a concept’s central form – a unitary structure within every concept that stores a compressed subset of its information and gives that information default influence in cognition. In Experiment 1, participants endorsed the strong belief that form properties of familiar categories will be present in category members forever. In Experiment 2, participants exhibited the same strong belief for form properties of newly learned categories. In both cases, they rejected this strong belief for non-form properties. These findings indicate that central forms may play a significant role in the fixation of beliefs within different domains – such as functional fixedness, stereotyping, and fixed mindsets – suggesting a universal mechanism for the development of belief fixation. The substantial benefits of this belief fixation to the cognitive system are also discussed.

articles.title: LLMs are transforming persuasion: A scoping review of LLM-powered social bots
articles.authors: Desislava Bocheva; Patricia Hajszan; Joanne Hinds
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified concerns about their capacity to shape human attitudes, beliefs, and behaviours across politics, health, education, and marketing. This scoping review synthesises evidence from 200 academic, policy, and industry sources to examine whether LLM-powered social bots can persuade, how effective they are, and the mechanisms driving persuasive effects. Findings suggest that LLM-generated content can match or exceed human persuasive performance while being difficult to distinguish from human-authored communication. Persuasive effects appear shaped by personalisation and adaptive interaction, vary across individual differences, and may be amplified through coordinated activity across social networks at scale. However, evidence remains mixed and context-dependent, with limited understanding of longer-term behavioural outcomes. These findings suggest that as AI systems become increasingly embedded across society, anticipating and responding to adaptive and scalable forms of LLM-powered persuasion may become one of the defining challenges of the AI era.

articles.title: Rare on screens but on everyone's mind: a systematic review of misinformation prevalence, exposure, and concentration
articles.authors: Sacha Altay
articles.abstract:
How much misinformation do people encounter? Published estimates range from a fraction of
one percent to strong majorities. We systematically reviewed 443 studies reporting 1048
estimates of misinformation prevalence, exposure, sharing, and concentration. In behavioural
studies, misinformation is a median 1.3% of what people consume online; it reaches 12.0% of
people at least once and makes up 13.0% of what they share. In surveys, 57.7% say they have
seen misinformation and 19.8% say they have shared it. In content analyses, 23.0% of items are
classified as misinformation. How misinformation was identified (by fact-checkers, domain lists,
researchers, or classifiers) and at which level (sources or items) explained more of the variance
between estimates than what the study was about; platform and topic explained less. The top 1%
of users account for a median 70% of misinformation sharing or exposure. These results help
contextualize the diversity of misinformation estimates.

articles.title: Subtractive Epistemology at the Metadata Layer: How the Scholarly Record Registers Retraction and Not Refutation
articles.authors: Tomasz Witkowski
articles.abstract: In the 25 highest impact factor journals of general and internal medicine, 61 systematic reviews included at least one study since retracted, and among those examined the retraction arrived after publication in 74% of cases. Retraction notices are dated, name the paper and are machine readable, yet nothing obliged anyone to carry them into the syntheses that relied on them. That is the favourable case. The controlled vocabularies through which the scholarly record registers subtractive events supply a standardised entry for every event triggered by misconduct or procedural defect and none for an honestly derived claim turning out to be wrong. The absence follows from the shape of responsibility rather than from schema design: a publication has a keeper who answers for it, a claim has none. Systems that answer questions about what is known must now resolve the current state of the corpus continuously and cannot decline, making them the first agents to bear, for reasons unconnected with methodology, the obligation that produced derogation in law and the withdrawal of recommendations in medicine. A minimal form for an act of withdrawal would cost the addition of terms to vocabularies that already exist. Who would issue it remains open.

articles.title: Statistical Foundations for Estimating Conditional and Score-Related Standard Errors of Measurement
articles.authors: Wilco Emons
articles.abstract: Measurement uncertainty is typically expressed by the standard error of measurement (SEM). However, the SEM provides only a global measure of precision and may obscure important differences in precision at different latent trait levels. Several methods have been proposed for estimating trait-related (conditional) standard errors of measurement (CSEM). Even though CSEM estimators have been available for decades, surprisingly little research has systematically examined their shared underlying conceptual principles and their sampling properties. This paper fills this gap. First, different conceptualizations of conditional measures of precision and accuracy are explored. Second, a general framework for estimating CSEMs within the framework of classical test theory is developed. Third, the sampling properties of CSEM estimators (bias, variance, and accuracy) are studied using simulations. The paper concludes with general recommendations and suggestions for future research.

articles.title: The impact of cognitive hints on mathematical problem solving: A webcam-based eye-tracking study
articles.authors: Anna Boros; Marzena Binkiewicz; Agnieszka Glica; Artur Pokropek
articles.abstract: This study investigates the impact of cognitive hints on mathematical problem-solving performance and the role of individual learner characteristics in engaging with hints, while simultaneously evaluating the technical feasibility of webcam-based eye-tracking with a single calibration session for large-scale learning analytics. Utilizing a webcam-based eye-tracking approach, we recorded the gaze patterns of 5th-grade students (n = 134) as they solved mathematical tasks across four thematic sets. The study employed a within-subject design with rotated thematic sets and on-demand access to step-by-step hints. Data were analyzed using Linear Mixed Models (LMM) to account for the nested structure of the observations. A key methodological objective was to determine whether lower-quality webcam data, which can be easily gathered at scale without compromising participant privacy, can still reliably support the analysis. Findings indicate that while hints have a negligible effect on high-performing students, they significantly reduce the knowledge gap for students with lower initial ability levels. Furthermore, a significant learning effect was observed for subsequent tasks within the same thematic set. Despite the inherent noise in webcam-based data, the eye-tracking metrics explained a substantial part of the variance between experimental conditions. We found that students with higher levels of math anxiety and intrinsic motivation exhibited significantly longer total fixation time on hints once accessed and a lower overall fixation count in this area. Additionally, female students demonstrated a general tendency for higher visual engagement with hint areas, regardless of whether they chose to open them.

articles.title: Emotion recognition in neurotechnology: A scientific and technical fact check
articles.authors: Marie Luise Schreiter
articles.abstract:
Consumer neurotechnology systems that are claimed to be able to infer human emotions from facial expressions, voice, and physiological signals are increasingly deployed in domains such as marketing, education, human resources, and mental health.  As these systems have moved beyond clinical and research settings into consumer markets, their purported capacity to infer users’ internal states has become increasingly relevant to everyday life. More recently, emerging neurotechnologies have extended these claims by suggesting that emotional states can be detected directly from neural data using artificial intelligence, thereby bypassing outward behaviour altogether. These technologies are often promoted on the premise that emotions can reliably be measured objectively, enabling more precise, efficient, and equitable decision-making. However, the scientific and technical foundations underlying these claims remain contested.
In this article, we examine the scientific basis and methodological reality underlying claims regarding emotion classification in neurotechnology. We will evaluate the basic assumptions that are embedded in emotion recognition claims: That 1) emotional states can be objectively and reliably inferred from bodily or brain data and 2) emotional states are associated with stable and sufficiently specific behavioural, physiological, or neural signatures that permit reliable inference and 3) recordings from forehead, in-ear devices or consumer EEG in the form of headbands, glasses, or earbuds can deliver technically good-enough signal to inform about the internal emotional states of an individual user. 
Based on current findings, we are sceptical about claims regarding consumer emotion recognition systems. These systems currently face fundamental conceptual, empirical, and practical limitations. We conclude that the current enthusiasm surrounding AI-based emotion recognition reflects an overconfidence in the objectivity of data-driven systems as well as current technological capabilities. A more realistic appraisal of the technical state of the art and transparent discussions of limitations of these technologies is necessary, particularly when they are deployed in high-stakes contexts or in vulnerable groups. Clarifying these limitations is essential for responsible development, evaluation, and governance of emotion recognition in neurotechnology.

articles.title: The Bridge-or-Trap Model of Companion AI: When Emotional Support Connects or Substitutes.
articles.authors: Ho Nam Cheung
articles.abstract: AI companions are increasingly used for emotional support, yet their relational consequences appear sharply divergent. The same qualities that make these systems comforting, availability, nonjudgment, and low interpersonal risk, may help some users move toward human connection while drawing others away from it. This paper proposes the Bridge-or-Trap model to explain this divergence. The model argues that AI-mediated relief becomes bridge-oriented when it reduces the expected cost of approaching a real person and supports human-directed action, such as disclosure, repair, help-seeking, or re-entry into social settings. The same relief becomes trap-oriented when it remains contained within the AI relationship, preserving avoidance and reducing opportunities for corrective human experience. The model specifies five interacting constructs: anticipated interpersonal cost of human closeness, AI relational reinforcement, relational-orientation state, ecological protection and affordance, and adaptive relational resilience. It further proposes that repeated AI-contained relief may produce path-dependent substitution, with entry and exit thresholds that can be tested empirically. Drawing on attachment theory, social anxiety research, resilience theory, social ecology, social exchange theory, and emerging evidence on AI companionship, the model reframes the central question from whether AI companions help or harm to when emotional support becomes a bridge back to people and when it becomes a substitute for them. The paper identifies three decisive tests: target-specific transfer, viable-alternative boundaries, and asymmetric recovery from AI-contained substitution.

articles.title: Duration-Dependent Bias and Variability in Short-Interval Time Reproduction: Evidence for Separable Timing and Control-Related Mechanisms
articles.authors: Aliza Naseer; Elena Gorbunova
articles.abstract: Time-reproduction performance can reflect both systematic distortions in temporal estimates and variability in the response used to express those estimates. The present study examined whether these aspects show different patterns across short target durations and participant groups. Sixty-seven HSE University students initially completed a PsychoPy-based time-reproduction task; five were excluded for insufficient valid trials, leaving 62 participants (40 International, 22 Russian). Participants reproduced five target durations (1.4, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, and 2.6 s). Performance was quantified using signed error, absolute error, and coefficient of variation (CV). Signed error showed a strong duration effect, F(4, 240) = 78.35, p < .001, ηp² = .566, whereas neither the group effect, F(1, 60) = 3.74, p = .057, nor duration × group interaction, F(4, 240) = 1.26, p = .285, was significant. Shorter intervals were over-reproduced and longer intervals under-reproduced, consistent with central tendency. Absolute error showed effects of group, F(1, 60) = 8.86, p = .004, ηp² = .129, duration, F(4, 240) = 2.50, p = .043, and their interaction, F(4, 240) = 3.60, p = .007, ηp² = .057. CV likewise showed effects of group, F(1, 60) = 10.57, p = .002, ηp² = .150, duration, F(4, 240) = 18.27, p < .001, ηp² = .233, and duration × group, F(4, 240) = 6.55, p < .001, ηp² = .098. The findings indicate that directional bias and response variability provide non-equivalent information about temporal reproduction. The behavioural results are compatible with contextual calibration of temporal estimates and with additional influences on response consistency, but they do not identify specific cognitive or neural mechanisms.

articles.title: The Unequal Selves Model: How Children Develop Self-Views in an Age of Economic Inequality
articles.authors: Eddie Brummelman
articles.abstract: Economic inequality is on the rise globally. How do children form self-views in an age of economic inequality? I offer a developmental model—the Unequal Selves Model—addressing this question by bridging insights from the psychological, educational, and sociological literatures. To support the model, I draw on qualitative, observational, survey, experimental, and intervention research, including cross-cultural studies, with a broad focus on childhood and adolescence (ages 4–18). The model identifies three pathways. Specifically, in contexts of economic inequality, children make social comparisons with worse- or better-off others (comparative self), face socioeconomic stereotypes (stereotyped self), and imagine their futures while receiving few opportunities for upward social mobility (disillusioned self). As a result, children from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds may come to see themselves as less worthy, deserving, competent, and capable of growth, while children from socioeconomically advantaged backgrounds may develop excessive achievement pressure. These gaps may widen in contexts with greater economic inequality and have downstream consequences (e.g., for mental health and academic achievement). The model informs theory and practice by positioning children’s self-views not as merely personal afflictions but as reflections of broader structural conditions.

articles.title: Evidence of Preserved Function in Semantic Dementia
articles.authors: Chelsea-Leigh Marie McKenzie; Melissa E Meade; Marieke Mur; John Paul Minda; Stefan Kohler
articles.abstract: This narrative review examined clinical assessments and empirical research on semantic dementia to understand the nature of preserved semantic function alongside impairment across different disease stages. The first section describes the clinical characteristics, staging, and diagnosis of semantic dementia, and concludes by summarizing the implications of these characterization differences. The next section presents a collection of studies with tasks specifically designed to explore spared semantic processing in semantic dementia. The final section synthesizes and discusses these findings and their utility in leveraging remaining cognitive processing. We conclude that a complete and accurate clinical picture of semantic dementia, and an understanding of semantic memory more generally, requires considering both impaired and spared aspects of conceptual processing and relevant cognitive functions that support semantic memory. The findings summarized in this review will be useful to researchers and clinicians interested in episodic and semantic memory.

articles.title: Proposition-Based Theory Specification (PBTS): A Structured Workflow for Analyzing and Refining Verbal Theories in Psychology
articles.authors: Andreas Glöckner; Tilmann Betsch; Daria Lisovoj; Jennifer Biehl; Jasper Zeno Siol; Fiona tho Pesch; Susann Fiedler
articles.abstract: Many theories in psychology are formulated as verbal narratives. Although verbal theories can be scientifically useful, there are no commonly accepted standards for making their inferential structure, definitions, boundary conditions, and links to observation explicit. This can leave unclear what a theory predicts in a given situation, whether it applies, which statements constitute the theory, or which version is current. We introduce Proposition-Based Theory Specification (PBTS), a structured, low-threshold workflow for improving verbal theory specification and analysis. PBTS requires researchers (a) to represent a theory as source-traceable verbal propositions, (b) to connect propositions through explicit implications, (c) to define all concepts and uncommon operators, and (d) to provide and document operationalizations and auxiliary assumptions. The workflow supports independent reconstruction, structured comparison, consensus building, versioning, and the assessment of theory-specification reproducibility. We provide step-by-step guidelines for specifying existing and new theories and for analyzing ambiguities, inconsistencies, tautologies, and missing elements. Evidence from an initial feasibility demonstration, a published case study, and two waves of the ManyTheorists collaboration indicates that substantively focused researchers can apply PBTS across a broad range of social psychological theories. PBTS complements rather than replaces mathematical, computational, and other formal approaches and can serve as an accessible intermediate or documentation layer.

articles.title: Socio-functional model of attitudes towards migrants: the role of institutional distrust, sense of threat and conspiratorial thinking
articles.authors: Nina Holičková; Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: Across three studies the current paper unpacks negative attitudes towards migrants in the context of the socio-functional model that binds together the sense of threat, institutional distrust, and conspiratorial thinking. Using a comprehensive multi-country dataset (Study 1) and two longitudinal studies from Slovakia and Czechia (Studies 2 and 3), the paper delves into the roots of anti-migration stances among European citizens. In Study 1 (N = 41,455), we analysed the ESS wave 10 data about conspiracy beliefs, institutional distrust, migration policy preferences, and the sense of threat allegedly posed by migrants. Study 2 (N = 938) shows that, at the between-participants level, conspiracy beliefs about the Russian invasion of Ukraine, institutional distrust and attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees are associated. No clear effects hold at the within-participants level, though. Finally, Study 3 (N = 856) shows that conspiracy mentality – rather than specific conspiracy beliefs about migration – is bidirectionally associated with the sense of threat allegedly posed by the migrants, pointing to conspiratorial thinking as a generalised metacognitive tendency to construe outgroup intentions and actions as malignant. Jointly, the studies explain the logic of anti-migration attitudes as immersed in the socio-functional model in which threat appraisals, conspiratorial thinking and attitudes towards outgroups are intertwined.

articles.title: What language models say about themselves can mislead users: evidence from schizotypy scales
articles.authors: Yifan Zhang; Kuzma Strelnikov
articles.abstract: A user can ask a conversational agent whether it feels lonely, whether it trusts people, or whether it perceives things that are not there. The system answers in the first person, and the answer invites an impression of what the agent is. Questions of this kind are the content of psychological questionnaires. We formalised this interaction by asking five large language models to answer as humans and giving them two validated instruments, the Multidimensional Schizotypy Scale (MSS) and the Schizotypal Personality Questionnaire (SPQ), with 30 iterations per model at the API default settings. All models departed from human normative values, and they did so in different directions. Among GPT models, GPT-4o showed the highest Negative and Positive scores, while GPT-5.4 showed lower Positive but elevated Disorganized scores. Gemini-3-flash showed elevated Negative and Interpersonal scores with suppressed Positive and Disorganized MSS scores, and Claude Opus 4.6 showed the largest elevations on Positive, Disorganized and total SPQ scores. Profiles were stable across repetitions, so a user who probes a model in this way receives a coherent and reproducible impression of a mind with unusual beliefs, social withdrawal or disorganized thinking. That impression reflects the model selected rather than any internal state: the scales were validated for human self-report, and the scores describe response tendencies produced by a prompt. We discuss two consequences for human-computer interaction: for users interpreting conversational agents that answer in the first person, and the use of language models for the interaction with human respondents, where the synthetic sam

articles.title: How Culture Shapes the Communication of Pain: A Systematic Review on the Affective Component and Future Directions
articles.authors: Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers; Camille Saumure; Daniel Fiset; Stéphanie Cormier; Caroline Blais
articles.abstract: Inequities in pain care persist globally, yet how culture—understood here as shared systems of norms, values, beliefs, and practices—shapes pain communication remains unclear. This systematic review examined cultural variation in the affective experience, regulation, and expression of physical pain among neurotypical adults. PubMed and PsycArticles were searched through December 8, 2025. Eligible studies compared cultural groups or subgroups or examined underrepresented populations using monocultural designs. Quantitative studies were appraised using STROBE- and Cochrane-informed criteria and qualitative studies using CASP; findings were synthesized narratively. Sixty-six studies were included (56 quantitative, 10 qualitative). Cultural differences were reported in 17 studies of affective experience and 31 of regulation, whereas evidence for pain expression was sparse and inconsistent: in some groups, self-reports suggested stoicism, whereas direct measures indicated greater expressivity. Major gaps also emerged in cultural representation, with most studies including a Western, English-speaking group while several world regions remained underrepresented. Key recommendations include broadening cultural representation, improving the reporting of culture, and developing cross-culturally valid measures of pain expression. The review was preregistered on OSF (September 1, 2022) and was mainly supported by the Canada Research Chair in Cognitive and Social Vision.

articles.title: The Adaptation Dilemma: Cultural Fit Does Not Guarantee Safety during Mental-Health Interactions with LLMs
articles.authors: Maya Low; Ian Gold; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: People increasingly take mental-health concerns to general-purpose AI chatbots. A first wave of safety research has begun to map LLM failure points in this context. When that work considers culture, it usually reads the problem as a lack of fit: if the model does not match the user, the fix is to make it match more closely. We argue that this perspective is incomplete, because cultural fit and safety are not the same thing. By safety we mean the absence of harm caused by the interaction itself. We sort these harms into two classes: imposition, where the model forces its default on a user it does not fit, and collusion, where it adapts to a framing that keeps the user unwell. Because a response that fits a user’s own framing is more credible to them, moving a model toward that framing lowers the risk of imposition while raising both the likelihood of collusion and the damage collusion does when it occurs, so improved cultural sensitivity trades one exposure for another rather than reducing exposure overall. We argue that the reinforcement learning layer increasingly pushes these models toward collusion, while the safeguards in current use are poorly suited to detecting that failure or to limiting the harm it does. We propose a taxonomy of six culture-related failure modes, three of imposition and three of collusion. We argue that evaluating safety requires an anchor outside the user’s in-the-moment approval: responses must be assessed against the harms and benefits the interaction produces for the user, judged both by an external standard and against the goals the user has stated for their care.

articles.title: Impact of the proportion of emotional faces on ensemble perception of group emotion.
articles.authors: MOURGUES; Guillaume T. Vallet; Simon Rigoulot
articles.abstract: In everyday life, we frequently interact with crowds with  faces showing various emotional expressions. Ensemble coding allows the visual system to efficiently extract average group emotion in groups  of faces. However, this process is biased as emotional intensity of the group is often overestimated. This amplification effect is reported to increase as a function of group size. Yet, it remains unclear whether this effect is driven only by the number of faces or could be influenced by another factor, the proportion of emotional faces in the group. The present study tested whether the amplification effect is driven by group size or the proportion of emotional faces within the group. Emotional valence (anger vs. happiness) was also manipulated as a potential influence of the amplification effect. Twenty-one participants estimated the average emotion intensity in groups of 4, 8, or 16 male faces, with 25%, 50%, or 75% of faces showing either happiness or anger. The amplification effect was operationalized as the proportional estimation error between the actual and estimated proportion of emotional faces. The results showed that larger groups were associated with greater amplification than small groups, that amplification increased when the proportion of emotional faces was higher, and that it was consistently stronger for anger than for happiness. These findings suggest that amplification may not depend only on group size, but also on the proportion of emotional faces, and that valence could modulate this effect. Together, the results highlight the role of structural and emotional factors in shaping how people perceive group emotions.

articles.title: Quality Control Exclusion Gaps: How routine processing of sensor data threatens the validity, generalizability, and racial diversity of research using psychophysiological methods
articles.authors: Boluwatife Dogari; Alicia Carmichael; Brandon P. Labbree; Donna Walter; Richard Gonzalez; Nicholas Paul Camp
articles.abstract: Scientists have long used physiological recording to study bodily processes underlying emotions. However, sensors are often affected by hair or skin characteristics that impair the accuracy of their measurements in Black individuals. We draw attention to an underrecognized consequence of such recording biases: differential exclusion of Black participants during Quality Control (QC) stages of the data pipeline, what we call the QC exclusion gap. These routine procedures receive less attention than other stages of the research process; yet, disparate participant exclusions during QC can undermine the internal and external validity of research utilizing physiological recording. Using Electrodermal Activity (EDA) as an illustrative example, we walk through QC analyses of Black (N= 72) and White (N=68) participants’ Skin Conductance Levels (SCL) during a baseline passive listening task. Black participants exhibited significantly lower SCL (M = 4.13μS, SD = 2.49) than White participants (M = 7.95μS, SD = 3.19), p < .001. As a result, Black participants’ EDA data received lower quality grades during QC, leading to differential attrition during triage. We offer immediate recommendations to compensate for the QC exclusion gap, such as integrating quality monitoring feedback into recruitment procedures and reporting exclusion rates by demographic group, and identify broader directions for sensor development and analytical methods. Quality control is often considered a prelude to data analysis; by attending to who is excluded or included, however, we can design a more inclusive science.

articles.title: Age-Related Cognitive Slowing and Wrong-Target Errors on the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality Across the Adult Lifespan
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Katerina Denaxa; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Petros Roussos; Maria Roussou; Ion Beratis; Chrysanthi Nega
articles.abstract: Age-related differences in cognitive test performance must be characterised for each assessment format before scores can inform individual interpretation. This cross-sectional study examined age-related differences on the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), an immersive adaptation of the Trail Making Test, across the adult lifespan. Specifically, it examined whether completion time and wrong-target errors increased with age, whether the age association differed between Parts A and B, whether it was linear or accelerated at older ages, whether it held within each of three adult developmental periods, namely early (19–39 years), middle (40–59 years) and late (60–90 years) adulthood, and which of the exported and derived scores carried the age signal. The sample comprised 230 healthy adults aged 19–90 years (131 women). Part-level mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts tested the linear, quadratic and part-specific age terms; age-band and age-balancing robustness analyses followed, together with a comprehensive, multiplicity-controlled examination of all 26 TMT-VR scores and a direct comparison of their age associations. Older age was strongly associated with longer completion time and moderately with more wrong-target errors on both parts. The associations were linear across the adult range on the modelled scales, with no evidence of acceleration at older ages, and the completion-time slope per decade was of similar size within each developmental period. The completion-time Age × Part interaction was not clearly supported; the absolute Part B minus Part A difference grew with age while the B/A ratio did not. This is compatible with proportional slowing across parts, without establishing equivalent slopes or an absence of executive ageing. Error-adjusted time, which combines duration with correctness, was among the most age-related scores at every level, but it correlated .99 with completion time and its age association was no stronger, making it an economical summary rather than additional evidence in healthy adults. Sex and education were unrelated to the outcomes beyond age; mean selection distance varied too narrowly across participants for an age association to be detectable. Completion time, error-adjusted time and wrong-target errors are therefore the TMT-VR scores on which age referencing should build.

articles.title: ADHD and Creativity: Contribution of ADHD Trait Dimensions and an Exploration of Other Contributing Factors
articles.authors: Han Fang; Anouk Scheres; Lisa I. Horstman; Emma L.M. Laan; Mats N.J. Akkermans; Eva Hermans; Rutger Carelse; Anne M. den Dulk; Martine Hoogman
articles.abstract: ADHD is associated with impairments but also strengths like creativity. How inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity contribute to creativity, and how potential factors influence and contribute to the link, remain unclear. This study examined the unique contribution of inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity to creativity (divergent thinking and creative achievement) and explored the influences of novelty seeking, extraversion, persistence, hyperfocus, and self-restraint in these associations across two independent studies. Data were obtained from two independent university student samples (n = 158, n = 122) via online testing. Divergent thinking was assessed using the Alternate Uses Task; creative achievement, ADHD traits, and potential influencing and contributing factors were measured through self-report questionnaires. Inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity correlated with creativity in both samples: hyperactivity-impulsivity was the stronger predictor. Among all the potential contributing factors, only hyperfocus accounted for part of the association between inattentiveness and creative achievement. Our findings indicate that hyperactivity-impulsivity is the dominant ADHD trait dimension in the association with creativity. Hyperfocus accounted for part of the associations between inattentiveness and creative achievement, suggesting it may be a factor contributing to this association. Understanding positive phenotypes associated with neurodevelopmental conditions can optimize psychoeducation, reduce stigma, and improve the quality of life for those affected.

articles.title: Communicating the Economic Impact of Science Funding Cuts Changes Attitudes and Motivates Action
articles.authors: Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Mallory Harris; Danielle Cosme; Angela Fagerlin; Ellen Peters; Clio Andris; Colin Cooke; Emily B. Falk; Joshua S. Weitz
articles.abstract: Federal science funding cuts in the United States negatively impact research, healthcare, and the economy. Despite prior research investigating strategies to communicate scientific findings to the public, there is substantially less evidence on strategies to communicate how policy shapes the process and societal impact of science. Here, we demonstrate that across political divides, behavioral interventions that interactively communicate the impact of science funding cuts influence policy support, awareness, and intentions to take action in support of science funding. In two preregistered experiments with politically-balanced samples (N=5,177), we tested novel text, quiz, and map-based interventions illustrating economic losses resulting from science funding cuts. Across the political spectrum, the interventions robustly decreased approval of funding cuts and increased perceived knowledge and perceived negative local impact. We scaled these interventions via a public website (https://scienceimpacts.org/); a third study analyzing data from >24,000 website users revealed converging evidence of effectiveness. Crucially, we demonstrate that even simple text interventions that highlighted local economic impact effectively changed attitudes. However, adding active engagement via interactive quizzes and maps selectively increased action intentions (e.g., contacting representatives, sharing information). Surprise in response to the information, and time spent actively engaging with impact maps, predicted intervention effects on policy approval, knowledge, action intentions, and sharing behavior. Overall, interactive interventions revealing community-level economic impact changed attitudes and increased action intentions related to science funding cuts.

articles.title: Online Discourse is Falsely Polarized by Self-Selection
articles.authors: Will Schulz; Claire Elizabeth Robertson; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ashwini Ashokkumar; Lisa Oswald; JungHwan Yang; Simon Munzert; Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Andrew Markus Guess
articles.abstract: We present comprehensive evidence quantifying the magnitude and scope of false polarization (i.e. the impression that opinions on political issues are more polarized than they actually are) on social media, driven by users' selective posting behavior. Using more than a decade of social media behavior connected to individual ideological attitudes in 1.7 million posts, a series of controlled experiments, and a large global survey covering 40 countries (total N = 49,222), we find that (1) strong ideologues post their opinions significantly more often than moderate individuals, and (2) extreme attitudes are posted more often than moderate attitudes. This general pattern replicates robustly across 40 countries, spanning diverse political cultures. Indeed, across studies we find extreme opinions are overrepresented on social media by at least 6% and up to 22% compared to their true prevalence in our samples. Furthermore, the opinions that users post are more hostile and toxic than the beliefs they keep to themselves.  These results were not explained by political interest or consistent left-right differences, suggesting that political extremity has an independent effect on social media behavior. Thus, most of the observed polarization of online discourse in recent years may be attributable to the systematic over-representation of pre-existing extreme political views, rather than the causal effects of platforms.

articles.title: What the Tally Hid: Screening Live-Observation Codes for Saturation, Floor Effects, and Degeneracy Before Piloting
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract: We set out a pre-piloting screening protocol for live-observation coding instruments (Table 1), usable in any brief structured behavioural-coding task, with a worked case study and a Monte Carlo calibration. In 15 stranger dyads a ten-code sheet produced a healthy-looking composite (M = 26.63, SD = 9.64), yet four engagement codes ran at 74-94% of their protocol maximum, three withdrawal codes were floored at 0-8%, and only three carried usable variance. Resampling the deposited counts (40,000 pilots per size), detection under the all-code conjunctive rule is 100% at every pilot size; one code (monologue) was never observed, and the all-code result is reported as a primary finding, with false positives against no-pathology nulls reaching 32.3% at N = 2 and falling to 9.3% at N = 4. In a sensitivity analysis excluding monologue and silence, detection remained high but non-monotonic (91.0% at N = 4; 87.1% at N = 6), with a closely comparable false-positive profile (6.1% at N = 4). Threshold distance and degeneracy, rather than pilot size, govern screening. The practical rule that follows is to report, for each code, its mean as a percentage of its protocol maximum, its between-unit variance, and its signed distance to the nearest threshold, rather than a recommended pilot N. The protocol and its two generalizable principles are offered as provisional and unregistered, pending independent replication on a second bin-level dataset. All counts derive from a single non-blinded coder, a limitation discussed throughout.

articles.title: Reframing Acculturation:  When (and Why) Acculturation Science Warrants a Systems Explanation
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Karen Phalet
articles.abstract: Acculturation has always been understood as a process of change, and contemporary research examines that change from several complementary perspectives, including developmental trajectories, reciprocal intergroup relations, ecological contexts, situated cultural processes, and multilevel social change. The field therefore contains many elements of a systems account without a shared architecture for relating them. This article offers a selective integrative review and metatheoretical synthesis using complex dynamic systems theory (CDST). CDST provides a coordinating framework that complements existing acculturation theories and encounter-level models of adaptation. It distinguishes five explanatory questions distributed across different traditions: what form change takes, who or what influences whom, how change moves across levels of organisation, where broader conditions become relevant, and how processes unfolding at different rates become linked. We organise these questions through five dimensions: nonlinear dynamism, relational reciprocity, multilevel emergence, situated adaptation, and multiscale temporality. Together, they provide a way to examine how patterns of acculturative change depend on prior experience, relationships, local conditions, levels of organisation, and processes unfolding at different rates. For each type of systems claim, we specify a linear-additive alternative and the evidence needed to distinguish between them. Power differences and prior history are treated as conditions that can shape how the system operates and changes. The framework therefore shifts attention from average associations between acculturation variables and outcomes toward explaining how acculturative change is organised, when different processes become connected, and when a systems explanation adds value beyond conventional models.

articles.title: Acculturation as a Situated Transactional Process
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract: Acculturation research commonly links broad preferences for heritage-culture maintenance and participation in the receiving society to psychological and sociocultural adjustment. Yet meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence shows that these associations are often weak, heterogeneous, and limited over time, suggesting that broad preferences alone cannot explain why cultural engagement leads to different outcomes across situations. This conceptual article develops a situated transactional framework within a broader complex dynamic systems account. Building on established work showing that acculturation is contextual, domain-specific, and interactional, the framework specifies how these influences come together within concrete encounters. It proposes a process in which locally relevant conditions shape appraisal, the mobilization of culturally patterned resources, response, relational and institutional reception, multidimensional outcomes, and feedback into later encounters. The article also distinguishes the adaptation process, understood as the continuing person-environment transaction, from adaptation outcomes, including psychological, sociocultural, relational, and externally observed consequences. By organizing these elements into an explicit recursive architecture, the framework generates testable predictions about context-specific responses, reception, multidimensional outcomes, learned response patterns, and structural change. It thereby provides a concrete empirical agenda for testing whether these mechanisms improve explanation and prediction beyond broad-orientation and contextual-moderation accounts.

articles.title: Fetching a Problem's Solution from a Computer Does Not Lead to an Impoverished Affective Footprint
articles.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Johannes Bernau; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Problem solving relies on purely internal processing (IP) or extended processing (EP) which additionally draws on external resources like computerized equipment. IP can initially cause negative affect due to effort or cognitive conflict, followed by positive affect after success. Such affective dynamics matter as they influence learning, well-being, and cognitive control. Yet, little is known about affect in EP, which this study examined. Participants solved alpha-numeric problems (is “D+4=I” correct?). IP required mentally counting up letters from “D”, while EP involved revealing the correct answer (“H”) by hovering a cursor over a box. Affect was measured using affective priming (Experiment 1), facial muscle activity (Experiment 2), and explicit ratings. We hypothesized that IP produces more negative affect during problem solving but more positive affect afterwards compared to EP. Results provided little support for such a general claim. Affective priming suggests that IP-related operations like matching men-tal representations to sensory input can indeed cause positive affect, which can however also be part of EP. Facial muscle data indicated broadly comparable affective dynamics between IP and EP. These results add an affective spin to the cognitive impartiality hypotheses (Clark 2011), which suggests that neither IP nor EP is privileged by problem solvers.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs. Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Theorising arts engagement as a health-promoting behaviour
articles.authors: Daisy Fancourt; Robert West; Andrew Steptoe; Sharifa Abdulla; Naoki Kondo; Pier Luigi Sacco; Agustin Ibanez
articles.abstract: Arts engagement encompasses a diverse range of human creative practices ubiquitous in every human culture. This Perspective advances a conceptual argument for classifying arts engagement as a health-promoting behaviour, drawing on evolving health behaviour theories and ontological definitions and models. We balance theoretical critiques against this conceptualisation (namely normative instrumentalist and dual valence arguments) alongside accumulating empirical evidence for its value, drawing on experimental and epidemiological research demonstrating associations and causal effects across psychological, cognitive, physiological, and social outcomes. We consider the practical opportunities that could emerge from integrating arts engagement into behavioural monitors, applying behaviour change frameworks, and formalising classification within behaviour change ontologies. Finally, we explore future research directions that a health behavioural framing suggest, include cross-cultural epidemiology, ecological momentary assessment, biomarker integration, exposome-informed models, and One Health frameworks.

articles.title: Gaze on IPCC climate maps carries behaviour-specific signals for intended low-carbon action
articles.authors: Étienne Serbe-Kamp; Ayshan Aliyeva; Candelaria Belen Krick; Candela I. Jantus; Yaning Han; Joaquin Navajas; Bahador Bahrami; Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Climate maps are among the most widely shared products of climate science, yet their effect on the people who look at them is measured almost entirely with questionnaires. We recorded gaze with mobile eye-trackers while people freely viewed climate-projection maps from the IPCC Interactive Atlas, and asked whether how someone looks carries information questionnaires miss. It does, for only one of the three outcomes we tested. Gaze improved prediction of intended low-carbon behaviour in viewers the models had never seen, beyond a broad battery of climate measures and in every model tried. The same features said nothing about how anxious those viewers were, or which audience segment they placed themselves in. Attention to climate information is therefore not a general marker of engagement. It tracks readiness to act. Because a visualisation can be designed around where people look, this opens a route to evaluating climate communication while people are looking.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic lives. This raises the question of which individuals are more likely to rely on GenAI in their schoolwork, with reliance defined as a dispositional tendency to turn to GenAI in preference to one’s own effort or teacher support, as well as difficulty initiating schoolwork without it. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model of the associations between executive functioning (EF) difficulties and reliance on GenAI through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage= 17.4 years, 55.2% girls), with analytic samples of 735 and 839 GenAI users, respectively. Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.33, ps < .001). Consistent with the hypothesized model, a sequential indirect association through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Specific indirect associations through perceived usefulness were consistently observed in both groups, whereas those through habitual use alone received more limited support despite the strong association between habitual use and reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF difficulties as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be particularly relevant to understanding the indirect association between EF difficulties and reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the relevance of self-regulatory capacities for understanding individual differences in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: ‘Why me?’ - The influence of perceived fairness of climate policies on adoption intentions of high impact climate actions across cultural contexts
articles.authors: Mario Herberz; Tobias Brosch; Claudia R. Schneider
articles.abstract: The unresolved question of how efforts to reduce carbon emissions should be fairly distributed across society constitutes a major hurdle to widespread cooperation on climate change mitigation. While perceived fairness has been established as a key characteristic of broadly supported climate policies, its affective underpinnings and its relevance for individual-level adoption of climate actions, as well as the added value of addressing fairness concerns in climate policies remain understudied. Here, we investigate the association between the perceived fairness of governments promoting the adoption of high impact climate actions and adoption intentions, the affective processes involved in fairness judgments, and the extent to which two climate policies addressing perceptions of unfairness succeed in increasing intentions to adopt climate actions. Across three pre-registered studies conducted in Switzerland, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom (Ntotal = 1063) we demonstrate that perceived fairness positively predicts adoption intentions, and this more strongly so than the perceived impact of climate actions. We found anger, psychological reactance, and lack of enthusiasm to be affective correlates of lower perceived fairness. Reducing the cost of adopting high impact climate actions and mandating societies’ highest emitters to reduce their carbon emissions to increase self-interested and distributional fairness, respectively, successfully increased adoption intentions. Evidence on potential moderators of these effects remained largely inconclusive. While practical challenges in the study of the behavioural effects of climate policy design remain, systematically accounting for inequalities and perceived unfairness seems to be key to the widespread adoption of high impact climate actions.

articles.title: Assessing complex belief structures with the triads task: Reliability and validity
articles.authors: René Dutschke; Gundula Thiele; Martin Schoemann; Caroline Surrey; Stefan Scherbaum
articles.abstract:
Research on attitudes and beliefs often relies on assessing people’s agreement with several explicit
statements. We promote a different approach, focusing on the interconnectedness of beliefs and
their cognitive and affective components. Here, we present the triads task as a procedure to
measure complex belief networks. Leaning on similarity and difference judgments for three
concepts at a time, the triads task allows us to derive similarity scores for each pair of concepts in
a topic domain, which provide insights into belief networks of individuals and groups.
Furthermore, we propose a procedure to translate similarity scores into belief network
visualizations, inspired by cognitive-affective maps (CAMs). For a sample of 56 participants, we
show that similarity scores are retest reliable in a two week interval (averaged individual retest
correlation: r = .78) and that participants communicatively validate our visualization procedure.
We highlight the benefits of the triads task in measuring belief networks and further discuss this
procedure with regards to its potential as a research and intervention tool.

articles.title: A priori power analysis for ANOVA interaction effects with the anovapowersim R package: a short introduction
articles.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles.abstract: Although power analysis has become increasingly accessible over time, researchers still find it challenging to compute power for complex ANOVA interactions. anovapowersim is an R package that enables users to easily specify between, within, and mixed interactions of varying complexity and simulate power based on a target effect size. This tutorial provides a short introduction to the package's core functionality, along with worked examples and sample R code.

articles.title: AI’s Frontline
articles.authors: Alex Taylor; Jina Suh; Marlyn Thomas Savio; Sinead O'Dwyer; John Caesar De Villa
articles.abstract:
1.	AI’s safety and reliability depend on a globally distributed workforce
2.	Data workers feel an ambivalence towards their work: operating in a space of tension between monotonous and potentially emotionally taxing work, and feelings of individual and collective agency in contributing to new tech. 
3.	The space of tension opens up a space for thinking productively about the importance of data work and the active role data workers can play in shaping AI development.

articles.title: Measuring Up:  Accessible Approaches for Improving Measurement Practices in Psychological Science
articles.authors: Julia Feld Strand; Violet Aurora Brown
articles.abstract: The conclusions psychologists draw are only as sound as the measurements they are based upon. Despite the foundational role of measurement in psychological science, many areas suffer from insufficient attention to measurement practices. Although improving measurement practices is widely recognized to be important work—indeed, reliability and validity are taught in introductory psychology courses at the high school and college level—psychometrics has a reputation of being inaccessible to those without formal training. This paper provides a framework to facilitate asking and answering questions about measurement, with the goal of providing researchers without formal training in psychometrics with an accessible entry point to evaluating the measurement tools in their research area. Specifically, we present four questions that researchers can pose of the literature to guide careful evaluation of the measurement landscape in their subdiscipline, focusing on issues related to reliability, validity, and variability in task administration and scoring. In each section, we provide examples of nonempirical and empirical work that can either be conducted in a standalone study or incorporated into ongoing research projects.

articles.title: Chatbot and Problematic Integration: Two Tests among U.S. Users
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are token-based, probabilistic engines that produce most likely answers based on trained models and user input. In this work, I draw upon the problematic integration (PI) theory to conceptualize human-AI interaction (HAII) as communication processes that are aimed to address users’ problematic probabilistic orientations (PP). I propose that (1) PP prompt people to seek answers from AI chatbots and (2) that the extent to which chatbot responses address PP shapes interaction outcomes. Two studies tested these propositions using national age-matching samples of AI chatbot users in the United States (age range=18-85 years; mean age=41 years). Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey and Study 2 was an interactive experiment where participants talked to chatbots about one of twenty validated and pretested life concerns and rated chatbot-generated responses addressing their concern. Findings lend partial support to my propositions and offer insights into how AI chatbots may shape communication and human cognition.

articles.title: Now You See Me: Associations between Student Outcomes and Instructor Visibility in Online Learning Contexts
articles.authors: Lindsay Ackerman; William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Online classroom environments may be associated with compromised student engagement and learning outcomes and behaviors, partially arising from a lack of instructor visibility. We tested the effect of watching instructor-led videos on learning outcomes in online environments. Study 1 (N = 600) was a randomized experiment testing whether participants who watched videos of an instructor delivering information reported higher engagement and understanding compared to participants who read equivalent text. In a small, applied Study 2 (N = 30, in an online course), we investigated classroom associations between watching instructor-led videos and subjective (e.g., self-reported engagement) and objective (e.g., time spent on course page) student learning outcomes and behaviors. In the classroom study, watching the instructor-led videos was associated with course engagement, connection to the instructor, and objective learning behaviors. However, in the experimental study, those who read the text performed better than those who watched the videos, though applications to classroom contexts may be limited. This work provides insight into the utility of visual and audio instructor representation in facilitating positive learning outcomes for students in online classrooms and invites educators to consider how best to engage students in online courses.

articles.title: Beyond delay: Discounting rewards for sustained self-control
articles.authors: Justin Wahlers; Jonathan Westlake; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Steven Seung-Suk Kang; Delwyn Catley; Seung-Lark Lim
articles.abstract:
Conventional intertemporal choice measures (e.g., delay discounting) often focus on the
cost of waiting for a reward. Yet, achieving many long-term health goals also requires
continuously exerting self-control while forgoing an immediately rewarding alternative. To
quantify these subjective costs, we introduced a novel abstinence discounting paradigm and
tested it in a consequential context: nicotine use. Abstinence discounting assessed one’s
preference for larger monetary rewards contingent on maintaining nicotine abstinence versus
smaller, noncontingent monetary rewards that do not require abstinence. Among e-cigarette users
(N = 253; Mage = 28.66, SDage = 4.22, 54.15% female, 45.85% male; 57.71% White, 20.16%
Black, 9.09% Hispanic, 6.32% Mixed), abstinence discounting related more closely and
consistently with nicotine dependence, craving, and cessation motivation while explaining
unique variance in these outcomes beyond delay discounting. These findings support extending
intertemporal choice research beyond the temporal distance of outcomes to consider the
sustained self-control demands required to achieve them.

articles.title: Engagement begins at recruitment: Comparing videoconference verification to passive online screening for participant retention and study engagement
articles.authors: Andrea Howard; Johanna Peetz
articles.abstract: Researchers who conduct studies online increasingly struggle with fraudulent respondents, programmable bots, inattention or carelessness, and ineligible impostors. This study tested whether participants in a longitudinal intervention study who were recruited using videoconference eligibility verification—meeting participants one by one on Zoom to verify their identities—were more engaged in the study tasks and showed better longitudinal retention. Using existing data from a sample of Canadian young adult women (N = 1,257), we compared participants who were screened via videoconference to participants who were passively screened (i.e., possessed valid email addresses) and participants who were pre-screened members of a commercial participant platform (Prolific.com) on seven measures of retention and six measures of engagement with study tasks. Results showed that videoconference verified participants had better rates of study initiation and retention, with over 90% completing all study waves. However, we found no meaningful differences between recruitment streams as a function of time to survey completion, engagement with the study’s intervention activities, or honest responding. Videoconference eligibility verification may be a practical tool for recruiting participants likely to remain enrolled in longitudinal research and limit attrition.

articles.title: An Open-Source Standardized Pipeline for Equitable Observations of Interactive Behavioral Dynamics: Theory-driven Measurement, Analysis, and Masking
articles.authors: Arkadiusz Białek; Wim Pouw; James Trujillo; Fred Hasselman; Babajide Owoyele; Natalia Siekiera; Joanna Raczaszek-Leonardi; Travis J. Witshire
articles.abstract: Behavioral observation has a longstanding tradition in psychology. However, its reliance on manual coding makes observational methods costly and prone to biases that arise from the inherent limits of coding schemes and from the subjectivity of human raters. Behavioral observation research therefore has drawbacks in terms of applicability, accessibility, reproducibility, and equitability. Computer vision (CV) methods have promise in this regard. In the context of quantifying human movement, CV approaches to pose estimation are becoming increasingly precise and have the benefit of being non-intrusive, reproducible, and low-cost. With such methods, human movement in videos can be processed as multivariate time-series data, offering a basis for a more comprehensive analysis of individual, interpersonal, and social dynamics, opening up the possibility for the widespread study of diverse populations in out-of-lab real-world contexts. Fulfilling such a promise goes beyond technical progress, it requires a theory-driven implementation of new accessible observational methods made equitable to learn. To showcase this promise, we present a CV pipeline with analyses of the temporal dynamics of dyadic interactions, including a cross-cultural investigation of movement fluidity in sibling cooperation during task-focused interactions and longitudinal assessments of infant-caregiver coordination during free-play sessions. The pipeline incorporates a pedagogical computational notebook, pose estimation (YOLOv8), theory-driven linear and non-linear time series analysis, and a CV method for more privacy-aware video data archiving. Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it.

articles.title: Exposure-Blind Resilience: A Scoping Review of Resilience, Recovery, and Adaptation in Israel After October 7
articles.authors: Adrian Mendelson; Yossi Levi-Belz; Yael Segal Elbak; Dalia Moallem; Rinatia Maaravi-Hesseg; Ziv Ben-Zion
articles.abstract: After the October 7, 2023, attack and the prolonged war that followed, research on resilience, recovery, and adaptation in Israel expanded rapidly. We conducted a prospectively registered scoping review of 147 peer-reviewed quantitative publications drawn from 125 independent samples to examine how resilience and adaptation were conceptualized, which resources were associated with favorable outcomes, and what evidence supported protective mechanisms. No publication operationalized resilience relative to the adversity participants experienced. Instead, resilience was predominantly measured as a self-reported capacity, and adaptation was most often inferred from low symptom levels rather than preserved functioning or broader positive adjustment. Personal resilience and individual psychological resources showed comparatively strong associations with favorable outcomes. However, the reliance on self-report resilience measures limits the interpretation of these associations as effects of distinct resources. Belonging showed a more consistently favorable pattern in a smaller literature, whereas findings for social support, family resources, and collective resources were less consistent. Formal tests of adversity-buffering effects were uncommon, predominantly cross-sectional, and indicated context-specific rather than general protection; prospective evidence regarding mechanisms was similarly sparse. No randomized trial tested a resilience-promoting intervention against a non-active comparator. The literature, therefore, identifies numerous correlates of favorable outcomes but provides substantially less evidence about when these resources constitute resilience or alter adaptation in the face of adversity. Future research should prioritize exposure-sensitive definitions, multidimensional outcomes, longitudinal designs, and temporally ordered tests of mechanisms.

articles.title: Speech Onset Time at Home or in the Lab: The Role of Testing Environment and Experimenter Presence.
articles.authors: Giorgio Piazza; Natalia Kartushina; Christoforos Souganidis; James E. Flege; Clara Martin
articles.abstract: Psycholinguistic research has become increasingly reliant on online experimentation, which has also grown more attractive for studying speech production. However, concerns remain about data quality in online settings and the absence of experimenters to ensure participant engagement. In this pre-registered study, we used two tasks—picture naming and reading aloud—to test whether the lexical frequency effect (Low Frequency words > High Frequency words) on speech onset times can be reliably detected in online environments (run at Home), both with and without experimenter supervision. Participants completed the same tasks under four conditions, varying by Supervision (between-subjects: Supervised vs. Unsupervised) and Environment (within-subjects: Lab vs. Home): Lab-Supervised, HomeSupervised, Lab-Unsupervised, and Home-Unsupervised. Frequency effects emerged across all conditions except Home-Supervised for the reading aloud task, where the effect was in the expected direction but non-significant (~12 ms). All other conditions yielded consistent frequency effects (~17–38 ms), comparable to previous online and lab-based findings. Notably, participants were faster at home than in the lab (~10 ms), and unsupervised settings yielded the largest effect sizes, suggesting that experimenter presence may inadvertently dampen subtle effects, possibly due to increased self-monitoring or reduced comfort. These findings validate the use of online platforms for speech production research and highlight the nuanced influence of supervision on experimental outcomes.

articles.title: Beyond Pre-Post Comparisons: A Comprehensive Effect Size Framework for Intensive Longitudinal Interventions via Time-Varying Modeling
articles.authors: Xiaohui Luo; Yue Liu; Hongyun Liu; Laura Francina Bringmann
articles.abstract: Intensive longitudinal interventions (ILIs), which deliver repeated interventions in people’s daily lives while intensively tracking their psychological states, offer unique opportunities for ecologically valid, real-time, and personalized support. However, there is a striking mismatch between the richness of the data these studies generate and the simplicity of the methods used to evaluate them: evaluations still rely largely on pre-post mean comparisons that collapse dozens or even hundreds of observations per person into a few summary statistics. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a comprehensive effect size framework based on Bayesian multilevel time-varying autoregressive (TV-AR) models within the generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) approach. The framework organizes effect sizes along four dimensions: subject level (population-average, individual-specific, and between-group), parameter type (mean level, autoregressive effect, and variance), temporal scale (integrated and time-specific), and study phase (active intervention and post-intervention decay). These metrics move researchers beyond whether an intervention works to when effects emerge, plateau, or fade, how the intervention reshapes the dynamics and stability of a process, and for whom it is effective. We demonstrate the framework with data from a mindfulness-based ILI targeting negative affect, in which an intervention and a control group were assessed before and during the intervention, and provide openly available annotated R code and a tutorial. Overall, the framework provides a practical and flexible toolkit for evaluating ILIs, supporting the broader shift toward a more dynamic, process-oriented, and personalized intervention science.

articles.title: Why the body comes first: Effects of experimenter touch on infants’ word finding
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; Ruth Tincoff; Christopher Baker; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
The lexicon of 6-month-olds is comprised of names and body part words. Unlike names, body part words do not often occur in isolation in the input. This presents a puzzle: How have infants been able to pull out these words from the continuous stream of speech at such a young age? We hypothesize that caregivers’ interactions directed at and on the infant’s body may be at the root of their early acquisition of body part words. An
artificial language segmentation study shows that experimenter-provided synchronous tactile cues help 4-month-olds to find words in continuous speech. A follow-up study suggests that this facilitation cannot be reduced to the highly social situation in which the directed interaction occurs. Taken together, these studies suggests that direct caregiver-infant interaction, exemplified in this study by touch cues, may play a key role
in infants’ ability to find word boundaries and suggests that words linked with caregiver touches may comprise early vocabulary items.

articles.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Realistic, misleading AI-generated audio content is a new threat to digital-media consumers. This study examined the effects of misleading AI-generated podcasts that presented false claims about nanoparticles in sunscreen (Experiment 1; N = 463), or microwaves damaging foods (Experiment 2; N = 500). U.S. participants either received a misleading podcast, misleading article, or a neutral podcast (control).
