To test interventions, misleading podcasts were preceded by either a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can deceive, an active inoculation that added an educational activity, or no intervention. The podcast and article produced comparable increases in misinformed beliefs. Both inoculations significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information and attenuated the podcast’s impact on beliefs. Results demonstrate that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as text-based misinformation, and that brief AI-source-focused inoculations can mitigate, but not eliminate, its persuasive impact. Findings inform interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.

articles.title: Gambling disorder symptoms as an indirect marker of microtransaction spending in video games
articles.authors: Charles-Etienne Benoit; Szymon Pałubinski; Akito Miura; Takahide Etani; Floris Tijmen van Vugt; Piotr Kałowski; Andrzej Cudo
articles.abstract: Video games have gained a lot of popularity over the past decades, generating large global revenue, mostly through in-game monetization referred to as microtransactions. Game developers have studied the psychological mechanisms in video game monetization presumably to increase potential revenues, which could for some gamers exacerbate negative personality traits. This is particularly true for microtransactions which may associate with gaming disorder symptoms and gambling disorder symptoms. There is currently insufficient research as to how the various forms of microtransactions relate to symptoms of gaming disorder and gambling disorder. We collected questionnaire data from 461 gamer participants. In order to explore the structure and interrelations between the variables, network analysis was applied. Our results align with previous findings that showed that the amount of money individuals spend on microtransactions increases with the risk of gaming disorder symptoms. However, we demonstrate that gambling disorder symptoms relate only indirectly to online spending through a direct link to physical game purchases. This finding is interesting considering the immaterial nature of microtransactions. Altogether, our findings highlight the need to disentangle gaming and gambling disorder symptoms and microtransactions, isolate psychological markers of problematic behavior, and aim to develop support or preventive technologies to come to the help of vulnerable gamers.

articles.title: Social influence and information cascades in experience-based decisions
articles.authors: Kiri Kuroda; Simon Kai Ciranka; Dirk U. Wulff; Ralf Kurvers
articles.abstract: Many consequential decisions are made in environments where outcome probabilities are not explicitly described but must be inferred from experience. In most modern environments, this information search takes place in the presence of others. Yet, the role of social influence in experience-based decisions has been largely overlooked, leaving it unclear how personal and social information combine to shape what people sample, when they stop searching, and what they finally choose. Here, we address all three decision stages. In a preregistered study, participants could freely sample two options before making a final choice, either alone (solo condition) or while observing the final choices of their group members (group condition). We developed a modeling framework and show that social influence left sampling unaffected but altered stopping and choice. Participants searched longer when the group was more divided and stopped earlier when the majority choice agreed with their own personal sampling information. Consequently, they drew fewer samples and encountered fewer rare events than solo participants. When choosing, group members copied others' choices only when their personal information was ambiguous. Comparing decision sequences in groups with a solo baseline, complemented with agent-based simulations, showed that this strategy gave rise to mild information cascades, with decisions in groups being more similar to each other than in a solo baseline. Our results reveal how social influence shapes search, stopping, and choice, and how these individual-level decision rules scale up to collective dynamics.

articles.title: The context-dependent evolution of structure learning and metacognition
articles.authors: Rochelle Kaper; Megan A. K. Peters
articles.abstract: Humans learn multiple probabilistic regularities at once, and often without feedback, which may be aided by metacognitive evaluations throughout learning. To understand this learning-metacognition relationship, we must first characterize how both capacities co-evolve as environmental structures are internalized, especially when feedback is unavailable. Here, participants learned a two-level probabilistic environment in which stimulus co-occurrences were embedded within a sequence, using unfamiliar fractals and familiar line drawings in a two-session, within-subjects design (N=63; N=50 completed both sessions). For each stimulus set, we measured learning across six repeating exposure-test cycles, using a cover task during exposure phases and forced-choice questions in test phases; test questions also included confidence judgments. Results revealed stimulus- and structure-dependent learning and metacognitive signatures. First, learning dynamics differed across stimuli: fractal sequence test accuracy outpaced co-occurrence accuracy, but vice versa for line drawings. Further, confidence increased across blocks, and was higher for line drawings as well as co-occurrences and first but not second sequence selections. Finally, both metacognitive sensitivity and test accuracy increased in successive exposure-test cycles for fractals, but metacognitive sensitivity remained stagnant for line drawings even as test accuracy improved. These results demonstrate that structure learning and metacognitive processes are highly context- and complexity-dependent rather than being completely generalizable. This study informs future directions for refining theories of learning without feedback, including how people evaluate their own learning and uncertainty and the interaction of both cognitive abilities with task design, stimuli, and environmental structures.

articles.title: Integrating science and design in the development of Detour: A mobile intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Maartje Luijten; Ken Koontz; Hanneke Scholten
articles.abstract: Digital smoking cessation interventions for adolescents and young adults (AYAs) often either lack a strong evidence base or fail to engage their intended users. Integrating psychological science with design-based methods offers a promising route to interventions, yet the processes behind such integration are rarely reported in detail. In this paper, we describe the development of Detour, a mobile smoking cessation intervention for AYAs, redesigned from an earlier app (HitnRun) using the Bloombox Toolkit to integrate science and design throughout. We describe how six psychological mechanisms including smoking cue devaluation and delay discounting were translated into intervention components. We used an iterative, interdisciplinary process involving behavioural scientists, app designers, and an ongoing youth advisory board. Additionally, we included over 380 AYAs across focus groups, play tests, and qualitative questionnaires. We then reflect on our experience integrating design and science for intervention development and share practical challenges encountered, including budgeting for interdisciplinary teams, retaining youth participants, and regulatory delays. By reporting these processes and challenges transparently, we aim to support other researchers in designing digital health interventions that are both scientifically grounded and engaging for their target users.

articles.title: Spatial biases in Arithmetic: The Effect of Operation Order and Visual Spacing on Calculations
articles.authors: Martyna Sroka; Michał Obidziński; Krzysztof Cipora; Mateusz Hohol
articles.abstract: Visual layout is known to affect computational performance, yet its relation to response format and numerical proficiency remains unclear. This preregistered study examined whether spatial presentation modulates arithmetic problem-solving. We conceptually replicated Experiment 3 of Landy and Goldstone's (2010) study using the Precedence and Proximity Task in a forced-choice format. Additionally, we assessed arithmetic fluency using a speeded test. A total of 201 adults solved 200 mixed addition–multiplication expressions in which spacing either aligned or conflicted with order-of-operations rules. Operation order was also manipulated. Participants were faster and more accurate in congruent spacing conditions, whereas incongruent spacing increased operation-order errors, especially when problems began with addition. A subgroup of participants showed disproportionately poor performance under incongruent spacing, suggesting a prepotent susceptibility to misleading grouping cues. The spacing effect persisted despite differences in task format and response procedure compared to the original study, supporting its robustness. Higher arithmetic fluency was associated with higher accuracy and shorter reaction times in the Precedence and Proximity Task. These findings corroborate that visuospatial layout biases symbolic computation and that individuals differ in their susceptibility to it.

articles.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles.title: Designing for Realistic Self-Assessment: Reducing Illusions of Competence in Human–Technology Interaction
articles.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Humans frequently overestimate their unaided problem-solving abilities after receiving cognitive support—a bias known as illusion of competence. Such miscalibration harms the ability to seek and sustain support and thus undermines adaptive reliance on technology. In four experiments, we examined how subtle interventions can reduce this bias during technology-assisted problem solving. In Experiment 1, short metacognitive prompts inviting reflection on the contribution of cognitive support abolished the bias. In Experiment 2, the intervention of emphasizing the external origin of the support was tested. The emphasis was implemented by framing the support as coming from a humanlike (a robot face) or a nonhumanlike (a soft-ware window) entity. Both emphases of external origin reduced the bias to a similar extent. Moreover, engaging in unaided problem solving also abolished and even reversed the bias, leading to an illusion of incompetence. We failed to replicate these findings after methodolog-ical refinement in Experiment 3 that included more pronounced external support. When keep-ing refinements but again using less pronounced support, replications succeeded in Experiment 4. Our findings demonstrate that minimal interventions can enhance a problem solver’s meta-cognitive accuracy when receiving cognitive support. We discuss implications for the design of cognitive human-computer interactions that promote realistic self-assessment and thus sus-tainable collaborations.

articles.title: Normative and Maladaptive Personality Traits in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative and Hierarchical Analysis of HEXACO and PID-5
articles.authors: Martin Weiß; Johanna Hepp; Katja Isabell Seitz; Yun-Loe Laura Lai; Nikolaus Kleindienst; Sylvia Steinmann; Katja Bertsch; Inga Niedtfeld
articles.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of personality pathology invite the question of how normative and maladaptive trait systems jointly characterize borderline personality disorder (BPD). This study examined how the HEXACO model of personality and the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders trait system, operationalized with the Personality Inventory for DSM–5, differentiate individuals with BPD from mentally healthy control (HC) individuals, both separately and jointly.
Methods: Data from two assessment waves of a large clinical research program were combined into a final sample of 575 participants (233 with BPD, 342 HC). A joint item-level PCA was conducted to examine seven- and eleven-component solutions, and a Bass-Ackwards principal components analysis was conducted to examine the joint hierarchical structure of HEXACO and PID-5 items. Both instruments were administered as self-reports. 
Results: Compared with HC, individuals with BPD showed lower HEXACO Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness, and higher Emotionality, as well as higher scores on all PID-5 domains, particularly Negative Affectivity and Disinhibition. In the combined domain model, low Extraversion and high  PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism uniquely predicted BPD status. At the facet level, low Social Self-Esteem (HEXACO) and high Emotional Lability (PID-5) were especially discriminative. Joint item analyses yielded a sevencomponent solution in which six components corresponded closely to the six HEXACO factors and a dominant seventh component represented broad maladaptivity, with PID-5 items loading positively and HEXACO items largely loading inversely. Group differences were almost entirely confined to this broad component. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that BPD is characterized by both a broad maladaptivity dimension and a more specific trait profile involving affective instability, interpersonal insecurity, irritability, and reduced behavioral control. The findings support integrating normative and maladaptive trait models in  the dimensional description of BPD, while indicating that the dominant joint dimension cannot be interpreted unambiguously as a substantive general factor of personality pathology.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: Trust and Intellectual Humility as Necessary Conditions for AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Recently, AI models demonstrated a remarkable ability to facilitate opinion change, a notoriously difficult task between human communicators. Here, we focus on the dispositions that characterize message recipients, specifically identifying trust in AI, intellectual humility (IH), and their interplay as key factors in acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Across two studies with an online British sample (N=294), we replicated findings showing significant attitude change regarding legal immigrants following brief interactions with GPT. Crucially, our findings reveal that opinion change is contingent on higher IH and greater trust in AI, independently and jointly, predicting greater acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Experimentally capturing the centrality of open-mindedness (IH) and source sensitivity (Trust) highlights how epistemic vigilance constrains AI’s persuasive impact and sheds new light on the persuasion literature by revisiting the role of source credibility. Future research should examine whether these dispositional effects extend to long-term behavioral patterns across broader real-world contexts.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles.title: Selective reproduction of spatial–emotional mappings in large language models
articles.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Fumiya Yonemitsu; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: The vertical-valence metaphor refers to the association between emotional valence and vertical space, whereby positive and negative emotions are linked to upward and downward directions, respectively. While this mapping has been robustly observed in human cognition, it remains unclear whether such associations are also reproduced in artificial intelligence systems. The present study investigated the vertical-valence metaphor in ChatGPT. In Experiments 1–3, ChatGPT-4 showed a consistent pattern in which “up” was evaluated more positively than “down,” and emotional words were spatially organized such that “joy” was placed above “sadness,” with “surprise” positioned in between. This pattern persisted even when the coordinate system was reversed. In Experiments 4–6, we compared silicon and human samples and observed a more nuanced pattern. While the vertical-valence mapping was largely preserved across both groups, the intermediate positioning of “surprise” was not consistently reproduced in ChatGPT-5.2. An additional pilot experiment indicates that this reduction in differentiation may be influenced by prompt language, although the relative contributions of model characteristics and language could not be determined. Exploratory analyses revealed that the horizontal-valence metaphor showed less consistent patterns across all the experiments, indicating lower robustness. Taken together, these findings suggest that large language models do not uniformly reproduce human cognitive mappings but instead exhibit a graded pattern of representation. Robust mappings are preserved, whereas intermediate or weaker mappings may be compressed or destabilized.

articles.title: How Employees Experience (Im)balance with W-ICTs: an Ideal Type Analysis of Digital Well-being
articles.authors: Lore Geldof; Ann DeSmet; Alice Verlinden; Elfi Baillien
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The rapid digitalization of work has intensified employees' connectivity to work-related information and communication technologies (W-ICTs), creating both opportunities and risks for digital well-being. While prior research highlights these ambivalent effects, little is known about how employees emotionally experience digital (im)balance with W-ICTs. Hence, we aim to develop a typology detailing such emotional experiences.
Design/Methodology/Approach: Drawing on 40 qualitative interviews (60% female; Mage = 40.25; SD = 9.16), this study abductively develops an experiential typology of digital (im)balance with W-ICT using Ideal Type Analysis. The identified types capture variations in emotional experiences (i.e., affective and cognitive) and digital connectivity processes (DCPs; i.e., interference, boundary blurring, exposure, and time displacement).
Findings: Eight Ideal Types are identified, comprising four experiences of digital imbalance and four experiences of digital balance. The types differ in emotional valence with configurations of DCPs. A comparison of the types show distinct emotional experiences while similar DCPs may occur. This is contextualized in the organisational setting.
Originality: By integrating emotional experiences and DCPs, the typology advances a configurational understanding of employee digital well-being. By contextualizing the types in organizational conditions, the findings suggest that highly connected work environments are not inherently tied to experiences of imbalance.

articles.title: Social readiness and public legitimacy of vaccine mandates: comparative evidence from three countries
articles.authors: Uwana Evers; Joshua Lake; Katie Attwell
articles.abstract: Vaccine mandates are used to increase vaccine uptake during infectious disease emergencies; however, they expose enduring tensions between collective protection and individual autonomy. Existing research treats public opinion toward mandates as a binary – recording only whether people support or oppose them. This study conceptualizes mandate attitudes as comprising two distinct dimensions – perceived public-health protection and concern for rights/autonomy – and examines these in survey data from Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973). In this framework, mandate legitimacy encompasses both perceived collective benefits and perceived infringements on individual autonomy. Analysis revealed divergent patterns: the protection dimension was more strongly associated with institutional trust and vaccination behavior across all three countries, while rights-based attitudes were more variable. Moreover, trust in health-relevant institutions was more robustly associated with the protection dimension than trust in political institutions or media, but this did not extend uniformly to rights-based attitudes. In France, rights-based attitudes were independent of health system trust; in Italy, rights attitudes were unrelated to national government trust, suggesting rights-based objections operate partly independently of institutional confidence. Feeling compelled to vaccinate against COVID-19 was negatively associated with both dimensions across all countries, indicating coercive vaccination experiences may deplete legitimacy capital available for future mandate deployment. Findings suggest that general mandate approval can conceal substantial rights-based resistance, and that institutional trust is insufficient to reduce rights-based mandate resistance Communication strategies that build health institution trust, minimize coercive framing, and are sensitive to political contexts might sustain the public legitimacy required for effective pandemic preparedness.

articles.title: Narrative Entropy
articles.authors: Devin R Wright; Fritz Breithaupt; Anthony F. Beavers; Jacob G. Foster; Jisun An
articles.abstract: Narrative Entropy Theory (NET) proposes that we inhabit narrative environments: ecosystems of cultures, communities, and personal histories constructed from overlapping stories. Narrative entropy is a dynamic, relational property of these ecosystems: the degree of constraint and uncertainty over the interpretive possibility space available within them. At relatively lower entropy, interpretive activity concentrates around recurrent structures, makes narrative and shared worlds easier to navigate and facilitates shared meaning and experience. At relatively higher entropy, more possibilities remain available, which makes interpretation less anticipable and preserves opportunities for interpretive plurality, perspective-taking, and the generation of new meaning. In this way, narrative environments shape how meaning is interpreted and shared and which experiences and perspectives become available for recognition. NET connects the structure of these environments to cognition, communication, and social coordination while treating narrative as both organized structure and embodied activity. We provide an initial empirical demonstration using 475,716 English-language news articles from sources in 65 countries. We operationalize narrative entropy through topic attention, microframe complexity, and narrative fluency (the compressibility of traversal through narrative networks) and compare these measures with national indices of expressive freedom. All measures covary with these indices in the predicted directions and together account for more than one-third of the cross-national variance in the World Press Freedom Index. Together, these results show that narrative environments leave measurable traces in the artifacts they produce, making their structure empirically tractable for scientific inquiry.

articles.title: Physical endpoint contact enhances visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback in virtual reality
articles.authors: Ryan George King; Guy Wallis
articles.abstract: When reaching for a visually defined target, sensory information not only guides the preparation and execution of the reaching response but also serves as a crucial source of error feedback. Research on visually guided reaching has typically emphasised the contribution of visual feedback to movement preparation and execution.  However, visually guided reaching also depends on non-visual sensory information. Here, we focus on the role of haptic endpoint feedback and visual hand feedback and how they interact to regulate behaviour. Thirty-six participants completed a rapid reaching task using a virtual reality head-mounted display, allowing us to manipulate endpoint haptic feedback and visual feedback of the moving hand. Participants completed a vibrotactile feedback condition, providing vibration feedback to the fingertip upon target touch, and a vibrotactile and physical contact feedback condition, providing additional physical surface contact. On 25% of trials, the virtual hand disappeared after movement initiation. The addition of physical contact led participants to initiate movement earlier, increase movement times, and spend proportionally more time decelerating, resulting in improved endpoint accuracy. Across kinematic measures, the effects of physical contact did not interact with visual hand feedback. Additionally, of six presence and embodiment items, only the item asking whether touch felt like one's own differed between conditions. Overall, these findings suggest physical contact improves visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback alone. However, this advantage appears to be selective, increasing the realism of touch rather than overall presence or embodiment and not compensating for a loss of visual feedback of the hand.

articles_hidden.title: Normative Data for PID-5 Items, Facets, and Domains in a Large American Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Ian Shryock; Sara J Weston; Maureen Zalewski; David M Condon
articles_hidden.abstract: In the alternative model of personality disorders (AMPD), the criteria for personality disorder diagnosis are bifurcated into the assessment of self and interpersonal function (Criterion A) and the presence of maladaptive personality traits (Criterion B).  While the Personality Inventory for the Diagnostic and Statistics Manual, Fifth Edition (PID-5) (R. F. Krueger et al., 2012) enables the assessment of these traits, a remaining challenge to implementing Criterion B is the question of what constitutes the presence of a maladaptive trait. In the present study of over 190,000 Americans, we report descriptive norms of the PID-5 items, and facets, domains, and personality disorder composites for a normative sample, as well as for 14 sub-samples that are grouped by age and gender, and we provide item response parameters for each of the subscales. We also include facet and domain descriptive norms for the 100- and 25-item versions of the PID-5. These data provide resources for researchers and clinicians alike enabling the further study of personality disorders and implementing the AMPD in clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Structural Stigma and LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Erica Szkody; Steven Hobaica; Laura Jans; Tyra Bergstrom; Ya-Wen Chang; Arielle C. Smith; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural stigma has been shown to have negative consequences on LGBTQ+ youth's mental health. Most research has focused on stigma at the national or state level, limiting understanding of how local institutions and environments influence mental health. In the current study, we sought to examine the association of multiple layers of structural stigma (e.g., at the county and state levels) on depression and anxiety severity, substance use, and mental healthcare access, for LGBTQ+ youth in the United States. Thus, we recruited 609 LGBTQ+ youth (Mage = 15.6, SDage = 1.17; 71.9% White) to complete survey measures about their mental health and access to care. Further, we extracted 2023 data from Project Implicit and the Human Rights Campaign to create factors of structural stigma at the county and state levels. Consistent with existing literature, our results demonstrate that structural stigma, particularly when examined at the county level (as opposed to the state level), may exert significant impacts on mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and substance use severity for LGBTQ+ youth.

articles_hidden.title: Test-retest reliability of multiple-target search: Eye movements and performance metrics
articles_hidden.authors: Kayley Birch-Hurst; Jamie Cooper; Isabella Foot; Oli Muckleston; Kait Clark
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual search plays a critical role in life-saving careers such as radiology and airport security. Professional searches often contain multiple-targets and while some work has explored factors that affect search performance in this context (e.g., personality, search strategy), paradigms and measures with low test-retest reliability are inappropriate for investigating individual differences. Understanding variability in multiple-target search is an important endeavour, but the test-retest reliability of multiple-target search performance and eye movement metrics remain unknown. Seventy-three undergraduate participants completed a multiple-target search task (0, 1, or 2 target ‘T’ shapes, presented at high or low salience, amongst distractor ‘L’ shapes) across two sessions separated by 1-3 weeks. We measured accuracy, response time, and eye movements, and assessed performance across single-, dual-, and no-target trials. Analyses revealed varying test-retest reliabilities: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for accuracy measures ranged from poor (.25 ≤ ICC < .4) to moderate (.4 ≤ ICC < .6), with low-salience (difficult) targets producing higher reliabilities than high-salience (easy) targets. Response time measures were more reliable than accuracy measures, ranging from moderate (.4 ≤ ICC < .6) to good (.6 ≤ ICC < .8). Eye-tracking measures (number of fixations, fixation duration, initiation time, saccade rate, saccade amplitude, saccade duration) had the best reliabilities, ranging from good (.6 ≤ ICC < .8) to excellent (ICC ≥ .8). These results indicate that only some multiple-target search metrics are suitable for assessing individual differences. Future work should integrate performance and eye-tracking measures when considering individual differences in visual search with multiple targets.

articles_hidden.title: Young Children Engage in Choice-Relative Moral Reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Talia Waltzer; Gail D. Heyman; Alan Leslie; Sydney Levine
articles_hidden.abstract: A central challenge in moral reasoning is evaluating actions not only by their outcomes, but also by the alternatives that were available at the time of choice. The present study examined whether preschool-age children engage in this form of choice-relative moral reasoning. Using a child-friendly version of the trolley problem, 3- to 5-year-old children (N = 124, 51% girls) judged a protagonist who moved a barrier to protect three children’s cookies from being eaten by a mean squirrel. Children typically judged this action as morally good when no better alternative was available, even when it caused harm to another child. However, they judged the same action as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. These findings suggest that preschool-age children evaluate actions in light of available alternatives rather than solely on the basis of outcomes. Thus, even young children appear to consider what else could have been done when making moral judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Targeting Emotion Intolerance Beliefs in Young Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial of An Online Single-Session Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Riley McDanal; Hein Kim; Pau Ortells-Faci; Nicholas R Eaton; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Traditional psychological interventions pose various access barriers related to time, geography, provider availability, and cost. Online, self-directed single-session interventions (SSIs) can mitigate such access barriers. However, SSI effect sizes are highly heterogenous. Targeting core transdiagnostic processes may improve SSI consistency. This randomized controlled trial (registration NCT07034027 via clinicaltrials.gov) evaluated a novel SSI targeting the transdiagnostic construct of emotion intolerance beliefs. Method: Participants aged 18-29 reporting deficits in emotional nonreactivity abilities (N = 550) were randomized to the SSI condition or the control and completed questionnaires assessing emotion intolerance beliefs and related constructs at baseline, post-activity, and two-week follow-up. Multilevel modeling was used to assess differential proximal and distal change in emotion intolerance beliefs. Participants in the SSI condition also provided ratings of perceived intervention teaching effectiveness. Results: The first hypothesis — that proximal reductions in emotional intolerance beliefs would be greater for SSI participants than for control participants — was supported at p < 0.001, with a near-medium Cohen’s d effect size derived from a standard regression. This differential benefit was not sustained at follow-up. The second hypothesis — that participants would self-report the activity “somewhat” helped them learn to be nonreactive — was not sufficiently supported, as the mean rating was slightly below the preregistered cutoff. However, participants provided positive views of the intervention. Conclusions: The SSI is a strong candidate for future testing as an on-demand intervention during states of acute distress. Future efforts should examine the conditions under which acute benefits might be sustained.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition From AI-Generated and Human Faces: Performance, Mental Health, and Demographic Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Vowels; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial emotion-recognition tasks are widely used to investigate social-cognitive differences across mental health conditions, but their
scientific value depends on the faces used to measure performance. Established photographic databases are difficult and expensive to
expand, and many provide little ethnic diversity. AI-generated faces offer a more representative, flexible, and scalable alternative,
provided they capture the same clinically relevant individual differences as photographs of human faces. We compared 161
photorealistic AI-generated faces with 72 images from FACES, an established human-photograph set. Prolific participants contributed
83,206 valid trials; 77,238 trials covering the six shared emotions entered the primary comparison (accuracy \textit{n} = 1,047; response
time \textit{n} = 1,046). AI-diverse expressions were recognised more accurately (89.12\% vs.\ 81.72\%) and faster (2.29 vs.\ 2.64 s) than
FACES expressions, while AI-diverse and AI-White performance did not differ significantly. The AI task retained the individual differences needed for research: lower accuracy on both sources was associated most consistently with psychotic-like experiences and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with magnitudes aligned with previous literature. AI-diverse and FACES accuracy correlated at \textit{r} = .56, and corrected split-half reliability was .70 and .60, respectively. Women were more accurate than men; participant ethnicity was unrelated to performance. Higher AI accuracy indicates that the expressions were clear; it does not show general psychometric superiority, possibly because very easy items can compress differences among high performers. The combination of clear expressions, comparable symptom sensitivity, and broader representation shows that generative AI can modernise a core social-cognition research tool while making stimulus design more controllable, expandable, and shareable.

articles_hidden.title: To whom should punishment communicate? Children's and adults' perceptions of punishment's message
articles_hidden.authors: Young-eun Lee; Sophie Noëlle Charles; Larisa Heiphetz
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do people punish? Legal and political theories describing punishment as expressive argue that one of punishment's functions is to communicate information (e.g., which behaviors are unacceptable). While this work emphasizes communicating to transgressors, punishment may also show victims that others take their pain seriously. In two studies, we asked how laypeople perceive the communicative nature of punishment. Study 1 found that adults (n=156), but not 4- to 7-year-old children (n=84), evaluated communicating punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims. Study 2 (n=188 adults and n=87 children) revealed that adults also evaluated communicating the reason underlying punishment to transgressors more positively than communicating it to victims, whereas 5- to 7-year-old children showed a more balanced evaluation of the two targets. Indeed, children provided more favorable evaluations than did adults of scenarios that did not include transgressors as targets of punishment's message. Together, these findings suggest that adults, but not children, consistently prioritize informing transgressors over informing victims, potentially contributing to social responses to wrongdoing that place insufficient emphasis on victims’ informational and emotional needs.

articles_hidden.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles_hidden.title: Drawn to Belong, but Not Just Anywhere: Identity Complexity, Uncertainty, and the Allure of Extremist Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Blaya-Burgo; Michael A. Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract: People often identify with radical groups before engaging in violence, yet the psychosocial processes that make these groups appealing warrant closer examination. Across two studies, we examined whether identity complexity moderated the relationship between self-uncertainty and positive attitudes toward and willingness to join radical groups. In Study 1 (N = 164), we experimentally manipulated identity complexity and self-uncertainty. Contrary to our hypotheses, neither manipulation nor their interaction significantly predicted attitudes toward or willingness to join a hypothetical radical group. Given the sample limitations and the limited effectiveness of the uncertainty prime, Study 2 (N = 259) provided a more rigorous test by manipulating identity complexity while examining naturally occurring self-uncertainty. Again, identity complexity and its interaction with self-uncertainty did not predict either outcome. However, higher self-uncertainty was associated with greater willingness to join the radical group, whereas younger age and greater identity centrality (but not complexity) predicted more positive attitudes toward and greater willingness to join it. These findings suggest that the prominence of a specific identity, rather than the complexity of one's broader identity structure, may be more relevant to understanding openness to radical groups and may inform identity-based approaches to prevention and countering violent extremism and deradicalization efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating conflicting visual 3D shape cues
articles_hidden.authors: Jovan Kemp; Fulvio Domini
articles_hidden.abstract: How does the visual system handle discrepant estimates of depth from conflicting visual cues? One possibility is that less reliable cues are suppressed in favor of cues that are more likely to produce veridical depth estimates. This can be accomplished by a statistically robust implementation of the Bayesian framework for cue integration. However, suppression relies on the assumption that individual cues generally produce consistent depth estimates, an assumption that may not hold. Alternatively, the cues may be integrated via a vector summation, as proposed by the Intrinsic Constraint theory, regardless of whether they conflict. Using an absolute depth judgment task and a two-interval forced-choice (2-IFC) task, we evaluate cue integration for a range of cue-conflict ratios. Participants were shown 3D corrugated surfaces with depths specified by a set ratio of the binocular disparity cue and monocular cues composed of texture and shading. In the depth judgement task, participants adjusted the depth of the 3D surface until it matched the target depth specified by a 2D reference. Discrimination thresholds measured from the component cues in isolation were additionally used to parameterize the Bayesian robust model. The results showed the matched depth systematically varied with the cue-conflict ratio. The vector summation model produced a better fit to the data than the Bayesian robust model. In the second task, participants performed a 2-IFC task discriminating between surfaces with the same cue-conflict ratio. The discrimination thresholds extracted from this task were again better predicted by the vector summation model. These results indicate that cues are integrated directly rather than through statistically robust mechanisms, challenging the dominant Bayesian account of cue integration.

articles_hidden.title: Rational decisions in multi-step environments with few rollouts
articles_hidden.authors: Sixing Chen; Kristopher T. Jensen; Marcelo G Mattar
articles_hidden.abstract: People routinely make decisions by mentally simulating the potential outcomes of their actions. However, this process appears computationally intractable in real-world situations involving sequences of decisions with exponentially many possible futures. How the brain efficiently evaluates temporally extended decisions despite limited cognitive resources remains a fundamental puzzle. Here we present a mathematical theory showing that for decisions in multi-step environments, the rational strategy is to perform only a few mental simulations, formalized as rollouts. This is because the first rollouts provide substantially more information than later ones despite taking a similar amount of time, so the opportunity cost of additional simulations quickly outweighs their marginal benefit. Our framework demonstrates that this efficiency relies on the correlated reward structure of naturalistic environments, which allows information from one rollout to generalize to many related future paths. This theory also explains why, under resource constraints, many shallow rollouts are preferable to fewer deep ones; why apparently myopic decisions can arise without explicit temporal discounting; and how to relate the dynamics of planning to evidence accumulation models. We validate predictions of our theory in two behavioral experiments, which confirm that humans achieve higher reward rates with few rollouts and dynamically adjust their simulation depth based on available cognitive resources. These findings reveal how the brain balances the depth and breadth of mental simulation to make effective decisions under computational constraints, providing a unifying account of planning that bridges computationally intensive search algorithms in machine learning and the remarkable efficiency of human decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays
articles_hidden.authors: Joonkoo Park; Shimin Hu; Ruoyu Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: This technical note presents mathematical derivations that establish the relationship between numerosity and the Fourier power spectrum of dot arrays, a standard stimulus in biological and psychological research in numerosity perception (e.g., DeWind et al. (2015); Park and Huber (2022). We derive a closed-form solution for the radially averaged power spectrum of images depicting arrays of identical dots as a function of dot number, radius, spacing, and spatial frequency. We also demonstrate that an unconventional distillation of the Fourier coefficients, as done in Paul et al. (2022), reveals an artifactual relationship between that metric and numerosity.

articles_hidden.title: Representations of Change Support Object Individuation in Infancy
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Mazalik; Justin Halberda
articles_hidden.abstract:
“One can never step in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man.” This ancient puzzle by Heraclitus highlights that the world, and ourselves, are constantly changing. But to raise these puzzles, one must engage the concept of CHANGE. Developmental research shows that even infants represent highly abstract notions, including objects, agents, cause, and number. Here, we ask whether they also represent CHANGE.

We adapted the individuation paradigm pioneered by Xu and Carey (1996), in which two objects emerge sequentially from behind an occluder, preventing spatiotemporal cues about the number of objects. Infants must instead rely on contrastive featural/kind information. Prior work shows that before 12 months, infants fail to individuate objects differing in basic-level category (e.g., duck vs. truck), but succeed with broader distinctions (e.g., object vs. agent).

Here we show that infants can use the contrast between a continuously changing object and a static object to infer the number of entities present. This effect cannot be
explained by saliency alone, as infants’ longer looking at unexpected outcomes differs
from any preference for the more salient changing object, and is striking in light of
reports that infants at this age fail to individuate objects by color alone (Leslie, 1998).
Representing change opens a new avenue for research: What types of change are
encoded? Over what timescales? Embedded in which cognitive systems? By 8 months,
infants already appreciate change as a core property of the world.

articles_hidden.title: Does confidence indicate face-identity matching accuracy for own-race and other-race faces?
articles_hidden.authors: Geraldine Jeckeln; ALICE O'TOOLE
articles_hidden.abstract: Confidence reliably indicates face-matching accuracy for same-race faces. However, it is unclear whether this holds for other-race faces. We examined the confidence-accuracy relationship for same- and other-race faces in Caucasian and African American participants. To eliminate response bias in observers’ confidence-scale use, we measured confidence using a confidence forced-choice task, rather than with confidence ratings. Participants completed two consecutive face-matching trials and selected the trial on which they felt more confident. Results showed an other-race effect for face-matching accuracy, but not for the confidence-accuracy relationship. We also examined whether comparative-trial difficulty predicted confidence decisions. For African American participants, difficulty predicted confidence for same- and other-race decisions. For Caucasian participants, difficulty predicted confidence for same-, but not other-race, decisions. Confidence predicted accuracy for same- and other-race faces, with difficulty consistently guiding confidence for same-race faces. These findings enhance our understanding of how confidence decisions are formed and guide cross-race identification decisions.

articles_hidden.title: Research practices and transparency in Slovak social sciences: A national analysis based on random sampling of publications (2013-2022)
articles_hidden.authors: Marcel Martončik; Ivan Ropovik; Peter Babincak; Gabriel Baník; Jaroslava Bočanová; Denisa Fedáková; Richard Gamrát; Samar Issmailová; Klára Kačmariková; Pavol Kačmár
articles_hidden.abstract: The credibility of the social sciences has been increasingly questioned, with concerns centering on limited transparency, replicability, questionable research practices, and incomplete reporting. Most evidence on these problems comes from self-report surveys, which are subject to recall and self-presentation biases. Analyzing the published literature offers a complementary approach that reveals what the scientific record contains. In this study, we examined the research, reporting, and transparency practices of Slovak social science literature published between 2013 and 2022. We coded a stratified random sample of 998 articles from two national registries and Scopus. For each record, we extracted methodological, statistical, bibliometric, and transparency-related characteristics, and applied granularity-related inconsistency of means (GRIM) tests to assess the internal coherence of reported results. Open science practices were rare and showed little improvement over the decade: data were shared in 5.0% of empirical studies, code in 4.1%, only one study was preregistered, and none was published as a Registered Report. More consequentially, standard reporting was frequently incomplete: sample size justification was present in 12.3% of applicable studies, effect sizes and confidence intervals accompanied all analyses in 32.0% and 7.1% studies, respectively, and reliability evidence and missing data handling were often absent. Among studies reporting sufficient detail for GRIM testing, 19.4% of assessed values were inconsistent, and 30% of these studies contained at least 25% inconsistent values. The findings suggest that the credibility of this literature is constrained primarily by insufficient reporting standards. Reforms should prioritize complete methodological reporting, with more demanding open science practices to follow.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Scalar Choice: Foraging as a Policy Framework for Decision Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Zahra Rezaei; Juan F. Ramirez-Villegas; Ian Q Whishaw; rob sutherland; Majid H Mohajerani
articles_hidden.abstract:
Foraging is a fundamental form of decision-making, requiring animals to search, evaluate resources,
allocate effort, manage risk, and coordinate behavior. Much of foraging neuroscience reduces this
behavior to scalar choice, using reward magnitude, delay, effort, risk, or opportunity cost to explain
whether an animal stays or leaves, accepts or rejects, harvests or switches. We argue that this
approach leaves a defining feature of foraging underdeveloped. Animals do not simply compare
values at isolated decision points. They implement policies that organize state-dependent patterns
of approach, inspection, consumption, transport, withdrawal, persistence, and disengagement over
time. Here we propose a policy-centered perspective in which the primary explanatory unit is the
mapping from internal and external states onto an organized repertoire of actions. This framework
retains the normative strengths of optimal foraging theory while broadening the interpretation of
departures from its predictions. Apparent suboptimality may reveal hidden costs, latent state variables,
or changes in policy organization rather than a simple failure of valuation. This perspective
also reframes the neural problem. Understanding foraging as policy points to a distributed neural
basis that integrates valuation, spatial memory, action selection, risk regulation, and behavioral
sequencing. By shifting the unit of analysis from scalar choice to policy organization, foraging provides
a principled bridge across behavioral ecology, decision neuroscience, reinforcement learning,
and research on artificial agents.

articles_hidden.title: What's The Function? Eigenfunctions Shaping (Non)Parametric Growth Curves
articles_hidden.authors: Suryadyuti Baral; Emilio Ferrer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Growth Curve Models (GCMs) are central tools for analyzing longitudinal data in psychology and are estimated under the Multilevel Modeling (MLM) or the Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) frameworks. Despite their flexibility, both approaches require researchers to predefine functional forms or loadings, aiding interpretation but risking model misspecification. We propose functional principal component analysis (FPCA) as a nonparametric extension of these models, where estimated eigenfunctions can inform the functions used in MLMs and the loadings in SEMs.
     
We evaluate FPCA’s ability to recover underlying functional structure in longitudinal data and assess its robustness to violations of key assumptions, including orthonormality of data generating functions and independence of random effects. Sample size and time points are varied to reflect realistic intensive and sparse longitudinal designs. FPCA is fit to training data, and the resulting eigenfunctions inform GCM loadings evaluated on held-out test data. Results show that FPCA accurately recovers generating functions under orthonormal conditions, with improved estimation under higher sample sizes and larger number of time points. GCMs informed by eigenfunctions show good fit and parameter recovery when assumptions are met. An empirical illustration demonstrates how FPCA can uncover functional patterns and guide model specification. Indeed, FPCA can be a valuable nonparametric complement to conventional longitudinal models.

articles_hidden.title: Does internalized homonegativity lower sexual satisfaction? A longitudinal assessment among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM) in Canada's three largest cities
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Meora Kowall; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Aki Gormezano; Jérémy Lelièvre; Daniel Grace; Trevor Adam Hart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Internalized homonegativity is associated with lower sexual satisfaction among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Though internalized homonegativity is commonly seen as an antecedent to lower sexual satisfaction, existing research tends to be cross-sectional, limiting our ability to make causal inferences. This has important implications for GBM sexual health and clinical interventions. The goal of this study is to examine the longitudinal associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction.

Methods: We analyzed data from a longitudinal study of GBM in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal, Canada (N = 1307). Using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), we analyzed data from baseline up to two years of follow-up to model the within-person changes between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction. The RI-CLPM allows us to account for the stable, trait-like differences between individuals that may inflate correlations, thus allowing for a stronger estimate of within-person variation over time.

Results: Although there were no cross-lagged associations between internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction, we found that participants who scored higher on internalized homonegativity also tended to score lower on sexual satisfaction after accounting for within-person variation, suggesting these effects are due to stable between-person differences.

Conclusion: Cross-sectional associations are likely due to stable between-person differences affecting both outcomes, suggesting that internalized homonegativity and sexual satisfaction are independent processes. From a clinical perspective, internalized homonegativity may be useful in identifying potential issues with sexual well-being, but reducing internalized homonegativity may not be sufficient in alleviating these outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Inflated Statistics Lead to Incorrect Inference: How (Not) to Make Cognitive Network Group Comparisons
articles_hidden.authors: Chun-Ying Tu; Martin Chodorow; Patricia J. Brooks; Emilia Ezrina; Virginia Valian
articles_hidden.abstract: Semantic networks are an increasingly popular method for examining the structure of cognitive representations. We identify a pervasive error in group-level network comparisons. This error, embedded in popular statistical software (SemNeT; Christensen & Kenett, 2023), artificially inflates statistical power by (1) treating bootstrap (re)samples as independent observations and (2) failing to treat the standard deviation of the bootstrapped distribution as a standard error. Study 1 illustrates the problem with a representative study; Study 2 documents the error in 42 published studies that use semantic network analysis. Using verbal fluency data from monolingual (N = 94) and bilingual adults (N = 93), Study 3 demonstrates that, in both naive random walk and correlation-based networks, parametric test statistics improperly become significant and increase in magnitude as the number of bootstrap samples increases, without any change in the underlying data. In contrast, percentile bootstrap confidence intervals based on within-iteration contrasts and permutation tests indicate no reliable group differences (i.e., the confidence intervals include 0, and the observed differences fall within the central 95% of the null distributions). Given the pervasiveness of the inflation error in published research, we suspect that many group differences of semantic organization have been overstated.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Health Literacy Across Psychology Students and Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Eileen Richter; Konrad Schöniger; Maya Schulze; Luisa Frede; Korbinian Moeller; Ronny Redlich; Markus Spitzer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health misconceptions are widespread, yet it remains unclear how accurately psychology students distinguish such misconceptions from evidence-based information, whether this differs across stages of psychology education, and how their performance compares with that of large language models (LLMs). 
We evaluated the accuracy of 150 psychology students, including 70 first-semester and 80 more advanced students, in classifying 15 mental health myths and 15 facts. Additionally, we used Chat GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek V3.2, and GLM-5 to classify the same statements across 80 independent runs per statement and model. 
Students classified mental health myths more accurately than facts, and advanced students outperformed first-semester students in classifying both statement types (myths: 87.7% vs. 75.2%; facts: 69.3% vs. 55.4%). A binomial generalized linear mixed-effects model indicated that group differences in classification accuracy varied between myths and facts. LLMs generally showed higher accuracy than both student groups in classifying statements, although performance varied substantially across models, particularly for facts. Item-level analyses revealed partly distinct error patterns: students and LLMs struggled with some of the same facts, whereas they also showed relative advantages on specific statements. 
These findings suggest that mental health literacy differs significantly across stages of psychology education and that, although current LLMs perform strongly on this classification task, some item-specific errors recurred across repeated runs. Examining which misconceptions and facts remain difficult may help identify specific gaps in both psychology education and AI-generated mental health information.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of self-efficacy on depressive symptoms among college students: A reassessment of Desai and Lueke (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Desai and Lueke, we conducted a reanalysis of the evidence supporting their mediation framework relating generalized self-efficacy to depressive symptoms in college students. We demonstrate that the observed pattern of covariation can be represented equally well by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not assume the directional sequence proposed in the original investigation. In this alternative specification, generalized self-efficacy, perceived stress, college maladjustment, and depressive symptoms are conceptualized as indicators of a broader latent construct, core self-evaluation. These findings illustrate a fundamental limitation of observational research: identical covariance structures can often be explained by multiple competing models. Consequently, correlational data alone provide limited grounds for favoring one theoretical interpretation over alternative explanations. Consideration of rival models should therefore be a routine part of efforts to draw conclusions about psychological processes and mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Robust Measurement of Habits with the Forced-Response Task A Multiverse Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: José Juan León; Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; David Luque
articles_hidden.abstract: Instrumental behavior reflects a balance between two systems: an outcome-oriented, goal-directed system and a cognitively efficient habit system that gradually gains control with repeated instrumental responding in stable contexts. While overtraining reliably induces habits in animal models, human participants often retain goal-directed control when their performance is assessed using devaluation paradigms. To address this translational gap, the forced-response method has emerged as a promising approach for studying goal-directed and habitual behavior by constraining the time available to respond. This method imposes a dual task in which participants must respond accurately to an instrumental discriminative stimulus at a specific time signaled by a sound. Because the onset of the discriminative stimulus varies across trials, the time available for response preparation is systematically manipulated. Restricting this time can unmask stimulus-driven responses when the goal-directed system has insufficient time to override them. Although the forced-response method has become increasingly popular, its use has also been accompanied by growing flexibility in data analysis, creating a potential “garden of forking paths.” Using four independent datasets, we generated 48 a priori valid preprocessing pipelines to assess variability in two discrete measures of habitual behavior—the proportion of habits and the habit index—as well as their split-half reliability and the proportion of habits as a continuous function of the available response time, modeled using generalized additive models. Results indicated that both habit measures were generally robust across preprocessing pipelines. The proportion of habits was more sensitive to specific preprocessing choices, particularly accuracy and timing-synchrony exclusion criteria, but also showed greater reliability. In all cases, however, the resulting variability was small. Reliability analyses yielded acceptable estimates in most analytic universes. Overall, these findings support the forced-response method as a robust paradigm for studying habit formation and expression in humans.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Control Neural Correlates of Negative Affective in Psychosis Spectrum Disorders: A Laboratory and Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Takakuni Suzuki; Margo W Menkes; Maureen Walton; Melvin G McInnis; Jian Kang; Tara A. Niendam; Ivy Fei Tso; Stephan F. Taylor
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum (SZ) and bipolar-spectrum disorders (BD) report experiencing heightened negative affect (NA), which can be operationalized as stable traits and dynamic states. While cognitive control is a potential underlying mechanism, identifying neural underpinning of NA has been challenging. This could be due to the lack of such investigation, but also a comprehensive framework to investigate the association specificity. Data were collected from 105 participants (34 SZ, 34 BD, 37 healthy control [HC]) on the five-factor model of personality traits, cognitive control electroencephalography (EEG), and self-reported mood and contexts via ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Cognitive control indices of EEG were extracted as event-related potentials (ERPs) and time-frequency theta-band activities from three flanker tasks varying in valence (neutral, unpleasant, and pleasant). Participants with SZ and BD generally reported higher NA traits, lower Extraversion, lower Conscientiousness traits, higher Psychoticism, and high average and fluctuation in EMA NA-related experiences than HC participants. Participants with SZ experienced more EMA unpleasant events, were more upset by them, and put more effort into avoiding them. EEG theta-band power from the arrow task was associated mostly with NA-related traits and tendency, and theta-band power from the unpleasant task was associated with EMA unpleasant event occurrence and reactions. ERPs and theta phase activities did not relate to any traits or daily experiences, and no other traits and experiences were related to EEG measures. Cognitive control EEG theta-band power was associated with trait and state NA specifically, potentially reflecting a transdiagnostic indicator of cognitive control and neural mechanism underlying stress-vulnerability in SZ and BD.

articles_hidden.title: Rhythm of Thought: Tracing the Dynamics of Deliberation in Reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Jérémie Beucler; Wim De Neys
articles_hidden.abstract: When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to engage in further reasoning. But what people actually do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes leads to better answers remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four possible functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort), together with expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a clear temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly prominent as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these evolving dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation also showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted subsequent increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

articles_hidden.title: A randomised controlled trial of Detour: a multi-component app-based intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles_hidden.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Hanneke Scholten; Maartje Luijten
articles_hidden.abstract: Cigarette smoking is a leading cause of preventable death, and adolescents and young adults (AYA) report the highest levels of smoking across age groups. Yet, quitting before 30 years can reduce most health risks attached to smoking. Unfortunately, there is a paucity of effective interventions catering to AYAs specifically. In the present pre-registered randomised controlled trial, we tested the efficacy of Detour, a multi-component app-based intervention, against a digital self-help brochure (N = 613; Mage = 20.9 years). The intervention period was five weeks long with one pre-quit week and four post-quit weeks. Quit day was on the first day of the second intervention week. Participants filled questionnaires at the start and end of the intervention, as well as three and six months later. The primary cessation outcome was 14-day point prevalence of smoking at 6-month follow-up. Secondary cessation outcomes included smoking prevalence at post-test and 3-month follow up, and weekly smoking at all time points. Contrary to our hypotheses, the Detour group did not report higher abstinence rates than the brochure group at any time points. Unexpectedly, the Detour group reported higher weekly smoking levels than the brochure group at all time points. These results could potentially be attributed to the comparison of Detour with an active control group, and technical limitations of the Detour app. Future studies can consider having an additional inactive control group to tease out general intervention effects and designing simpler interventions with a special focus on functionality and technological smoothness.

articles_hidden.title: From Treating to Preventing Distress through Psychological Prehabilitation – A  Novel Theoretical Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Baliousis; Lauren Charlotte Heathcote; Chloe Grimmett; Lynn Calman; Christopher Meek; Nima Moghaddam; David Dawson; Mike Rennoldson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: In cancer prehabilitation, physical components predominate and psychological preparation is often overlooked. Yet up to half of patients develop distress during treatment, which undermines adherence, recovery, and quality of life. Psychological care remains largely reactive and lacks a unifying theoretical framework for prevention. Preventing distress poses three challenges: building resilience; doing so before patients have experienced treatment stressors; and tailoring this to each patient.

Methods: Following conceptual review guidance, we selected theories that address these challenges and integrated them into one framework.

Results: We synthesised five theoretical traditions (stress and resilience, social identity, affective forecasting, stress inoculation, and narrative identity) into four areas for assessment and intervention, framed as questions for the patient. What do I bring? covers beliefs about illness and treatment, coping and emotion regulation, and social support and group memberships. Where am I heading? covers how patients expect treatment to feel, including underestimating their ability to adapt. What do I need? uses stress inoculation to build and rehearse coping, with imagery for stressors that cannot be simulated. Who am I (becoming)? links these through the patient's personal story, from past coping to future recovery. The framework specifies testable mechanisms; for example, limited resources and skewed forecasts may predict distress during treatment. It maps onto universal, targeted, and specialist levels of provision.

Conclusions: The framework provides a theoretical basis for preventing distress through Psychological Prehabilitation for Cancer Treatment. It can guide intervention design, staff training, and evaluation. Research priorities are to test its mechanisms, evaluate it as a complex intervention, and develop brief screening tools that predict future distress.

articles_hidden.title: Visuospatial Orienting in Working Memory is Preserved in Adults with ADHD Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães; Amy Louise Atkinson; Richard John Allen; Valerie Camos
articles_hidden.abstract: People with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are reported to have pervasive deficits in working memory (WM), yet mechanistic explanations for such deficits are lacking. Research suggests that attentional mechanisms such as reward-based prioritisation and visuospatial orienting are intact in this population (Atkinson et al., 2025; Superbia-Guimarães et al., 2022, 2023). To further examine these mechanisms, we investigated the hypotheses that deficient visuospatial orienting during encoding and maintenance are at the root of WM deficits in adults with ADHD symptoms.  Eighty-four symptomatic participants (Mage = 28.4 years, SD = 4.6) and 107 controls (Mage = 29.4, SD = 4.4) had their symptoms assessed with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. They each took part in one of two experiments involving an item (colour or unfamiliar shape) recognition memory task that incorporated pre- and retro-cues. Across both experiments, we found strong evidence of beneficial pre- and retro-cueing effects upon memory accuracy and reaction time (RT). However, we found no evidence for the expected group differences nor the interaction between symptom status and cueing condition. There was also no evidence for correlations between ADHD symptom scores, recognition accuracy, RT, and cueing benefits. Therefore, attentional mechanisms are unlikely to explain deficits in WM in individuals with symptoms of ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: Evolutionary Theory Makes Predictions About Cognition Beyond Rational Optimization
articles_hidden.authors: Cameron Turner; Thomas L. Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Evolution by natural selection produces the appearance of design in minds, brains, and behavior. While rational models of cognition are usually considered to be consistent with evolution, they are rarely derived from distinctively evolutionary assumptions. Bayesian modeling, reinforcement learning, rational analysis, and resource rational analysis all postulate optimization objectives of coherence in information use or maximization of expected value, potentially under resource constraints. However, cognition is performed by an individual within a lineage where success is determined by the persistence of the lineage across generations. Here, we present a signal detection model that shows how this distinctly evolutionary objective produces predictions that depart from those of rational models. We find that the source of environmental uncertainty determines cognitive design, with weak priors being favored in environments dominated by change. This ensures offspring vary so that some profit against novel challenges, and is favored even at the expense of accurate decision making. Cognitive structure should reflect stable environmental trends, but in fluctuating environments selection strips structure away to release behavioral diversity. We highlight that evolution maximizes the geometric mean number of offspring over generations, an objective that recurs across optimization problems where outcomes accumulate sequentially, including in finance, control engineering, and information theory.

articles_hidden.title: Maladaptive Personality Traits and Statement Validity Assessment. Mapping DSM-5 Trait Domains and Facets onto Lying, Suggestibility, and Autobiographical Memory Quality
articles_hidden.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Merle Hurtmanns; Johannes Zimmermann
articles_hidden.abstract: Statement validity assessment (SVA) requires experts to weigh a witness’s personality when judging motives for deception, expectable statement quality, and suggestibility. We propose the maladaptive trait model of the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders as a common language for these steps and test its expectations with low-stakes paradigms at the domain and facet level. In a German community sample (N = 258), we administered the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Short Form, a matrix cheating task, the Lying in Everyday Situations scale, an online Gudjonsson Suggestibility Scale, and self-ratings of memory quality and imagery vividness. We report correlations between all 5 domains and 25 facets with all criteria, with confidence intervals, false-discovery-rate correction, and Bayes factors. Self-reported lying was positively related to Antagonism and Disinhibition, with motive-specific patterns; contrary to preregistration, so was Negative Affectivity. Memory clarity and imagery vividness were related to Detachment, Negative Affectivity, and several of their facets. No trait was related to behavioral dishonesty or suggestibility; Bayes factors mostly favored the null. Facets improved cross-validated prediction where they diverged from their domain.
