For SVA, the results support using antagonistic and self-protective profiles in motive analysis and lowering expectations of detail and vividness for detached and depressive witnesses.

articles_hidden.title: Why do suicide rates increase in the spring and decrease in the fall? Insights from Canadian suicide rate and death rate data spanning 2010 to 2020
articles_hidden.authors: James Christopher Wiley
articles_hidden.abstract: In 1952, the psychiatrist Erwin Stengel hypothesized that suicide becomes rarer in times when the value of life within a society is lower, when death is more common. In Canada, suicide rates and death rates present with consistent seasonality between years, fluctuating inversely with one another. However, the typical pre-pandemic seasonality seen in death rates was broken during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, as a consequence of inordinate deaths occurring at an odd time of year. This offers a unique opportunity to observe whether suicide rates were inversely disrupted. The present study models weekly Canadian suicide rates using death rates, from time series data spanning 2010 to 2019. Results indicate that suicide rates decrease on average by 0.27 standard deviations per 1 standard deviation increase in the death rate. This model is then used to predict 2020 suicide rates, using 2020 death rates. Predictions account for 11.6% of the variation in actual 2020 suicide rates. Furthermore, actual 2020 suicide rates display a negative disruption at the same time as the 2020 death rate positive disruption, and this suicide rate disruption is mimicked by our model predictions. Overall, results are interpreted as being favorable towards Stengel’s theory. As alternative interpretation, we suggest that non-suicide-related deaths preferentially remove potential suicides from the population. Overall analysis suggests that elevated death rates during colder seasons are driven by increases in cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart attacks) and communicable disease transmission relative to warmer seasons, resulting in suppressed suicide rates.

articles_hidden.title: Memory experiences under psychedelics – an exploratory prospective online study
articles_hidden.authors: Samuli Kangaslampi; Kim PC Kuypers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Rationale

Case reports and early clinical research suggest classic psychedelics can occasion intense recall and processing of autobiographical memories. Such memory experiences have seen very little study more recently, although they may hold importance for both therapeutic effects and potential iatrogenic harms.

Objectives

This prospective, exploratory study aimed to assess 1) the extent and content of memory experiences in naturalistic psychedelic use, as well as their associations with 2) elements of set and setting, 3) emotional breakthroughs and psychological insights, and 4) longer-term changes in well-being and later subjective evaluations of the experience.

Methods

English-speaking adults (N = 66, Mage = 34.91, 60.1% male) planning to take a classic psychedelic were assessed online before, 1-3 days, and 3-5 weeks after taking the psychedelic with self-report instruments.

Results

On average, participants spent around a quarter of their psychedelic experience recalling past events, although variance was high. Positive and recent memories were most commonly recalled. Four in ten participants recalled usually avoided memories, nearly half potentially traumatic experiences, and a quarter memories of events they had never recalled before. Memory experiences, especially recalling avoided memories, were associated with more emotional breakthroughs and psychological insights and higher evaluations of the experience as useful, but did not predict changes in well-being.

Conclusions

Recalling past events of one’s life may form a major, largely neglected element of many psychedelic experiences and be associated with therapeutic processes. Recalling apparent memories never remembered before under psychedelics may be more common than previously thought and needs careful study and consideration.

articles_hidden.title: (Un)informed Consent: To What Degree are Research Participants 'Informed' by Common Consent Procedures in Psychology under EU Data Protection Law?
articles_hidden.authors: Luisa Jansen; Annika Iris Külpmann; Dara Hallinan; Franziska Boehm; Malte Elson
articles_hidden.abstract: There is reason to believe that consent forms in psychological research may routinely not fulfill the requirements for consent outlined in EU data protection law. Where this is the case, the legitimacy of the research conducted may be undermined. However, so far, there is only preliminary data to support the proposition that compliance may not be the norm (Hallinan et al., 2023a). We present the results of a content analysis of a sample of psychological research reports and consent forms used in those studies. We contacted authors of studies published between 2019 and 2021 and asked them to share the corresponding consent materials, resulting in N = 101 sets of papers and consent forms. We evaluated the compliance of consent forms with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and systematically compared the data collected as part of empirical research, as reported in publications, with the details provided in the respective consent forms given to research participants. Results indicate that all consent forms lack essential information for participants, particularly regarding the data controller, the data collected in the study, and participants' legal rights, even when studies involve collecting sensitive data (n = 58). We discuss the shortcomings and present ways forward for psychological researchers to facilitate both the sharing of research data and the protection of their participants’ privacy, when enabling participants to make the consent they give actually informed.

articles_hidden.title: The Experimental Study of Habitual Behavior in Humans: A Review of the Validity of Current Protocols
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Martínez-López; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Miguel A. Vadillo; David Luque
articles_hidden.abstract: Although habits play a key role across psychological science, current laboratory methods may limit our understanding of these behaviors. The dual‑system framework defines habits as context-triggered, outcome‑insensitive responses that emerge gradually with repeated instrumental training. Many human experimental paradigms have been developed to test this characterization of habits. However, most of them fail to provide clear evidence of habit formation, suggesting a gap between habit theory and existing methodologies. We systematically review evidence on the construct validity of fourteen paradigms in which training amount was manipulated. We also reanalyze publicly available datasets from studies using these paradigms to assess the psychometric reliability of their measures. Paradigms that mirror classical approaches derived from habit theory have consistently failed to induce habits, whereas recent approaches have revealed training effects. However, these novel paradigms often rely on broader operationalizations that substantially diverge from traditional definitions. Among the paradigms reviewed, the forced‑response task stands out as capable of inducing habitual behavior while providing a narrowly operationalized measure with reliability estimates ranging from .74 to .83. Finally, we argue that strengthening the credibility of the field will require greater attention to the psychometric properties of habit measures, including precise operationalization, reliability, and systematic validity testing.

articles_hidden.title: How Long Do Refutational Text Effects Last? Evidence From a Six-Month Follow-Up Study of Misconceptions in Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Varea; Silvia Guerrero; Paula Barrios; Ileana Enesco
articles_hidden.abstract: This work analyzes the effectiveness of refutational texts in correcting misconceptions in psychology and the stability of that change. To this end, it focuses on two variables: the level of engagement with the texts and the specific nature of different myths. The prevalence of misconceptions in the fields of developmental psychology and educational psychology was assessed, and the three most widespread misconceptions, related to adolescence, educational videos, and learning styles, were identified. Using a pre-test/post-test design with a six-month follow-up and an equivalent control group, the study compared reading refutational texts (R) with reading plus producing a summary (RS). A total of 328 psychology students participated and the rejection of the three misconceptions was assessed one week after the intervention and six months later. At Post-test I both intervention groups showed significantly higher probabilities of rejecting all three misconceptions than the control group, with stronger immediate effects observed in the RS condition. At Post-test II, six months later, these effects were attenuated, although rejection remained above baseline levels. The learning styles misconception, which was considered to involve a deeper conceptual framework, showed the greatest resistance to long-term change. Overall, refutational texts promoted conceptual change, but their effects were not fully stable over time and differ between misconceptions, highlighting the need for interventions to be repeated and tailored to each type of myth.

articles_hidden.title: Altered Self-Other Distinction in Motor and Cognitive Domains in Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder: Evidence from a Multi-Site Behavioral Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ekaterina Pronizius; Celine De Meulemeester; Nita Bislimi; Sarah Kathryn Fineberg; Ingmar Heinig; Martin Horký; Inga Niedtfeld; Magdalena Helísková; Pavla Horká Linhartová; Thea M McAfee
articles_hidden.abstract: Self–other distinction (SOD), defined as the ability to separate self- from other-related mental representations, has been proposed as a core mechanism in borderline personality disorder (BPD), yet experimental evidence remains limited. In this preregistered, multicenter study (Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Germany, USA), we assessed motor SOD (Automatic Imitation Inhibition Task, AIT) and cognitive SOD (Visual Perspective-Taking, VPT) in 290 adults (131 BPD, 159 healthy controls), alongside a Stroop-based inhibitory control task. Overall, individuals with BPD showed slower and less accurate performance across tasks. In the AIT, BPD exhibited reduced motor SOD relative to healthy controls, reflected in increased imitative interference. These effects were robust to covariate adjustment and not explained by demographic or clinical factors. In the BPD sample, symptom severity was neither associated with motor SOD performance nor interindividual differences in self-reported childhood maltreatment. In the VPT task, the BPD group showed greater egocentric bias than controls, with effects varying depending on covariate inclusion (e.g., ADHD symptoms, age, cognitive control). Within the BPD group, childhood maltreatment moderated the association between symptom severity and VPT egocentric bias, such that greater childhood maltreatment and greater symptom severity were associated with increased bias. Overall, findings indicate selective, context-dependent alterations of SOD in BPD, characterized by heightened imitative interference and increased egocentric bias rather than a global deficit. Early adversity appears to shape variability in cognitive SOD in BPD.

articles_hidden.title: Safety, Compatibility and Reconnection: Understanding Restorative Nature Through the Lens of Chronic Low Back Pain
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Smith; Kayleigh Wyles; Patricia Schofield; Sam William Hughes
articles_hidden.abstract: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is a pervasive and debilitating condition that is often resistant to conventional pain management strategies. This has driven a growing interest in novel psychosocial approaches, such as the use of restorative nature-based environments as part of pain self-management strategies. However, many assumptions regarding restorative nature spaces are based on the perspective of healthy individuals. A population living with cLBP may conceptualise or identify restorative nature spaces differently, given such factors as risk of reinjury or physical limitations. Two focus groups were conducted with a cLBP group (n = 7, Mage = 55.57, 6 females) to explore what a restorative outdoor nature space means through the lens of chronic low back pain. Thematic Analysis generated four Themes (Safety, Confidence, and Control; Embodied Capability; Reclaiming Self Beyond Pain; and Engagement with Living Nature). The present study highlights the necessity of inclusion of lived experience and perspective when discussing how best to incorporate restorative nature spaces into pain self-management or green social prescribing frameworks for the chronic pain community. Future research can build upon the present research to codesign tailored nature-based interventions for people with a lived experience of chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Intrinsic connectivity signatures of anxiety sensitivity from connectome based predictive modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Dahyun Won; Hakin Kim; Justin Minue Kim; Juyoen Hur
articles_hidden.abstract:
Anxiety sensitivity (AS) is a dispositional trait characterized by the fear of anxiety-related 
sensations based on beliefs that they may have harmful physical, cognitive, or social 
consequences. Despite its clinical significance as a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor, the 
intrinsic neural architecture underlying individual differences in AS remains poorly understood. 
We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) to resting-state fMRI data from a 
non-clinical sample (N = 86) to identify whole-brain intrinsic connectivity patterns predictive 
of individual differences in AS. In an exploratory follow-up analysis, we applied the trained 
model to an independent dataset to examine whether its predictive utility extended to panic 
symptom severity, a clinically related but distinct construct. The CPM model significantly 
predicted individual differences in AS (prediction 𝑅2  = .07, 𝑝𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑚  < .005) and was 
characterized primarily by reduced insula-temporal, insula-frontal, and temporo-parietal 
connectivity. However, the model did not significantly predict panic symptom severity in the 
independent sample. These findings suggest that individual differences in AS are reflected in 
distributed patterns of intrinsic functional connectivity involving the insula and broader 
cortical systems, providing a network-level characterization of the intrinsic neural architecture 
associated with AS.

articles_hidden.title: From Digital Workbooks to Digital Schoolbooks: Pre-Practice Instructional Support in Authentic Digital Mathematics Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Eileen Richter; Lukas Wesenberg; Felix Krieglstein; Nicklas Jakob Elia Vaupel; Peat Schmolke; Korbinian Moeller; Markus Spitzer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Digital learning platforms provide extensive support for learning mathematics but this support
typically happens during practice. However, less is known about whether instructional support
provided before practice by digital learning platforms is associated with better subsequent
performance in authentic large-scale digital learning settings. Here, we examined different
forms of instructional support embedded in a digital mathematics learning platform used in
schools across Germany. Initially designed primarily as a digital workbook for practicing
mathematical problems, the platform was recently extended toward a digital schoolbook by
adding blackboards that learners can access before practice to obtain additional instructional
support. In particular, Explore blackboards provide opportunities to inspect and connect
mathematical relationships, whereas Secure blackboards organize relevant definitions, rules,
examples, and relationships before practice. Using large-scale log data from 9,293 learners
across 74,801 problems and a within-subject design, we compared learners’ performance on
mathematical problems in a baseline condition (Exercise Only), in which they received no
additional instructional support, with their performance in three other conditions in which they
received instructional support before practice (i.e., Explore, Secure, and Explore & Secure).
We observed significantly lower error rates following all three forms of instructional support
relative to the Exercise Only condition. These findings extend previous work by showing that
instructional support provided by a digital learning platform before practice is associated with
better subsequent performance in an authentic, large-scale learning setting. More broadly, they
highlight the potential value of providing instructional support before practice on digital
mathematics learning platforms.

articles_hidden.title: Lived Experiences of Adulthood with Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder: A Qualitative  Analysis of Diagnosis, Support, Employment, and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Quinn; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) encompasses lifelong neurodevelopmental difficulties that can affect cognitive, behavioural, and everyday functioning. Research and support have frequently focused on childhood and developmental outcomes, while comparatively less attention has been given to experiences of FASD during adulthood. Understanding the challenges and support needs of adults with FASD is therefore important for recognising the lifelong implications of the condition and informing appropriate support.
Methods: This qualitative study explored experiences of living with FASD during adulthood, with particular attention to diagnosis, support, employment, and mental health. Secondary qualitative data were collected from publicly available online sources, including social media posts and material published by FASD support organisations. Written and transcribed material relating to personal experiences of FASD was analysed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns and themes within participants' accounts.
Results: The analysis identified themes relating to FASD diagnosis that were consistent with issues reported in previous research. The findings also highlighted the perceived importance of appropriate and ongoing support in adulthood. Participants' accounts indicated that support could have implications across multiple areas of life, including employment and mental health. The findings further highlighted the value of incorporating the perspectives and experiences of people living with FASD when considering education, support, and approaches to FASD prevention.
Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of recognising FASD as a lifelong condition and extending attention beyond childhood development to the experiences and support needs of adults. Greater consideration of the lived experiences of people with FASD may help inform approaches to adult support, education, and prevention. Further research involving adults with FASD is warranted to better understand their long-term experiences and identify effective forms of support across different areas of adult life.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The Weight of Early Stress and Trauma: An Analysis of How Adverse Childhood Experiences, PTSD, and CPTSD Influence Adult Obesity Rates’
articles_hidden.authors: Lynn Holleran; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have been associated with adverse health outcomes in adulthood, including obesity. Psychological responses to childhood adversity, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD), may also be relevant to this relationship. However, the associations between childhood adversity, PTSD/CPTSD, and adult obesity remain incompletely understood. This study examined the relationships between ACEs, PTSD, CPTSD, and body mass index (BMI) in adults.
Methods: A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted using an anonymous online survey. Participants were recruited through social media and referrals. Ninety-five adults aged 18–73 years (M = 39.98, SD = 14.43; 69% female) completed measures of ACEs using the Adverse Childhood Experiences Questionnaire (ACEQ), PTSD and CPTSD using the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ), and demographic and self-reported height and weight measures from which BMI was derived. Correlational, regression, and between-group analyses were conducted to examine associations between ACE scores, PTSD/CPTSD severity, and BMI.
Results: ACE scores significantly predicted BMI (β = .69, p = .03), accounting for 4.9% of the variance. Participants with obesity reported significantly higher ACE scores than participants classified as healthy weight (p = .037). Positive but non-significant associations were observed between BMI and PTSD severity (r = .14) and CPTSD severity (r = .18). Participants meeting criteria for CPTSD reported significantly higher ACE scores than those who did not meet CPTSD criteria (p = .008). Female participants also reported significantly higher ACE scores than male participants (p = .027).

Conclusions: The findings provide evidence of an association between greater exposure to childhood adversity and adult BMI, consistent with previous research linking ACEs with obesity. Higher ACE exposure was also associated with meeting criteria for CPTSD, while associations between PTSD/CPTSD severity and BMI were comparatively weak and did not reach statistical significance. Given the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and relatively small sample, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the mechanisms linking childhood adversity, trauma-related psychopathology, and obesity and to investigate implications for integrated approaches to trauma and obesity prevention and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Over-the-Counter Painkiller Use in the United Kingdom and Taiwan, A Cross-Cultural Analysis of Self-Medication, Pain Perceptions, and Dependency Considerations
articles_hidden.authors: Liwei Kuo; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Pain is a complex biopsychosocial phenomenon that can substantially affect quality of life. The use of over-the-counter (OTC) painkillers is an important aspect of pain management, particularly where medications are readily accessible without a prescription. Understanding patterns of OTC painkiller use, and the factors associated with self-medication may help inform approaches to responsible pain management across different cultural contexts.
Methods: This cross-cultural study investigated OTC painkiller use among members of the public in the United Kingdom and Taiwan. An online questionnaire examined participants' pain perceptions, self-medication practices, painkiller use, demographic characteristics, and considerations relating to dependency. Patterns of OTC painkiller use, and self-medication preferences were compared between the two populations.
Results: Despite differences in the accessibility of OTC painkillers between the United Kingdom and Taiwan, the reported rates of painkiller use were similar between the two populations. No significant differences were identified in preferences for self-medication. Although reported levels of dependency were low, concerns relating to dependency were identified as an important consideration in participants' use of painkillers in both regions.
Conclusions: The findings indicate that accessibility alone may not explain differences in OTC painkiller use across cultural contexts. Pain perceptions, self-medication practices, and considerations relating to dependency may contribute to how individuals approach OTC pain management. Further research is warranted to examine the cultural and psychological factors underlying OTC painkiller use and to inform culturally sensitive approaches that support the responsible use of non-prescription pain medications.

articles_hidden.title: Local average treatment effects on latent outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Sanford R Student; Joshua B Gilbert; William Young
articles_hidden.abstract: Instrumental variables (IV) regression models for causal inference have received increased attention in psychology with continuous, observed variables. Yet, latent outcomes are ubiquitous in psychology and research designs involving non-binding treatments and encouragement/manipulation designs are widespread. We consider IV with a binary instrument and treatment to estimate the \textit{local average treatment effect} on a latent variable, or the latent local average treatment effect (LLATE). The LLATE is the average of heterogeneous latent treatment effects for the population of individuals who comply with treatment assignment. Heterogeneous treatment effects imply that a single-group SEM with residual normality of the outcome is misspecified. We propose a multiple-group estimator that allows for this heteroskedasticity, enables tests for heterogeneous treatment effects, and characterizes compliers. The multiple-group estimator recovers the LLATE with trivial bias, while two single-group estimators and a two-step procedure using factor score estimates as observed outcomes all yield small but persistent bias. Testing for heterogeneous treatment effects is possible but limited to larger samples. We conclude that IV with a latent outcome is a viable means of estimating causal effects on latent outcomes, and that the multiple-group approach is usually the safest way to do so.

articles_hidden.title: Trust in AI Versus Human Clinicians: A Study of Diagnostic Judgements and Transparency
articles_hidden.authors: Ye Yang; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for use in healthcare, including clinical diagnosis, with potential to support clinicians and address pressures on healthcare systems. However, public trust remains an important consideration in the adoption of AI-based clinical decision-making. This study investigated perceptions of and trust in AI and human clinicians, particularly when their diagnostic judgements were either consistent or conflicting. The study also explored whether concerns regarding transparency and liability influenced preferences for medical AI.

Methods: An experimental vignette and questionnaire-based study was conducted to examine participants' responses to diagnostic judgements made by AI and human clinicians. Vignettes presented scenarios in which AI and human clinicians provided either the same or conflicting diagnostic judgements. Participants' levels of trust and preferences regarding medical AI were assessed, alongside their concerns about transparency and liability.

Results: Participants demonstrated greater trust in human clinicians than in AI clinicians. However, agreement between AI and human clinicians' diagnostic judgements was associated with increased trust in the resulting diagnosis. Participants who expressed greater concern about transparency reported lower levels of trust in medical AI. The findings therefore indicate that perceptions of AI-based diagnosis may be influenced not only by whether the diagnosis is consistent with that of a human clinician, but also by concerns surrounding transparency and accountability.

Conclusions: Trust in AI-based clinical diagnosis appears to remain lower than trust in human clinicians, although agreement between human and AI diagnostic judgements may increase confidence in AI-supported decisions. Concerns regarding transparency may represent an important barrier to trust and acceptance. Developing transparent standards and clearly communicating how AI-based clinical decisions are generated and governed may therefore be important considerations in the adoption of medical AI.

articles_hidden.title: Pain Management Across Cultures: A Qualitative Study of Chinese and British Perspectives
articles_hidden.authors: Xiang Li; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Pain is a prevalent health concern, but perceptions of pain and approaches to its management may be shaped by cultural and sociocultural factors. This study explored differences in attitudes towards pain and pain management between Chinese and British participants and examined factors that may influence these perceptions.
Methods: A qualitative study was conducted with 14 participants, comprising eight Chinese and six British participants. Participants completed a questionnaire concerning pain-related health perceptions and subsequently participated in semi-structured online interviews exploring their attitudes towards pain and the factors influencing their views. Interviews were conducted with participants' consent, recorded and transcribed, and analysed using thematic analysis. Ethical approval was provided by the University of Glasgow Ethics Committee.
Results: No clear difference in pain-related knowledge was identified between Chinese and British participants. However, cultural and sociocultural factors appeared to influence attitudes towards pain management. Traditional cultural beliefs were associated with greater resistance to the use of analgesic medication among Chinese participants. Differences were also observed in preferred approaches to pain relief, with Chinese participants more frequently referring to physiotherapy or naturopathy, while British participants more commonly favoured pharmacological approaches. Women generally described more positive approaches to pain management than men. Family, tradition, interpersonal relationships and healthcare infrastructure were identified as important influences on pain-related perceptions and management strategies.
Conclusions: The findings suggest that pain-related perceptions and management preferences are influenced by a combination of cultural and wider sociocultural factors. Understanding these influences may help inform culturally responsive approaches to pain management. Given the small sample and qualitative design, the findings provide an exploratory account rather than evidence of population-level differences between Chinese and British populations.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive constraints govern collective outcomes in strategic network formation
articles_hidden.authors: Hicham DAHMOU; Frédéric Moisan; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles_hidden.abstract: Social networks are built through local decisions, yet the value of a connection depends on paths that individuals cannot fully observe. How such bounded information shapes collective outcomes remains unclear. Here we develop a computational model in which agents revise costly links using a limited view of the network, optimism about connections beyond that view, and stochastic choice. Starting from the inefficient empty-network equilibrium, the model reaches near-efficient structures when decision noise is low and optimism lies in an intermediate range: agents must value unseen opportunities enough to initiate connectivity, but not so strongly that continued linking displaces the removal of redundant ties. This favorable regime narrows as groups grow, although broader visibility partly restores it and agent heterogeneity preserves its qualitative form. Earlier action or link receipt is associated with eventual hub status, while stable differences in agent-level decision parameters are associated with persistent payoff ranks across repeated networks. Introducing one agent that builds and then sheds links without considering payoffs reduces total payoff on average in small groups but increases it in larger groups, where sustained building can benefit others at the builder's expense. These results identify a scale-dependent balance between exploration, local visibility and payoff-guided link removal through which bounded individual decisions can generate high total payoff and structural inequality.

articles_hidden.title: An Experience Sampling-Integrated Digital Navigator Model for Personalised Mental Health Care
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Montauti; Samuel Badu; Dan W Joyce; Xiaoxiao Hou; Abigail Jones; Oladayo Bifarin
articles_hidden.abstract:
The digital navigator role emerged to support the integration of digital health tools into clinical care. These roles typically involve onboarding patients, supporting digital literacy, facilitating data collection, and providing technical troubleshooting. However, the integration of digital health data into routine clinical practice, and its uptake by clinicians, has remained inconsistent.
In this perspective paper, we propose an adaptation of the existing digital navigator model in which the role extends beyond patient onboarding, data collection, and technical support. Instead, we conceptualise this role as an extension of mental health nursing practice, where digital health platforms serve as tools to enhance data collection, interpretation, and clinical decision-making. We argue that the established competencies of mental health nurses, including assessment, formulation, and personalised care planning, position them uniquely to translate granular digital health data into meaningful insights that can be effectively integrated into routine clinical care.

articles_hidden.title: The Behavioral Cost of Memory-Driven Attentional Capture: Eye-Movement Evidence for Post-Capture Attentional Dwell
articles_hidden.authors: Keyang Liu; Chen Wang; Qiang Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: During visual search, task-irrelevant distractors matching current visual working memory representations can capture attention, but less is known about how their influence continues after capture. Using a memory–search dual-task paradigm with eye tracking, we distinguished initial oculomotor selection from processing after distractor fixation and examined their associations with working memory capacity (WMC). Memory-matching distractors produced longer overall search RTs and were more likely than neutral distractors to receive the first fixation. When the critical distractor was not fixated, memory matching produced no reliable additional search-time cost. When it was fixated, however, memory matching prolonged conditional dwell time. WMC showed no clear association with the memory-matching effect on first fixation, whereas higher WMC was associated with less additional post-capture dwell. These findings indicate that the influence of memory matching can persist after attentional selection. The behavioral cost of memory-driven distraction may therefore reflect not only whether a distractor is selected, but also how processing unfolds after selection, with WMC-related differences more clearly expressed in post-capture processing than in initial oculomotor selection.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptibility of Error Outcomes Shapes the Direction of Post-Error Adjustment: Evidence From 6.7 Million Moves in Online Chess
articles_hidden.authors: Yunjeong Jeong; Younggyu Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether post-error slowing requires noticing the error is unresolved, because in laboratory tasks errors and the noticing of them covary. Chess separates them: engine evaluation identifies errors that leave no trace on the board, whereas material loss is visible. Analysing 1.06 million event observations from 222,099 games played by 2,014 players, we found that the sign of the adjustment reversed with the visibility of the outcome. Blunders that left material intact were followed by slower moves (+0.154 within-person SD), whereas the two conditions in which material disappeared were followed by faster ones (-0.493, -0.631). The conditions differed by 0.65 SD in all five rating tiers, and neither error magnitude nor the change in legal move count accounted for this. Reliability approached .70 for material loss but was near zero for blunders. Post-error adjustment followed two patterns, divided by whether the outcome was visible.

articles_hidden.title: Genetic Evidence Linking Prefrontal Surface Area to ADHD, Major Depression, and Smoking Initiation
articles_hidden.authors: rui wang; Yifan Du; Yunkai Yang
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and smoking behaviour exhibit substantial comorbidity and evidence of sequential occurrence. However, the shared upstream neurodevelopmental structural basis underlying this psychiatric–addiction cascade remains poorly understood.
Methods: This study applied a high-dimensional imaging-genetics framework. First, an exploratory Mendelian randomization (MR) screening was conducted across 3,935 UK Biobank imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) to prioritize candidate brain structural targets. Subsequently, univariable MR, multivariable MR (MVMR), and serial mediation analyses were used to characterize the potential temporal and causal cascade, with MRlap applied to account for potential sample overlap and weak instrument bias. Finally, Bayesian colocalization with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and functional network annotation were integrated to explore potential molecular mechanisms.
Results: High-dimensional screening prioritized left rostral middle frontal gyrus (rMFG) surface area as a core upstream structural phenotype. Genetically predicted larger left rMFG surface area showed consistent directional evidence of association with lower risks of ADHD, MDD, and smoking initiation. MVMR analyses showed that the conditional direct association between left rMFG surface area and smoking initiation was substantially attenuated and was no longer statistically detectable after adjustment for psychopathological liability, although limited conditional instrument strength warranted cautious interpretation. Exploratory MRlap-adjusted pathway analysis suggested a substantial relative contribution of the prespecified sequential pathway, with the product of path coefficients corresponding to an exploratory estimate of approximately 65.51% of the estimated total effect. Bayesian colocalization (PP.H4 = 0.911) and functional mapping further suggested BDNF-AS and neurodevelopment-related modules as potential molecular mechanisms.
Conclusions: Structural developmental vulnerability of the prefrontal cortex does not appear to relate to smoking initiation through an independent direct pathway. The association between genetically predicted left rMFG surface area and smoking initiation may be partly consistent with a pathway involving ADHD and MDD; however, this interpretation remains exploratory because of limited conditional instrument strength and the pairwise nature of the pathway analysis. These findings provide a neuroimaging-genetics perspective on cross-diagnostic comorbidity and suggest a potential role for shared neurotrophic regulatory mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Embedding qualitative data in LLM semantic space: A tutorial on conceptualization, measurement, and validation
articles_hidden.authors: Toshizumi Muta
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language model embeddings give any text coordinates in a semantic space, where the cosine between two coordinates indexes their similarity. Standard qualitative practice cannot quantify such closeness: open-ended answers become nominal variables, which represent only difference under dummy codes. Psychometrics obtains such closeness from responses, as the correlations among a scale's items. Whether the cosine can substitute for the correlation is therefore open. We tested it against established findings in open data, each with an agreed structure: the Big Five, PANAS in two languages, Schwartz's values, Pineo-Porter occupational prestige, and the ISEAR and Kjell narratives. Linguistic structure alone did not reproduce the psychometric structure. The item texts recovered part of it, and none of it where a relation carries a sign. They fall far short of a random split-sample ceiling. Read from the other side, that is a finding about questionnaires: a scale's wording does not carry what its respondents give it. Embeddings supply a semantic layer between raw language and conventional coding, where the material that neither psychometrics nor hand coding reaches belongs. A category label—an occupation, a diagnosis, a brand—becomes coordinates rather than a dummy variable. An open-ended answer becomes coordinates without a coder. Cut into segments, a long answer becomes a path, along which departures, returns, and drifts can be drawn and tested. What any of it means, however, stays with the analyst. We supply the conceptual background, an R package, and a tutorial: no training, no Python.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Attentional Spreading within Form-Based Perceptual Groups: An ERP Study
articles_hidden.authors: Tetsuko Kasai; Kei Kobayashi
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research has shown that spatial attention can spread to to-be-ignored objects that share similar shapes with objects at attended locations during relatively late stages of visual processing (Kasai et al., 2011). Such attentional spreading may be associated with perceptual grouping by shape similarity. However, this possibility remains unclear, partly because other grouping factors may have been confounded in the previous study. The present study aimed to examine the time course of attentional spreading associated with shape similarity, while distinguishing shape similarity from collinearity. Participants were required to sustain their attention to one visual field and respond to infrequent target shapes (circles or squares) presented at the attended location. The stimuli consisted of rapidly presented pairs of ovals or rectangles arranged bilaterally, with the two objects differing in luminance contrast and width. Behavioral performance was impaired for rectangle pairs compared with both oval pairs and dissimilar pairs, suggesting that attentional allocation to the attended location was affected by geometric relations between objects. Time-resolved electrophysiological measures further showed that similar-shape pairs (ovals or rectangles) reduced the lateralized attention effect around 260 ms after stimulus onset, suggesting attentional spreading based on shape similarity. This effect was also evident around 300 ms for rectangle pairs, which additionally involved collinearity. These findings suggest that geometric relations among spatially separated objects shape how attention is guided across space and time.

articles_hidden.title: The Environmental Includes the Social: On the Psychological Structure of Altruistic and Biospheric Values
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Eric Neef; Quinn J Hundgen; Siegmar Otto; P. Wesley Schultz
articles_hidden.abstract: A substantial body of research has discussed the close relationship between altruistic (i.e., human-oriented) and biospheric (i.e., nature-oriented) motivations. Some researchers posit that they reflect a single, other-oriented construct, while others have shown discriminant validity between the two. Using values as representations of motivation, we reconcile these conflicting positions. Building on and extending the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, we propose that biospheric values inherently encompass altruistic values. We provide support for the proposed extended Inclusion Model across a series of studies: an exploratory analysis (Study 1: N = 222, U.S. sample), a pre-registered study (Study 2: N = 791, U.S. sample), and a large-scale secondary data analysis (Study 3: N = 85,796; 52 countries). We find that, across much of the world, individuals who hold strong biospheric values also tend to hold strong altruistic values. However, holding strong altruistic values does not likewise imply holding strong biospheric ones. Biospheric and altruistic values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly, whereas biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values did. Using bifactor modeling in line with the Inclusion Model resolves interpretational challenges arising when treating both values as unidimensional (i.e., lack of discrimination) or correlated (i.e., suppression). Bifactor results suggest that effects previously attributed to biospheric values may partly reflect their altruistic core. Interventions can reach broader audiences by appealing to altruistic motivation, and interventions targeting environmental motivation may also tap into altruistic motivation. Future work should determine the boundaries of this model, further explore global heterogeneity, and test its practical implications.

articles_hidden.title: Public attention to artificial intelligence predicts helping between humans across 86 countries
articles_hidden.authors: Chenxi Li; Xiaoxue Hu; Xue Wang; Mengchen Dong
articles_hidden.abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has provoked debate about its consequences for human social life. Yet, whether and how public attention to AI shapes human relationships globally are largely unknown. In a global online game, we linked daily country-level AI attention from Google Trends to more than 1.5 million player-day records of voluntary helping among 9,167 players across 86 countries. Higher national attention to AI predicted increased helping behavior between players, an association robust across samples, measures, and specifications. This link was corroborated by quasi-experimental analyses around OpenAI DevDay, a major AI event, showing that helping rose in proportion to countries’ attention responses and shifted upward at the event date. The response was stronger where a shared human identity was likely salient and AI-related change likely felt pressing. Amid narratives casting AI as a threat to humanity, strengthened interpersonal bonds may mark a collective human adaptation to its rise.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptibility of Error Outcomes Shapes the Direction of Post-Error Adjustment: Evidence From 6.7 Million Moves in Online Chess
articles_hidden.authors: Yunjeong Jeong; Younggyu Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether post-error slowing requires noticing the error is unresolved, because in laboratory tasks errors and the noticing of them covary. Chess separates them: engine evaluation identifies errors that leave no trace on the board, whereas material loss is visible. Analysing 1.06 million event observations from 222,099 games played by 2,014 players, we found that the sign of the adjustment reversed with the visibility of the outcome. Blunders that left material intact were followed by slower moves (+0.154 within-person SD), whereas the two conditions in which material disappeared were followed by faster ones (-0.493, -0.631). The conditions differed by 0.65 SD in all five rating tiers, and neither error magnitude nor the change in legal move count accounted for this. Reliability approached .70 for material loss but was near zero for blunders. Post-error adjustment followed two patterns, divided by whether the outcome was visible.

articles_hidden.title: Altered Self-Other Distinction in Motor and Cognitive Domains in Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder: Evidence from a Multi-Site Behavioral Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ekaterina Pronizius; Celine De Meulemeester; Nita Bislimi; Sarah Kathryn Fineberg; Ingmar Heinig; Martin Horký; Inga Niedtfeld; Magdalena Helísková; Pavla Horká Linhartová; Thea M McAfee
articles_hidden.abstract: Self–other distinction (SOD), defined as the ability to separate self- from other-related mental representations, has been proposed as a core mechanism in borderline personality disorder (BPD), yet experimental evidence remains limited. In this preregistered, multicenter study (Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Germany, USA), we assessed motor SOD (Automatic Imitation Inhibition Task, AIT) and cognitive SOD (Visual Perspective-Taking, VPT) in 290 adults (131 BPD, 159 healthy controls), alongside a Stroop-based inhibitory control task. Overall, individuals with BPD showed slower and less accurate performance across tasks. In the AIT, BPD exhibited reduced motor SOD relative to healthy controls, reflected in increased imitative interference. These effects were robust to covariate adjustment and not explained by demographic or clinical factors. In the BPD sample, symptom severity was neither associated with motor SOD performance nor interindividual differences in self-reported childhood maltreatment. In the VPT task, the BPD group showed greater egocentric bias than controls, with effects varying depending on covariate inclusion (e.g., ADHD symptoms, age, cognitive control). Within the BPD group, childhood maltreatment moderated the association between symptom severity and VPT egocentric bias, such that greater childhood maltreatment and greater symptom severity were associated with increased bias. Overall, findings indicate selective, context-dependent alterations of SOD in BPD, characterized by heightened imitative interference and increased egocentric bias rather than a global deficit. Early adversity appears to shape variability in cognitive SOD in BPD.

articles_hidden.title: Intergenerational differences and inheritance of marriage between born “around 1975” and “after-1995” groups based on China
articles_hidden.authors: Jingxi Zheng; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract: Marriage is a union under socialised norms, the typical model being monogamy. It provides for the smooth development of society and a perennially active economic market. The globalised rise in late marriage and divorce rates is to some extent a reflection of life choices and attitudes towards marriage. China is a densely populated country, and after the one-child policy, most families has a pyramidal structure; in 2021, the Chinese government officially enacted the three-child policy, with the aim of stimulating and encouraging people to have more children. However, with the rapid development of the economy, modernisation and industrialisation, there are dynamic changes of individuals’ consideration. The target group for this study is parents who have experienced a change in fertility policy who born around 1975, and their children, the millennials born after 1995. Seven pairs of families were recruited to join the study through snowball sampling. The study used a qualitative approach, with volunteers first completing a demographic questionnaire; semi-structured interviews allowed participants to explore and consider in depth, and asynchronous interviews compensated for the fact that some participants were unable to have simultaneous one-to-one communication online. The researcher forms four themes: the importance of marriage, love and cruelty in marriage, opposite sex kinship and mate choice, and women in marriage. The analysis concluded that there are indeed similarities and contradictions in intergenerational perceptions of marriage, as well as differences between individuals and family units. Inheritance is mainly in the identification of marital behaviour and marital and family pressures, and differences revolve around the two generations' starting points for marriage and attitudes to non-mainstream marriage trends. However, parental influence on children is also externalised into acting styles such as reinforcement, correction, and avoidance to spousal choices due to the unique patterns of the individual internalised system.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Puppetry on Pro-Social and Anti-Social Behaviours: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kenneth Gear; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the potential benefits and barriers to the utilization of puppets within behaviour intervention of children during their pre-operational stage of development. It presents a  systematic qualitative review of studies that either aim to reduce antisocial behaviour or develop pro social behaviour. Works included educational and clinical settings and development of pro social behaviours such as inclusion and sharing, and reduction of anti-social behaviour such as refusal to comply and aggressive behaviours. The literature was searched using scholarly databases, with additional articles sourced from snowball method of similar reviews. Papers were included based on specific selection criteria and multiple validity and reliability measures. The wider field of research regarding puppetry within behaviour highlighted the overlap of socio-cognitive factors with the psychological principles and concepts of modeling, shared cognition, mediation and social influence being present among studies. From the review, utilizations of puppetry differed and overlapped among studies with modeling, mediation, performance and pedagogy all being utilized to develop and/or reduce behaviours. With majority of studies predominantly exploring the development of pro social behaviour, no significant differences between processes in reduction or development of behaviour were determined. Key themes among all studies were (1) internalization and interaction, (2) direct communication, (3) indirect communication, (4) play and indirect therapy, and (5) rehearsal and imitation. Benefits highlighted were the strengthened communication and dual development of three-party relationships in the sense that facilitators and researchers gained greater insight of participants’ perspective via indirect and direct communication, and vice versa. Though all studies reported positive behavioural change, there are barriers regarding the assessment of behavioural change and determination of purpose and intent.

articles_hidden.title: Epigenetic mechanisms of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review of Human and Preclinical Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: June Kang; JeYoung Jung
articles_hidden.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) produces clinical and behavioural effects persisting weeks to months beyond stimulation. This persistence is typically attributed to LTP- and LTD-like synaptic plasticity, yet short-lived synaptic events alone cannot explain it; epigenetic mechanisms, the leading candidate substrate, have never been systematically evaluated. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC to June 2026 (2,089 records; 1,941 de-duplicated). Twenty-two studies were eligible: ten human, ten preclinical, and two invasive cervical-VNS studies retained for sensitivity analysis. Among 18 interventional studies, 17 reported significant epigenetic change (94%; p = 1.45×10⁻⁴), driven by the controlled animal tier (10/10; p = 0.002); the human stream alone (5/6) was non-significant (p = 0.22). Adjusting for publication bias, the pooled signal held under a moderately conservative null (p₀ = 0.7, p = 0.020) but not a strongly conservative one (p₀ = 0.8, p = 0.15). Effects spanned histone modifications, DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and epigenetic enzymes. Histone acetylation was the most compelling pathway, supported by causal pharmacological rescue in rodent rTMS and tDCS models. DNA methylation showed an "epigenetic homeostat" pattern, normalising stress-induced aberrations at promoters including BDNF and COMT. Non-coding RNAs formed the largest stream, with circulating miR-146a-5p recurring across rTMS trials. BDNF emerged as a convergent node, also predicting rTMS response via baseline methylation and circulating microRNAs. Coverage is skewed: rTMS and tDCS dominate, tVNS is sparse, tACS/tRNS uninvestigated. NIBS is consistently associated with epigenetic remodelling across mechanisms and species, positioning chromatin regulation as a primary substrate for durable neuromodulatory after-effects.

articles_hidden.title: Bringing our tribes together:  The promise and peril of interdisciplinary research on epistemically suspect beliefs
articles_hidden.authors: Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Raunak M Pillai; Steve Rathje
articles_hidden.abstract: Epistemically suspect beliefs are studied across multiple disciplines, yet these literatures have developed largely in parallel. We argue that integrating research from clinical, social, cognitive, and political psychology offers an important opportunity to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the origins and consequences of these beliefs. In particular, research on social identity can help explain how people select information and social environments, evaluate evidence, and process information in ways that affirm their identities. Extending these insights to clinical contexts raises new questions about how social and personal identities shape susceptibility to certain beliefs, including in emerging information environments shaped by artificial intelligence. However, interdisciplinary research faces substantial institutional and psychological barriers. Academic incentives often reward disciplinary competition, simple theories, and surprising findings over integration, encouraging researchers to defend disciplinary identities and caricature competing perspectives. Building a robust science of beliefs therefore requires a culture of cooperation that prioritizes explanatory utility and theoretical synthesis over disciplinary dominance, and needs to be supported by interdisciplinary funding, hiring, training, conferences, and journals.

articles_hidden.title: Antecedents of ecospirituality across cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Ira Billet; Adam Baimel
articles_hidden.abstract: The idea that humanity and nature are spiritually connected—ecospirituality—is a core aspect of cultural and religious worldviews around the world. Sociocultural factors, like religion, urbanization, and socioeconomic status, are hypothesized to shape people’s spiritual connections with nature, yet there are no systematic cross-cultural surveys of ecospirituality that can speak to these hypotheses. We present the results of a study assessing the associations between ecospirituality and these three sociocultural factors using a cross-cultural sample of religious individuals from 15 countries spanning the 5 major world religions (N = 11,186) and a sample of religious and non-religious individuals from the United States (N = 3,329). The overall pattern of results suggested that greater religiosity, urbanization, and socioeconomic status contribute to greater ecospirituality across cultural and religious contexts. Results in the sample of individuals in the United States largely departed from the results found across other countries in the cross-cultural sample, even other Western majority-Christian societies. This research contributes to our understanding of how sociocultural factors that are rapidly changing in many parts of the world may shape people’s connections with the natural environment.

articles_hidden.title: Disentangling between- and within-person effects of HIV PrEP and treatment attitudes on condom use and bacterial STIs among sexual minority men
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Adam Hart; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Yangqing Deng; Syed Noor; David M. Moore; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Daniel Grace; Nathan Lachowsky; Joseph Cox; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling
articles_hidden.abstract: HIV treatment attitudes and HIV PrEP are associated with sexual behavior that elevates the risk for bacterial STIs (B-STIs) among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Using a longitudinal multi-site study (Engage Cohort Study, 2017-2024), we modelled direct and indirect within- and between-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on condomless anal sex (CAS) and incident B-STIs among 1863 HIV-negative GBM. We modelled up to four years of follow-up visits using multi-level mediation analysis, with CAS as a mediating variable between HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs. We found direct within-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs, such that participants were more likely to report incident B-STIs at time points if they reported using PrEP and being more optimistic about HIV treatments; there were no indirect within-person effects through CAS. In contrast, we found both direct and indirect between-person effects. Specifically, participants who reported more PrEP use or who were more optimistic about HIV treatments over the course of the study were more likely to report incident B-STIs. Further, these effects were partially mediated by CAS. Given that we found within-person PrEP use is associated with increased CAS and STIs, and the general increase in adoption of PrEP over time, there is a need to expand biomedical intervention programs for B-STIs prophylaxis by integrating them with social and informational interventions about B-STIs risks, especially for GBM who use HIV PrEP.

articles_hidden.title: Is there a “shape bias” for places?
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Kirsten Mark; Moira Rose Dillon
articles_hidden.abstract: Early emerging biases support our learning of new words, like a tendency to extend novel nouns referring to objects to other objects of the same shape. The present work tests the generalizability of this “shape bias” in another foundational domain of everyday life — the domain of places. Adults and 6-year-old children, but not 3-year-old children, extended novel nouns to places of the same shape over places composed of the same-colored walls, regardless of whether places were described by novel nouns in labeling phrases or in more place-relevant prepositional phrases. All age groups, by contrast, showed a shape bias for objects that matched many features of the place stimuli. This relatively delayed shape bias for places suggests that at least some word-learning biases may emerge separately for different domains.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamics of Perceived Rejection in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Haya Fatimah; Marina Bornovalova; Lijuan Wang; Fallon Rachael Goodman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal rejection is typically studied using trait questionnaires or in laboratory settings, while its temporal dynamics that may characterize important individual differences are often overlooked. This study examined perceived rejection in daily life as a dynamic process and its specificity from negative affect.

Method: 89 community adults, including 46 with DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), completed a 28-day EMA protocol with five prompts per day, yielding 9279 observations after data screening. Dynamic structural equation modeling was used to estimate equilibrium (typical level), inertia (persistence over time), innovation variance (magnitude of momentary perturbations), and stationary variance (overall within-person variability) for perceived rejection.

Results: Perceived rejection dynamics were associated with negative affect dynamics. After controlling for the corresponding negative affect components, SAD diagnosis and several interpersonal vulnerability measures (e.g., separation anxiety) remained associated with perceived rejection dynamics. When SAD diagnosis and interpersonal vulnerabilities were considered together, separation anxiety was uniquely associated with higher equilibrium, greater inertia, and greater stationary variance, whereas SAD was uniquely associated with greater log innovation variance; need to belong and rejection sensitivity were additionally associated with higher equilibrium.

Conclusions: Perceived rejection appears to reflect a distinct interpersonal dynamic process beyond negative affect. Within this process, a person’s typical level of perceived rejection, momentary perturbations, the persistence of deviations from the person’s typical level, and overall variability showed different patterns of association with SAD and interpersonal vulnerabilities, suggesting that these dynamic features capture different aspects of perceived rejection.

articles_hidden.title: Not all effort is equal: Invested and demanded effort in nicotine abstinence
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Wahlers; William Hart; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Katie Garrison; Seung-Lark Lim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Understanding the connection between perceived effort and nicotine abstinence requires recognizing not only how much effort people anticipate exerting, but why they anticipate exerting it. The Invested and Demanded Effort Model (IDEM) provides a framework for distinguishing between perceptions of effort associated with favorable and unfavorable psychological conditions for abstinence.

Method
E-cigarette users between the ages of 21 and 35 in the United States were recruited via Prolific (N = 253; Mage = 28.66, SDage = 4.22, 54.15% female, 45.85% male; 57.71% White, 20.16% Black, 9.09% Hispanic, 6.32% Mixed). We assessed anticipated invested and demanded effort toward nicotine abstinence (adapted Invested and Demanded Effort Scale [IDES]), states that make quitting feel difficult (e.g., e-cigarette dependence motivation, craving), goal-directed states that support quitting (e.g., cessation motivation), and abstinence-related traits (i.e., trait self-control, self-efficacy).

Results
Anticipated invested effort was associated with greater goal-directed states that support quitting including cessation motivation, cessation confidence, and willingness to bear the cost of abstinence whereas anticipated demanded effort was associated with greater states that make quitting feel difficult including e-cigarette dependence motivation, behavior, and craving and less willingness to bear the cost of abstinence. These findings were not attributable to confounding with trait self-control and self-efficacy.

Conclusions
Anticipated effort had no universal connection with abstinence-related states but depended on whether effortful control is attributed to one’s volition irrespective of self-control demands (invested effort) or the demands of abstinence (demanded effort). These findings bolster IDEM and extend its relevance to self-control contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Reducing Measurement Error in Forecaster Evaluation Using the Wisdom of Crowds
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Helmer; Nikolay Petrov; Sophie Ma Zhu; Ezra Karger; Edgar C. Merkle; Mark Himmelstein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Forecasting skill is often measured by the average error between forecasters’ predictions and the ground truth, but the inherent uncertainty in event outcomes adds an additional layer of measurement error onto skill estimation. Intersubjective measures offer an alternative approach to skill measurement: comparing forecasters’ predictions to those of their peers, typically to aggregated forecasts from groups of peers. A key advantage of this approach is that forecasts can be scored in real time, without having to wait for the ground truth outcome to be realized. However, it has another more subtle advantage as well: aggregate predictions can be less noisy than ground truth outcomes, leading to a potential reduction in this additional
measurement error. In a simulation study, we demonstrate conditions under which crowd aggregates provide a more reliable indicator of the optimal forecast for a given event than a single realized ground truth outcome, leading to skill measurement with reduced measurement error. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of intersubjective methods in a real-world forecasting study in which 894 participants made both forecasts and metapredictions, i.e., predictions of what others might forecast. As in our simulation, intersubjective measures capture forecasting ability more efficiently than do ground-truth scores, demonstrating their usefulness for identifying high-performing forecasters.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a treatment pathway to reduce violence risk in psychosis:  from risk assessment to complex intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Whiting; Belinda Lennox; Seena Fazel
articles_hidden.abstract: Violence perpetration is an important adverse outcome for psychiatric services to reduce. Clinical services for psychosis, such as Early Intervention in Psychosis services, represent a key opportunity for prevention, but this is challenging without specialist expertise and resource for violence risk assessment and management. One innovation to address this is a scalable clinical prediction tool for violence, OxMIV, which has been developed using contemporary statistical approaches and been found to be both feasible to use and more accurate than clinical judgement alone in these settings. However, assessing risk does not reduce violence unless it leads to effective interventions being offered more consistently to those who are most likely to benefit. Evidence-based, population health approaches for linking individual risk estimates to intervention pathways have been successfully implemented elsewhere in medicine. Here we adopt such an approach for assessing and reducing the risk of violence in psychosis, presenting a framework for using OxMIV to support decision-making around allocating resources for further assessment and offering interventions that address modifiable risk factors. To develop, implement and test the effectiveness of such clinical pathways, assessments of risk and linked interventions should be studied together as complex healthcare interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Kudos to CUDOS: Resurrecting Mertonian Principles to Remedy Politicized Science
articles_hidden.authors: Cory J Clark; Medhini Urs
articles_hidden.abstract: Science is the most effective system humans have developed to understand reality. Like all systems, it is flawed and subject to bias and error. Reforms such as the Open Science movement seek to address these issues by institutionalizing long-standing Mertonian norms (communalism, universalism, disinterestedness, organized skepticism), helping scientists escape their biases and discover truth. However, other actions within scientific institutions have introduced ideological and political values into the truth-seeking domain, including harm-based censorship, DEI policies, positionality statements, and endorsements of political candidates and positions, among others. These developments can deprioritize epistemic quality and decrease public trust in science. Because the politicization of science arising within the academy has occurred primarily from one direction (i.e., left-wing), some strategies to counteract this bias have been to prioritize ideological/political diversity in hiring, or to encourage scientists to stay away from weighing in on political issues altogether. We argue that these well-meaning solutions to the problem of politicization compounds non-epistemic values in science, thereby risking further loss in public trust. Effort should be directed to restoring Mertonian norms that historically underpinned scientific credibility so that epistemic rigor can be improved and the issues of politicization can be solved without introducing more politics.

articles_hidden.title: Priority Maps, Featureful Processing, and the Superior Colliculus
articles_hidden.authors: Wayne Wu; Neeraj J. Gandhi; James P. Herman
articles_hidden.abstract: The priority map has been used to explain how locations are prioritized for attention and behavior. Priority maps provide a test case for how computational models and neural data can be integrated. Focusing on the superior colliculus (SC) as a paradigm neural substrate for priority maps, we raise two questions: (1) What does priority mean computationally? (2) Since priority maps are featureless, how can this be integrated with recent work on feature coding in SC? We argue that the priority map remains computationally unclear because the nature of priority remains unsettled. Given emerging evidence for “featureful” coding within SC, we challenge the priority map’s featureless assumption as applied to SC and suggest an alternative: a featureful priority matrix where feature dimensions remain distinctly represented.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Attributed Innateness Beliefs Moderate the Heritability of Psychological Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Jern
articles_hidden.abstract:
People vary in how strongly they believe their psychological traits are innate. Using a 
twin/sibling design (N = 5,844; 1,043 MZ and 2,607 DZ families), I tested whether such 
beliefs moderate the heritability of 11 traits spanning sexuality, personality, attitudes, and 
health behavior. Innateness beliefs significantly moderated heritability for all traits: 
individuals who considered a trait more innate showed higher heritability for that trait. The 
effect was more trait-specific than indicative of a general essentialist tendency and largely 
driven by the individual's own belief rather than shared familial or genetic factors 
(religiosity and risk-taking were partial exceptions). A stringent sensitivity analysis reduced 
the number of significant traits from 11 to 6, indicating that for some traits the moderation 
may at least partly reflect a confound between extreme trait scores and innateness beliefs. 
The low heritability of innateness beliefs is consistent with largely non-genetic beliefs 
gatekeeping the expression of genetic variation.

articles_hidden.title: A Bayesian Structure Inference Account of Biases in the Formation and Updating of Group Moral Impressions
articles_hidden.authors: Jieyun Li; Fuying Chen; Yi Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: Evaluating a group's morality requires integrating its members' behaviors to form an impression, and updating these evaluations as new information emerges. We captured both impression formation and updating within a single Bayesian nonparametric framework: observers infer latent structures from group's behavioral distributions, thereby generating systematic biases in both static and changing contexts. During moral impression formation, when a group exhibits both common (dense) and rare (sparse) moral behaviors, the structure inference account (formalized by the Chinese Restaurant Process, CRP) predicts a sparsity bias, where rare behaviors trigger the inference of more latent structures. This opposes the "Common Is Moral" (CIM) heuristic, which predicts a density bias anchored to the high-frequency majority. Behavioral and computational modeling results (Experiments 1a-1b) showed a sparsity bias better explained by structural inference rather than frequency heuristics. Representational Similarity Analysis (Experiment 2) further revealed that observers' mental representations of groups organize around these inferred structures. Critically, moving to moral impression updating (Experiment 3), we found that impression biases track the shifting valence of newly sparse information. We captured the underlying structural evolution by extending the framework to changing environments via the Recurrent CRP (RCRP). Together, these findings suggest that the formation and updating of moral group impressions can be understood under a single cognitive perspective, implying that social biases could be mitigated by strategically altering information distributions.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Adaptation of the Attachment-Focused Connect Parenting Program for Ukrainian Families in Canada Affected by War and Displacement
articles_hidden.authors: Hanna Usatenko; Roksolana Malyi-Prasol; Anh-Thu Vu; Patti Ranahan; Olha Kochubeinyk; Janet Mainland; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract:
War and forced displacement deeply strain parent–child relationships. The ongoing war in Ukraine has intensified the need for family support. Culturally adapted, evidence-based parenting interventions for displaced Ukrainian families remain limited. This study describes the cultural adaptation of Connect, a trauma-informed, attachment-focused, evidence-supported parenting program for Ukrainian parents of children aged 8–17, affected by war and displacement and residing in Canada since 2022. The Cultural Adaptation Process (CAP) model guided iterative adaptation, while the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications to Evidence-Based Interventions (FRAME) documented modifications retrospectively, and the Ecological Validity Model (EVM) was used to examine cultural relevance. Informed by contextual realities, lived experiences, and cultural values, the adaptation involved a multistage, top-down and bottom-up interaction with stakeholders. 
Twenty-two modifications were identified across planning, pilot implementation, and refinement, most commonly related to cultural values, as well as intervention delivery. Core Connect structure related to attachment, reflective parenting, and intervention functions were preserved, while examples, role plays, and procedures were contextually aligned. Feedback from 22 parents was collected through guided group discussion and an anonymous online survey. Group discussion transcripts were analyzed using qualitative content analysis, and survey results were summarized descriptively. Participants indicated strong acceptability alongside qualitative reports of cultural fit, and emphasized greater understanding of children, parenting confidence, self-regulation, and greater parent–child mutuality. Cultural adaptation was systematically documented while preserving core intervention functions and informing future implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Relational generalization through memory integration: building knowledge beyond direct experience
articles_hidden.authors: Lainey Costa; Cheyna Warner; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory allows us to remember the past but also form complex knowledge combining information obtained across time. As a key example, relational generalization helps us infer new information by connecting related information acquired separately (AB & BC, therefore AC). Associative inference across arbitrary associations of visual objects has been the most fruitful paradigm, but how it relates to real-world knowledge acquisition is unclear. A more naturalistic paradigm is self-derivation of knowledge, assessing the ability to integrate two related, real-world facts to infer a novel fact. However, because of the rooting in verbal material and semantic memory, it is unclear to what degree the two paradigms assess a common underlying process. Here we tested the degree to which an individual's self-derivation performance can be predicted from their general verbal retrieval abilities and a standard associative inference task with arbitrary object pairs. Results showed that associative inference and verbal fluency separately positively predicted self-derivation of knowledge. Associative inference predicted self-derivation even after controlling for individual differences in associative memory strength. Finally, we found that resistance to interference in the associative inference paradigm may serve as an alternative measure of memory integration. These findings demonstrate that self-derivation of knowledge and associative inference are underpinned by the same process of memory integration across experiences and reinforce the validity of both laboratory measures to assess relational generalization. More broadly, they show that the knowledge humans form depends not only on what they encode, but also on how effectively they integrate across memories.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking and predicting physical task failure using machine learning
articles_hidden.authors: Darias Holgado; Juan Eloy Arco; Priscilla Bartschi; Daniel Sanabria; Nicolas Place
