articles_hidden.abstract: Task failure during sustained exercise is often defined mechanically as the inability to maintain a prescribed force, yet cessation may reflect a developing decision to disengage. This study characterized the temporal dynamics of this process and tested whether imminent task failure could be anticipated from multimodal signals. Twenty-three healthy adults performed a sustained isometric knee extension at 20% maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) until task failure. During exercise, auditory probes required participants to indicate whether, since the previous probe, they had thought about or felt the need to stop. Neuromuscular function was assessed before and immediately after exercise, and seven subjective dimensions were reconstructed using Temporal Experience Tracing. Probe-level data were entered into ridge-penalized within-participant Cox proportional hazards models using physiological-behavioral, subjective, and full feature sets; discrimination was quantified with Harrell’s C-index. Participants reached failure after 549 ± 336 s. The first “yes” response occurred at 45% of individual task duration, showing that disengagement-related thoughts preceded failure. Force output remained stable, whereas knee-extensor EMG increased; MVC force, voluntary activation, and 100-Hz doublet amplitude decreased post-exercise, confirming central and peripheral fatigue. Cox models ranked probes by proximity to failure above chance in all participants. The experiential (C-index = 0.988 ± 0.003) and full models (0.984 ± 0.002) outperformed the physiological-behavioral model (0.882 ± 0.014; p < 0.001) and anticipated failure ~50–54 s before cessation. Perceived physical fatigue, mental fatigue, frustration, reduced motivation, EMG activity, and “yes” responses were the main contributors. Task failure reflects a cumulative, multimodal process rather than physiological failure.

articles_hidden.title: Reframing the Unconscious: A Conceptual Mapping of Jungian Analytical Psychology onto Indian Knowledge Systems
articles_hidden.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles_hidden.abstract: Carl Jung engaged Eastern thought throughout his career, writing psychological commentaries on The Secret of the Golden Flower, the Tibetan Book of the Dead, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga, yet this engagement remained impressionistic rather than systematic. No existing review pairs his core constructs with named terms from classical Indian philosophy. This paper proposes a term-by-term conceptual correspondence between six constructs of Jungian analytical psychology and six terms drawn from Sāṃkhya, Patañjali's Yoga, and Advaita Vedānta. It does not introduce a new theoretical model, acronym, or unifying framework. The paper follows Jaakkola's Theory Synthesis template for conceptual articles, distinguished from Theory Adaptation, Typology, and Model approaches. Four criteria guided term selection: definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity. Each correspondence was checked against primary Jungian texts and established secondary scholarship in Indology. Six correspondences are proposed: Collective Unconscious–Mahat, Archetypes–Tattva, Persona–Vyavahārika, Anima/Animus–Puruṣa/ Prakṛti, Shadow–Kleśa, and Individuation–Svarūpa-bodha. A central divergence emerged alongside these resemblances. Jung's individuation preserves a differentiated, related self, while Advaita's deeper vocabulary points toward non-dual dissolution of that self. This paper treats the divergence as a substantive finding, not a flaw in the method. The mapping offers culturally grounded vocabulary for teaching analytical psychology in Indian settings and for developing culturally resonant counseling language, illustrated through a brief clinical vignette. Risks of essentialism, translation distance, and untested clinical application are named explicitly, with concrete directions proposed for future empirical and textual work.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition From AI-Generated and Human Faces: Performance, Mental Health, and Demographic Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Vowels; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial emotion-recognition tasks are widely used to investigate social-cognitive differences across mental health conditions, but their
scientific value depends on the faces used to measure performance. Established photographic databases are difficult and expensive to
expand, and many provide little ethnic diversity. AI-generated faces offer a more representative, flexible, and scalable alternative,
provided they capture the same clinically relevant individual differences as photographs of human faces. We compared 161
photorealistic AI-generated faces with 72 images from FACES, an established human-photograph set. Prolific participants contributed
83,206 valid trials; 77,238 trials covering the six shared emotions entered the primary comparison (accuracy \textit{n} = 1,047; response
time \textit{n} = 1,046). AI-diverse expressions were recognised more accurately (89.12\% vs.\ 81.72\%) and faster (2.29 vs.\ 2.64 s) than
FACES expressions, while AI-diverse and AI-White performance did not differ significantly. The AI task retained the individual differences needed for research: lower accuracy on both sources was associated most consistently with psychotic-like experiences and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with magnitudes aligned with previous literature. AI-diverse and FACES accuracy correlated at \textit{r} = .56, and corrected split-half reliability was .70 and .60, respectively. Women were more accurate than men; participant ethnicity was unrelated to performance. Higher AI accuracy indicates that the expressions were clear; it does not show general psychometric superiority, possibly because very easy items can compress differences among high performers. The combination of clear expressions, comparable symptom sensitivity, and broader representation shows that generative AI can modernise a core social-cognition research tool while making stimulus design more controllable, expandable, and shareable.

articles_hidden.title: Semantic Information Shapes Gaze Patterns During Naturalistic Movie Viewing: Evidence from computational models of vision and language
articles_hidden.authors: Xing Su; Aditya Upadhyayula; Jeffrey M. Zacks
articles_hidden.abstract: When people watch everyday activity or movies, the eyes are drawn by visually salient features, and also by features that are semantically meaningful. However, saliency and meaning often co-occur, making it difficult to isolate their individual influence on gaze. Here we leveraged a large language-image model (CLIP: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) to isolate these influences. Eighty-one participants watched four movies of everyday activities and eye movements were recorded. CLIP embeddings were used as a metric to measure semantic content and were compared with the gaze maps. The embeddings were generated for both upright and inverted frame versions, because frame inversion selectively disrupts semantic information while preserving saliency. Upright CLIP embeddings predicted viewers’ gaze patterns better than inverted embeddings, and this advantage persisted even after accounting for low-level saliency and other random-noise controls. Finally, temporally aligned action descriptions predicted gaze better than shuffled descriptions across multiple text-based representations, suggesting that action meaning itself carries information about where viewers look. Together, these findings suggest that gaze during naturalistic movie viewing is sensitive to semantic information at fine temporal scales, and that computational vision-language models provide a useful approach for studying cognitive processes in naturalistic environments.

articles_hidden.title: Visual, Vocal, and Verbal Markers of PTSD: A Parallel Affective Computing Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Yuanyuan Yang; Daiil Jun; Brett Welch; Allison Sylvia; Joel Gregory Sprunger; Jeffrey M. Girard
articles_hidden.abstract: Current PTSD assessment methods often compromise diagnostic precision for scalability, limiting clinical effectiveness. We propose a digital task-shifting framework that utilizes computational techniques to enhance assessment capacity while preserving clinician judgment. We implemented two structured trauma-activation tasks (trauma account and impact statement) via telehealth to elicit disorder-relevant behavioral signals, then quantified PTSD-related behaviors across modalities: verbal, vocal, and visual. Parallel unimodal statistical analyses prioritized interpretability. Comparing 49 individuals with PTSD and 44 trauma-exposed controls isolated PTSD-specific effects. Bayesian generalized linear mixed models revealed significant main effects of group across all modalities with group-by-task interaction effects specifically in verbal and vocal modalities. These findings demonstrate digital task-shifting can capture clinically meaningful variations in PTSD within a scalable framework, complementing traditional assessment methods. Strong interaction effects indicate context-dependent shifts and constrained stylistic patterns across modalities. This approach provides objective indicators of distress to potentially support clinical assessments and research via telehealth.

articles_hidden.title: Losing nuance in camouflaging research: the unintended harms for research, clinical practice, and public discourse
articles_hidden.authors: Ailbhe McKinney; Connor Tom Keating; Holly Elizabeth Anne Sutherland; Rae Field; Jiedi Lei
articles_hidden.abstract: Camouflaging refers to the conscious or subconscious suppression of autistic (or neurodivergent) behaviours, and/or the use of compensatory strategies, to navigate social interactions with the aim of being perceived as neurotypical and to keep safe. The field is currently at an important turning point: camouflaging is now firmly established within autism research, but its rapid movement into public discourse and clinical practice has outpaced conceptual and measurement precision. In this Personal View, we identify two related challenges. First, existing conceptualisations often capture only one slice of the relationship between camouflaging and other outcomes (e.g. mental health), treating camouflaging as unidimensional and its associations with outcomes as linear, potentially obscuring more complex and heterogeneous relationships. Current frameworks similarly tend to quantify camouflaging behaviours without in-depth functional analysis to capture differences in agency, context, and cognitive mechanisms that may give rise to different behaviours and outcomes. We propose a multidimensional framework to capture these distinct but interacting processes and support more precise mechanistic research. Second, simplified clinical and public narratives increasingly frame camouflaging as uniformly harmful and “unmasking” as inherently desirable. We argue instead for a nuanced, neurodiversity-affirming approach centred on safety and personal autonomy. Applying the multidimensional framework clinically may help practitioners understand when, why, and how camouflaging is helpful or harmful for a particular person in a particular context.

articles_hidden.title: The influence of visual manipulations on behavioural, physiological and perceptual responses in the heat:  A multi-experiment, mixed methods approach
articles_hidden.authors: Harry Mayes; Liam Satchell; Martina Navarro; Daniel Muller; Finlay Morgan; Juan Ignacio Badariotti; Danny White; Mike Tipton; Zac Schlader; Soichi Ando
articles_hidden.abstract: Thermal perception is essential for human survival through its influence on behavioural thermoregulation. Existing literature suggests that thermal perception can be altered by simple visual manipulations, but this has not been empirically investigated using more contemporary immersive tools such as virtual reality or during exposure to high ambient environments. We tested the hypothesis that visual manipulation, using virtual reality (VR), would alter thermal perception during both rest and exercise in ambient temperatures above ≥ 35 °C. Across three separate experiments, participants cycled at a fixed intensity in 35 °C (experiment 1, n=16), rested in 40 °C (experiment 2, n=12), or completed a fixed-RPE protocol in 35 °C (experiment 3, n=12). Participants completed three visits for each experiment; a ‘hot’ VR environment, a ‘cold’ VR environment, and No VR environment. A single, participant-blind, block randomised controlled, cross-over design was employed. Key outcome measures were thermal comfort, thermal sensation, behavioural thermoregulation, and thermophysiological variables. Additionally, participants were interviewed to explore their perceptual experience in depth, and this added insightful data about their experiences. Visual manipulation had no effect on thermal sensation, thermal comfort, behavioural thermoregulation or any other thermophysiological variables (all p > 0.05). It is concluded that visual manipulations using virtual reality do not alter thermal perceptual, behavioural thermoregulation or thermophysiolological variables during rest or exercise in the heat, but interview data suggest participants believed the VR environments had more of an effect than elucidated quantitatively. These novel findings provide evidence that the hue-heat hypothesis may only exist in thermoneutral environments, further research should confirm this in other (e.g. cold) environments.

articles_hidden.title: China–US Differences in Attributions of AI Consciousness and Moral Status
articles_hidden.authors: Ali Ladak; Nick Corvino; David Moss; Bradford Saad; Jeff Sebo; Matti Wilks; Lucius Caviola
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite AI’s global reach, little is known about how laypeople outside Western contexts think about whether AI systems can be conscious—capable of subjective experience—or whether they could have moral status—warranting moral consideration. In a preregistered main and replication study, we compared such attitudes among laypeople in China and the US (main sample: N = 820; replication sample: N = 910). Across a range of measures, Chinese participants were more open to AI consciousness and moral status than US participants. For example, a larger proportion of Chinese than US participants judged it in-principle possible that AI could be conscious (86.3% vs. 39.6%) and have moral status (89.1% vs. 54.0%). While both countries, on average, leaned against current AI systems being conscious, Chinese participants’ average ratings were higher than US participants’. Chinese participants also, on average, rated a hypothetical future AI system—an exact digital copy of a human brain with a physical body—as having comparable consciousness and moral status to a chimpanzee, while US participants, on average, rated the same system close to an ant. These differences may reflect more positive general attitudes towards AI and greater animism (measured by the belief that non-living things can have a spirit or soul) in China than in the US. Despite these diverging attitudes, participants in neither country supported protecting advanced AI systems at the expense of humans or their own country. Yet participants in both countries supported international cooperation regarding conscious AI, pointing to an opportunity for collaboration in global AI governance.

articles_hidden.title: Sadism is Linked to Greater Habituation to Schadenfreude
articles_hidden.authors: Drew M. Parton; Emily Pappalardo; David Skylan Chester
articles_hidden.abstract: People sometimes enjoy being passive spectators to others’ pain (i.e., schadenfreude). Yet, sadistic individuals actively inflict such pain themselves for the pleasure it brings. What differentiates those who passively versus actively enjoy others’ suffering? In individuals predisposed to enjoying others’ suffering, diminishing hedonic returns from schadenfreude may motivate sadistic pursuits to better satisfy hedonic goals. To test this, 297 undergraduates from a Minority Serving Institution reported their sadistic tendencies and then repeatedly watched and reported their enjoyment of two blocks of videos that either depicted people being moderately harmed or non-harmful pleasant scenes. Sadism was positively correlated with schadenfreude (i.e., participants with more sadistic tendencies reported greater enjoyment of the harm videos than those lower in sadism). Yet, sadism was also linked to a greater habituation to schadenfreude, in which more sadistic individuals showed steeper drops in their enjoyment of harm videos over subsequent videos than others, even when we adjusted for corresponding declines in their enjoyment of non-harm videos in the control condition. Indeed, the extent to which sadism was linked to greater enjoyment of harm videos more than halved over the course of the task.

articles_hidden.title: Ensuring quality in research, 'Authorship Effect' & Conflict of Interest. Response submitted to BMJ Mental Health in response to 'Clinician perspectives on the utility and acceptability of OxSATS: a qualitative study of a novel structured suicide risk assessment tool
articles_hidden.authors: Alastair Cockburn; Karen Lascelles; Leah Quinlivan
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper is a response to the recent BMJ Mental Health publication, 'Clinician perspectives on the utility and acceptability of OxSATS: a qualitative study of a novel structured suicide risk assessment tool.’1 We outline several methodological limitations, including a dissonance between the participants’ responses and the study conclusions, recruitment, reflexivity, and conflict of interests. We conclude with highlighting the importance of scientific standards and academic integrity in producing trusted, unbiased, good quality research.

articles_hidden.title: Dual-Task Interference Elicits Reactive Adjustments in Neural Correlates of Performance Monitoring
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Löschner; Marco Steinhauser
articles_hidden.abstract: Interference in dual-tasking poses a challenge both for task performance and for effective performance monitoring. The question emerges whether the brain copes with such interference not only reactively but also proactively by engaging adjustments in anticipation of interference. The present study investigated how two key correlates of performance monitoring, the error-related negativity (Ne/ERN) and the error positivity (Pe), adjust to interference in dual-tasking. In a Psychological Refractory Period paradigm, participants completed two tasks separated by a long or short stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA). Next to the actual SOA in a trial, we manipulated the expected SOA in blocks of trials by varying the frequency of short and long SOAs. This allowed participants to form expectations regarding the occurrence of dual-task interference, thereby creating conditions under which proactive adjustments to performance monitoring would be advantageous. While expecting short SOAs led to a proactive slowing of the first task in line with capacity-sharing accounts of dual-tasking, neural correlates of performance monitoring indicated a reactive but not proactive adjustment for the Pe. Following an erroneous response on the first task, the Pe was reactively reduced and later reappeared after the correct response of the second task, a pattern previously labeled adaptive rescheduling. For the Ne/ERN, no clear evidence for either a reactive or a proactive pattern emerged. Taken together, these findings suggest that performance monitoring adjusts reactively to dual-task interference in order to prevent interference between temporally overlapping processes while maintaining effective performance monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: The effects of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information on implicit and explicit evaluations: A replication and extension of Rydell et al. (2007)
articles_hidden.authors: Benedek Kurdi; Ming Ma; Nicholas Surdel; Melissa J. Ferguson; Jeremy Cone
articles_hidden.abstract: Rydell et al. (2007) documented a dissociative pattern of updating such that implicit (automatic) evaluations changed continuously, whereas explicit (controlled) evaluations changed asymptotically in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information. The present project consisted of two preregistered experiments (total N = 1,090). In Experiment 1, implemented as a close replication, implicit evaluations changed asymptotically, whereas explicit evaluations changed continuously, thus deviating from the original result. In Experiment 2, designed as a test of boundary conditions, neutral statements were omitted from the learning phase, and implicit evaluation measurement was improved. Here, implicit and explicit evaluation change were both asymptotic. These results demonstrate that the functional trajectories of evaluative updating are highly variable across independent investigations. Given that these divergent patterns are challenging to reconcile with any single existing account, they underscore the value of grounding future research in quantitative models of learning.

articles_hidden.title: Sex-Differences in the Relationship between Methamphetamine-Use Experience and Spatial Memory in Non-Treatment Seeking Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Alisha Schaefer; Hyeon Jung Heselton; Hillary Schwarb
articles_hidden.abstract: Methamphetamine remains a public health concern in the United States, and its use has been associated with detrimental effects on memory. More specifically, spatial memory deficits after methamphetamine exposure have been heavily researched in the rodent literature and sex-differences have been reported. However, the effects of methamphetamine on spatial memory in human studies remain underinvestigated and sex differences have not been considered. The current study recruited 30 community-dwelling people with recent or current methamphetamine-use experience, and 30 without methamphetamine-use experience people matched on sex and age. All participants completed a computerized spatial reconstruction task where they studied arrays of randomly positioned objects and then, after a short delay, attempted to reconstruct the remembered study array. Accuracy for both the general spatial arrangement and specific object-location bindings as well as various types of spatial-errors were evaluated. Data indicated that both groups were able to remember global features of the task similarly (i.e., the general spatial arrangement). However, large group differences were evident when specific object-location associative binding was assessed. These group differences were driven by males such that males, but not females, with methamphetamine-use experience were significantly impaired at remembering specific object-location pairings. Together, these findings underscore the need to further characterize spatial memory deficits in people with methamphetamine-use experience as such impairments may have detrimental effects on everyday function and spatial navigation. Furthermore, these findings emphasize the need for sex-balanced samples when studying spatial memory in this population, thus affording the opportunity to investigate possible sex differences.

articles_hidden.title: The virtual crime scene:  Virtual reality context reinstatement as a means to increase the quality of eyewitness statements.
articles_hidden.authors: Jeroen Timmer; Peter W. de Vries; Jordy F. Gosselt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Eyewitness statements often determine the direction and the success of police investigations. However, eyewitnesses’ recollection of events may become inaccurate or even incorrect over time. Moreover, eyewitnesses’ expressed confidence in the quality of their statements tends to be a rather weak indicator of actual quality. The current study explores how different types of context reinstatement compare in terms of quality of eyewitness statements and how they influence the confidence-quality relationship. Of particular interest is a new type of context reinstatement: virtual context reinstatement.
Methods: Participants (N = 98) were asked to take part in a group experiment in which an incident was staged. A week later, participants were subjected to virtual context reinstatement (VCR), physical context reinstatement (PCR), mental context reinstatement (MCR), or a no context reinstatement (control) procedure, and were subsequently asked to give an eyewitness statement. 
Results: During free recall, eyewitness statements in both the VCR and PCR conditions contained significantly less confabulated details compared to statements of participants in the control group. During cued recall, participants in the VCR condition reported more correct details in their statements than participants in the MCR and PCR conditions. Moreover, VCR appears to result in a stronger confidence-quality relationship compared to the other types context reinstatement. 
Conclusions: PCR and VCR showed fewest confabulated details in eyewitness statements and are therefore most beneficial to police investigations. The stronger confidence-quality relationship as a result of VCR can help to support the decision-making process of police investigators and other professionals who rely on eyewitness statements.

articles_hidden.title: Gender Gap in Eco-friendliness: Is It Mostly in Our Head?
articles_hidden.authors: Olena Vitkovska; Veronika Job; Christina Bauer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Do women want to engage in more eco-friendly behaviors compared to men? Popular 
media sometimes suggest as much, but it is unclear whether such portrayals reflect actual gender 
gaps or stereotypes (i.e., shared beliefs about gender differences that may not align with reality). 
To address this, we examined both in two studies: Study 1 (N = 274, convenience sample) and 
Study 2 (N = 615, US census-representative sample), using frequentist and Bayesian analyses, 
thus testing for both the presence and the absence of a gender gap in eco-friendly behavioral 
intentions and attitudes. Overall, we found strong and consistent evidence for stereotypes. The 
means indicate that gender stereotypes were driven by perceptions of women as highly 
compatible with eco-friendliness, whilst men were perceived as moderately compatible. At the 
same time, evidence for gender gaps in eco-friendly intentions and attitudes was weaker. Study 1 
found no evidence for a gap, whereas Study 2 found small effects on two out of four measures. 
Overall, this research shows that perceptions of women as more eco-friendly than men are 
largely driven by gender stereotypes rather than by the extent to which men and women actually 
differ in their eco-friendly behavioral intentions and attitudes. Thus, the present research 
counters essentializing views of men and women.

articles_hidden.title: The role of spontaneous strategy use in younger and older adults' visuospatial memory
articles_hidden.authors: Gerard Campbell; Rebecca Hart; Richard John Allen; Claudia Christina von Bastian; Melanie Rose Burke; Mario Parra Rodrigues; Victor Kenji Medeiros Shiramizu; Louise A. Brown Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous strategy use may contribute to age-related changes in visuospatial memory. We aimed to establish which strategies are associated with young and older adults’ working memory and long-term memory performance, using ecologically valid stimuli. Across four experiments, we investigated younger (18–37 years; total N = 192) and older (63–85 years; total N = 192) adults’ strategy use when remembering coloured objects within everyday virtual scenes. Participants attempted to recall object-colour or object-location bindings from working memory. In-task spontaneous strategy use was also comprehensively assessed via theory-driven, repeated Likert scale probes. Participants subsequently completed an incidental or intentional long-term memory task assessing item (objects only) and associative memory (object-colour/object-location associations) for the working memory task stimuli. All experiments revealed age-related deficits in working memory and long-term memory, although item long-term memory exhibited smaller effect sizes than associative long-term memory. Regarding strategies, younger adults used verbal coding to a greater extent than older adults, who generally exhibited a reduced strategy repertoire. Importantly, verbal coding was consistently associated with better working memory performance. Regarding object-colour associations, using semantic strategies was associated with better intentional, but not incidental, long-term memory, showing the importance of task foreknowledge in strategy selection. For object-location binding, verbal coding was positively related to both incidental and intentional long-term memory. Object-colour associations may therefore be more amenable to strategic semantic encoding than locations. The findings highlight that strategy use is associated with age effects in visuospatial memory and have implications for developing strategy-based interventions to improve visuospatial memory.

articles_hidden.title: PixelSurvey: A YAML-based open-source framework for creating surveys
articles_hidden.authors: Francisco Garrido-Valenzuela; Oded Cats; Sander van Cranenburgh
articles_hidden.abstract: Surveys are among the most widely used tools in behavioral, social, and psychological research. At the same time, visual information is increasingly recognized as central to how humans perceive, evaluate, and decide, underscoring the need for survey infrastructures that systematically and reproducibly integrate images. However, existing platforms, such as Qualtrics or Google Forms,  face significant limitations when it comes to incorporating image-based experimental designs and are not open-sourced. PixelSurvey, an open-source, modular framework for designing, deploying, and sharing survey experiments, addresses this gap. Built around human-readable YAML “recipes” that fully specify survey structure, logic, and stimuli, PixelSurvey allows the inclusion of image-based experimental designs. While initially conceived to address the complexities of visual data, its underlying structure is stimulus-agnostic, allowing researchers to easily extend its use to broader survey applications beyond just images. Additionally, it ensures transparency, reproducibility, and ease of sharing. Its standardized architecture supports different question types and image-based experiment paradigms, while its modular design enables community-driven extensions. By lowering technical barriers and embedding open-science principles, PixelSurvey provides a versatile and sustainable platform for advancing the study of human perceptions, preferences, and decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a treatment pathway to reduce violence risk in psychosis:  from risk assessment to complex intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Whiting; Belinda Lennox; Seena Fazel
articles_hidden.abstract: Violence perpetration is an important adverse outcome for psychiatric services to reduce. Clinical services for psychosis, such as Early Intervention in Psychosis services, represent a key opportunity for prevention, but this is challenging without specialist expertise and resource for violence risk assessment and management. One innovation to address this is a scalable clinical prediction tool for violence, OxMIV, which has been developed using contemporary statistical approaches and been found to be both feasible to use and more accurate than clinical judgement alone in these settings. However, assessing risk does not reduce violence unless it leads to effective interventions being offered more consistently to those who are most likely to benefit. Evidence-based, population health approaches for linking individual risk estimates to intervention pathways have been successfully implemented elsewhere in medicine. Here we adopt such an approach for assessing and reducing the risk of violence in psychosis, presenting a framework for using OxMIV to support decision-making around allocating resources for further assessment and offering interventions that address modifiable risk factors. To develop, implement and test the effectiveness of such clinical pathways, assessments of risk and linked interventions should be studied together as complex healthcare interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Subgroup Relationships and Individual Differences  in Musical Synchronization
articles_hidden.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Chihiro Honda; Davide Lionetti; Pieter-Jan Maes; Marcelo Wanderley; Caroline Palmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Musicians demonstrate strong auditory-motor synchronization abilities during group performance, although most empirical studies have examined only solo or dyadic performance. We investigated musical synchronization in four-person groups performing simple and complex rhythms. Each musician's spontaneous production rate for familiar melodies provided individual difference measures of intrinsic rhythms. Participants were randomly assigned to quartets and synchronized their drumming while they performing rhythms based on Binary or Ternary Meters in Simple (1:1 isochronous) and Complex (2:3 polyrhythmic) Rhythm conditions. An unexpected perturbation cue instructed members to switch to the opposite meter, from Ternary to Binary or vice versa. Simple rhythms yielded greater synchrony and shorter relaxation times for returning to stable synchronization following perturbations than Complex polyrhythms. History-dependent effects, reflecting carryover from previous states, were observed when musicians switched between Ternary and Binary rhythms. Quartets with larger individual differences in spontaneous production rates had longer relaxation times to achieve stable coordination. Social interaction ratings indicated greater perceived relationship toward the dyadic partner than toward the four-person group in the Complex Rhythm condition, but not in the Simple Rhythm condition, consistent with in-group (partner) and out-group (group) roles. These findings were largely consistent across North American and European testing sites, suggesting that group and subgroup relationships generalize across sites.

articles_hidden.title: Better Safe Than Sorry? Risks and Benefits of Neuroticism in Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Larissa Lucia Wieczorek; Eva Bleckmann; Solomiia Myroniuk; Bertus F. Jeronimus; Sanne Booij; Jenny Wagner; Albertine Oldehinkel
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroticism is known for detrimental outcomes, but it may also serve beneficial functions in adolescence, where avoiding and protecting oneself from threats becomes crucial. We examined potential benefits of neuroticism based on longitudinal data of two samples of Dutch adolescents, one population (n = 2229, 51% female) and one clinic-referred (n = 543, 34% female) sample. Neuroticism was measured with parent-ratings of the temperament dimensions fear and frustration and used to predict a diverse set of outcomes in the domains lifestyle choices (e.g., substance abuse) and social resources (e.g., social skills) between ages 11 to 19. High neuroticism conveyed heightened risk but four key observations refine this picture: (1) higher fear related to more social skills and prosocial behavior among adolescents in the clinic-referred sample; (2) fear generally related to fewer risks than frustration; (3) controlling for childhood adversity (e.g., low socioeconomic status, parental divorce) removed links between fear and most detrimental outcomes; (4) both fear and frustration were consistently associated with parent-rated social behavior problems, while other associations varied across neuroticism scales and measurement points. Altogether, we provide initial evidence that, under certain conditions, neuroticism can be beneficial in adolescence, especially among vulnerable individuals and in the social domain.

articles_hidden.title: Safety, Compatibility and Reconnection: Understanding Restorative Nature Through the Lens of Chronic Low Back Pain
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Smith; Kayleigh Wyles; Patricia Schofield; Sam William Hughes
articles_hidden.abstract: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is a pervasive and debilitating condition that is often resistant to conventional pain management strategies. This has driven a growing interest in novel psychosocial approaches, such as the use of restorative nature-based environments as part of pain self-management strategies. However, many assumptions regarding restorative nature spaces are based on the perspective of healthy individuals. A population living with cLBP may conceptualise or identify restorative nature spaces differently, given such factors as risk of reinjury or physical limitations. Two focus groups were conducted with a cLBP group (n = 7, Mage = 55.57, 6 females) to explore what a restorative outdoor nature space means through the lens of chronic low back pain. Thematic Analysis generated four Themes (Safety, Confidence, and Control; Embodied Capability; Reclaiming Self Beyond Pain; and Engagement with Living Nature). The present study highlights the necessity of inclusion of lived experience and perspective when discussing how best to incorporate restorative nature spaces into pain self-management or green social prescribing frameworks for the chronic pain community. Future research can build upon the present research to codesign tailored nature-based interventions for people with a lived experience of chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating effects of day-to-day variations in environmental exposure on the human brain: study protocol for the Day2Day Environment project
articles_hidden.authors: Kim Falkenstein; Claire Pauley; Simone Kühn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Understanding how daily environmental exposures influence the human brain and mental health is increasingly important in the context of global urbanization and climate change. Previous studies have focused primarily on long-term environmental factors or isolated features like green space and air quality, neglecting the interaction between multiple exposures encountered in everyday life. This protocol paper describes the study design and dataset of the Day2Day Environment project, an ongoing study investigating how real-world, day-to-day environmental variability affects brain structure, function, and well-being.
Methods: This dense longitudinal study collects multimodal data from 30 participants over 25 testing sessions, including neuroimaging and tracking of physiological, behavioral, and environmental variables. Using wearable devices, geographic ecological momentary assessments, and GPS-based geospatial tracking, we collect data on air quality, noise, light exposure, physical activity, stress, cognition, and affect. Neuroimaging measures include T1- and T2*-weighted images during rest and tasks, quantitative multi-parameter mapping, high-resolution proton density imaging of the hippocampus, and diffusion tensor imaging sequences.
Conclusion: The Day2Day Environment dataset offers a unique opportunity to study short-term neuroplasticity in response to the dynamic interplay between multiple environmental exposures. Furthermore, the diversity of measurements in this dataset may be valuable for addressing research questions beyond environmental neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Norms for a German version of the Phenomenological Control Scale: Measuring the capacity for creating and controlling experience
articles_hidden.authors: Moritz Schiltenwolf; Marie Luise Schreiter; Peter Lush
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to create experiences which misrepresent reality and thereby meet strategic goals is a stable trait that varies substantially in the general population. The capacity for such phenomenological control can be measured by response to imaginative suggestions for a variety of experiences, for example, hallucination in various modalities, amnesia, paralysis or motor actions which are experienced as involuntary. Here we present norms for a German translation of the Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS;  Lush et al., 2021).  Data were collected from a representative sample of native-German speakers (N=299) using a single-session online screening procedure. We show that the translated scale is psychometrically sound, and in line with the results of the original scale in terms of mean scores, distribution and internal consistency. All analyses, code, data, materials and the full questionnaire script are made freely available. Other researchers in the field of psychology are welcome to access and encouraged to use the German norms for the Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS-GER), for example, to assess the degree to which trait phenomenological control may be involved in other psychological effects.

articles_hidden.title: AI-based detection of suicidal ideation in text: model development and evaluation for a student mental health chatbot
articles_hidden.authors: Lotenna Olisaeloka; Leonard Ruocco; Richard Munthali; Melissa Vereschaagin; Yuqian Zhuang; Angel Wang; Tiana Mori; Chris Richardson; Kristen Hudec; Daniel Vigo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Conversational digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) require mechanisms for recognizing expressions of suicidal ideation (SI) and initiating appropriate safety responses. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection approaches could provide a scalable safeguard; but systems designed for real world deployment must consider accuracy alongside computational efficiency, transparency, and appropriate response pathways. 

Methods: We developed a lightweight SI-detection system for integration into Minder, a mental health chatbot intervention for students. The detection pipeline combined a fine-tuned Sentence-BERT (SBERT) encoder with a nonparametric, anchor-based decision layer. The encoder was trained on 220,833 sentence-level text samples from public social media datasets. Fine-tuning used partial unfreezing and Batch-All Triplet Loss, with three configurations (Light, Medium, Heavy) compared on a development set. Each text input was encoded as 768-dimensional embeddings, then compared, using cosine similarity, against an expert-curated reference set of statements spanning suicidal ideation, intent, planning, and method. Inputs exceeding a development-set threshold were flagged as containing SI. The selected model was evaluated on a held-out test set and benchmarked against four open-weight generative language models under zero-shot prompting. 

Results: The Light fine-tuning configuration was selected for its strong performance and better preservation of the embedding space’s broader semantic structure. On the held-out test set, it achieved precision 0.91, recall 0.92, specificity 0.92, F1 0.91, and accuracy 0.92. A stricter threshold raised precision to 0.98 but lowered recall to 0.34. This trade-off informed a proposed workflow in which high-confidence detections trigger an immediate supportive response and crisis resources, while intermediate scores prompt clarification and re-evaluation. The system performed comparably to Phi-4 (accuracy 0.93, F1 0.92) while using roughly one-eighteenth of its storage and fewer than one-hundredth of its parameters. 

Conclusion: These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of a computationally efficient, domain-grounded approach for SI detection in informal text. Keeping the decision logic separate from the encoder makes the system auditable and allows the flagging criteria to be inspected and iteratively refined. Prospective evaluation using contextually representative chatbot conversations is required before deployment, including assessment of missed disclosures, user acceptability, and clinical governance.

articles_hidden.title: Constructing Composite Scores for Multidimensional Educational Assessment Batteries: Evaluating Alternative Psychometric Models in K–12 Reading Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Tongtong Zou; Jon Weeks; Jason D. Yeatman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Educational assessment batteries often measure constructs that are conceptually multidimensional yet sufficiently coherent to support interpretation through a single summary score. While the literature on essential unidimensionality has primarily focused on individual scales, less attention has been given to how multidimensional assessment batteries can be represented by a composite score, particularly in developmental contexts where construct shift and structurally missing assessments pose additional challenges. This study examines the construction of an essentially unidimensional composite score using the Foundational Reading Skills Assessment Suite from the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading (ROAR) as an empirical example.

Four alternative modeling approaches were evaluated, including a unidimensional Rasch model with fixed guessing parameters (1PL-G), a three-parameter logistic model (3PL), a bifactor model, and a Projective IRT model. The resulting composite scores were compared with respect to model fit, score agreement, measurement precision, reliability, external validity, and robustness to varied assessment combinations across developmental stages.

Results indicated that although multidimensional models provided improved statistical fit, the resulting composite scores were highly consistent across modeling approaches and demonstrated comparable validity evidence. Furthermore, the composite scores exhibited stable measurement properties across developmental stages and were generally robust to variations in assessment composition, supporting the interpretation of a common underlying reading construct despite meaningful differences among subskills. Consequently, the choice of composite model should be guided by the intended use of the score and the trade-offs among model complexity, measurement precision, interpretability, and operational feasibility rather than by model fit alone.

articles_hidden.title: Degree Distributions in Psychological Networks: When Centrality Conveys Consequential Information
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan JaeHong Park; Mijke Rhemtulla; Omid V. Ebrahimi; Denny Borsboom
articles_hidden.abstract:
Network analysis is an increasingly popular methodological tool in the
social, clinical and behavioral sciences because of its ability to represent
phenomena as systems of interconnected variables. A key result is a set
of centrality indices intended to quantify the “importance” of individual
vertices. However, debate over centrality in psychological networks has
rarely considered that the relevance of these indices may depend on the
broader configuration of edges described by a graph’s degree distribution.
Many real-world systems self-organize into distinct degree distributions,
yet their implications for psychological networks remain understudied. We
used Monte Carlo simulations of weighted threshold cascades to examine
when different graph structures give rise to consequential central vertices.
Differences between cascades initiated at the most and least central vertices
were greatest under moderate activation thresholds and most pronounced
in scale-free graphs. By contrast, selection of the most central vertex mattered
relatively less in the case of small world graphs. Taken together,
these results indicate that centrality should be interpreted as one feature of
a network’s broader structural organization rather than as an isolated measure
of substantive importance or intervention relevance, with the utility
of these metrics contingent on the topology in which they are embedded.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Equivalence Testing with the Updated TOSTER R Package
articles_hidden.authors: Aaron R Caldwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of methodological guidance, researchers continue to misinterpret non-significant results as evidence for the absence of an effect. Equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST) provides a principled alternative, but adoption remains limited by software accessibility and lack of training. The TOSTER R package, originally developed by Lakens (2017), made TOST accessible to experimental psychologists. This paper describes a major update to the package that expands its scope with (1) a unified t-test interface supporting both equivalence and minimal effect testing, (2) a simplified hypothesis testing interface returning standard R objects, (3) tools for computing and testing standardized effect sizes and correlations, (4) robust and resampling-based alternatives including bootstrap and permutation tests, (5) equivalence testing for ANOVAs, and (6) power analysis and sample size planning. Each capability is demonstrated with worked examples. TOSTER is also available as a jamovi module for researchers who prefer a graphical interface.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Up:  Accessible Approaches for Improving Measurement Practices in Psychological Science
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Feld Strand; Violet Aurora Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: The conclusions psychologists draw are only as sound as the measurements they are based upon. Despite the foundational role of measurement in psychological science, many areas suffer from insufficient attention to measurement practices. Although improving measurement practices is widely recognized to be important work—indeed, reliability and validity are taught in introductory psychology courses at the high school and college level—psychometrics has a reputation of being inaccessible to those without formal training. This paper provides a framework to facilitate asking and answering questions about measurement, with the goal of providing researchers without formal training in psychometrics with an accessible entry point to evaluating the measurement tools in their research area. Specifically, we present four questions that researchers can pose of the literature to guide careful evaluation of the measurement landscape in their subdiscipline, focusing on issues related to reliability, validity, and variability in task administration and scoring. In each section, we provide examples of nonempirical and empirical work that can either be conducted in a standalone study or incorporated into ongoing research projects.

articles_hidden.title: Episodic Health Behavior: A Cognitive Event-Based Perspective on Health Behavior Change
articles_hidden.authors: Darko Jekauc; Jeffrey M. Zacks
articles_hidden.abstract: Health behavior research has generated extensive knowledge about motivational and volitional determinants of behavior, yet it often treats behavior as an aggregate outcome rather than specifying the unit through which action is cognitively organized and enacted. This paper introduces episodic health behavior as health-relevant action represented and regulated as discrete behavioral episodes. Drawing on research in event cognition, we define behavioral episodes as temporally bounded and contextually situated units of action with specific initiation conditions, unfolding trajectories, and end states that can be prospectively anticipated, enacted, and retrospectively experienced. We argue that this framework addresses a structural mismatch between aggregate measurement and the episodic organization of behavioral enactment. The episodic perspective reframes core phenomena in health psychology: the intention-behavior gap reflects temporal and contextual misalignment between momentary intentions and behavioral opportunities, planning specifies actionable episode representations, habitualization increases efficiency in the initiation of recurrent episodes, and behavior change can be understood as a transformation in the frequency, regularity, and stability of episodic chains. The framework provides a theoretical rationale for intensive longitudinal designs, event-contingent assessment, within-episode measurement, and phase-sensitive interventions, particularly for recurrent health behaviors. It also identifies boundary conditions concerning participant burden, measurement reactivity, missing data, and analytic complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness at the Edge of Death: Dark Retreat, Near-Death Experience, and Generative Brain Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Miller; Zach Buck; Alex Zhu; Andrew Holecek
articles_hidden.abstract:
Near-death experiences (NDEs) and advanced contemplative practices such as dark retreat are frequently reported to involve vivid inner imagery, encounters with non-ordinary agents, moral insight, and panoramic life reviews. Despite growing empirical interest, these experiences remain theoretically fragmented across neuroscience, psychology, and religious studies. In this paper, we develop a unified computational account of NDEs, dark-retreat phenomenology, and Tibetan Buddhist bardo (“between two, gap” often glossed as “transitional process”) models using the active inference framework.
We argue that these experiences arise from lawful generative dynamics that emerge when sensory input is radically attenuated, action relevance collapses, and autobiographical self-models lose precision. Under these conditions, the brain enters a regime of offline inference in which deep priors governing identity, value, and meaning become available for revision. In extended darkness, previously unconscious processes may be brought into the light of consciousness, allowing the practitioner to relate to them rather than from them. Life review is interpreted not as episodic memory replay, but as hierarchical compression and reweighting of autobiographical information under conditions of severe constraint. Archetypal and deity-like figures are interpreted as agentive generative hypotheses that stabilize cognition when narrative selfhood can no longer organize experience, helping to explain their cross-cultural recurrence and exceptional salience.
Dark retreat is examined as a trainable analogue of the dying process (a form of bardo yoga) that allows these dynamics to unfold gradually rather than catastrophically, on the practitioner’s terms rather than on death’s involuntary and non-negotiable terms. Integrating phenomenological reports, contemplative theory, and predictive-processing models, we show how moral salience, karmic imagery, and self-transcendent insight can emerge without invoking metaphysical assumptions. Taken together, this framework reframes experiences at the edge of death as principled reorganizations of generative self-models, offering a tractable scientific account of meaning-making under maximal uncertainty and self-evidencing across increasingly refined levels of self-modeling.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamics of Perceived Rejection in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Haya Fatimah; Marina Bornovalova; Lijuan Wang; Fallon Rachael Goodman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal rejection is typically studied using trait questionnaires or in laboratory settings, while its temporal dynamics that may characterize important individual differences are often overlooked. This study examined perceived rejection in daily life as a dynamic process and its specificity from negative affect.

Method: 89 community adults, including 46 with DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), completed a 28-day EMA protocol with five prompts per day, yielding 9279 observations after data screening. Dynamic structural equation modeling was used to estimate equilibrium (typical level), inertia (persistence over time), innovation variance (magnitude of momentary perturbations), and stationary variance (overall within-person variability) for perceived rejection.

Results: Perceived rejection dynamics were associated with negative affect dynamics. After controlling for the corresponding negative affect components, SAD diagnosis and several interpersonal vulnerability measures (e.g., separation anxiety) remained associated with perceived rejection dynamics. When SAD diagnosis and interpersonal vulnerabilities were considered together, separation anxiety was uniquely associated with higher equilibrium, greater inertia, and greater stationary variance, whereas SAD was uniquely associated with greater log innovation variance; need to belong and rejection sensitivity were additionally associated with higher equilibrium.

Conclusions: Perceived rejection appears to reflect a distinct interpersonal dynamic process beyond negative affect. Within this process, a person’s typical level of perceived rejection, momentary perturbations, the persistence of deviations from the person’s typical level, and overall variability showed different patterns of association with SAD and interpersonal vulnerabilities, suggesting that these dynamic features capture different aspects of perceived rejection.

articles_hidden.title: An Integrative Somatic Approach to Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy:  Theoretical Foundations and Biological Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Devon Christie; Manesh Girn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) has demonstrated transdiagnostic efficacy across a range of psychiatric conditions and is increasingly conceptualized through third-wave cognitive–behavioral frameworks. These frameworks, including Contextual Behavioral Science (CBS) and the psychological flexibility model, emphasize processes such as cognitive insight, belief revision, and narrative meaning-making as central to therapeutic change in PAT. While valuable, they often under-specify the embodied, autonomic, and relational dynamics that patients and clinicians frequently identify as central to both therapeutic benefit and potential risk

In this paper, we introduce Integrative Somatic Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy (ISPAT), a process-based framework that extends psychological flexibility by explicitly centering interoceptive processing, autonomic nervous system regulation, and co-regulated relational presence as core mechanisms of change in psychedelic-assisted therapy. Drawing upon complexity science, trauma-informed somatic psychotherapy, and contemporary neurobiological models of psychedelic action, ISPAT conceptualizes the human psyche as an embodied, relational, and dynamic adaptive system. 

Within this framework, psychedelics are understood as controlled perturbations that temporarily relax rigid patterns of cognition, affect, interoceptive-autonomic functioning, and interpersonal relating. ISPAT articulates how somatic awareness, autonomic regulation, and relational safety can scaffold psychological flexibility across preparation, medicine, and integration phases, helping guide psychedelic-induced reorganization toward coherence rather than fragmentation. By expanding PAT beyond cognicentric formulations, ISPAT offers a scientifically grounded and clinically actionable framework for understanding how psychedelic pharmacology interfaces with embodied and relational processes to shape therapeutic outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: As life happens: Prospectively studying the temporal dynamics of autobiographical and collective narratives
articles_hidden.authors: Ziming Cheng; Öykü Ekinci; Samuel Fynes-Clinton; William Fisher; Karl Szpunar; Buddhika Bellana; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: Autobiographical and collective experiences both contribute to memories for lifetime periods, but how these narratives evolve over time remains unclear. The COVID-19 pandemic allowed us to prospectively track the development of these narratives as a new lifetime period unfolded. Across nine surveys conducted during 2020-2021, participants wrote pandemic “chapters” for their autobiography and for a history book. We used natural language processing (NLP) to track measure features of lifetime period narratives. First, Automated Autobiographical Interview Scoring and Structural Topic Modelling provided evidence of distinct mnemonic representations: autobiographical narratives contained more episodic detail and personal topics, while collective narratives focused more on public topics. We also found differences between narrative types in how the use of personal and public topics changed over time. Second, Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) quantified the semantic similarity between pairs of narratives, providing evidence of increasing integration between autobiographical and collective narratives, and that both types of narratives remained anchored to the origin narrative for the lifetime period. Intersubject similarity analyses on USE data revealed that pairs of narratives from participants residing in the same region (European Union, North America and United Kingdom) had slightly higher similarity that different-region pairs. Interestingly, different-regions pairs showed steeper increases over time suggesting that despite initial differences, the pandemic gave rise to a shared narrative representation across regions. Our prospective method provides insights into how autobiographical and collective narratives converge and stabilize as a lifetime period is being lived – effects impossible to investigate from a fully retrospective standpoint.

articles_hidden.title: EFFECTS OF SELECTED PSYCHOLOGICAL SKILLS INTERVENTION ON SELF-CONFIDENCE AMONG BENDEL INSURANCE FOOTBALL CLUB PLAYERS
articles_hidden.authors: Celina Abayomi; F. M. Adeyeye; Adewunmi C. M.
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The study was designed to establish the effectiveness of selected psychological skills interventions in improving self confidence among Bendel Insurance Football Club players. To guide the study, one research question and one corresponding hypothesis was raised and  formulated. 
Methods: The study adopted a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design. The population comprised players of Bendel Insurance Football Club. The sample consisted of 49 players aged between 19 and 26 years. Data collected using Athletic Self-Confidence Scale were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics involving Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) at the 0.05 level of significance.
Findings: The findings of the study revealed significant improvements in psychological characteristics of involving self-confidence of players in the experimental group compared with the control group which indicated that the intervention significantly increased players' self-confidence of players. The study concluded that selected psychological skills interventions are effective in enhancing self-confidence of Bendel Insurance Football players, which is necessary for improved competition performance. Consequently, it was recommended among others that football clubs should incorporate structured psychological skills training programmes into their routine training schedules to ensure that mental preparation that builds self-confidence receives the same level of attention as physical, technical, and tactical training.

Keywords: Athletic Self-Confidence Scale, Bendel Insurance Football Players, Psychological Skills Intervention, Self-Confidence.

articles_hidden.title: Psychosocial Characteristics and Objective Performance in Immersive Virtual Reality: Associations of Social Support, Psychological Distress, and Education with Psychomotor Speed and Cognitive Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Katerina Denaxa; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos
articles_hidden.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) can quantify cognitive and psychomotor performance, but interpreting its scores requires establishing whether they also vary with psychosocial characteristics. This study examined associations of perceived support, psychological distress, and education with immersive performance across adulthood, including whether support associations differed by interaction mode, age, or education. Two hundred and two adults aged 19–90 years completed a five-mode VR Fitts' law task, the Trail Making Test in VR (TMT-VR), the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales. Hierarchical mixed-effects models retained the repeated task structure; multiplicity-controlled exploratory analyses examined the complete 26-variable TMT-VR battery and focused moderation tests. In the Fitts task, distress showed no clear association with task time or the application-defined Accuracy Index, and education added no independent task-time association beyond age. Higher support accompanied slightly slower adjusted task times, opposite to expectation, without supported differences by mode, age, or education. In TMT-VR, age and Part were the principal correlates of completion time. Support, distress, and education did not show broad associations with completion time, wrong-target errors, or error-adjusted time after multiplicity correction. One exploratory association survived correction: participants reporting more support showed a smaller increase in wrong-target errors from Part A to Part B, with no difference in overall error level. Distress was unrelated to every TMT-VR outcome after correction, including the application-defined mean selection distance. Within this generally high-support, low-symptom sample, psychosocial differences between participants were therefore not consistent correlates of conventional immersive cognitive outcomes. This finding informs the interpretation of non-clinical assessments without implying that support or distress is unimportant within an individual. Longitudinal studies should test whether changes in a person's psychosocial circumstances accompany cognitive change during healthy ageing or cognitive vulnerability. The support association with the Part B minus Part A error increment shows how a contrast between task demands can carry information that neither the overall error level nor completion time captures; it is exploratory and requires replication.

articles_hidden.title: Preferred Terminology for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Among ADHD-Related Interest Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Dodgson; Carolynn Hare; Renee Leow-Guerville; Rachel Mack; Katarina Jovanovic; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract:
The conversation surrounding disability and mental health has changed dramatically in recent decades, with many groups advocating for the use of new language and forms of social analysis. We examined preferences for different Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) related terminology, including person/identity first language, and describing ADHD as either a form of neurodiversity or a disability. Three ADHD interest groups participated: people with ADHD (n=232), parents of ADHD people (n=79), people who work in an ADHD-related field (n=172), and members of the public (n=134; total N=536). All groups preferred person-first language, and framing ADHD as something that you have. Opinions of identity-first language, and framing ADHD as something you are were correlated with one another, but not our measure of ADHD identity; we therefore believe these to reflect a preference for grammatical correctness, rather than a statement on one’s views of ADHD as an identity.

Keywords: ADHD, Neurodiversity, Disability, Terminology

articles_hidden.title: Cox versus Discrete-Time Models in Behavioral Research: A Simulation Study of Predictive Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Hyungjun Park; Mike W.-L. Cheung
articles_hidden.abstract: The Cox proportional-hazards model is the standard for survival prediction, although discrete-time models are often recommended as an alternative in behavioral research. Discrete-time models theoretically handle the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events better, but whether this theoretical advantage translates to better predictions under behavioral-research conditions has not been systematically tested. The present study compared six survival prediction models (Cox, elastic-net Cox, gradient-boosted Cox, random survival forest, logistic hazards, and multi-task logistic regression) via simulation under all combinations of sample size, number of time points, event rate, and hazard distribution. Each model's predictive performance was evaluated by the concordance index, mean absolute error, and integrated Brier score. Results on the concordance index and mean absolute error were broadly comparable across all six models in every condition tested. Results on the integrated Brier score showed that the Cox-family models consistently performed worse than the discrete-time models and random survival forest, although this was attributed to how the Cox-family models estimate baseline hazards, not how they handle the proportional-hazards assumption or tied events. Overall, concerns about the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events overstate the case against the Cox model. The Cox model remains a reasonable default for prediction, with discrete-time alternatives favored when probabilistic calibration matters; whether the calibration advantage is substantial enough to justify the additional implementation effort remains unclear. Possible directions for future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A scoping review of community engagement and implementation outcomes for approaches  to adapt mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Tschida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth are commonly adapted for use in community-based settings and, more increasingly, with community-engaged  research methods (Stahmer et al., 2005). However, it is unknown which adaptation method, including what level of community engagement, may be most effective and feasible for (1) enhancing the fit of mental and behavioral health EBPs with autistic client needs in a community 
service context and, (2) improving implementation and intervention outcomes (Dickson et al., 2021). Using the Model for Adaptation Design and Impact (MADI; Kirk et al., 2020) and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research (Key et al., 2019), this scoping review aimed to fill this research gap by assessing approaches to adapt mental and behavioral health EBPs for autistic youth served in community-based settings from existing literature. Data sources included PsycInfo, PubMed, and Web of Science. Article eligibility criteria included (a) reported in English, (b) describes EBP adaptation, (c) includes children with autism spectrum diagnoses and/or their caregivers, and (d) considers community-based mental and behavioral health settings. Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines, an initial literature search (n = 349) was followed by title and abstract screening (n = 230), full text review (n = 121), and data charting and analysis (n = 37). Frequencies were obtained for MADI and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research domains reported and assessed across studies. Qualitative content analysis also was used to yield more nuanced descriptions of each adaptation approach and related context, feasibility, and empirical support (Graneheim & Lundman, 2004). Context 
surrounding adaptation, common factors for feasible and effective adaptation methods, and two effective and feasible exemplar methods to were identified. Overall, this scoping review contributes to science found at the intersection of autism research, implementation science, and community-engaged research. Further, it has the potential to inform and improve efforts to adapt and implement EBPs in community-based settings and consequently improve wellbeing among 
autistic youth and their families.

articles_hidden.title: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation as a tool to causally modulate the human hippocampus
articles_hidden.authors: Craig McFarland; Miriam Klein-Flugge; Helen Barron; Valentina Mancini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Non-invasive brain stimulation has, until recently, had limited effect on deep brain circuits critical for memory. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising tool to address this limitation. By delivering spatially focused acoustic energy, TUS enables targeted modulation of deep brain structures such as the hippocampus. TUS therefore provides new opportunities to causally modulate activity in neural circuits important for memory.
Objective: This perspective discusses how TUS provides a potential methodological advance for human memory research, examining the mechanistic basis of the technology, emerging empirical evidence, and outstanding interpretative and technical limitations.
Methods: We synthesise human and animal TUS studies targeting hippocampal and other memory-relevant circuits, compare TUS with alternative brain stimulation approaches and discuss potential clinical applications for TUS in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and medial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE).
Results: TUS provides a tool to modulate activity in deep circuits that have been inaccessible to other forms of non-invasive brain stimulation. Human TUS studies to date document changes in neurochemistry, functional connectivity, and memory-relevant behaviour. Moreover, clinical studies in AD and mTLE report memory improvement and seizure reduction, respectively. To guide future work, we outline five critical considerations: uncertain directionality of effects, individual differences in delivered acoustic dose, state-dependence of outcomes, evidence of lasting synaptic modification, and standardisation of protocols.
Conclusions: TUS holds promise for studying and enhancing human memory. Realising this potential will require concurrent neuroimaging or electrophysiology to verify target engagement, and close attention to individual differences in dose and brain state, together with cross-laboratory standardisation.

articles_hidden.title: Social Isolation and Ambition: A Two-Wave Correlational Study of School Ostracism and Goal Abandonment in High-Achieving Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandr Anikeev
articles_hidden.abstract: Independent student research project examining the relationship between chronic school peer ostracism and thoughts of abandoning ambitious personal goals in high-achieving adolescents. Across two independent samples (Wave 1, N = 82, CIS-based Co-founder ecosystem; Wave 2, N = 35, international communities), we find a robust positive correlation between school ostracism and goal-abandonment ideation (pooled N = 117; r ≈ 0.61). A formal Baron-Kenny mediation analysis supports full mediation through school burnout. This OSF project contains the manuscript, anonymized Wave 2 data, and a reproducibility analysis script.

articles_hidden.title: Resilience Beyond Symptom Reduction: A Dual-Dimension Model of Distress and Adaptation Under Continuous Traumatic Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Netali Mor; Rivka Tuval-Mashiach; Yifat Reuveni
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Traditional trauma models often view resilience merely as the absence of clinical symptoms. Applying the dual-continua framework to Continuous Traumatic Stress (CTS) during the ongoing Swords of Iron war, this study examined whether psychological distress and positive adaptation function as distinct, coexisting dimensions among civilians under active threat, while mapping differential predictors for each dimension.
Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 674 Israeli adults approximately 18 months following the war's outbreak. Validated measures assessed trauma exposure, sociodemographic, clinical distress (depression, anxiety, PTSS), individual resilience, and post-traumatic growth (PTG). Dimensionality was evaluated via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), further supported by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and followed by multiple regression analyses predicting each dimension. 
Results: PCA and SEM analyses confirmed two empirically distinct dimensions: Distress (encompassing depression, anxiety, and PTSS) and Adaptation (encompassing resilience and PTG). Trauma exposure extent, younger age, and female gender significantly predicted higher scores across both dimensions. Conversely, receiving mental health treatment and lower income uniquely predicted Distress, whereas active combat participation uniquely predicted Adaptation. 
Conclusions: Psychological distress and positive adaptation coexist under CTS through shared and dimension-specific mechanisms, supporting a nuanced model of continuous adaptation. Interventions during prolonged adversity should not rely solely on symptom reduction; psychological care must incorporate a dual-dimension model to simultaneously relieve distress and actively cultivate adaptive resources. Limitations: Reliance on traditional 'post'-trauma instruments limit the precise assessment of dynamic adaptation during ongoing CTS, and the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptions and Outcomes of Artificial Intelligence Among Back-office Employees: A Systematic Literature Review
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Igorevna Efremova; Oliver Runswick; Myanna Duncan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace is rapidly evolving. Employees’ perceptions of AI are of increasing interest, particularly in relation to their psychological wellbeing and performance outcomes. This systematic review extends existing research by synthesising recent empirical evidence on the impact of AI among back-office employees across a range of industries and functions, an occupational group that is particularly exposed to AI-driven technologies. Following PRISMA guidelines, eight databases were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published in English between January 2022 and January 2026. A total of 40 eligible studies were included in the review. Findings indicated that employee perceptions of AI were largely positive, although experiences across industries and occupations varied. AI adoption and performance outcomes were commonly related to perceived usefulness, ease of use, and the extent to which the organisation was ready to adopt AI. These outcomes were also associated with fears of job displacement and de-skilling, but these relationships were unexamined quantitatively. AI’s workplace value appears contingent on employee perceptions and organisational context, rather than just on the technology. 

Key words: AI at work, AI adoption, back-office employees, technology acceptance

articles_hidden.title: Perspective taking is context-dependent: The relation among perspective taking, sleep, and affect in an acute psychiatric sample
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Michelle Bowers; Courtney Beard; Chloe Hudson
articles_hidden.abstract: Perspective taking is a central component of social cognition linked to interpersonal functioning and psychiatric symptomatology. Although it is traditionally viewed as a stable trait, emerging evidence suggests it may fluctuate with momentary contextual factors. In the current study, we investigated the longitudinal association between perspective taking, sleep, and affect in a clinically heterogenous psychiatric sample. Participants were 900 patients (M age = 36.33, SD = 14.50, 58.89% female, 78.89% non-Hispanic White) who completed the Interpersonal Reactivity Index Perspective Taking subscale, Positive and Negative Affect Schedule, and the Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index throughout a two-week partial hospital program. Our multilevel modeling results indicate that greater positive and lower negative affect were significantly associated with more frequent perspective taking.
