Sleep duration was not significantly associated with perspective taking. The results support a shift toward conceptualizing perspective taking as a contextually sensitive process in psychiatric populations.

articles_hidden.title: Critical Perspectives Towards Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and How They Contribute Towards ADHD Attitudes Among Related Interest Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Dodgson; Carolynn Hare; Renee Leow-Guerville; Rachel Mack; Katarina Jovanovic; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract:
From its earliest conceptions, some have challenged the concept of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) as pathologization of normal childhood behavior. In this study we aimed to examine how different conceptions of ADHD contribute to attitudes towards ADHD. We asked participants about whether they felt ADHD was a Disability, a Scientific or Social Construct, and whether they viewed ADHD through the medical model and social model of disability. Additionally, we collected a measure of attitudes towards ADHD and misconceptions about ADHD. Three ADHD interest groups participated: people with ADHD (n=232), parents of ADHD people (n=79), people who work in an ADHD-related field (n=172), and members of the public (n=134; total N=536). We found that having ADHD, being a parent of an ADHD child, and working in and ADHD-related field all predicted more positive attitudes and lesser endorsement of the ADHD-related misconceptions. Knowledge about ADHD was the most consistent predictor for positive attitudes. The social construct view of ADHD was associated with more negative attitudes towards ADHD, and greater endorsement of ADHD-related misconceptions. Viewing ADHD as a disability was inconsistently associated with an improvement in attitudes (ADHD and professionals groups only), and inconsistently with a reduction of misconceptions (parent and public groups only). We conclude that examining ADHD as a social construct or through the social model of disability may not be an appropriate tool for stigma reduction for ADHD. 

Keywords: ADHD, Neurodiversity, Disability, Social Model of Disability, Social Constructs

articles_hidden.title: Shared Dimensions, Divergent Patterns: Multidimensional Well-Being Among Cultural Majority and Minoritized Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Jozefien De Leersnyder
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents adapt constantly to their social environments, which can support certain functions while limiting others. In intercultural contexts, adolescents share institutions but hold different social positions and cultural references. Consequently, similar overall well-being scores can mask entirely different combinations of health, relationships, and material conditions—a limitation of single total scores. Well-being and acculturation research approach this problem differently. Well-being research provides broad theories but typically focuses on global indicators within Western majority samples, while acculturation research studies adaptation in intercultural contexts but primarily examines minorities and separates psychological adjustment from sociocultural competence. Researchers currently lack a common multidimensional framework to capture well-being variations among adolescents sharing an intercultural environment. We addressed this gap in 1,385 Belgian-majority and Turkish–Moroccan minoritized adolescents using exploratory and multigroup factor analyses, which supported a broadly comparable five-domain structure. This demonstrates that a common framework can apply across groups while accommodating meaningful differences in how well-being is experienced and organized. Item-level differences formed a mixed profile rather than a consistent advantage for either group. Cross-sectional Gaussian graphical models revealed differences in overall edge-weight structure and global strength, with greater aggregate connectivity in the Turkish–Moroccan network, though no individual edge difference survived correction. Across both groups, the strongest associations clustered within domains alongside cross-domain links. These findings suggest that adolescent well-being is better understood as a multidimensional system than as a single score: shared dimensions can coexist with different profiles and relational organization. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these patterns reflect contextual conditions, cultural orientations, or their interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring cultural and individual differences in the hierarchy of moral concern: Evidence from student samples across 41 cultural groups
articles_hidden.authors: Işıl Ayça Akkuş; Charlie R Crimston; Kelly Kirkland; Brock Bastian; Bastian Jaeger
articles_hidden.abstract: Disagreement about the rights and protections owed to different individuals underpins many important historical and current debates (e.g., on the abolishment of slavery, the feminist movement, abortion, and environmental protection). Recent work on moral concern (i.e., the subjectively felt moral obligation to consider an individual’s welfare and interests) has uncovered a seemingly robust hierarchy. For example, people extend most moral concern toward family and friends, followed by ingroup members (e.g., a co-worker), outgroup members (e.g., a foreign citizen), the environment (e.g., a coral reef), and, lastly, criminals (e.g., a murderer). However, these studies were all conducted in a few countries from the Anglosphere, raising doubt about the cross-cultural generalizability of the results. We analyzed a data set with 6,665 participants recruited from 41 cultural groups to explore cultural and individual variation in the hierarchy of moral concern. We find that (1) on average, across the 41 cultural groups, 11 of the 13 rankings in the typical hierarchy of moral concern replicated, pointing to substantial cultural similarities; (2) countries that are culturally more similar to the reference sample from the initial U.S. study showed a more similar hierarchy; (3) some rankings (e.g., prioritizing family and friends over human ingroups) replicated more often than others (e.g., prioritizing human outgroups over the environment) across countries; and (4) both cultural and individual differences were largest most pronounced examining people’s concern for non-human animals and the environment.

articles_hidden.title: Loneliness and alcohol use in alcohol use disorder: A longitudinal within-person analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Kräplin; Michael A Rapp; Jan Luca Wiedenhöft; Gianna Spitta; Louisa Diallo; Shuyan Liu; Tobias Banaschewski; Andreas Heinz; Fabian Arntz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Alcohol use is a major public health concern and a leading cause of preventable disease and death worldwide. Loneliness has been identified as a psychosocial risk factor associated with negative mental health outcomes such as increased alcohol use and alcohol-related problems through stress-relieving or self-medication processes. In turn, alcohol use may exacerbate loneliness through social and interpersonal consequences. Our goal was to examine the longitudinal dynamics of these factors in a population with alcohol use disorder (AUD).
Methods: Data were drawn from the Collaborative Research Center Transregio (TRR) 265 longitudinal cohort study, which included adults with AUD who were assessed across four waves with 4 months in-between waves. Alcohol use was measured by frequency, quantity, binge drinking of alcohol, and the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). Subjective loneliness was assessed using the UCLA Loneliness Scale. Dynamic panel models were used to examine within-person associations over time. Gender and age were tested as moderators.
Results: Analyses revealed no evidence that loneliness predicts subsequent alcohol consumption frequency, quantity, or binge drinking episodes. However, elevated loneliness was associated with lower subsequent AUDIT scores. This relationship was significantly moderated by baseline age, specifically, the negative association was more pronounced among older birth cohorts. In contrast, alcohol use did not significantly predict subsequent loneliness across any indicator. No evidence of gender interactions was observed.
Conclusions: The relationship between loneliness and alcohol use appears asymmetric rather than bidirectional, characterized primarily by fluctuations in problematic drinking rather than consumption levels in an AUD sample over four waves with four-month intervals. Diverging from self-medication hypotheses, loneliness was associated with fewer alcohol-related problems, particularly among older adults. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between alcohol consumption and alcohol-related problems and of using within-person approaches to understand their dynamic interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles_hidden.title: Effectiveness of Culturally Adapted Group CBT for ADHD Among Indian University Students: A Large-Scale Comparative Study from Greater Noida
articles_hidden.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) persisting into adulthood is associated with significant academic and functional impairment among university students in India. However, culturally adapted, scalable psychological interventions remain limited.
Objective:   To evaluate the effectiveness of a culturally adapted 26-session group CBT compared to a supportive academic group for university students with ADHD.
Methods:  IEC-approved study (Ref: IEC/IILMU/PSYCH/2026/01, dated 15 March 2026) included 674 university students (21-26 years) meeting DSM-5-TR criteria from Greater Noida. Allocated to Group CBT (n=337) and Supportive Academic Group (n=337) based on counselling centre availability. Primary outcome: CAARS. Secondary outcomes: NIMHANS Battery. Assessments at baseline, post-intervention (12 weeks) and 3-month follow-up. Intent-to-treat analysis with LMM, MLE. Written informed consent obtained.
Results:  LMM revealed significant Group × Time interactions for all outcomes. CBT showed greater reductions in inattention [F(2,1344)=268.42, p<.001, d=2.31, 95% CI 2.12-2.50, 41.6% reduction] and hyperactivity-impulsivity [F(2,1344)=189.76, p<.001, d=1.58] and improvements in executive function [F(2,1344)=312.55, p<.001, d=1.18, 21.0% increase]. Gains maintained at 3-month follow-up. Mean attendance 89.3%, fidelity 92%, no adverse events.
Conclusions:  Culturally adapted group CBT is effective, feasible and scalable for Indian university students with ADHD and may be implemented in university counselling settings.
 Keywords: ADHD, group CBT, executive function, university students, India, culturally adapted

articles_hidden.title: A Bayesian method for representing the process of accumulating evidence over time: The case of forgetting curve models
articles_hidden.authors: Yui Furukawa; Kensuke Okada
articles_hidden.abstract:
In the practice of cognitive modeling, comparing and organizing proposed models plays a crucial role in refining psychological theory. Secondary data analysis provides a useful framework for such evaluations, enabling researchers to assess models across multiple datasets. Bayes factors (BFs) are valuable tools for evaluating the generalizability of cognitive models in this context. However, a standardized framework for model evaluation using BFs across multiple secondary datasets has yet to be established.
This study proposes a Bayesian model comparison method for assessing the generalizability of cognitive models, focusing on how evidence changes as secondary datasets accumulate over time. The proposed method enables (1) quantitative evaluation of model support across all datasets, (2) evaluation of how model support changes as datasets accumulate, and (3) parameter interpretation alongside model comparison. Using the forgetting curve as an illustrative example, we confirmed the method’s basic properties under the examined simulation conditions and examined its usefulness using secondary datasets.
In the simulations, BF-based model comparison supported the data-generating model under many examined conditions, and the method produced outputs corresponding to the intended properties. In the empirical study, the most strongly supported model differed across retention-interval subsets. The exploratory expectation of a publication-year-related shift from the power model to the linear model was not supported. Overall, the results illustrate how the proposed method can be used to evaluate model support across multiple datasets and to trace how evidence accumulates over time.
The Stage 1 protocol received in-principle acceptance on 13 May 2026 and is available at https://osf.io/z74cn.

articles_hidden.title: What are the merits of identifying as neurodivergent? Assessing the effects of neurodiversity labels on the evaluation of and stigmatizing attitudes towards people exhibiting autistic traits.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Maya Kaiser; Laura Jungnitz; Milena Sophia de Bruin; Luc Weilandt; Marie Ballhause; Felix Strakeljahn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
With the neurodiversity movement gaining traction, people with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and other diagnoses have begun self-identifying as neurodivergent and report that this manner of disclosure boosts their self-esteem and well-being. However, little is known about how self-labelling as neurodivergent changes public perception about the people self-labelling as neurodivergent. This study explores how neurodiversity labels influence stigmatizing and empowering public perceptions of people displaying ASD-typical characteristics.

Methods
In a three-armed online-experiment, 1215 participants received a text-vignette describing a male adult with everyday life challenges typically associated with ASD. The man was either labelled as neurodivergent/neurodiverse, autistic, or not labelled. Participants then rated the described man in terms of social, general, and self-regulation competencies and answered questionnaires on stigmatizing and empowering beliefs about the presented person and/or people like him.

Results
In the neurodiversity-label and no-label conditions, ratings on social competencies and emotional stability were higher than in the autism condition. The crucial stigmatization components blame and desired social distance were significantly lower in the neurodiversity- and autism-label conditions than in the no-label condition.

Conclusion
Across all public perception outcome categories, using a neurodiversity label provided the optimal balance of benefits. This highlights how self-identifying as neurodivergent (rather than by one’s diagnosis) may be a way to circumvent some public stigma when disclosing one’s challenges and warrants further investigation into the generalizability and stability of such effects.

articles_hidden.title: Mediators and moderators of the relationship between maternal childhood adversity and offspring´ outcomes during early childhood: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Rabasa Serrano; Sandra Doval; Belén Fernández; Marta Giménez-Dasí
articles_hidden.abstract:
Maternal adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) can lead to intergenerational effects beginning in the earliest stages of offspring development. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the biopsychosocial pathways linking maternal ACEs to offspring outcomes from birth to age 3. The systematic review evaluated both mediators and moderators of these associations, whereas the meta-analysis focused exclusively on mediation effects. A total of 41 studies were included in the systematic review and 26     in the meta-analysis, covering publications up to September 2025. 
Findings indicate that maternal mental health—including distress (c’ = 0.045, 95% CI: 0.011–0.086), depression (c’ = 0.020, 95% CI: 0.010–0.033), and anxiety (c’ = 0.018, 95% CI: 0.009–0.030)—emerged as the most robust and consistent mediator. Other mediators, such as physical health problems, parenting style (c’ = 0.011, 95% CI: 0.003–0.020), and broader psychosocial factors (c’ = 0.014, 95% CI: -0.001–0.034), showed more variable or context-dependent associations when integrating evidence from both the review and the meta-analysis. The systematic review also identified several biological moderators of intergenerational risk, including child sex, age, markers of cellular aging, and genetic factors. 
Taken together, these findings underscore the complex pathways through which maternal ACEs influence offspring development and highlight maternal mental health as a key target for early identification and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Harmonizing Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) in Mental Health Research and Services: A Delphi Study on an EMA Core Item Set
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Rauschenberg; Annette Brose; Joshua M Smyth; Peter Kuppens; Peter Wilhelm; Inez Myin-Germeys; Harald Baumeister; Christine Knaevelsrud; Pascal-M. Aggensteiner; Patrick Bach
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) captures experience and behavior as they occur in daily life, yielding intensive longitudinal data that are well suited for modeling within- and between-person processes and outcomes. However, heterogeneity in EMA items across studies hampers comparability, data aggregation, and reproducibility.
Objective: To establish expert consensus on an EMA core item set, a standardized set of momentary variables from which comparable phenotypic indicators can later be derived. This minimum item set aims to be broadly applicable yet concise enough for use in large-scale research consortia and routine care while maintaining minimal completion time and assessment burden, adopting a nested structure (i.e., minimum core, extended core, add-on modules).
Methods: A Delphi study was conducted with support from an international expert panel (J.S., P.K., I.M-G., P.W., M.L.) and 50 invited EMA experts from the German Center for Mental Health (DZPG). Candidate items were derived from prior work, the international expert panel, as well as a narrative review. The items were iteratively refined between Delphi rounds based on aggregated ratings and expert comments. They were assigned to one of three layers – the minimum core, extended core, or add-on modules – according to their degree of generality, the minimum core comprising the most broadly applicable items. A priori consensus was set at ≥75% endorsement. Rating stability and qualitative agreement informed revisions. Experts additionally reported on current methodological EMA practices (e.g., sampling frequency, study duration).
Results: The EMA core phenotype was established in three rounds. Participation was n=41 in Round 1 (82%), n=43 in Round 2 (86%), and n=40 in Round 3 (80%). Of 69 initial item candidates, 37 partly revised items remained in the three-tiered structure. The finalized EMA minimum core (7 items) comprises four affect items, one item on social context, and two items on positive and negative events. The EMA extended core includes 5 additional items (total 12) on affect, social context, and activities. Completion time for both the minimum and extended core remains low. More specific items (e.g., self-esteem) are reserved for more specific EMA add-on modules.
Conclusions: The consensus-derived DZPG EMA core phenotype provides a consented, ready-to-use item set that balances information yield with minimal assessment burden. By harmonizing EMA assessment across studies, it facilitates comparability, data pooling, and reproducible research while supporting integration into large-scale digital mental health assessment and intervention pipelines. The EMA core will be maintained as a living, versioned measure. Ongoing initiatives include a prospectively specified, multi-study validation program of items, systematic variation of design and assessment procedures (e.g., answering formats), as well as cross-cultural adaptation of the EMA core phenotype.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Properties of the Swedish version of the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) in a mixed trauma sample – a comprehensive evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Kristina Bondjers; Albin Granlöf; Josefin Sveen; Filip K. Arnberg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. The International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) is the most widely used self-report measure of ICD-11 PTSD and Complex PTSD (CPTSD), but its psychometric properties have not been evaluated in a Swedish context, and few studies have examined its properties as a screening tool against clinician-assessed PTSD and CPTSD. 
Methods. In a Swedish adult trauma-exposed sample (N = 276), we examined internal consistency, test–retest reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, and the latent structure of the standard 12-item ITQ and an extended item pool with the 22-item developer version (D-ITQ) using confirmatory factor analysis. In a subsample assessed with the International Trauma Interview (n = 248), we evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of ITQ scores and algorithms and compared pattern of subscale scores across clinician-assessed diagnostic groups.
Results. Reliability was good for the ITQ total, PTSD, and DSO scores but low for affective dysregulation (α = .53). Factor models for the standard ITQ produced inadmissible solutions, with affective dysregulation and difficulties in relationships empirically inseparable (r = 1.09). The D-ITQ had no improper estimates but global fit remained inadequate and the two factors stayed highly correlated. ITQ sum score thresholds showed high overall accuracy, but levels of specificity were low on ≥ .80 sensitivity for PTSD. Algorithm-based classifications showed high specificity but modest sensitivity for PTSD and low positive predictive value for CPTSD. Subscale profiles matched ICD-11 expectations, with negative self-concept showing the largest divergence between PTSD and CPTSD cases. 
Conclusions. The Swedish ITQ is reliable and valid for symptom assessment and screening but is best complemented by clinical assessment. Persistent difficulty separating DSO factors, together with the two-item factors, suggests that a version of the ITQ with more items would be valuable for future research on the ICD-11 constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Lab culture and the PI
articles_hidden.authors: Rosanne L. Rademaker; Christine Pfund; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Academic scientists are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of mentorship and the cohesion of a lab community for research productivity and trainee well-being. Moreover, funding agencies have started to mandate action around mentorship and management of interpersonal relationships within labs. Here, we consider these aspects in the context of the broader culture of a lab and emphasize the crucial role that the principal investigator plays in shaping that culture. We propose a framework for thinking about lab culture in terms of norms, values, responsibilities, expectations, processes, and procedures. We describe how lab documentation can support a strong lab culture and mentoring environment by making the elements of lab culture explicit and clear, while still allowing for flexibility and continual revision. We outline practical ways to get started on lab documentation, discuss contexts beyond the lab, and suggest strategies for troubleshooting. We hope that our framework will foster intentional and thoughtful approaches to lab documentation.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluation Frameworks for Gambling Harm Reduction: A Rapid Evidence Review of Outcome Measurement Approaches for Assessing Interventions in the UK.
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan Statton; Imogen Martin; Phoebe Weston-Stanley; Sokratis Dinos; Colin Walsh; James Close
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Current intervention trials for gambling harm reduction are dominated by Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) based approaches, usually measured by clinically-related outcome tools such as the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). To understand the broader ecosystem of intervention and measurement beyond this, we systematically review current outcome assessment for gambling harm reduction interventions (excluding CBT) in the UK and other comparable regulatory markets. 
Design 
A pre-registered rapid evidence review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, an approach well suited to areas with policy and regulatory relevance. 
Methods and Outcomes
Keyword searching (e.g. “gambling AND treatment AND reduction AND efficacy”) was conducted on Scopus, PsycInfo, and Medline with additional grey literature searches. Screening criteria identified publications that reported non-CBT gambling harm reduction interventions, published in English, conducted within the UK or other comparable regulatory market, using adult (18+) population. Publications were assessed for the type of intervention reported and approaches to measurement and assessing efficacy of interventions. Records were appraised with Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and analysed through Critical Interpretive Synthesis. 
Results 
Thirty nine records were identified that met inclusion criteria. Several trends were observed. First, a default to clinical measures (e.g. PGSI being 18/39 records), indicating a continued reliance on pathology derived approaches to harm reduction. Secondly, though many interventions were holistic, and used holistic outcome measures, their definitions of harm reduction were lacking, or relied on the default to pathology. Thirdly, there was a trade-off between validated and bespoke outcome measures, making comparison challenging. 
Conclusion 
Overall, there was generally a disconnect between the mechanism that interventions sought to work on (being largely psychosocial) and their outcome measures (gambling behaviour/ cessation). Future work should generate a clear definition of harm reduction informed by lived experience. To enable such complex outcome measurement, a core outcome set should be developed, as has been previously achieved for drug and alcohol harm research.  Following this, a shared “harm and recovery” tariff could allow different, validated measures to interoperate within such a core outcome set.

articles_hidden.title: Timing Is Everything: Modeling the Temporal Dynamics of Suicidal Ideation
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Julian Rubel; Juan Martín Gómez Penedo; Miriam Ina Hehlmann; Tobias Steinbrenner; Jay Lawrynowicz; Wolfgang Lutz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Suicidal ideation (SI) is a critical clinical concern, yet most predictive approaches rely on static or aggregate measures that overlook its session-to-session dynamics. This study aimed to improve next-session SI prediction by integrating dynamic item-level data and identifying the clinical features that contribute most strongly throughout treatment. Methods: 
Data from 2,045 outpatients were analyzed across the first 10 sessions. A transformer-based time-series model was trained to predict next-session SI using prior-session item-level scores and was compared against a static elastic-net baseline. SHAP values were calculated to quantify feature contributions at both group and individual levels. Results: The dynamic model significantly outperformed the static baseline (average R² = .95 vs. .12), and performance remained improved even without autoregressive inputs (average R² = .24). While prior-session SI was consistently the strongest predictor, depressive affect, hopelessness, meaning in life, and anxiety-related symptoms also provided significant predictive value. SHAP analyses further revealed temporal fluctuations and patient-specific patterns in influential features. Conclusion: Dynamic, interpretable models using item-level data substantially enhance short-term SI prediction. These findings provide clinical insights into which symptoms are most relevant for specific patients at different times, supporting more responsive and personalized suicide risk monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Crying as a Dynamic Multilevel Regulatory Process: A Scoping Review and Integrative Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Giaquinto
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of research, emotional crying remains an insufficiently integrated phenomenon, with its biological, cognitive, and interpersonal functions often investigated independently. This scoping review maps the existing literature on emotional crying and proposes a multilevel conceptual model of crying as a context-dependent regulatory process. Fifty-seven studies were included (44 primary studies and 13 theoretical or review papers). Evidence was organized according to both crier and observer perspectives, revealing a multilevel architecture linking antecedent appraisals, physiological regulation, neural mechanisms, cognitive representations, and interpersonal communication. Across studies, crying was associated with experiences of helplessness, emotional overload, and meaning-making, while also functioning as a social signal capable of influencing support-related responses and interpersonal dynamics. Observer-focused research further indicated that the effects of visible tears depend strongly on contextual, relational, and interpretative factors. Overall, these findings suggest that crying is better understood as an emergent multilevel regulatory process rather than as a simple emotional discharge. The proposed framework highlights dynamic interactions among biological, cognitive, and social systems that shape internal regulation and organism–environment exchanges. Within this perspective, emotional crying can be interpreted through the Thermodynamics of Mind framework as a process involving hierarchical transitions between mental states. Ultimately, this model integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal accounts of crying while providing a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Ageing, Digital Literacy, and Interaction Modality in Immersive Virtual Reality: Psychomotor Performance, Cognitive Flexibility, and Their Processing-Speed Association
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Katerina Denaxa; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Petros Roussos; Maria Roussou
articles_hidden.abstract: Extended reality (XR) increasingly supports training and cognitive assessment, yet the age sensitivity of its interaction techniques is unclear. This study examined age, digital literacy, and interaction modality as correlates of psychomotor and cognitive-flexibility performance in immersive virtual reality (VR). Two hundred and two adults (19–90 years) completed a five-mode Fitts' law task (eye-gaze, head-gaze, controller ray-casting, virtual finger, and controller direct touch), the Trail Making Test in VR (TMT-VR), and a digital-literacy questionnaire. Age was associated with slower task times across modes, but controller direct touch carried the steepest relative age gradient yet remained among the fastest in absolute terms; technique altered relative age sensitivity without determining absolute efficiency. Higher digital literacy was associated with faster TMT-VR completion but not Fitts task times. A Fitts-derived speed score predicted TMT-VR performance beyond age and partly accounted for its age association, consistent with shared processing-speed variance; an exploratory full-battery extension confined the Fitts-score association to completion-time and error-adjusted-time indices and the digital-literacy association to error-adjusted-time indices, not wrong-target errors, mean selection distance, or relative Part B indices. Age-inclusive XR assessment should standardise interaction modality, evaluate rather than exclude mid-air di-rect selection, and interpret cognitive scores alongside digital literacy and psychomotor speed.

articles_hidden.title: How Many Factors Underlie the WAIS-5? Evidence From the Australian and New Zealand Standardization Sample.
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles_hidden.abstract:
The latent structure of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fifth Edition (WAIS-5) is the subject of recent psychometric debate. Although the publisher's initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a theoretically derived five-factor model, a recent independent evaluation of the US standardisation sample found that complementary exploratory and confirmatory analyses favoured a hierarchical four-factor representation. The present study examined whether these findings could be independently replicated using the published WAIS-5 Australasian standardisation sample (N = 677).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation, followed by Schmid-Leiman transformation and model-based reliability and dimensionality analyses. Confirmatory analyses compared competing oblique, higher-order, and bifactor models evaluated in the US sample.
Factor-retention procedures did not support the proposed five-factor structure. Exploratory analyses consistently recovered four interpretable factors corresponding to Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, with Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning failing to emerge as distinct latent constructs. Confirmatory analyses identified the same higher-order (4h3) and bifactor (4b3) models as the preferred representations of the data. Model-based reliability analyses indicated a dominant general factor with smaller contributions from the broad cognitive abilities. Despite modest differences in model parameters, the central conclusions closely replicated those of the US sample.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on early adversity and resting-state EEG from infancy to adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Haleigh M. Brown; Emma Hart; Josué Rico-Picó; Kathryn N. Gray; Man Chen; Sonya V. Troller-Renfree
articles_hidden.abstract: Early adversity is theorized to alter brain activity detectable via resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), positioning it as a scalable tool in creating a global biomarker of brain health. Yet, the consistency of the association between adversity and EEG across the pediatric literature is unclear. We systematically reviewed 34 papers (N = 4245 EEG recordings) and meta-analytically synthesized 19 papers (N = 2669 EEG recordings, 228 effect sizes) on the association between early adversity and resting-state EEG power. Using a Correlated and Hierarchical Effects Model, we found a small, yet robust association (r = −0.086, 95% CI [−0.132, −0.040]) that withstood sensitivity analyses, publication bias correction, and was comparable for both correlational and randomized controlled trial designs. We found power (absolute, relative) significantly moderated the association, though adversity type, frequency band, resting-state EEG procedure, developmental life stage at EEG, and study design did not. The systematic review revealed a similar pattern of findings while also highlighting inconsistent reporting practices. This robust but modest effect suggests adversity is measurably linked to brain activity. However, with substantial unaccounted for heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting practices, EEG's promise as a scalable biomarker will depend as much on methodological standardization as on further biological characterization.

articles_hidden.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles_hidden.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 82% in 2025. Among 652 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 135 times; fewer than 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 30% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 40% referenced a missing file —shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable

articles_hidden.title: Memories of a shameful episode: Multiple access routes towards understanding self-memory integration
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Lukaschewski; Rebekka Heinen; Emil Eva Rosina; Carlos Alexandre Gomes; Frans Schalkwijk; Kristina Liefke; Oliver T. Wolf; Albert Newen; Nikolai Axmacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Shame, a self-conscious emotion, plays a crucial role in understanding the interplay between autobiographical memory and the self. Self-incongruent memories—particularly those eliciting shame—are often difficult to integrate with the self and may persist in a distressing and fragmented format. At the same time, it remains unclear how phenomenological, semantic, and behavioral access routes to autobiographical memory uniquely capture the effects of interventions and provide complementary insights into how such memories are represented and transformed. Here, we investigated the effects of a novel experimental shame-induction procedure and subsequent manipulations aiming to reduce self-incongruence. Healthy participants (N = 75) were instructed to sing a difficult song in front of a committee providing negative social feedback; salivary cortisol levels and subjective ratings indicated successful induction of shame and psychosocial stress. Participants were then assigned to self-affirmation, reframing, or control conditions. Phenomenological analyses revealed no significant group differences. By contrast, participants in the self-affirmation condition mentioned “not remembering” less often, produced semantically more similar narratives, used more negative emotion words (trend), and showed better recall for central objects from the shameful scene. Participants in the reframing condition produced more semantic jumps per sentence, indicating a less linear recall structure. Correlational analyses revealed associations across semantic, phenomenological, and object-memory variables. Finally, an exploratory factor analysis identified three representational profiles reflecting emotionally elaborated recall, a shame-prone defensive style, and a structural–behavioral dimension. These findings support a model of multiple access routes to autobiographical memory and highlight their convergence and divergence.

articles_hidden.title: Studies reporting bodily feedback effects on motivation have poor evidentiary value: a critical review and z-curve analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles_hidden.abstract: The embodied view of cognition holds that cognitive and emotional processes are grounded in our bodily experiences and physical interactions with the world. In line with this view, embodied motivation studies have purported to show that enacting motivation-related postures, expressions, and actions can elicit or modulate their corresponding motivational states. While theory-building reviews on the topic have accepted these studies’ conclusions at face value, a closer reading of key articles reveals several statistical issues that cast doubt on their veracity. The present review shows that evidence for bodily feedback effects on motivation relies on: (1) studies using multiple measures of motivation, and dismissing results from those that do not support hypotheses, (2) analytical degrees of freedom inflating the false positive rate, and (3) reviews on the topic interpreting non-significant hypothesis tests as if they were significant. Supporting this analysis of the literature, a z-curve on 52 significant results reported across 18 articles indicated little, if any, evidentiary value, with a dismal estimated replicability rate of 22%. In sum, there is little credible evidence that bodily postures modulate motivational states.

articles_hidden.title: Estimating Effects of Time-Varying Special Education Regimes Using Targeted Maximum Likelihood
articles_hidden.authors: Bryan Keller; Lindsey Liu; Yingqi Huan
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal treatments are common in social science research but are often reduced to ever-versus-never exposure indicators that obscure their time-varying nature. This study shows how causal questions can be clarified by defining treatments through explicit intervention regimes rather than collapsed summaries. We introduce this framework by linking the longitudinal setting to single-time-point causal inference and extending it to time-varying exposures, sequential identification assumptions, and estimation using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). We also address practical challenges, including missing data and positivity violations. Using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Kindergarten Class of 1998-1999 (ECLS-K), we examine the effect of special education participation on 5th-grade mathematics achievement. Comparing static and dynamic regimes, we find meaningful differences: always-treated versus never-treated contrasts yield the largest negative estimates, while rule-based dynamic regimes produce substantially smaller effects. These results highlight the importance of well-defined interventions for interpreting longitudinal treatment effects.

articles_hidden.title: Lifetime Engagement in the Activities of Parenthood (LEAP): Capturing personal transformation and the thinking and feeling work of parenthood across the lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Katia Manariti; Caroline Gurvich; Edwina R Orchard; Sharna Jamadar
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenthood contributes to lasting changes in brain structure, function, and cognition, with emerging evidence suggesting a neuroprotective effect against cognitive ageing. Long-term environmental complexity is a recognised contributor to cognitive reserve. We recently proposed that the enduring cognitive and emotional demands of parenthood represent a unique form of environmental complexity. However, the absence of a well-defined construct capturing lifetime engagement in parenthood limits our ability to examine its impact on the parental brain. This qualitative phase of a mixed methods study examines how parents conceptualise the cognitive demands of caregiving across the lifespan, providing a conceptual foundation for the Lifetime Engagement in the Activities of Parenthood (LEAP) scale. Twenty-nine parents (21 mothers, 8 fathers) participated in one of five focus groups exploring the psychological and environmental demands of parenthood. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist framework. Three themes were developed: thinking work, feeling work, and personal transformation, each enduring and evolving from the peripartum period into late life. Taken together, these findings position lifelong engagement in parenthood as a form of environmental complexity that may influence normative ageing and contribute to cognitive reserve in late life.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: The cascade from basic visual processing to social dysfunction: An extended path model in a transdiagnostic sample of youth.
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly Mathis; Scott D. Blain; Laura Rose Locarno; Carly A Lasagna; Colombi Costanza; Katharine N. Thakkar; Cynthia Z. Burton; Ivy Fei Tso
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Social dysfunction is widespread across psychiatric disorders, but treatments remain limited. Identifying underlying mechanisms could inform novel treatment approaches that meaningfully improve clinical outcomes. We previously showed that basic visual processing deficits cascade through gaze perception and emotion recognition to impair theory of mind. Here, we test an extended model assessing whether this cascade ultimately predicts real-world social dysfunction via theory of mind in an expanded sample.

Methods
A combined sample of 202 psychiatric patients with varying levels of social dysfunction and healthy individuals completed basic visual processing tasks, a multi-level social cognition battery that included measures of gaze perception, emotion recognition, and theory of mind, and clinical assessments of social functioning. A five-level path model evaluated the sequential cascade from visual processing to gaze perception, emotion recognition, theory of mind, and social functioning.

Results
The extended five-level path model demonstrated good fit to the data. Poorer basic visual processing sequentially predicted deficits across intermediate social cognitive domains, culminating in theory of mind, which directly predicted worse social functioning.

Conclusion
These findings indicate that basic visual deficits cascade through social cognitive steps to impair everyday social functioning. As a candidate shared mechanism contributing to social dysfunction, basic visual processing represents a promising target for psychiatric interventions.

articles_hidden.title: The Implicit Trait Function: Effectiveness as a Function of a Trait-Driven Antecedent Disposition
articles_hidden.authors: Stijn Schelfhout; Femke Timmerman; Eva Derous
articles_hidden.abstract: An implicit trait policy (ITP) comprises of a form of general domain knowledge (GDK), for which a worker’s knowledge of effectiveness interacts with (trait-driven antecedent) dispositions like agreeableness. Through this interaction, an ITP succeeds in predicting and explaining effective work behavior. Studies therefore use an ITP as a validation mechanism in research that aims to predict and explain future work behavior like situational judgement tests (SJTs). Currently, ITP literature still debates the nature and the validity of the ITP concept, while also pointing towards methodological problems in the field. The present study introduces the implicit trait function (ITF) that transforms the dimension of a trait-driven antecedent disposition into the dimension of effectiveness, for both workers as well as behavioral responses. Proactive and retrospective applications of this function demonstrate that an ITP exhibits ample levels of construct-related validity, provided that the measuring instrument, the measurement scoring key, and the subsequent ITP calculations are properly facilitated. The ITF thus renders a comprehensive framework that not only integrates key contributions from the ITP literature but also addresses contemporary challenges within the field.

articles_hidden.title: Collaboration, Creation, & Imagination: Exploring the Effects of Co-Imagination on Divergent Thinking
articles_hidden.authors: Zoe Fowler; Clin KY Lai; Roger Beaty; Brendan Bo O'Connor
articles_hidden.abstract: Creativity is essential in adaptively navigating the challenges of the future. While creativity research reveals the complex ways social context can influence creative outcomes, research on how we imagine the future has only just begun to explore imagination as a collaborative process (i.e., collaborative imagination, or co-imagination). How does collaborative imagination influence creative cognition? Across two studies (N = 162), we assess how imagining the future collaboratively rather than individually influences engagement in divergent thinking during imagination. This work quantified divergent thinking by measuring the semantic distance between all words spoken by a given participant in the narrative (i.e., Divergent Semantic Integration, or DSI). Study 1, run with university students in-lab, found no significant effects of collaborative imagine vs. individual imagine tasks on DSI scores. Exploratory analyses including social connection found that participants in the co-imagine condition had significantly higher DSI scores, though this model also revealed social connection related negatively to DSI scores. Study 2, run over video call with Prolific participants, did not replicate these findings. Together, these studies consider underexplored questions at the intersection of collaboration, imagination, and creativity, and provide tools for future research to investigate creative cognition in co-imagination.

articles_hidden.title: Psychotic-like experiences and neurobehavioral reward processing in adolescents who use cannabis
articles_hidden.authors: Shelley Gresko; Elizabeth Thompson; Meghan A. Gonsalves; Gillian LeBlanc; Elizabeth Lorenc; Jane Metrik; Michael Frank; Sarah Ryan; Emily Olenik; Leslie Brick
articles_hidden.abstract: Importance: Cannabis use (CU) in adolescence is linked to increased risk of developing psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) that can lead to lifelong impairment. A candidate mechanism may be disruptions in reward processing supported by dopamine but this association has not yet been tested in adolescents with CU and PLEs. The objective of the study was to assess the interrelation between CU, PLEs, and neurobehavioral markers of reward processing (behavioral reward motivation, tissue iron signal [1/nT2*], an indicator of dopamine-related neurophysiology). Methods: Participants were adolescents (aged 14 - 17) with either >11 lifetime cannabis episodes or <5 lifetime cannabis episodes (controls). CU quantity was assessed with the Daily Sessions, Frequency, Age of Onset, and Quantity of Cannabis Use Inventory. PLEs were assessed with the Achenbach Youth Self-Report Thought Problems Scale. Reward motivation (proportion of hard choices) was assessed using a behavioral task. 1/nT2* was derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging. Hypotheses, formulated during data collection as recognition grew of the risk factors of developing PLEs with CU, were: PLEs will magnify negative associations between CU and reward motivation; the positive association between greater CU and PLEs will depend on subcortical 1/nT2*. Results: 81 participants included 47 control and 34 cannabis group participants: mean [SD] age, 15.53 [1.12]; 52 female (64%). There was a significant interaction between CU and PLEs on reward motivation (OR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.10, 5.27, p=0.028), depending on reward amount and effort required. At high PLEs, the cannabis group, compared to controls, were less motivated to work for a reward when effort required was low and medium.  Associations between CU quantity and PLEs depended on 1/nT2* (at high 1/nT2*, CU positively predicted PLEs). Daily concentrate hits interacted with 1/nT2* in the left putamen (β=51.58, 95% CI, 12.07, 91.09, p=0.01) and right thalamus (β=70.93, 95% CI, 12.32, 129.54, p =0.02), daily cannabis grams in the left putamen (β=73.34, 95% CI, 12.32, 129.54, p=0.02), right putamen (β=101.69, 95% CI, 41.72, 161.67, p=0.001), and right thalamus (β=102.38, 95% CI, 28.00, 176.77, p=0.01). Conclusions and Relevance: Adolescent CU was associated with alterations in dopamine-relevant neural and behavioral indices as a function of PLEs. Behaviorally, this manifested as less reward motivation and strategic action. Consistent with prior research on psychosis-spectrum vulnerability and dopamine-related neurophysiology, elevated 1/nT2* was observed to moderate the link between CU and PLEs in key subcortical brain regions. Longitudinal studies are needed to understand the timing and mechanism of neurobehavioral reward processing alterations.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Formal Theory of Cognitive Effort: Application of Linear Control Theory to a Simple Cognitive Model of Controlled Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Clay B. Holroyd
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive effort is a defining feature of cognitive control but theories about its origin and purpose have long been controversial. Recently, it has been proposed that cognitive effort can be understood using linear control theory, a mathematical formalism developed in the engineering literature to control dynamical systems. On this view, effort levels reflect the energy required by the cognitive control system to support representational states that deviate from the intrinsic dynamics of the cognitive system. Although this approach has been used to characterize the energy landscape of neural networks abstracted from the human structural and functional connectome, it has yet to make contact with neurocomputational models of cognitive control. Here we demonstrate the potential of this approach by applying LCT to a classic computational model of cognitive control, and discuss its broader significance in the context of other models of cognitive effort and future studies that can test the theory.

articles_hidden.title: Interference in Long-Term Memory: Competition between Intentionally and Incidentally Acquired Memory Traces Leads to Forgetting
articles_hidden.authors: Melinda Sabo; Şahcan Özdemir; Anna Lena Mantei; Daniel Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract: Forgetting is a fundamental feature of human memory, yet questions remain about how long-term memories become vulnerable to interference. While previous work has focused on exploring interference between intentionally encoded long-term memories, it is less clear to what extent incidentally acquired long-term memories can also disrupt intentionally encoded ones. We address this question across two experiments (total N = 88). Participants encoded object-location associations into long-term memory. Afterwards, they completed a working memory task in which the same objects reappeared in the same or shifted locations (60° or 120°), or were absent, before a final long-term memory test. Results indicated that the interference induced via the working memory task impaired long-term memory retrieval, and that this effect was driven by swap errors. Occasionally, participants accidentally reported the task-irrelevant working memory location instead of the long-term memory one, indicating that they incidentally transferred the working memory task information to long-term memory. Experiment 2 sought to investigate the mechanisms underlying interference. Results showed that both maintenance and testing in working memory disrupted long-term memory, with the combination of maintenance and testing producing the strongest effects. These findings demonstrate that incidentally acquired long-term memories, especially those that underwent maintenance and testing in working memory, can disrupt intentionally encoded long-term memories.

articles_hidden.title: Novel perspectives on the affect regulation hypothesis of substance use: Introduction to special issue
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas Dora; Andrea M Wycoff; Jack Waddell; Andrea Howard; Kevin Michael King
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: The affect regulation hypothesis, the proposition that people use substances to manage how they feel, has organized addiction science for decades, yet empirical support varies markedly across methods. This special issue was assembled to examine the hypothesis through novel theory, rigorous empirical tests, and synthesis of existing evidence. Method: We introduce twelve contributions spanning theoretical proposals, (placebo-)controlled laboratory experiments, ecological momentary assessment (EMA), and longitudinal, cross-sectional, and qualitative designs. The studies address alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, and gambling across various populations, including recently suicidal psychiatric patients, pregnant adults, sexual and gender minority young women, Black men, and treatment-seeking individuals. We organize the contributions into five themes: affect regulation as a person-level vulnerability, laboratory tests of the hypothesis, real-time tests of negative reinforcement, studies of positive reinforcement, and an extension beyond substances. Results: Across contributions, no simple global verdict emerges. Within-person negative reinforcement was evident in some operationalizations, populations, and contexts but not others; positive affect and its dysregulation were more consistent correlates of use than negative affect; motive-response associations were substantially driven by expectancies; and affect regulation extended to gambling. Findings frequently diverged by substance and by timescale of measurement. Conclusions: The evidence summarized here supports not a refutation but a refinement of the hypothesis; one in which positive affect is at least as central as negative affect, and populations, timescales, expectancies, and context matter substantially.

articles_hidden.title: Personality dysfunction is an excellent marker of general psychopathology, particularly internalizing symptoms but less so for externalizing: A commentary on Martin, Kuer, & Sellbom
articles_hidden.authors: Josh Miller; Nathaniel Luke Phillips; Ashmita Ghosh; Leigha Rose; Donald R Lynam
articles_hidden.abstract: Martin and colleagues examined the separability of personality dysfunction (PF) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) using clinician ratings and self-reports in a sample of 289 adults receiving community-based mental health treatment. Using both confirmatory factor and bifactor analyses, the authors found that a general factor splitting across both BPD and PF best accounted for their variance. The authors concluded that PF and BPD “represent the same underlying construct,” with only modest unique variance left in BPD thought to be artifacts of its conceptualization in the DSM. In this commentary, we argue two basic points. First, there is simultaneously ample evidence that PF is an excellent marker of psychopathology writ large and comparatively little evidence that it will successfully delineate personality disorders from other forms of psychopathology, as has been suggested. Second, there is growing evidence that PF is a better marker of internalizing than externalizing forms of psychopathology. Without modification to the conceptualization and assessment of PF, we believe that current (and forthcoming) diagnostic models of personality disorder unduly focus on internalizing, distress-based presentations, which potentially exclude more purely externalizing forms such as (grandiose) narcissism and antisocial/psychopathic personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: The Description–Experience Gap in Loss Aversion
articles_hidden.authors: Nuno Busch; Thorsten Pachur
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans make different decisions under risk when they acquire information about their options through experience than when they learn it from a summary description. Research on this description–experience gap has largely focused on differences in probability weighting—for instance, how low-probability events are reflected in people’s decisions. Here, we show that the gap manifests much more broadly and also occurs with regard to the influence of outcomes. Specifically, we investigated how description- and experience-based decisions differ in loss aversion—the tendency for loss outcomes to have a greater impact on choice than equivalent gain outcomes. We first conducted a meta-reanalysis synthesizing raw data of all available datasets that directly compared description- and experience-based decisions involving mixed-domain lotteries (88,409 choices in total across N_Desc = 439 and N_Exp = 468). The results indicate that loss aversion, measured with cumulative prospect theory (CPT), is more pronounced in experience-based than in description-based choices. We then replicated this description–experience gap in loss aversion in a large-scale experiment with preregistered methods (19,435 choices by N_Desc = 202 and N_Exp = 202) tailored to address potential limitations of the studies included in the meta-analysis, and also showed the gap in an analysis that does not depend on estimating a latent loss aversion parameter. An analysis of the experience-based choices with a reinforcement learning model suggests that a possible mechanism for the apparently higher loss aversion in decisions from experience could be asymmetric learning after positive versus negative prediction errors during experiential sampling.

articles_hidden.title: From Friend to Foe: Stereotypes of Dogs are Ambivalent
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Palmer; Remy Frost; Sophia Ruppel; Anamarie C Johnson; Andrew Johnson; Clive DL Wynne
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on animal stereotypes often lacks nuance, focusing on animals broadly rather than specific subgroups or contexts. In Study 1, 172 participants listed stereotypes about Dogs, Aggressive Dogs, and Friendly Dogs in open-ended responses. We identified 17 themes for Dogs (e.g., “good companions”), 15 for Aggressive Dogs (e.g., “dangerous to children”), and 20 for Friendly Dogs (e.g., “affiliative”). In Study 2, we examined stereotype endorsement, policy support, and how related belief systems influenced endorsement. Using items created from Study 1 responses, 305 participants rated their personal endorsement of stereotypes (Dogs, Friendly Dogs, or Aggressive Dogs). We found that greater belief in stereotypes about Dogs and Aggressive Dogs decreased support for policies to improve welfare, and only stereotypes about Aggressive Dogs predicted increased support for restrictive policies. We found that beliefs in essentialism and dominance theory consistently predicted greater stereotype endorsement.

articles_hidden.title: Ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Gaurav Mahajan; Caroline J Charpentier; Valentin Guigon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Computational research depends on complex, linked operations. In cognitive neuroscience, these operations often combine multiple data types, specialized toolboxes, custom scripts, and changing computing environments. Open science practices, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) principles, and data standardization have improved how research objects are shared and described. However, they do not guarantee that the same analysis can be rerun to reconstruct the original result. This limitation becomes more consequential as AI-assisted coding tools are accelerating code development, with the potential to strengthen good practices, but also to amplify weak ones. Related problems have long been addressed in software engineering and machine learning operations through practices that make code, data, environments, and execution steps traceable. Drawing from these practices, we present ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience. We emphasize simple, low-cost decisions that can be implemented early and scaled as
projects become more complex.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Foreboding Amid Prosperity: Phantom Anxiety Theory and Abstract Pessimism
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
The analyses drew on 38 independently conducted international surveys involving more than half a million respondents. The results demonstrate that higher national levels of human development, as indexed by the Human Development Index (HDI), are associated with more pessimistic expectations about the future. Leading theories of optimism/pessimism, negativity, threat processing, resource loss, and the determinants of hope predict patterns that are inconsistent with the empirical findings.
This article posits the existence of endogenous anxious arousal analogous to the vigilance observed in prey animals. Such vigilance promoted survival in the environments that shaped the human nervous system but is evolutionarily mismatched to the modern world. Phantom anxiety theory predicts the observed effect—abstract pessimism—and specifies the conditions under which it should intensify; both predictions are supported by the data. The hypothesis of endogenous anxious arousal in humans also offers a new perspective on anxiety disorders and the evolutionary origins of sapientization.

articles_hidden.title: The Longitudinal THRIVE study Protocol: Social and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Risk and Resilience in Young People with a History of Childhood Adversity
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Maximilian König; Pauline Wessels; Hannah Dorsman; Antoinette Haverhals; THRIVE consortium; Peter Bos; Geert-Jan Will; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction
Childhood adversity (CA) is among the strongest predictors of mental health problems. CA refers to experiences that are likely to require significant adaptation by an average child and that represent a deviation from the expectable environment. CA-related alterations in social and cognitive functioning may result in the thinning of social networks and increases in stressful peer interactions, which subsequently lead to mental health problems. The THRIVE study takes a longitudinal approach to investigate these proposed prospective relationships by examining whether and how social, cognitive, and neurobiological mechanisms interact to shape friendship support, stressful peer interactions, and mental health functioning over time.
Methods and analysis
The ongoing THRIVE study aims to recruit 288 participants aged 18-24 years who retrospectively self-report CA. This longitudinal study comprises six sessions in total. Participants complete an online baseline assessment of mental health, social support, stress experiences, and early life experiences, followed by an in-unit deep-phenotyping session. Assessments include self-report measures, cortisol measures, computerized cognitive tasks, and functional neuroimaging paradigms assessing stress and social evaluation. Participants subsequently complete four online follow-up assessments at 3-month intervals. Using data collected at the in-unit session, we aim to test whether CA is associated with biased emotion processing, blunted feedback learning and enhanced stress responses, and whether social support from peers may moderate these effects. The longitudinal design further enables us to test whether CA contributes to mental health problems through its impact on cognitive functioning, which over time leads to reduced social support and increased social stress. By elucidating how cognitive and social functioning contribute to mental health outcomes following CA, the THRIVE study aims to inform the development of interventions that foster resilience in young people.
Ethics and dissemination
The THRIVE study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee Leiden-The Hague-Delft (NL80017.058.21). The study was co-created with the Augeo Youth Task Force, a panel of young adults with lived experience of CA, who contribute throughout the research process. Findings will be disseminated through scientific publications, conference presentations, preprints, and public engagement activities.

articles_hidden.title: Electrophysiological signatures of statistical segmentation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Liesa Ravijts; Isabella Toselli Prequero Sbrocco; Brent Vernaillen; Rodrigo Dal Ben; Débora de Hollanda Souza; Louisa Bogaerts
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning (SL), the ability to extract regularities from continuous sensory input, is widely studied using segmentation in embedded pattern learning (EPL) paradigms. Different electrophysiological measures, including event-related potentials (ERPs), steady-state responses (SSRs), and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs), have been proposed as neural signatures of statistical segmentation. However, the extent to which these measures provide consistent evidence remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of EEG and MEG studies to assess the evidence for these signatures in the current literature. After screening 635 records, 39 studies (46 experiments) contributed to the quantitative synthesis. We conducted separate meta-analyses of four signatures: N1 and N400 pattern-onset effects, emergence of pattern-rate SSRs, and suppression of item-rate SSRs. The results provided some evidence for an N400 effect and strong evidence for pattern-rate SSR enhancement, whereas neither N1 nor item-rate SSR effects reached statistical significance. No moderation effects were observed across the tested characteristics, with the exception of contrast type, which significantly moderated the N400 effect. A comparative model further indicated that pattern-rate SSRs provided the most robust evidence of statistical segmentation. We discuss how our results inform the interpretation of these signatures as neural indices of statistical segmentation and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: LEWIS: Lund Everyday Waste Image Set of Naturally Sourced, Normalised, and Evaluated Waste Images
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Prip Wrisberg; Annika Wallin; Philip Pärnamets
articles_hidden.abstract: Waste sorting is a cognitively demanding task with high environmental stakes. To support research on the categorisation and decision processes underlying waste sorting behaviour, this paper introduces an evaluated stimulus set of 790 images of naturally occurring waste items. The images were sampled from Danish and Swedish household waste, visually standardised, and evaluated by 526 Swedish participants on real-world frequency, how good an example they are of their waste category, and ease of categorisation. The resulting database offers a valuable resource for experiments in categorisation, judgment and decision-making, and sustainability interventions, enabling researchers to study real-world categorisation with both experimental control and ecological validity.

articles_hidden.title: Factors structuring lexical development intoddlers: The effects of parental education,language exposure, and age
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Camila Scaff; Laia Fibla; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract:
A growing body of research suggests that individual variation in young children's word comprehension (indexed by response times and accuracy) is structured and meaningful. In this paper, we assess how children’s word comprehension correlates with three factors: socio-economic status (indexed by maternal education), lingual status (based on language exposure), and age. We present results from 91 2- to 3-year-old children using a paired forced-choice task built on a child-friendly touch screen. Effects associated with maternal education and exposure to the tested language (French) were small, and they were greater for accuracy than response times. This pattern of results is compatible with an interpretation whereby the greatest effects of these two variables are on cumulative knowledge (vocabulary size) rather
than on processing. Effects for age were larger and affected both accuracy and response times. Finally, response time variation did not mediate the effects of socio-economic status on accuracy or vice versa

articles_hidden.title: From Vulnerability to Flourishing: Genetic Sensitivity, Family Environment, and Social Support in Intergenerational Trauma and Resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Vera Bekes; Judit Gervai; Aranyi Tamas; Adel Schein; Zsofia Nemoda
articles_hidden.abstract: Intergenerational trauma research has increasingly emphasized the role of both psychological and biological factors in shaping vulnerability and resilience across generations. The present study examined whether gene × environment interactions involving the DRD4 dopamine receptor exon 3 genetic variant could predict trauma-related and positive mental health outcomes among second- and third-generation offspring of Holocaust survivors. Altogether 256 offspring (175 children and 81 grandchildren) of Holocaust survivors completed self-report measures of childhood adversity, family vulnerability and resilience, current social support, and mental health outcomes, and provided genetic sample. Results showed that Family vulnerability and Social support predicted trauma-related and resilient outcomes, respectively, and that carrying the DRD4 7-repeat allele amplified sensitivity to both adverse and protective environments. Childhood family vulnerability predicted posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms significantly only in DRD4 7-repeat allele carriers but not among those without it, while current social support predicted resilience and flourishing also more strongly in 7-repeat allele carriers. Our findings provide empirical support for the DRD4 7-repeat allele as a differential susceptibility variant in an intergenerational trauma context, indicating that the same genetic variant that increases vulnerability in adverse family environments also enhances capacity for flourishing in supportive contexts. The findings suggest that more vulnerable individuals might also be capable of exceptional thriving, given a supportive environment, and that offering family-based and parenting interventions, and community building initiatives for trauma-affected families have the potential to reduce negative and increase positive mental health outcomes, not only in childhood but throughout the lifespan.

articles_hidden.title: Configurations of Mother-Child and Father-Child Attachment Relationships as Predictors  of Child Social Competence: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Or Dagan; Carlo Schuengel; Sheri Madigan; Glenn I. Roisman; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Marinus H. van IJzendoorn; Marije Verhage; Robbie Duschinsky; Abraham Sagi-Schwartz; Jean-François Bureau
articles_hidden.abstract: Attachment theory posits that early child-caregiver relationships shape socioemotional development. Social competence has received particular attention both because it is theoretically expected to be shaped by early attachment relationships and due to its well-established associations with children’s mental health and adjustment. However, most research has examined a single child-parent relationship, typically the child-mother dyad, overlooking the simultaneous attachment relationships many children form with other significant caregivers. In this study, we used individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis to test whether mother-child and father-child attachment configurations uniquely predict children’s social competence. This pre-registered two-step IPD meta-analysis included studies that assessed child attachment relationships with both mothers and fathers using observational measures, and children’s social competence using parent, teacher, or observer reports.
