Effects computed for 16 studies, comprising 1,585 children, were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Children with two insecure attachment relationships showed significantly lower social competence compared to those with one or two secure attachments (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35]). No difference was observed between children with one versus two secure attachment relationships. We found no evidence that the number of disorganized attachment relationships predicted social competence. Across attachment configurations, mother-child and father-child attachment relationship quality did not differentially predict social competence. The presence of at least one secure attachment relationship, whether with the mother or father, may buffer against the risks of having two insecure attachments for children’s social competence. These findings add to the growing evidence that attachment relationships with mothers and fathers are similarly important in predicting key developmental outcomes. In contrast, organized versus disorganized attachment configurations were not reliably associated with social competence, raising both methodological and conceptual questions.

articles_hidden.title: Steering Generative AI Toward Developmentally Supportive Learning: The SCAFFOLD Framework and a Pilot in a School Setting
articles_hidden.authors: Olga Muss
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents are the fastest-growing users of Large Language Models (LLMs) and many LLM-powered toys are entering homes, transforming their environment. Yet these tools were not designed for their educational, emotional, and developmental needs. Children are particularly vulnerable because their skills are immature, knowledge limited and they are undergoing sensitive periods of development, when the foundations are being laid. Safe, developmentally and pedagogically grounded design for interactions with LLMs are therefore essential for limiting risks and harvesting benefits of this technology. This thesis presents the Steered Contextual AI Framework for Orchestrating Learning Dialogue (SCAFFOLD), which builds upon its technical framework, a layered reliability framework that surrounds LLM-generated text and speech with external verification, targeted repair, and safe fallback, to enable to steer LLM’s behavior towards its conceptual framework that operationalizes the knowledge from developmental psychology and neuroscience, science of learning, science of education and pedagogy and the science of human-computer interactions. Model-agnostic and privacy-preserving, SCAFFOLD helps educators to configure interactions with AI that support safety, learning and development, with transparency and modularity. The thesis includes a piloted minimal SCAFFOLD prototype tested in a classroom with 12–16-year-olds using an LLM-powered social robot in a multi-user co-creation task, where students collaboratively designed a mnemonic on a previously covered topic. Preliminary findings showed that, compared to a prompt-only LLM, the SCAFFOLD prototype elicited more student activity, engagement, and on-topic participation. Co-creation level was associated with post-test knowledge scores after controlling for prior knowledge. These findings provide initial evidence for SCAFFOLD's feasibility and potential to support engagement and learning in educational settings.

articles_hidden.title: COVID-19 Impacts and Child Psychological Distress: A Twin Direction-of-Causation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Mandeep Singh; Hongcui Du; Callie W. Little; Sara Ann Hart
articles_hidden.abstract: COVID-19 disrupted children's social, economic, and psychological circumstances, yet the causal direction of this association with child distress remains unresolved. We applied twin Direction of Causation (DoC) modeling to 579 twin families (183 MZ, 396 DZ pairs; grades 3–12) from the NatPAT COVID 2022 survey. COVID-19 impacts were modeled as a latent construct spanning social, economic, and COVID-specific stress domains; distress was indexed by anxiety and perceived stress. The two constructs showed different genetic and environmental influences: COVID-19 impacts were predominantly environmental, distress substantially heritable, yet were strongly associated (r = .706). Modeling favoured a unidirectional path from COVID-19 impacts to distress per our preregistered tiebreaker (β = .703, p < .001; ΔAIC = 0.29), although this small margin does not rule out a bidirectional relation. These findings suggest that reducing pandemic-related disruptions, rather than targeting stress responses alone, may help protect child mental health during future societal disruptions.

articles_hidden.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles_hidden.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a genetics of mental disorders as complex dynamical systems: A symptom-specific and symptom-interactive approach
articles_hidden.authors: Omid V. Ebrahimi; Michel Guillaume Nivard; Ludvig Daae Bjørndal
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychiatric genetics has largely mapped genetic liability onto diagnoses and symptom sum scores. Yet these disorder-level phenotypes are heterogeneous composites: individuals sharing a diagnosis may exhibit markedly different symptoms; the same symptoms recur across multiple disorders; and symptoms influence one another over time. Genetic analyses based on such aggregates may therefore obscure symptom-specific biological signals and overlook the dynamic processes through which genetic liability becomes expressed clinically. We propose a complementary symptom-specific and symptom-interactive framework that conceptualises psychiatric disorders as dynamic systems of mutually influencing symptoms. This framework distinguishes three forms of genetic influence: direct effects of genetic risk on individual symptoms; indirect effects propagated through symptom-to-symptom pathways; and examinations of how genetic risk moderates the strength, persistence, and activation potential of symptom interactions. We show how various genetic and psychometric methods can be integrated to investigate these processes. We identify four priorities for psychiatric genetics research that can be advanced by adopting this framework: improving symptom-level phenotyping; distinguishing disorder-specific and transdiagnostic symptoms; modelling mediated genetic effects across symptoms; and testing whether genetic liability shapes symptom co-activation and their temporal dynamics. Reframing psychopathology as systems of interacting symptoms could sharpen genes-to-phenotype mapping, clarify heterogeneity in illness trajectories, and align psychiatric genetics more closely with novel mechanistic theories of mental disorders and the goals of precision psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Attention Bias in Perfectionism:  Prolonged Dwell Time on Critical Faces Partially Mediates a Link Between Perfectionistic Concerns and Psychological Distress
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Prestele; Christine Altstötter-Gleich; Stephan Koenig; Ulrike Basten
articles_hidden.abstract: Perfectionism is a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor implicated in emotional disorders, including depression and anxiety. Yet, the mechanisms through which perfectionism contributes to psychological distress are only partly understood. A candidate mechanism is attention allocation during social interactions, as attention to evaluative cues may influence subsequent perceptions and affective responses. The present study used eye tracking to examine whether perfectionistic concerns (PC) and perfectionistic strivings (PS) are associated with attention biases toward socially evaluative cues, as indicated by prolonged dwell time on facial expressions of criticism as opposed to appreciation in a free viewing task. For 148 participants (82% female, 1% diverse; age: 18 – 57 years, M = 24 years, SD = 6.4), the proportional dwell-time on critical faces was related to self-reported PC as well as state and trait measures of psychological distress (unpleasant mood and depressiveness). In latent-variable analyses, PC showed small to moderate positive unique associations with the proportional dwell time on critical faces. Path analyses further indicated that this dwell time partially mediated the associations of PC with unpleasant mood and depressiveness. These findings provide novel evidence that PC are linked to biases in attention toward social cues of criticism, suggesting a pathway through which PC may contribute to psychological distress. More broadly, the results underscore the importance of considering attentional mechanisms in models of perfectionism and emotional disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Psychometric Validation of the ‘Psychedelic Flourishing Scale’
articles_hidden.authors: Frederick Pattisson; Sunjeev Kamboj; Devon Stoliker; Rosalind McAlpine
articles_hidden.abstract: Positive psychological changes following psychedelic experiences are widely studied, yet no validated instrument has been developed specifically to assess the breadth of enduring change that individuals attribute to those experiences. We therefore conducted a two-part programme of research to evaluate an existing measure and to develop and validate a more comprehensive scale. In Part 1, a preliminary psychometric analysis of the 11-item Mindset Questionnaire (MQ) was conducted using data from two psilocybin studies (N = 97). Its items were strongly intercorrelated (mean inter-item r = .63) and predominantly reflected a single, relatively narrow dimension of change. Part 2 followed established scale-development procedures to define the broader construct of psychedelic flourishing and develop the Psychedelic Flourishing Scale (PFS). A three-round Delphi study involving 17 experts established the construct definition and generated a 41-item pool. The PFS was then evaluated in a pre-registered cross-sectional survey of 1,296 adults who reported previous serotonergic (“classic”) psychedelic use. The sample was randomly divided for exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, with the structure extracted in the exploratory half rather than specified in advance. In the confirmatory subsample, a model comprising five correlated facets showed good fit (RMSEA = .053, CFI = .965) and fitted better than a unidimensional model, although a four-factor model performed similarly. A full-sample bifactor model indicated that 87.8% of the common variance was attributable to a general factor, with high general-factor reliability (ωh = .960), supporting use of a single total score. Scores showed high test-retest reliability over a median interval of approximately three weeks (ICC = .890) and were more strongly associated with theoretically related constructs, including presence of meaning (r = .45) and well-being (r = .42), than with extraversion (r = .22) or socially desirable responding (r = .17). The MQ appears to assess a narrow dimension of perceived change, whereas the PFS provides a psychometrically robust measure of broader positive psychological change attributed to psychedelic experiences.

articles_hidden.title: The Functional Connectivity of Hallucinations in Psychiatric Disorders and Neurodegenerative Disorders: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Ren; Huyen Ngoc Pham; Xiong Xiong; Shun-Chin Jim Wu; Emilio Fernandez-Egea; John T. O’Brien; Graham Murray; John suckling
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Hallucinations span psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders, yet unified neurobiological or consciousness-based explanations remain uncertain. Functional connectivity (FC) provides a network-level view with highly heterogeneous findings.
Methods: Following PRISMA, we included studies with FC of hallucinations to ask whether it is sensitive to hallucinations, can distinguish different disorders, and if adopted theories are explanatory. 
Results: 198 studies were included, with far fewer studies in neurodegenerative (35) than psychiatric disorders (163). Across conditions, hallucinations consistently involved dysconnectivity among default mode (DMN), salience (SN), central executive (CEN), sensory systems, and subcortical circuits. Shared alterations included disrupted SN modulation of sensory gating, altered DMN-sensory coupling and within DMN coherence, limbic system involvement, and reduced CEN regulation of perceptual networks. Disorder‑specific patterns were evident: psychiatric hallucinations preferentially involved auditory-language networks, cortico‑striatal circuits, and salience hubs, whereas neurodegenerative hallucinations were characterised by visual and attentional network dysfunction, including dorsal and ventral attention systems and visual cortices.
Conclusions: FC is sensitive to hallucinations and shows different disorder-linked patterns while revealing shared mechanisms, supporting the transdiagnostic nature of hallucinations at the level of functional brain networks. Despite the involvement of multiple transdiagnostic networks, the current literature does not converge on a unified cognitive or consciousness-based theory of hallucinations, underscoring a critical theoretical gap and the need for integrative models.

articles_hidden.title: Can Large Language Models Simulate Child-Like Theory of Mind?
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Brand; Tobias Wingen; Oliver Christ
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified debates about the validity of using silicon samples, of artificial participants simulated by AI. This question is especially relevant for developmental psychology, where valid simulation requires models not only to solve tasks, but also to reproduce age-typical limitations in cognitive ability. We tested whether standard autoregressive models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-4) and more advanced reasoning models can simulate such developmental trajectories in Theory of Mind (ToM). Six LLMs were prompted with child-age personas ranging from 2.5 to 6.0 years and completed classic false-belief tasks. Most models showed strong baseline ToM performance, and many also successfully downplayed their abilities in line with human developmental trajectories. However, performance varied substantially across model type, provider, and task. These findings suggest that silicon sampling may be promising for developmental research, but relying on silicon samples alone is not yet a valid method.

articles_hidden.title: Relationship Quality Moderates Depressive-Symptom Associations With Negative Self-Perceptions and Partner Metaperceptions
articles_hidden.authors: Nida Civici; Andrew Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is associated with persistent negative self-beliefs and altered social information processing. Although considerable research has examined self-perception in depression, less is known about how depressive symptoms relate to beliefs about how romantic partners perceive the self and whether relationship quality moderates these associations. The present study investigated associations between depressive symptoms, self-perceptions, metaperceptions of partner evaluations, and memory for self-referential information across multiple social perspectives. A sample of 171 adults in romantic relationships completed measures of depressive symptoms and relationship quality, an adapted Self-Referential Encoding Task assessing evaluations from the self, a romantic partner, and a neutral researcher, and a subsequent memory assessment. Higher depressive symptoms were associated with more negative self-perceptions and more negative beliefs about how romantic partners viewed the self, but not with perceptions attributed to the neutral researcher. Relationship quality moderated the association between depressive symptoms and negative self- and partner-related perceptions, with weaker associations observed among participants reporting higher-quality relationships. Memory analyses focused on self-reference effects across social perspectives. Memory sensitivity was higher for self- and partner-encoded items than for researcher-encoded items and for negative than positive items. However, there was no consistent evidence that depressive symptoms, relationship quality, or their interaction predicted these self-reference effects. These findings suggest that depressive symptoms extend beyond self-evaluation to include assumptions about how emotionally significant others perceive the self, with relationship quality shaping the strength of these associations. The findings underscore the importance of considering partner-related metaperceptions and relationship context when examining interpersonal processes associated with depression.

articles_hidden.title: Apples to apples: Stability and flexibility trade off only when measured at the same processing level.
articles_hidden.authors: Luca Moretti; Iring Koch; Tobias Egner
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive stability and cognitive flexibility are two crucial abilities supporting goal-directed behaviour. While cognitive stability designates our ability to maintain task-relevant information and shield it against distraction, flexibility allows to choose which information constitutes the task focus. Because of their complementary role, it has long been assumed that cognitive stability and flexibility are inversely related, such that promoting stability should impair flexibility, and vice versa. Recently however, a series of task-switching experiments have failed to observe such a mandatory trade-off, prompting a lively debate on the stability-flexibility relationship. In the present study, we aim to reconcile these findings with the trade-off view, by testing whether the stability and flexibility trade-off depends on the operationalization of these constructs. While previous studies gauged stability via the congruency effect and flexibility via task-switch costs, we here additionally measured cognitive stability via the valency effect. While the congruency effect indexes cross-task interference at the level of response selection, the valency effect is thought to reflect such interference at the level of task selection, which may more closely align with task-switching. Across three experiments and a re-analysis, we provide consistent evidence that manipulations reducing task switch cost increase the valency effect (and vice versa), but do not modulate the congruency effect. These findings suggest that stability and flexibility do trade off, but only when measured at the same level of processing (here, the task-selection level). We discuss the possible reasons why trade-offs may be level-specific, and future approaches to further investigate the stability-flexibility relationship.

articles_hidden.title: Translation and Validation of the Japanese version of the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (J-APEQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto; Shuhei Iimura
articles_hidden.abstract: Picky eating is a multidimensional eating behavior that has been studied primarily in children, although it is also observed in adults. The Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ) was developed to assess multiple dimensions of picky eating in adults, but a validated Japanese version has not been available. The present study aimed to develop and validate a Japanese version of the APEQ (J-APEQ) (Researcher-led translation) and to compare it with a translation generated using generative artificial intelligence (AI-generated translation). The researcher-led translation was completed by 892 Japanese adults, with 210 participants completing the scale again after three weeks. A separate sample of 939 participants completed an AI-generated translation. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original four-factor structure of the researcher-led J-APEQ, and a second-order factor model also showed acceptable fit. The composite score showed adequate internal consistency, while reliability was lower for some subscales, particularly Meal Disengagement and Taste Aversion. Test–retest reliability was moderate, and correlations with food neophobia, disgust, and eating-attitude measures generally supported convergent validity. The AI-generated translation showed a factor structure and reliability broadly comparable to those of the researcher-led translation. Measurement invariance analyses supported configural, threshold, metric, and partial scalar invariance between the two versions. In the present study, however, the researcher-led translation was the version formally validated and established as the Japanese APEQ (J-APEQ), whereas the AI-generated translation was included for comparison. These findings support the use of the J-APEQ for assessing picky eating in Japanese adults and suggest that generative AI may be useful as a tool for psychological scale translation, although human review and validation remain necessary.

articles_hidden.title: Memory reactivation levels remain unaffected by anticipated interference
articles_hidden.authors: Nursena Ataseven; I. Efsane Algın; Duygu Yucel; Berna Güler; Lara Todorova; Keisuke Fukuda; Eren Gunseli
articles_hidden.abstract: Most daily tasks require frequent information exchange between working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM). However, the factors that modulate the reactivation of LTMs in WM remain to be explored. Here, we tested the effects of anticipated perceptual interference (in Experiment 1) and anticipated dual task interference (in Experiment 2) on reactivation of LTMs in WM using contralateral delay activity (CDA) in the EEG. On each trial, participants saw one or three previously studied or novel objects that were tested after a brief retention interval. In half of the blocks, the retention contained perceptual distractors (Experiment 1) or dual task interference (Experiment 2). In both experiments, the CDA prior to the interference period was similar regardless of the anticipated interference. Additionally, we measured contralateral alpha power suppression as an index of spatial attention. We found that spatial attention allocated to the memorized objects’ locations also was not modulated with anticipated interference. These findings indicate that anticipating interference does not influence the extent to which WM is engaged in representing information stored in LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Healthy attachment for the parents? An investigation on the association between attachment parenting and parental mental health.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Hanna Laura Meder; Mira-Pauline Grapentin; Nora Imlau
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. Attachment parenting (AP) became popular for it promotes responsive caregiving, but has been criticized for over-extensively translating attachment research into challenging parenting standards, mirroring detrimental intensive-parenting beliefs that adversely affect parental health. Meanwhile, evidence on AP remains limited and assessments of AP-beliefs and AP-practice are lacking. This study aims to develop and validate an AP-questionnaire and test the associations between AP and parental mental health and explore the mediating role of intensive-parenting beliefs.
Methods. In a preregistered cross-sectional online-survey, 1664 parents (98.5% mothers) of children aged up to six years answered an extensive item-list assessing AP-beliefs and AP implementation into practice, an intensive parenting questionnaire, and mental health measures. Confirmatory factor analyses were used for AP-questionnaire validation and correlation- and mediation-analyses for exploring the association between AP and mental health.
Results. A 26-item AP-questionnaire was extracted that assesses AP-beliefs and AP- practice, both for the global AP-approach and seven individual core-principles. AP-indicators consistently showed small/minimal correlations with better mental health, whereas mediation analyses revealed parallel, opposing pathways: a positive, direct association from AP to mental health (possibly explained via parental fulfilment) and adverse indirect pathways through intensive-parenting beliefs (challenge-/self-sacrifice and essentialist-beliefs).
Conclusion. AP may be neither uniformly beneficial nor harmful. Rather, it can foster parental fulfilment which increases parental well-being, but also instil dysfunctional beliefs about sacrifice and unavoidable strain that increase parental-stress. To improve evidence-based personalized parenting-recommendations, longitudinal research is needed to disentangle when AP fosters positive parental identity and when it reinforces parental vulnerabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Material Life Satisfaction Increases Willingness to Engage in Costly Climate Action
articles_hidden.authors: Fabian Dablander; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles_hidden.abstract: Addressing climate change requires sustained public support for policies and willingness to engage in actions that may incur personal costs. Understanding the social conditions under which citizens are willing to support such measures is important for assessing the feasibility of ambitious climate action. Using data from a large, population-weighted survey of Dutch citizens (N = 22,749) and covariate adjustments informed by directed acyclic graphs, we estimate the effect of different facets of life satisfaction on willingness to contribute 1% of monthly household income to address climate change. We find a strong effect of material life satisfaction: individuals who are very satisfied with their material conditions are more than three times more likely to be willing to contribute than those who are not satisfied at all. In contrast, satisfaction with social life, physical health, and mental health show weak or negligible independent effects on willingness once material life satisfaction and relevant background variables are taken into account. We discuss the implications of our results for the design and acceptability of climate policies that are perceived as placing burdens on households.

articles_hidden.title: Human outcome-irrelevant value learning is insensitive to its monetary cost
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: When learning from reinforcement, individuals should assign credit selectively to features of their actions that causally determine outcomes. Yet, even when explicit instructions and extensive experience clarify which action features predict reward, humans assign credit to outcome-irrelevant features, leading to suboptimal choices. Here, we use computational modeling to test if this suboptimal credit assignment can be controlled depending on the monetary cost at stake. Specifically, we tested whether higher payoffs can increase control over outcome-irrelevant credit assignment. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task under low and high monetary stakes. Higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but, strikingly, had no influence on outcome-irrelevant values, which influenced choices to a similar degree. These findings demonstrate the automatic nature of credit assignment to outcome-irrelevant features, suggesting that associations between features and reward are formed despite clear instructions and their detrimental consequences for monetary gains.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles_hidden.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles_hidden.title: Educator Preparedness in Navigating Inclusive Education and Sensory Differences in Autism: Qualitative Exploration in Ontario, Canada
articles_hidden.authors: Stephanie Larmer; Gabrielle Czichrak; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Although Ontario, Canada follows an inclusive education model, little is known about the current status regarding the education of autistic students. Specifically, limited research has explored relevant facets of educator experiences and needs, a crucial component of successful inclusive education in autism. We aimed to explore existing gaps through open-ended questions in a questionnaire and follow-up interviews. First, educators and pre-service educators completed the open-ended questions as part of a larger questionnaire. Then, those who opted to participate completed follow-up interviews on their responses to the open-ended questions. The results revealed a pervasive lack of support for educators and pre-service educators and the consequences it can have for both them and autistic students. Specifically, participants detailed a wide range of desired professional development in autism and outlined a high prevalence of sensory experiences with autistic students, desiring guidance. Ultimately, participants emphasized the existing barriers to successful inclusive education in autism and explained the changes that would help in overcoming them. It was evident participants care for autistic students and desire change that leads to greater inclusion and success. This research demonstrates the value in listening to those responsible for implementing inclusive education in autism, providing decision makers with updated evidence based on direct experience that can guide professional development design and policies and may serve as an example for inclusive education more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles_hidden.title: The Unified Model Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Hsiu Ting Ting Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists describe their statistical models with diagrams. The conventions in use, path diagrams, multilevel panels, plate notation, and causal graphs, each grew inside one modeling tradition, and they disagree on basic symbols. As a result, one figure can stand for two different models. An ellipse with three arrows can show a factor model or a latent profile model. A labeled arrow can show a fixed slope or a person-varying slope. A mediation triangle can show a regression decomposition or a causal claim. This article introduces the Unified Model Graph (UMG), a notation built so that the figure identifies the model that was fitted. Three visual cues type every quantity: fill for observed versus latent, shape for continuous versus categorical, and outline for inferential role. Four edge types separate regression, covariance, deterministic, and mixture relations. Plates mark replication, and a badge states whether the figure makes a causal claim. Every well-formed UMG corresponds to exactly one family of distributions, and path diagrams, plate notation, and causal graphs are special cases; the formal results and proofs are in the supplemental material. The accompanying R package \pkg{} builds diagrams from code or from fitted lavaan, lme4, mirt, and brms objects, validates them, translates them to and from lavaan syntax, checks necessary identification conditions, derives testable implications, and generates model-implied data displays. A benchmark of eight R diagramming packages on ten representational features and ten operations locates what the notation adds. All materials, scripts, and outputs are openly archived.

articles_hidden.title: The Liege Mind-Blanking Scale: a comprehensive scale to assess the heterogeneity of mind-blanking cognitive and experiential aspects
articles_hidden.authors: Paradeisios Alexandros Boulakis; Marion Balla; Agustina Aragón-Daud; David Stawarczyk; Giovanni Briganti; Athena Demertzi; Steve Majerus
articles_hidden.abstract: Our minds are not always full of thoughts. Occasionally, people will report absence of any mental content, an experience termed mind-blanking (MB). So far, MB has been primarily quantified through experience-sampling paradigms. While experience-sampling has allowed researchers to study the behavioural and neurophysiological profile of MB, the practice of asking participants for thought categories, such as “an empty mind”, might undermine the richness and diversity of MB instances. In the present study, we adopted a self-reported, trait approach to MB. We developed a novel MB scale, the Liege Mind-Blanking Scale (L-MBS), with the aim to probe distinct types of MB experiences and relate them to different cognitive functions. A sample of 644 participants completed the L-MBS alongside a cohort of self-report questionnaires measuring trait mind-wandering, attention, memory, metacognition and arousal. The L-MBS showed adequate psychometric properties. Factor analysis validated the presence of 3 discrete factors: one related to the perceived experience of MB, one related to memory failures, and one related to blanking under pressure. Network analysis linked these factors to discrete cognitive domains. The experience of blanking correlated with metacognitive monitoring, while memory failures were associated with autobiographical memory difficulties. Overall, the L-MBS provides a quick, accessible and psychometrically validated measure of an individual’s beliefs about their blank experiences. At the same time, the presence of multiple MB factors suggests that MB is not necessarily a unitary phenomenon and most likely represents a clustering of different moments of no content.

articles.title: Representation Without Power: Far Right Electoral Success and Violence in Weimar Germany
articles.authors: Felix Haass; Alexander De Juan; Daniel Bischof; Henry Thomson
articles.abstract: Far right parties often win elections without gaining access to power. Do such outcomes pacify extremist movements, or can they fuel violence? We study this question in Weimar Germany after the July 1932 Reichstag election, when the Nazi Party became the largest parliamentary force but remained outside government. We digitize Nazi candidate lists and Prussian police records on street violence, linking riots to candidates' home towns. Using a regression discontinuity design around district list cutoffs, we compare towns whose Nazi candidates narrowly entered parliament with towns whose candidates narrowly missed. Post-election Nazi-communist violence was substantially higher in towns represented by elected Nazi MPs, while no discontinuity appears before the election. Mechanism evidence from perpetrator coding, stormtrooper mood reports, and membership records suggests that representation without power redirected frustration toward the movement's violent wing. The findings show that electoral representation can intensify anti-democratic violence when far right parties win mandates but remain excluded from power.

articles.title: The China Mirror  Learning through Difference in the Digital Age
articles.authors: Stéphane Grumbach
articles.abstract: Under conditions of rapidly increasing societal complexity, understanding other civilizations might become an epistemological necessity for fostering adaptive capacities. Drawing on Weber's Verstehen, Jullien's method of the écart, Luhmann's theory of observation, and Koselleck's conceptual history, we propose a method of differential displacement to compare not simply different situations, but their dynamics, with the aim of exposing implicit assumptions. As a case study, following Jullien, we examine what the categories through which China approaches the digital transformation can reveal to Europeans about its purposes and governance. The goal is neither to endorse nor to criticize China, but to move beyond the simplistic duality of democracy and authoritarianism and examine what the difference reveals about Europe's own categories. We further argue that persistent misunderstanding of others can progressively feed a misunderstanding of one's own transformation. Under conditions of complexity surge, comparison can become a mechanism of collective intelligence and adaptive learning.

articles.title: Disaggregating the AI elite: Gender, age, and education differences among professionals engaged in AI development
articles.authors: Matti Nelimarkka
articles.abstract: Amid the society-wide onrush of artificial intelligence, asking ‘who creates AI?’ holds great urgency. A questionnaire-based study conceptualising ‘AI elite’ as a narrower group than the conventionally considered ‘coding elite’ found that only 5% of the 16,808 engineering and technology professionals surveyed contributed significantly to their organisation’s projects for AI development, design, or deployment, with an additional 15% contributing somewhat. Examining predictors of AI-elite membership, path analysis revealed organisation position to be the strongest, suggesting a Matthew-effect pattern wherein pre-existing power informs control over AI. Gender shapes membership directly and indirectly (through education choices and access to senior positions), compounding women’s under-representation. Education likewise manifests both direct and mediated positive effects. Counter to expectations, variety in one’s everyday application of AI tools correlated negatively with participation in AI development. This evidence that the AI elite reproduces structural inequalities spotlights ramifications that warrant further research and well-targeted diversification efforts.

articles.title: An Overview of Public Administration Research: Insights From Publications in Leading Journals (2000–2024)
articles.authors: Vener Garayev
articles.abstract: This study examines paradigmatic changes, thematic developments and authorship patterns in public administration research by analyzing 4,317 articles published in Public Administration Review, Public Management Review, and Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory between 2000 and 2024. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques through Python software to analyze content of titles, abstracts, and metadata, the article identifies key thematic clusters and paradigmatic shifts across the period, shaped by global events, contextual challenges, and technological advancements. The findings reveal a transition from bureaucratic efficiency to participatory governance, from reform to resilience, and from administrative theory to data-driven governance. Additionally, analysis of authorship patterns reveals increasing collaboration and concentration of scholarly output among top prolific contributors. This study contributes to a growing body of literature on bibliometric and content analytical studies in public administration, offering a comprehensive, data-driven perspective on the field’s intellectual evolution over the past quarter-century.

articles.title: Building Bridges Through Infrastructure: Citizen Science and Institutional Integration in Air Quality Monitoring
articles.authors: Henri de Ruiter; Kirsten Vegt; Hester Volten; Margaret Gold; Janneke Elberse
articles.abstract: Citizens are increasingly using low-cost sensors to measure their surroundings, for example air quality. Sensor measurements offer greater temporal and spatial resolution and therefore have the potential to complement official monitoring practices. However, the integration of citizen science (CS) data into official frameworks is still limited. CS data are often perceived as “messy”, with barriers such as concerns about data quality, the absence of standard methodologies, and perceptions of unreliability. While these challenges are well-documented, the critical role of infrastructure in bridging CS data and institutional frameworks has received less attention. This study examines the case of Measure Together, a government-funded project and community that functions as a boundary organisation to bridge the gap between CS initiatives and institutional air quality monitoring. We explore how a CS infrastructure emerges through a combination of relational, organisational and technical factors aimed at making sense of CS data. We further analyse how this CS infrastructure is beginning to merge with official monitoring infrastructure, resulting in a hybrid infrastructure that seeks to combine local data and insights from CS with the standardised and rigorous approaches of official monitoring. Our analysis highlights critical tensions, including conflicts between local and generic data, the action-oriented expectations of many CS participants versus the long-term timelines of official infrastructure, and challenges around trust and standardisation. We conclude by identifying pathways to navigate these tensions, emphasizing the need for adaptive, participatory infrastructure that balance rigour with societal relevance, fostering greater integration between CS and official infrastructures.

articles.title: Peace or Push? Understanding Global Patterns of Refugee Return
articles.authors: Mae MacDonald
articles.abstract: Return is the main way refugee crises end, yet there have been few cross-national studies of when it actually occurs. A central expectation of the refugee regime is that refugees remain abroad while home is unsafe and return as security improves. Yet using a novel global dataset, I show that most returns occur during ongoing conflict, while many refugees remain abroad long after wars end. To explain these patterns, I argue that asylum countries and international organizations play major and underrecognized roles in shaping return, largely overlooked by existing micro-level research focused on refugees’ concerns about security at home. Return is substantially higher when refugees face exclusion policies or conflict in asylum countries, and when donor-funded UNHCR assistance lowers the costs of return. I introduce the Global Refugee Return Dataset, covering 293 origin--asylum dyads from 1980 to 2023, which documents returns systematically undercounted by UNHCR and provides new global data on de facto refugee conditions and UNHCR financing.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: “TikTok refugees”: Motivations and political correlates of international platform migration
articles.authors: Yibin Fan; Hai Wang
articles.abstract: This study investigates the motivations and political correlates of large-scale platform migration in a transnational context. While prior research has emphasized social and technological drivers, the political significance of migration remains underexplored. Building on theories of alternative political expression, political and media trust, and political efficacy, this study conceptualizes platform migration as an alternative political expression. Using an online survey of a group of users with sustained adoption of RedNote, we analyze the case of “TikTok refugees,” examining five motivational mechanisms – social influence, platform-use orientation, political expression, cultural openness, and collective identity frames – and a series of political characteristics with migration. The results show that lower political and media trust, lower external efficacy, and higher internal efficacy are significantly associated with affective and perceptual dimensions of migration. In addition, political expression and cultural openness emerge as the strongest motivators, while well-recognized motivations of social influence and platform-use orientation do not show statistically significant correlation. Taken together, the findings highlight platform migration as a complex, multidimensional behavior situated at the intersection of technological change and (geo)political dynamics.

articles.title: Double Adaptation: Negotiating Closeness and Managing Boundaries in Journalist–Politician Relations
articles.authors: Marina Urbanikova; Lenka Waschkova Cisarova; Iveta Jansová; Melanie Haberl; Folker Hanusch; Sophie Lecheler
articles.abstract: Closeness with politicians is both a professional resource and a potential risk for journalists, as it enables access to information but may compromise autonomy and integrity, particularly within today’s hybrid media environment. This study proposes the conceptual framework of double adaptation as a sensitizing, process-oriented lens for a more systematic understanding of how journalists manage boundaries with politicians, drawing on 96 semi-structured interviews with political journalists in Austria and Czechia. Double adaptation captures the dual process through which journalists adjust their practices in response to both immediate situational demands and structural conditions. Boundaries in journalist–politician interactions emerge through situational adaptation to specific contexts, requiring a careful balancing across multiple dimensions of closeness. The analysis identifies nine such dimensions, grouped into two domains: interactions and relationships. The study further identifies individual factors shaping situational adaptation, including symbolic and pragmatic approaches to boundary management, and situational factors such as personal affinity. Simultaneously, boundaries result from structural adaptation operating at organizational, professional, and systemic levels, influenced by digital transformation, economic pressures, and the professionalization of political communication. Together, these insights advance a more systematic and processual conceptualization of boundary management in political journalism by linking everyday interactional practices to broader structural transformations.

articles.title: A Royal Effect: The Impact of Princess Leonor of Spain’s University Choice on Admission Outcomes
articles.authors: Manuel T. Valdés
articles.abstract: In April 2026, Princess Leonor, heir to the Spanish throne, announced that she would begin a degree in Political Science at Carlos III University of Madrid (UC3M) in the forthcoming academic year. Since the announcement occurred nearly two months before students submitted their university admission applications, the Princess’s choice may have affected admission outcomes in three ways: by shifting preferences toward Political Science across universities, enhancing the attractiveness of UC3M across degree programs, or increasing demand for Political Science at UC3M over and above these two effects. Using public data on admission cutoff scores over an 11-year period and a difference-in-differences-in-differences model, I observe no general effect on Political Science across universities or on UC3M across degree programs. However, I do find a large and statistically significant impact of the Princess’ announcement on the admission cutoff score for Political Science at UC3M. The results emphasize how consequential the behavior of influential people might be, while also highlighting the volatility of decisions about university enrollment.

articles.title: Research on Gender Contradictions in Contemporary China: Structural Pressures, the Negativity of Marital Surplus, and the Gender Projection of Class Contradictions
articles.authors: Yuan Di; ZY Liu
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of a sustained decline in marriage and birth rates in China and intensifying gender tensions, traditional explanations centered on individual preferences or gender norms are insufficient to account for the structural mechanisms involved. Drawing on the economics of marriage and the family, this paper examines how rising costs of housing, weddings, bride price, childbearing, and education affect men's decisions to enter marriage, as well as how the expansion of higher education, the shortage of standardized professional employment, and the motherhood penalty shape women's opportunity costs associated with marriage. Building on these factors, together with declining expectations of economic growth, changing lifestyle expectations, and the rising utility of singlehood as an alternative, the paper proposes the “Dual Marriage Costs–Expectation Mismatch Integrated Model” (the Di Formula) and uses “marital surplus” to characterize the comprehensive net benefits of marriage relative to singlehood. The paper argues that contemporary gender relations in China involve more than a conflict of values, but separately rising direct marriage costs for men and opportunity costs for women, together with a widening structural mismatch between modernity-based expectations and real resource constraints. When marital surplus declines and eventually becomes negative, individually rational decisions to postpone or forgo marriage may, in aggregate, contribute to declining marriage and birth rates and intensified gender tensions. Marriage is therefore increasingly shifting from a traditional mechanism of family cooperation toward a high-cost, high-risk, long-term economic decision.

articles.title: Identifying a Conflict’s Cause: The Theme-Enablers Framework
articles.authors: Moorthy Muthuswamy
articles.abstract:
Conflict studies lack a replicable method for establishing causation because existing frameworks 
conflate an ideology-driven conflict's cause with dependent variables it produces. This bottom
up shortcoming necessitates a top-down approach beginning with a causal framework. The 
Theme-Enablers Framework identifies a conflict's animating theme, its institutional enablers, and 
the agendas they propagate as separable, measurable variables, enabling simultaneous internal 
and external causal validation from the same dataset. The framework is reproducible, falsifiable, 
and generalizable to ideology-driven conflicts for which comparable societal-level data on 
themes, enablers, and agendas can be assembled. This article introduces a methodological 
package combining the framework with difference-in-differences estimation and regression 
analysis to identify and validate causal structure. The methodology is tested on the Islamist 
movement across five world regions and 20 lands, then applied to out-of-sample data from 
Britain, America, India, Gaza, Afghanistan, and Iran. The results demonstrate how the 
framework identifies a conflict's root cause and distinguishes it from downstream effects. The 
designs converge on a much-overlooked cause with direct policy implications: religious leaders 
leverage the Sharia platform to radicalize communities and obtain political power.

articles.title: Zero FTE Does Not Mean Zero Work: Administrative Classification and the Political Economy of Academic Labor
articles.authors: Pan Liu
articles.abstract: Universities often assign faculty appointments through percentages, salary lines, workload allocations, and other administrative categories. Yet a zero-FTE or unpaid appointment can still carry substantive expectations. This study examines that apparent contradiction as a problem of academic labor. Drawing on Marxian political economy, with selective guidance from Labour Process Theory, I conducted a critical analysis of eight publicly available university policy documents governing zero-FTE, dry, courtesy, affiliate, unpaid, and conflict-of-commitment arrangements. The documents were purposively selected because they explicitly paired zero or absent local compensation with language about contribution, duties, effort, institutional benefit, or professional obligation. Across the policies, three patterns recur. First, zero often describes a budgetary or appointment status rather than the absence of work. Second, the organizational beneficiary of academic labor need not be the unit that bears its salary cost. Third, unpaid activity can remain institutionally visible when universities need to regulate time, contribution, or commitment, even when the same activity creates no local salary obligation. The analysis does not imply that every unpaid affiliation is exploitative, nor does it treat every uncompensated activity as surplus-value production in a strict Marxian sense. Instead, it shows how administrative classification can separate labor from the obligations attached to labor. The central asymmetry is simple: institutions are often better at preventing double payment than at preventing double work. Zero FTE is an administrative category. It is not a description of human activity.

articles.title: Cross-Validation as a Bandwidth Criterion for Geographically Weighted PCA: An Ethics of Ambiguity
articles.authors: Andrew Kampfschulte
articles.abstract:
Geographically weighted principal component analysis (GWPCA) summarizes
spatial multivariate structure through local eigen decompositions whose
output depends strongly on a bandwidth, conventionally chosen by
leave-one-out cross-validation (CV). While locating the bandwidth that minimizes CV, several competing minima are frequently observed. We focus on the implications of multiple ambiguous minima as the
object of study. We formalize it through the CV-equivalent set
($H_{\mathrm{CV}}$) of bandwidths that the data do not distinguish from the
CV minimum ($h_{CV}$) and show that bandwidths within this set differ materially in
their bias--variance composition and loading structure. Simulations across eight data-generating processes show that wherever the covariance subspace varied locally, the
equivalent set spanned roughly a quarter of the candidate range
grid, and the oracle bandwidth typically lay inside the set while
differing from $h_{CV}$. In applications to the Dublin voter
turnout and the Kola geochemical survey, the same ambiguity appeared,
and within-set disagreement between local loadings concentrated where
the local eigengap was small. We offer these findings as the first in-depth study of the characteristics of CV as used in GWPCA, and recommend reporting standards to include the equivalent set, and mapping the local eigengap.

articles.title: Beyond Screen Time: Context, Valuation, and Self-Limitation of Mobile Phone Use
articles.authors: Jean-Samuel Beuscart; Thomas Beauvisage
articles.abstract: Do people spend too much time on their phones? "Screen time" has come under scrutiny for its effects on health, cognition and sociability. In this paper, we conceptualize mobile phone use as a practice (Shove, 2003; Warde, 2005) and analyze how users evaluate and regulate their digital consumption. We draw on 45 in-depth semi-structured interviews with a diverse sample of French mobile phone users. We report three main findings. First, users’ accounts of their activity distinguish embedded activities and overflowing activities - that compete with other practices. Second, users' valuation of their digital activities depends not only on their nature (e.g. social media), but on their spatial and temporal context. Third, we identify four self-limitation strategies and show that context-based ones are the most effective.  These results contribute to the debates on digital overconsumption, and the role of platform design in generating the practices they claim to help people reduce.

articles.title: Digital Preservation in Academic Libraries: The University of Ibadan Experience
articles.authors: Agwu Patrick Uzodinma
articles.abstract:
This study examines digital preservation practice at Kenneth Dike Library (KDL), University of Ibadan, to identify infrastructure, practices, challenges, and context sensitive strategies for sustainable stewardship in Nigerian academic libraries. Using a descriptive survey of the 15 library and ICT professionals directly involved in preservation activities, the research measures awareness, available infrastructure, preservation practices, major constraints, and preferred sustainability strategies. Results indicate uniformly high awareness and consensus that core preservation practices (digitisation, backups, metadata application, use of preservation tools, and integrity checks) are performed regularly. The library possesses essential digital repository infrastructure and technical support, but respondents identify poor internet connectivity, inadequate funding, and unreliable power as the most significant obstacles. Staff training, adoption of open source tools, inter institutional collaboration, hybrid storage approaches, and increased funding were unanimously recommended as sustainable strategies. Crucially, respondents strongly endorsed the need for locally adaptable, context sensitive preservation frameworks; however, opinions diverged on the adoption of specific low bandwidth or offline first technical designs. The study concludes that while KDL demonstrates strong knowledge and commitment to digital preservation, long term sustainability requires targeted investment, infrastructure resilience, capacity building, and policy formalisation—preferably through solutions adapted to the Nigerian technological context.

Keywords – Digital Preservation, Academic Libraries, Nigeria, Digitisation, Repositories

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the New Science of Culture
articles.authors: Douglas Guilbeault; Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan; James Evans
articles.abstract:
Cognition and culture have long been treated as parallel objects of study, joined more by metaphor
than by mechanism. We argue they are co-constituted in a manner now empirically tractable:
subjectivities can be measured as local trajectories through a high-dimensional cultural field, and
the field is itself the aggregate of those trajectories. Recent advances in machine learning, including
embedding methods and large generative models, provide the first general framework for
measuring this co-constitution from micro-cognition to macro-social structure. Vector geometry
recovers individual conceptual structure, organizational communication, and large-scale
ideologies; captures multimodal cultural content beyond text; and generates testable predictions
about cultural emergence, including the simultaneous arrival of independent discoveries across
distant minds. We treat this predictability of simultaneous innovation as evidence for the co-
constitutive view: when the geometry of the cultural field is measurable, trajectories of cognitive
search through it become predictable. We then examine generative AI agents as simulators of
human subjectivity and as a qualitatively new coordinating substrate whose insertion into social
life introduces evolutionary dynamics unprecedented in human cultural history. We formalize this
reflexive condition as a Heisenberg-like Uncertainty Principle for generative AI: as instruments for
fixing a culture’s position grow more precise, our capacity to predict its trajectory degrades,
because the machinery of cultural description and cultural action have merged. We close with
ethical questions raised by AI-mediated cultural drift, recursive synthetic culture, and the limits of
human cultural agency, offering guidelines for safe, equitable, and privacy-preserving research on
AI and culture.

articles.title: Mapping Europe’s Digital Acquis. A Granular History of EU Digital Policymaking
articles.authors: Timo Seidl; Nir Kosti
articles.abstract: Over the last decade, digital policy has moved to the center of EU policymaking. Yet we have little systematic knowledge of how much of it the EU has produced, where it is made, or what it does. We map the EU's digital acquis from 1979 to today: we decompose every regulation, directive, and decision into nearly two million recitals and (sub-)articles and classify each with a two-stage pipeline that distills a human-validated ensemble of large language models into open encoder models. The share of digital provisions in newly adopted legislation rose from under one percent in the 1980s to roughly one in ten, and most sit outside the flagship digital acts. Testing two prominent claims, we show that digital legislation has become more assertive over time, with its obligations and prohibitions falling increasingly on private actors, and that it is more rights-oriented than the rest of EU law yet still more market- than rights-oriented, with the rights it invokes being mostly civil. We release our provision-level dataset, classification models, and a Python package for building granular legislative corpora: open infrastructure for measuring not just how much legislation there is, but what it says and does.

articles.title: Who Wants More War? Conflict Exposure, Perceptions of Public Opinion, and Preferences for Conflict Escalation in Israel
articles.authors: Nicholas Sambanis; Itamar Yakir
articles.abstract: We explore whether conformity to perceptions of public opinion shapes individual foreign policy preferences in the aftermath of a militarized conflict between Israel and Iran in June 2025. Exploiting naturally occurring variation in exposure to an Iranian missile attack, we measure Israelis' proneness to hawkish (vs. dovish) policy responses as a function of information concerning the majority's policy preferences. We find that Israelis shift their preferences to align with perceived majority opinion: when they perceive the public to be dovish, they support more dovish positions; whereas they become more hawkish when they perceive the public as hawkish. People who report having been exposed to Iranian attacks show stronger support for belligerence. Partisanship also matters as respondents are more likely to respond to cues aligned with priors that are consistent with their party's positions. We explore mechanisms of these patterns.

articles.title: Climate Change Coverage in The Guardian, 2010–2025
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Simon Wimmer; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Leading news outlets play a central role in shaping how political leaders and the public understand the causes, impacts, and solutions to climate change. Here, we provide the first comprehensive assessment of how The Guardian, a globally influential newspaper widely recognized for high-quality climate journalism, has reported on climate change between 2010 and 2025. We applied a validated methodology based on large language models to analyze N = 18,785 articles and evaluate to what extent reporting covers scientifically grounded causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and adaptation measures. We find that climate coverage increased markedly after 2018 and has remained structurally elevated relative to the preceding decade. Coverage of causes and mitigation is dominated by fossil fuels and renewable energy, whereas agriculture, overconsumption, carbon inequality, and economic growth are mentioned far less frequently. Aspects related to adaptation receive considerably less attention than aspects related to causes, impacts, and mitigation. Our findings highlight opportunities for more comprehensive coverage that better reflects full range of societal transformations needed to address climate change.

articles.title: Can Ethnic Divisions Explain  Poor Economic Growth in  Resource Rich Countries? The Case of the Middle East
articles.authors: Sinem Acar-Burkay
articles.abstract: This paper addresses the question of the effects of ethnic diversity on economic growth. It extends the cross-country growth regressions in Easterly and Levine (1997) by allowing for growth effects of natural resources to depend on the amount of ethnic fractionalization to see if ethnic diversity, natural resource abundance, and the interaction of the two can explain Middle Eastern Countries' poor economic performance. And, the answer is found to be “yes”: The resource curse applies in ethnically heterogeneous countries but not in homogenous ones.

articles.title: Local-Oriented Online Communities in Urban Communication Infrastructures: News Media, Engagement, and Emotion in 128 North American City Communities
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities (LOOCs) have become ubiquitous spaces for discussing national and local news as well as urban civic life, yet existing scholarship lacks a consistent framework to explain what shapes their behavioral and emotional outcomes across diverse contexts. This study applies Communication Infrastructure Theory (CIT) to conceptualize LOOCs as meso-level storytellers whose outcomes are shaped by their connections to broader storytelling networks. Analyzing 1,613,650 posts and 32,706,953 comments from 128 North American city subreddits over the full year of 2024, we examine how connections to mainstream media, local media, urban governance topics, and everyday urban life topics predict thread-level engagement and emotional expression. Results show that both mainstream and local media connections substantially increase engagement but correlate with more negative emotional expression. Urban governance topics increase behavioral engagement but elicit negative sentiment, whereas everyday urban life topics exhibit the inverse pattern, showing an engagement–negativity tradeoff.

articles.title: Political Talk in Nonpolitical Digital Spaces
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: In recent years, scholars in communication and media studies have increasingly turned their attention to political discourse that emerges incidentally within ostensibly nonpolitical digital contexts. These political discussions not only permeate diverse online platforms and communities, but also carry significant democratic potential. Despite growing interest in the phenomenon, existing research remains fragmented across distinct theoretical traditions and lacks a coherent conceptual understanding. This article addresses that gap by reviewing studies in three epistemological orientations—post-positivist, interpretive, and critical—that can guide the analysis of political talk in nonpolitical digital environments. In doing so, it highlights how this group of phenomena can be understood and interpreted with different theoretical assumptions, thereby enabling scholars to better assess their communicative and political significance. This review offers a foundation for more integrative and theoretically informed research on the various dimensions of political expression in digital networked publics.

articles.title: Toward non-textual representation of social anthropology: Modeling cultures as knowledge graphs
articles.authors: Manolis Peponakis; Sarantos Kapidakis; Martin Doerr; Eirini Tountasaki
articles.abstract: The study examines the emerging field of knowledge representation in the context of the semantic web and linked data, with a focus on knowledge produced within the social sciences - particularly in sociocultural anthropology. It starts from the premise that natural language, especially its textualized form, has long been the primary vehicle for producing and communicating anthropological research. Informed by theoretical approaches from information science, the study explores how computational methods may offer alternative modes of structuring and representing anthropological knowledge. It challenges the dominance of text as the sole representational medium and highlights the potential of semantic modeling to open new epistemological pathways. At the same time, it acknowledges the conceptual and methodological challenges involved in such a transition. This approach shifts emphasis away from metrics and programming, foregrounding processes of conceptualization, semantics, meaning, and reasoning as key to engaging with anthropological knowledge in digital environments.

articles.title: Climate Change Coverage in The Guardian, 2010–2025
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Simon Wimmer; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Leading news outlets play a central role in shaping how political leaders and the public understand the causes, impacts, and solutions to climate change. Here, we provide the first comprehensive assessment of how The Guardian, a globally influential newspaper widely recognized for high-quality climate journalism, has reported on climate change between 2010 and 2025.
