articles.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
articles.authors: Meg Small; Sally Dancer; Jonathan Wright; Blake Anthony Colaianne; Gillian Sommerville
articles.abstract: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

articles.title: The Symbolic Organisation of Political Antagonism: An Integrative Model of Cultural and Social Polarisation
articles.authors: Werner Binder; Matthias Revers; Marcus Morgan; María Luengo
articles.abstract: This article develops a cultural and relational model of political polarisation that integrates insights from currently disconnected streams of scholarship to conceive polarisation as a discursive and performative struggle over sacred meanings. Rather than treating polarisation as mere attitudinal divergence, we frame it as the symbolic organization of political antagonism. We identify three interrelated cultural dimensions and one social dimension. These are (1) ideological divergence as bifurcating responses to contested issues, conceptualized as morally and emotionally charged signifiers; (2) the ideological consistency of these divergent issues, enabling chains of signification held together by what we call 'linking signifiers' that mark group identity; (3) the mutual constitution of opposing semiotic chains and identities, which describes how antagonistic groups performatively mobilise opposing discourses to co-constitutively define themselves in relation to one another; and (4) social polarisation, which is based in e.g., inequalities, segregations, or violent conflicts.  We then present a pathway model which expresses how cultural and social polarisation drive or diminish one another over time. This model thereby offers a sociological theory of polarisation and depolarisation as interlinked processes rather than as separate phenomena requiring separate theories. This paper also maps out the implications of our model for empirical polarisation and depolarisation research.

articles.title: Who influences climate adaptation? Farmer and advisor social networks and differentiated benefits of participation in a climate adaptation fellowship program
articles.authors: Sara Delaney; Rachel E. Schattman; Janica Anderzén
articles.abstract: Due to ongoing and projected environmental change farmers and agricultural advisors need access to up-to-date and relevant information and advice to continue to be effective in their work. Education and advising services aim to transmit new information and facilitate change in behavior, often using peer-to-peer or cohort style approaches. However, given that learning and behavior is continuously shaped by interactions, we must understand the role of these interventions within broader climate adaptation networks. This study explores the social networks of a cohort of farmers and agricultural advisors who participated in a Climate Adaptation Fellowship program. Drawing on pre- and post-program surveys and interviews and longitudinal social network analysis, we first explore the range of sources that farmers and advisors in this cohort reported using for adaptation-related information, advice, and support. We also examine the impact of the program on the inter-cohort network and participants’ individual social networks. We find high diversity in the composition of interviewees’ adaptation networks. Farmers and advisors engage widely on adaptation, and while they use other farmers and advisors as resources for adaptation, they also draw on media, customers, friends, family, and the broader community. This heterogeneity has benefits for effective decision-making but also implies that messaging through single channels will only reach a limited audience. The analysis also shows that the program had variable effects among participants over time. There was a meaningful change in the social networks of approximately half of the fellows. While a subset of the group grew progressively more densely connected, others lost contact. We argue that this uneven engagement and impact is not a fault, but instead an invitation to capitalize on the energy of these most interconnected members and also find opportunities to engage those on the periphery over time. Programming can also be strategically expanded to a wider circle to help participants carry forward new learning.

articles.title: Concentration Without Representation
articles.authors: Burak Ozturan; David Lazer
articles.abstract:
A small fraction of users produces most of what circulates online, and the expectation that falling
publication costs would flatten this gradient has not been borne out. Two questions about that
concentration remain open. Published estimates of how concentrated sharing is vary by a factor
of three at comparable thresholds, with no account of why, and the demographic composition of
heavy sharers has received little systematic attention outside the study of misinformation, where
existing work does not separate the users who share the most from those whose shares reach the
most people. Using 38 million news shares by 493,237 registered US voters matched to their Twit-
ter accounts across 57 months, we address both. Observation-window length alone reproduces
the full factor-of-three range within a single dataset, holding population and content fixed. The
top one percent accounts for 22 percent of shares at a one-week window and 52 percent at 57
months. Two tests establish that the rise is compositional and not behavioral, since holding sample
size fixed does not flatten the curve and a cohort of the same users followed across all windows
stays near 21 percent throughout. Matching observation windows to prior studies that overlap our
own panel narrows the gap for comparable content almost entirely, while a residual gap against
misinformation-specific estimates reflects a difference in content class rather than window choice.
Ranking the same users by sharing volume and by audience reach identifies substantially overlap-
ping but still distinct populations, overlapping by 49.9 percent at the top one percent against one
percent expected by chance. Both elites are older and more Democratic than the panel, with mean
age rising from 40.5 years to 57.0 under activity ranking. Gender behaves differently. Male and
female users share at statistically indistinguishable rates throughout the activity distribution, and
a thirteen-point gap appears only at the extreme of the follower tail, where female share falls to
34.8 percent. Elite position is durable at the head of the distribution and close to memoryless in
the middle. The users who share the most only partly overlap with the users whose shares travel
furthest, and both groups are unrepresentative of the voting public in overlapping but distinct ways.

articles.title: Review bombing the video game industries: Sabotage as political consumer practice
articles.authors: Andrew Wirzburger
articles.abstract: Spaces of consumption have long been sites of tension and contestation between corporations and consumers. Since the late 2010s, review bombing has emerged as a persistent feature of this conflict. Consumers practice review bombing to take action in response to perceived grievances by inundating products with negative online reviews to drive down their aggregate ratings. Online reviews have been touted as part of a shift in power from producers to consumers championed by the logics of social commerce, and yet companies wield tremendous power over consumers. This study frames review bombing as sabotage, a withdrawal of efficiency. Through relational-ethnographic approaches to two cases of review bombing in the video game industries, the study argues that the efficacy of review bombing depends on a combination of spectacle and policy. While specific outcomes vary, review bombing is exceedingly effective at sabotaging the logics of the video games industries more broadly.

articles.title: Modelación Lógico-Proposicional y Reducción Forense Frente a la Infoxicación Procesal: Epistemología Jurídica "Desde Abajo" en la Defensa del Parque La Valvanera  /  Logical-Propositional Modeling and Forensic Reduction Against Procedural Information Overload: "Bottom-Up" Legal Epistemology in the Defense of La Valvanera Park
articles.authors: Luis Felipe Narvaez Galindez
articles.abstract:
RESUMEN:
El presente artículo analiza las asimetrías epistémicas y procesales en el litigio de derechos colectivos en Colombia. Desde la sociología reflexiva de Alvin Gouldner y la Investigación-Acción Participativa (IAP) de Orlando Fals Borda, se examina la resistencia comunitaria frente a la privatización del Parque La Valvanera en Pitalito, Huila. Se documenta la trayectoria del colectivo popular desde la tutela hasta el cauce contencioso-administrativo, abordando el ensayo decolonial con Enrique Dussel y categorías autónomas. Frente al dilema de Audre Lorde sobre las herramientas hegemónicas, se fundamenta cómo el repliegue provisional de los conceptos propios y la adopción de la lógica formal constituyeron una apropiación táctica de la racionalidad procesal dominante para salvaguardar un derecho material inminente, preservando la doctrina comunitaria para el debate sociológico formal. Asimismo, ante la infoxicación procesal desplegada por las demandadas mediante el aporte desarticulado de 800 MB de expedientes, se formaliza la introducción de un modelo algebraico booleano (V = A ∧ B ∧ C). Se expone la operacionalización de tres silogismos deónticos, una matriz de confesión cruzada y la extensión del modelo a defensas herméticas mediante prueba documental de puro derecho, situando la argumentación técnica como compuerta procesal hacia la Sentencia Anticipada (Art. 182A del CPACA).

ABSTRACT:
This article analyzes the epistemic and procedural asymmetries in public interest litigation in Colombia. Drawing upon Alvin Gouldner's reflexive sociology and Orlando Fals Borda's Participatory Action Research (PAR), it examines community resistance against the privatization of La Valvanera Park in Pitalito, Huila. The paper documents the collective's trajectory from an initial injunction (tutela) to administrative proceedings, addressing decolonial theory grounded in Enrique Dussel and bottom-up categories. Engaging with Audre Lorde's dilemma regarding hegemonic tools, it theorizes how setting aside indigenous concepts in favor of formal logic was a tactical appropriation of dominant procedural rationality to safeguard an urgent collective right, preserving autonomous doctrine for scholarly debate. Confronted with procedural information overload deployed by the defendants through the disorganized submission of 800 MB of files, the paper formalizes the introduction of a Boolean algebraic reduction model (V = A ∧ B ∧ C). It details three deontic syllogisms, a cross-party admission matrix, and the model's extension to airtight defenses via documentary evidence of pure law, positioning technical argumentation as the procedural mechanism for an Early Judgment under Article 182A of the CPACA.

articles.title: Examining Rising Life Satisfaction in Russia Amidst War: The Role of Perceived Socioeconomic Status Before and During the Ukraine War
articles.authors: Pavel Vlasov
articles.abstract: Previous research has firmly established life satisfaction within the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS) as a reliable measure for assessing perceived quality of life within Russia. In this paper, we present perceived socioeconomic status (PSS) within the RLMS as a latent measure introduced to help examine levels of life satisfaction in Russia before (prewar 2018-2019) and during the Ukraine war (wartime 2022-2023). Using exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modelling (SEM), the findings indicate that PSS is a robust measure that increases the explanatory power of prewar and wartime models and positively predicts life satisfaction in both periods. Contemporary wellbeing research consistently supports the view that a key mechanism in shaping life satisfaction lies in how certain demographic conditions are psychologically interpreted. Drawing on appraisal theory, the study thus suggests that subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position provide meaningful information for understanding wellbeing that cannot be captured by demographic characteristics alone. Moreover, in the RLMS, overreliance on demographic indicators is shown to obscure the subjective mechanisms through which individuals living through wartime conditions evaluate their life satisfaction and interpret their social positions. Overall, the paper emphasizes that future research on the RLMS should consider incorporating PSS in their analyses and further developing on how subjective appraisals of socioeconomic position capture aspects of life satisfaction that are simply immeasurable in demographic only models of the RLMS. Emphasis should be placed on the major social, economic, and political disruption caused by the war that become normalized over time.

articles.title: Representation of Police in Television, 2020 Anti-Police Movements, and Audience Reception
articles.authors: Jenny Lee
articles.abstract: Police television is one of the most popular genres of television in the modern age. With its continued popularity and high viewership, police television, from fictional to reality shows, is often the first introduction to the criminal justice system for many viewers. Prior research has also shown that many people believe that the information they see on police television is factual and reflective of reality, whether this information is fact checked or not. In fact, the police institution relies on its cultural power to sustain its status as maintainers of social order and of regulators of deviance. However, with the 2020 anti-police brutality movements, the public atmosphere around police undeniably shifted toward a more negative outlook than before. With this question, I seek to identify whether or not there has been a change in the way police officers are portrayed in television, and if so, how change has been implemented. In addition, I seek to find how police television continues to curate a specific image of police officers without ignoring the social movements that were present. Through the qualitative observation of two television shows, I explore the changes in portrayals of police officers across the two shows. I find that there are more varied portrayals of police officers in specific categories, yet police officers are still shown to be the sole method of maintaining social order and controlling deviance. The police television shows observed in this paper adhere to the promotion of “ideal cop” principles to show the effectiveness of police officers in regulating society.

articles.title: Defining Nature for Policy and Practice
articles.authors: Patricia Soranno; Stephen Posner; Courtney DeLoatch-Hill; Emerson Conrad-Rooney; Katie Arkema; Meena M. Balgopal; Gillian Bowser; Monika M. Derrien; Kevin C. Elliott; Tessa Francis
articles.abstract: What counts as "nature" is increasingly central to public policies, investment decisions, and scientific assessments, yet the term is often left undefined or implicit. Because nature is a complex, value-laden concept, a universal definition is unlikely to serve all uses, creating problems for comparability and auditability of claims. When users document what counts as nature and disclose the basis for their claims, measurement becomes more comparable, and accountability improves. We present a framework that pairs a concise definition with its purpose, context, and boundary rules, and apply it to develop a definition of nature that can reveal how benefits, harms, and stewardship responsibilities are distributed across people and places. Definitions should be treated as public commitments: articulating both a definition and a replicable process for revision makes governance more transparent, auditable, and open to legitimate contest.

articles.title: How bibliometric indicators align with REF 2021 peer review across disciplines
articles.authors: Junjie Shen
articles.abstract: Bibliometric indicators are increasingly used to approximate expert peer review, but how well they do so varies across disciplines in ways that remain poorly understood. Existing analyses of the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) have largely correlated metrics with individual article quality scores, within single fields and using restricted-access data. This study takes a complementary approach based on publicly available data: institutional REF 2021 output GPA is correlated with a consistent set of citation-based and journal-based indicators for all submitting institutions across fifteen Units of Assessment (UoAs). Comparing the two types of indicators side by side reveals a continuum of evaluation cultures. At one end, Physics tracks citation impact far more closely than journal rank (correlations of 0.85 versus 0.42, based on the share of outputs in the top 10% of each measure). At the other end, Business and Management Studies shows the reverse (0.59 versus 0.92), among the strongest journal-based correlations across all fields examined. Of the fifteen UoAs, nine correspond best with journal-based indicators and six with citation-based indicators, a divide that cuts across the usual STEM/non-STEM boundary. Indicator validity is therefore not a property of the metric alone but of the discipline’s evaluation culture, and research assessment should choose and interpret metrics field by field.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Green: The Production of Green Conformity in European Cultural Policy
articles.authors: Vânia Rodrigues; Catarina Santos-Silva; Olga Solovova
articles.abstract:
Ecological vocabulary is nearly absent until 2021, when greening became a cross-cutting programme priority, and rises abruptly thereafter. Green, climate and sustainable increasingly appear together as an interchangeable signal of commitment. Sustainable also retains its earlier organisational meaning, binding ecological claims to claims of institutional survival. Modernisation dominates the coded projects, framing sustainability as innovation, capacity-building and better practice. Transformative elements persist only as traces, and the vocabularies of degrowth, commoning and ecological justice are absent or residual across the whole corpus. The programme's explicit greening guidance appears to supply the very terms in which compliance is demonstrated.
The article argues that this narrowing is anticipatory and sincere, which makes it harder to contest than greenwashing. It contributes to debates on travelling cultural policy and multilateral cultural governance by showing how a transnational green idiom, composed largely in English, carries a sustainability paradigm across Europe while constraining the ecological futures cultural institutions can meaningfully articulate.

articles.title: Uncovering Student Thinking from Only the Answer: A GenAI Perspective
articles.authors: Tommy Stell; Darryl Chamberlain; Kelvin Rozier; Yaroslav Molkov; Russell Jeter
articles.abstract: Identifying the underlying reasoning behind a student’s response to a mathematical question is a time-intensive activity for instructors. This work seeks to answer if a Large Language Model (LLM) can be used to identify potential student thinking based solely on their final response. To evaluate the LLM’s identification of potential student thinking, we developed an ordinal scale which describes how well the LLM’s identification aligns with a content expert’s identification of potential student thinking. We then utilized this scale to evaluate the ability of the Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview LLM to identify potential student thinking in a variety of College Algebra questions. We show that the LLM was able to correctly identify the mechanism encoded in the distractor, in a little over half (55.25%) of cases. This work highlights the limits of current LLMs’ ability to identify potential student thinking and further highlights the necessity of instructors to provide targeted feedback based on student thinking.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz
articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. A bounded exploratory pilot applies the strategy to the publicly accessible, logged-out segment of ConsultaLEX, the Portuguese government portal for legislative and regulatory consultations. The pilot covers discovery, orientation, and authentication and assesses the availability of an entry point to expression and feedback. It identifies enabling conditions in programmatically named controls, structured consultation information, exact dates, and alternative authentication routes. Potentially constraining conditions involve relative deadlines, scripted navigation, registration and identity requirements, and human verification. Because no live commenting process was available, expression and feedback could not be inspected. The study therefore supports mechanism-level inferences rather than claims about participant exclusion or platform-wide conformance. These findings support treating accessibility as a necessary but insufficient condition for equal participation. The paper contributes a proof of concept connecting accessibility evidence to democratic analysis and identifies disability-led participant testing, live-process observation, and cross-platform comparison as priorities for future research.

articles.title: Why Do Immigrant Girls Participate Less in Organized Leisure Activities? The Role of Parental Influence Across the Transition from Adolescence to Adulthood
articles.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Frank van Tubergen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles.abstract: Research documents immigrant-native gaps in girls’ participation in organized leisure activities across Western Europe, particularly among Muslim immigrant-origin girls. While parental characteristics are often assumed to shape these gaps, less is known about which parental factors matter most and how their influence unfolds from adolescence into adulthood. Using German longitudinal data from CILS4EU and CILS4EU-DE, we address these questions by examining participation gaps among non-Muslim and Muslim immigrant-origin girls relative to native girls across the transition from adolescence to early adulthood.In doing so, we estimate a structural equation model that distinguishes between initial parental effects in adolescence, path-dependent effects linking adolescent and adult participation, and persistent parental effects in early adulthood. Differences in parental participation andsocioeconomic resources explain a substantial share of theimmigrant-native participation gaps, whereas parental gender values explain comparatively little. Although participation gaps narrow over time, they persist, primarily through path-dependent processes, as lower participation during adolescence is carried forward into adulthood. Persistent parental effects remain but are comparatively modest. While participation gaps are larger among Muslim immigrant-origin girls, the underlying mechanisms are broadly similar across immigrant-origin groups. The findings highlight how family-based inequalities shape participation trajectories and contribute to the production and reproduction of participation gaps across the life course.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Homeschooling as Racial Retreat: The Impact of School District and Leadership Diversity
articles.authors: Maranda Joyce
articles.abstract: What explains the decision to homeschool? This study examines whether local racial context influences families’ decisions to homeschool their children. I argue that many white parents exit public school systems due to concerns about the distribution of school resources to racial out-groups, particularly in racially diverse and resource-constrained districts. I conduct a state-representative survey of over 30,000 respondents to describe the homeschooling population in the United States. Then, using data from Virginia that link student and district leadership demographics (school board members and superintendents) to district-level homeschooling rates, I examine how racial composition and leadership diversity shape educational exit. I find that higher levels of non-white students and certain kinds of leadership diversity are positively associated with increased homeschooling, especially where resources are limited. By showing that homeschooling is often motivated by perceived racial threat, this study informs debates about the regulation and public subsidization of homeschooling.

articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz

This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: Harnessing Human–AI Interpretive Difference: Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: Recent debate over GenAI in qualitative inquiry centres on concerns that computational participation reinforces postpositivist dominance. Critical analysts propose excluding it, out-theorising it, or continuously inspecting its entanglements. In parallel, a growing body of work builds architectures to accommodate human-AI collaboration in interpretive inquiry. While most of this work relies on postpositivist assumptions, an emerging strand develops collaborative architectures grounded in interpretivism, an approach this article adopts. I propose that for computational interpretation to be part of interpretivist inquiry without being granted reflexivity or interpretive authority, it must be deliberately structured into an accountable, productive relationship alongside human interpretation. To that end, I outline Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism, an epistemological position resting on five propositions. First, productive epistemic non-equivalence holds that human and computational interpretation need not share an epistemic basis for their difference to be structured as a resource. Second, interpretive co-construction grounds computational interpretation in meanings negotiated between researcher and participant, rather than a decontextualised corpus. Third, productive divergence treats non-alignment between human and computational interpretations as a potential source of analytic insight. Fourth, interpretive traceability refers to the capacity to see the grounds upon which human and computational interpretations are made, rendering them accountable structurally. Fifth, reflexive engagement holds that computational participation can create occasions for the researcher to interrogate her relationship to her subjectivity. This position is operationalised through Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA). LICA deploys computational interpretation to anchor interpretive insights to the empirical material. It integrates explicit interpretive co-construction between participant and researcher in interviews, scrutinises divergence between researcher and computational interpretations, renders analytic reasoning traceable, and embeds the researcher's subjectivity into the computational process. Together, these features create the conditions for new insights to emerge from the interaction between human and computational interpretations.

articles.title: Do genes modify earnings trajectories following job loss?  Gene-environment interactions with endogenous and exogenous forms of job loss
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship; Arno Van Hootegem; Henri Salokangas; Gaia Ghirardi; Henrik Dobewall; Laura Jernström; Maria Vaalavuo
articles.abstract: Job loss is a disruptive event that results in long-term economic scarring, though effects vary across social groups. This study explores a new potential source of inequality in the impact of job loss by examining whether genetic traits can amplify or attenuate earning declines following job loss. To address bias from gene-environment correlations, we compare interactions between polygenic indices (PGIs) and both endogenous job loss (individual unemployment) and exogenous job loss (plant closures). We focus on PGIs for depression, educational attainment, and risk-taking. Using Finnish population register data linked to genetic information for approximately 10,000 individuals observed over ten years, we apply a difference-in-differences design. We find persistent earnings losses following job loss, with larger declines for endogenous unemployment spells. Genetic moderation is observed only for plant closures: individuals with higher depression-related PGIs experience greater earnings declines. No comparable interactions emerge for endogenous job loss or the other PGIs.

articles.title: The Qualitative Network Approach: A Methodological Framework and Tutorial for Relational Coding
articles.authors: Ivonne Lipsch-Wijnen; Femke Nijland; Vanessa Torres van Grinsven; Szilvia Zörgő; Gjalt - Jorn Peters
articles.abstract: Relationships between concepts are often interpreted during qualitative analysis but may remain implicit within coding structures, thematic descriptions, or analytical narratives. This article introduces the Qualitative Network Approach (QNA), a methodological framework for representing qualitative codes as interconnected elements. Its associated method, QNA network coding, specifies interpreted connections between pairs of qualitative codes according to relationship type and, where relevant, directionality. A four-step tutorial demonstrates how researchers can identify two concepts in the data for relational interpretation, identify and specify their relationship using the codebook, assign the three codes to the data fragment, and document a QNA network code. A worked interview example illustrates how individual QNA network codes can form a wider QNA network code structure. QNA may be useful when relationships between concepts are analytically important. By making relational interpretations explicit and traceable to the underlying data, QNA aims to increase the transparency and inspectability of qualitative analysis.

articles.title: Sentiment change points, not peaks, mark when public opinion has yet to settle
articles.authors: Chenying Weng; Yilun Chen; Huazhen Huang; Yiting Yang; He Gong; Hongkai Wang
articles.abstract: Timing interventions during public controversies requires more than identifying when sentiment is strongest: a peak does not tell us whether public opinion can still change. We analyzed about 1.34M Weibo posts about a controversial news event (Company T vs. Company L), separating sentiment strength by referent and tracking the resulting trajectories across the event. After sudden change points (SCPs) sentiment-strength trajectories and public expression continued to change; after peak points (PPs) they largely stabilized (mean absolute displacement 3.291 times; p = 0.035), and discourse-strategy composition changed around SCPs but stayed largely stable around PPs. SCPs, not PPs, are the candidate leverage points. This suggests that the strongest moment is where public opinion settles, so mitigation should act at the SCP.

articles.title: Examining the Multidimensional Structure of Subjective Well-Being: Evidence from Mexico
articles.authors: Carlos Alberto Arellano-Esparza
articles.abstract: Most research on subjective well-being (SWB) relies on the classic tripartite model of life satisfaction, positive affect, and negative affect, which may obscure its multidimensional character. Using nationally representative data from Mexico, this study compares alternative structural models of SWB through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, evaluating configurations that integrate eudaimonic, affective, and cognitive components to test whether a multidimensional structure provides a better statistical account of the data than a unidimensional alternative. Several competing models (correlated three-factor, hierarchical, and bifactor) display robust and largely equivalent fit. This multidimensional representation consistently outperforms a unidimensional one and remains largely stable across sex and region, indicating that no single structural model uniquely captures SWB, calling for more flexible approaches to its study.

articles.title: Integrating Green Marketing and Environmental Behavior to Predict Revisit Intention in Indonesian Ecotourism
articles.authors: Andina Fasha; Cheryn Kang; Lady; Budi Setiawan
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The escalation of ecotourism as sustainability-oriented travel highlights the inconsistency of tourists' responsible actions during visits, which is also known as the attitude-behavior gap, whereas environmental concern does not necessarily translate into action, as discussed in sustainable tourism literature.

Research Methodology: A quantitative approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, collected through questionnaire surveys from 478 tourists who had previously visited Ecotourism destinations in Batam City, Indonesia, using SmartPLS 4.

Results: The findings show how direct environmental experiences at the destination were more effective in encouraging responsible tourist behavior than pre-visit digital exposure, which presumes that it is more likely to develop revisit intentions as long-term destination loyalty.

Conclusions: The study highlights the importance of environmental behavior in fostering revisit intention within ecotourism destinations and suggests that direct interpretive experiences at the destination may play a more influential role in shaping tourists’ behavior than digital promotional exposure alone.

Limitations: This study was limited to one ecotourism site in Batam City, with cross-sectional self-reported data, which may have limited generalizability.

Contributions: This study extends sustainable tourism literature by integrating digital green marketing, environmental belief, and environmental interpretation into a unified behavioral framework explaining revisit intention through environmental behavior and offer practical insights for ecotourism managers to strengthen sustainable behavior and long-term destination loyalty through effective communication and interpretation strategies.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping disability inclusion in Canadian park employment: A scoping review of academic and organizational evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Dudney; Zeyad Ghulam; Tilak Dutta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The objective of this scoping review is to map how disability inclusion and accessibility are considered in Canadian park employment literature and organizational discourse. The review will identify and summarize both peer-reviewed literature and organizational evidence to examine how workplace accessibility and disability inclusion are addressed in these settings, and the extent to which they are absent. 

Introduction: Parks and protected areas in Canada are key public-facing service environments that increasingly emphasize accessibility and inclusion in relation to visitor experiences. However, less is known about how these organizations approach employment inclusion for people with disabilities, across both academic literature and organizational documents.  

Inclusion criteria: This review will include sources that concern employment-related stakeholders such as employers, employees, managers or other decision-makers (Population). Literature, policies, and other organizational discourse will be examined to determine the extent they consider disability, accessibility, and disability-inclusive employment (Concept). The search will be limited to Canadian parks and protected area organizations, with a focus on national, provincial, and territorial parks (Context). Sources will not be required to focus on disability and accessibility, provided they contain employment-related content. Both peer-reviewed literature and grey literature will be searched and reviewed. 

Methods: Peer-reviewed literature will include a search of the following collections: EBSCO (EconLit, Business Source Premier), ProQuest (ASSIA, PAIS Index, Policy File Index, Worldwide Political Science Abstracts, IBSS), and Web of Science (Core Collection: SSCI, SCI-Expanded, ESCI, AHCI, CPCI-SSH, CPCI-S, BKCI-SSH). Grey literature will be systematically searched through official websites of Canadian national, provincial and territorial park agencies in Canada, with targeted searches for employment and human resource policies and reports. Searches will not be restricted by date but will be limited to English-language sources. 

The targeted search will take place in September 2026. All identified sources will be imported into Covidence and screened in two stages (title/abstract and full text) against the inclusion criteria. Data will be extracted to capture document characteristics and accessibility or disability inclusion-related content. Findings will be reported using frequency counts and narrative descriptions to map key concepts, evidence types, and gaps. Any deviations from standard JBI scoping review methodology will be documented and justified.

articles_hidden.title: Insights from Facilitator Reflections and Participant Feedback: A Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training Model
articles_hidden.authors: Kate Dunne; Tara Doherty; Sinéad Hanrahan; Ruth Moran; Lorna Walsh; Caragh Tisdall; Ciara McManus; Seán Lacey
articles_hidden.abstract: The Cross-Institutional Research Integrity Training (CIRIT) consortium was established in 2021 by representatives of Irish Research Performing Organisations (RPOs) to collaboratively develop and deliver research integrity (RI) and open science training across the Irish research sector. Underpinning the CIRIT model is a virtue-based approach to RI in which participants work in small groups to engage in dialogue and reflect on moral conflicts and authentic research dilemmas using problem-based learning (PBL) and social constructivist pedagogy. This exploratory mixed-methods case study examined the effectiveness of the CIRIT model and explored its potential as a collaborative cross-institutional approach to RI training. CIRIT facilitators acted as insider researchers, conducting two post-seminar dialogical reflections over a twelve-month period. Seminar participants completed an anonymous post-seminar feedback questionnaire following five CIRIT workshops. A Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) framework informed the analysis of the dialogical reflections, while questionnaire findings were used to contextualise and complement the facilitators' reflections. Findings indicate that the CIRIT model successfully fostered participant engagement, dialogue, and reflective discussion while supporting the development of a collaborative RI community of practice. The findings suggest that collaborative cross-institutional, virtue-based approaches offer a promising model for strengthening RI training and provide a transferable framework that could be adapted within other national research systems, while highlighting the importance of adequate resourcing and institutional recognition.

articles_hidden.title: Searching for Serendipity
articles_hidden.authors: Isaac Tucker; Martin Gonzalez-Cabello; Olav Sorenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Serendipity would seem to preclude purposeful search. To understand the relationship between search behavior and the probability of a serendipitous discovery, we propose a formal modeling framework based on the 𝑁𝐾model. Our simulations suggest that searchers with a clear hypothesis convert good fortune into fitness or value far more effectively. Searchers that pursue their theories through incremental steps instead of long-distance jumps have the highest rates of serendipitous success. Our model also provides insight into the role of bias, inaccurate or incorrect beliefs, and the ruggedness of the terrain in determining the rate of serendipitous discovery. Our results demonstrate the distinct roles of intent and information in finding novel, valuable discoveries.

articles_hidden.title: Соотношение финансового и реального секторов как драйверов развития экономики: систематизация теоретических моделей в рамках 9-слойной схемы системы разделения труда // The Relationship between the Financial and Real Sectors as Drivers of Economic Development: Systematization of Theoretical Models within a Nine-Layer Scheme of the Division of Labor
articles_hidden.authors: Maksim Tsepkov
articles_hidden.abstract:
This meta-research is devoted to the systematization and conceptual comparison of key economic concepts that consider either the real sector and technological innovation, the financial sector, or state institutions as the fundamental drivers of economic development. Comparing traditional models is complicated by the fact that most authors focus on individual factors, ignoring complex interrelated relationships.

To overcome this limitation, nine-layer scheme of the division of labor of Petr Shchedrovitsky is used as an integrative analytical framework, encompassing levels from natural resources and production technologies to knowledge accumulation institutions and monetary systems. The study spatially visualizes the theoretical perspectives of Karl Marx, R. Hilferding, V. Lenin, J. Keynes, H. Minsky, J. Schumpeter, and C. Perez, as well as those of Latin American structuralism, Japanese "knowledge capitalism," and the Chinese school of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Positioning these concepts on a single map allows us to demonstrate their mutual complementarity at different phases of technological and financial cycles and lay the foundations for the synthesis of a comprehensive socioeconomic theory.

The study also identified four main phases of technological and economic cycles, during each of which the role of the financial sector shifts from stimulating to destructive. It is shown that state and national-institutional mechanisms (the Chinese model, the Japanese J-firm) are capable of blocking the speculative separation of the ninth layer from the real sector.

articles_hidden.title: Что такое жертва? Концептуализация виктимизации в опросах
articles_hidden.authors: Ruslan Kuchakov; Dmitriy Serebrennikov
articles_hidden.abstract: В статье рассматриваются основные подходы к концептуализации и операционализации понятия жертвы в виктимизационных опросах. На основе обзора более чем полувековой исследовательской традиции выделяются нормативный и конструктивистский подходы к определению жертвы и анализируются их следствия для дизайна опросных инструментов. Во второй части работы реконструируются три традиции операционализации виктимизации на материале пяти опросов: NCVS, CSEW, SES, ICVS и Всероссийского опроса жертв преступлений (RCVS). Авторы предлагают рассматривать эти исследования через матрицу двух измерений: фиксация факта (или стилизованного факта) виктимизации и фиксация самооценки респондента в качестве жертвы. Показано, что выбор стратегии измерения предполагает поиск баланса между юридической строгостью, обеспечивающей сопоставимость с официальной статистикой, и конструктной валидностью — способностью улавливать реальный опыт виктимизации, в том числе не распознанный самим респондентом. Другой компромисс — уже ресурсный — образует своего рода невозможную триаду: при ограниченном бюджете и времени интервью нельзя одновременно максимизировать содержательную широту опросника, лонгитюдную глубину и статистическую точность (надёжность) оценок. При этом сама лонгитюдная глубина достигается по-разному — от повторных кросс-секционных срезов, где каждая волна опрашивает новую выборку из той же совокупности, до панельных дизайнов, отслеживающих одних и тех же респондентов. Именно последние — панели с наблюдением за одними и теми же людьми — из-за бюджетных ограничений по сей день остаются редкостью.

articles_hidden.title: The chilean health model in the context of latin america. 40 years of economic crises, spending policies and reforms
articles_hidden.authors: Camilo Cid Pedraza; Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter analyzes the relationship between economic crises and health reforms in Latin America, with an in-depth focus on the Chilean case, from the origins of its health model to the present day, including a reflection on its possible future developments. The Chilean health model, as it is known today, was designed amid the international crises of 1975 and 1982 and the political crisis of the dictatorship, and it was consolidated during the economic growth of the 1990s. Its most significant reform, developed following the Asian crisis of 1997, resulted in the AUGE Plan, adopted in 2005, which increased access to a defined set of health conditions without changing the model's underlying structure. The 2008 global financial crisis, and later the 2019 social crisis, opened a new stage of debate over structural change, in which the segmentation between the public insurer (FONASA) and the private insurers (ISAPRES) has come to be seen as the central obstacle to an equitable and solidarity-based health system. The regional analysis shows that this relationship between crises and reforms is not unique to Chile, but follows a broader Latin American pattern, moving from market-oriented reforms in the 1980s and 1990s toward a growing consensus, strengthened by the COVID-19 pandemic, in favor of universal, solidarity-based public health systems.

articles_hidden.title: Are geographical and socioeconomic contexts exchangeable? On simple means versus random effects in the study of health inequalities
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo; Kani Khalaf
articles_hidden.abstract: Multilevel random-effects (RE) models are standard in social and geographical epidemiology. They rest on the assumption of exchangeability, which means that, before seeing the data, we have no reason to distinguish one group from another: group means become draws from one common distribution. RE models were developed for repeated measurements within individuals where a shared physiology underwrites the assumption, and partial pooling improves prediction. A silent transfer later applied the same machinery to schools, hospitals, neighbourhoods and, recently, to intersectional strata. There exchangeability fails twice: individuals are not repeated measurements of their group, and groups are social positions produced by directional forces such as racism, not draws from a common distribution. We review strict, conditional and tolerant readings of exchangeability and show that they agree: social and intersectional categories are not exchangeable, as this would paradoxically require the absence of the unjustified inequalities which are the very object of study. In many intersectional analyses, shrinkage erases the small and deviating strata, where inequality lives. Modelling injustice as dispersion around a mean domesticates rather than denounces it. For describing realised health inequalities we recommend Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA). Here, each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and uncertainty is reported openly rather than smoothed. RE models keep their legitimate uses, such as prediction, cluster-randomised trials and the propensity models of causal S-MAIHDA. Exchangeability is not a property of the software. It is a claim about the world, to be justified in every application.

articles_hidden.title: A Minimal Axiomatic Definition of Democratic Procedure: Count-Based Aggregation with Autonomy and Non-Coercion
articles_hidden.authors: Giulio Vidotto
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper proposes a minimal axiomatic characterization of democratic procedures by combining structural requirements with conditions concerning individual freedom. Rather than starting from substantive conceptions of democracy, the paper treats a decision procedure as a function from profiles of individual expressions to collective outcomes, and asks under which minimal conditions such a procedure may still be called democratic. Four conditions are taken to be jointly required: universal expression, count-dependence, autonomy of judgement, and absence of coercion.
The main distinction introduced by the model concerns two failures that are often treated together, although they occur at different levels: coercion in expression, where individuals cannot state what they judge, and lack of autonomy in judgement formation, where the judgement itself has been shaped by manipulation or systematic distortion. Once these two loci are separated, a procedure may satisfy universal participation and count-based aggregation, and nevertheless remain democratically defective because what is counted is either not freely expressed, or not autonomously formed.
Methodologically, the paper adapts a measurement-theoretic distinction, that between latent and observed variables, to normative procedural theory. The resulting account remains institutionally neutral: it does not presuppose elections, representation, deliberation, or any specific institutional form, but provides a formal language for analyzing collective choice mechanisms, including referenda, digital voting systems, and algorithmic forms of governance.

articles_hidden.title: One meal, not the next: a two-day RCT testing effects of increased plant-based availability on direct and later food choice
articles_hidden.authors: Lotte Patricia de Lint; Wilhelmina Elisabeth Adriana Metje van Rookhuijzen; Rachelle de Vries; Emely de Vet
articles_hidden.abstract: Replacing animal-sourced foods with plant-based alternatives benefits the environment, animal welfare, and public health. Nudges have been found to promote plant-based selection in the moment, but whether they influence later, non-targeted behaviors remains underexplored. Effects on non-targeted behavior could make interventions more effective if they promote consistency in later plant-based choice, or less effective if they trigger compensatory animal-based choice. In a two-day randomized controlled trial (n = 200), we evaluated a Nudge plus intervention delivered on day 1. The intervention combined an increased availability of plant-based to meat sandwich varieties (3:1 vs. 1:3) with a post-choice identity cue informing plant-based choosers that their choice signaled they care about the environment. We assessed intervention effects on targeted behavior (day-1 plant-based lunch choice) and non-targeted behavior (day-2 plant-based lunch choice and 24-hour animal product consumption). Furthermore, we tested whether such effects were mediated by environmental self-identity or moderated by plant-based eating motivation. The increased availability tripled targeted plant-based choice, from 22% in the Reference condition to 66% in the Intervention condition. We detected no main effects of the intervention on either non-targeted outcome, with equivalence tests indicating a negligible effect on 24-hour animal product consumption. There was no evidence of mediation via environmental self-identity or moderation by plant-based eating motivation. Increasing plant-based availability produced a large immediate positive effect on plant-based choice, while the Nudge plus produced no detectable compensatory shifts in non-targeted behavior. These findings support increasing the relative availability of appealing plant-based over meat-based options in food service settings.

articles_hidden.title: Dangers  of  non-objective constructions and  interpretations of history: Important assertions and  takeaways from an Indian context
articles_hidden.authors: Sujay Rao Mandavilli
articles_hidden.abstract:
This short and very brief paper in a way extends our previous papers and publications on historiography, 
though it is in many ways quite important to our core mission. Its importance cannot also not be 
discounted based on our general observation that non-objective and non-purposeful constructs of 
history are widely prevalent across the intellectual spectrum, and both from the left and the right, and 
various errors of omission and commission to this effect and deeply and foundationally entrenched. 
Therefore, it goes without saying that course-corrections are in order, and that the dangers of non
objective and highly biased and prejudiced constructs of history, especially those driven and propelled 
by ideology must be driven home to the broader and larger public. These assume added importance and 
significance in the Indian context for several reasons. Firstly, it precludes a scientific temper being 
inculcated among the laity, as they cannot trust mainstream scholarship any longer. Scientific constructs 
of history are also so important to relegate religion to the background eventually, and keep it in its 
place. Such constructs also lead to a culture of non-objectivity becoming deeply entrenched and it 
invariably begets counter-reactions from other ideologically driven groups. In addition, it is bound to 
severely compromise interdisciplinary approaches and integration across multiple periods and 
geographies all of which are so essential to the healthy growth of scholarship. In situations and 
circumstances where there are ideologically-driven ding dong battles as is presently the case, we may 
even need to adopt an outside in approach and educate the general public about non-objective and 
non-scientific constructs of history first. We are also at a loss to understand why a culture of service of 
historians to science, society, and the education system is not well-entrenched, and immediate course
corrections are in order to promote objectivity in mindset at all costs, and under all circumstances.

articles_hidden.title: Quais os impactos da Lei  de Acesso à Informação  (LAI)?
articles_hidden.authors: Jorge Lucas; Ana Paula Lima dos Santos; João Pedro Cavalcanti Silva
articles_hidden.abstract:
O estudo busca avaliar os impactos da implementação da Lei de Acesso à 
Informação (LAI) sobre a transparência pública, a accountability e o controle social no 
Brasil, com base em uma revisão sistemática de 32 trabalhos. Os resultados indicam 
efeitos principalmente institucionais e organizacionais: a LAI contribuiu para 
institucionalizar o direito de acesso à informação, expandir os mecanismos de 
transparência ativa e passiva, criar condições para o controle social e modificar 
práticas internas de gestão da informação. Contudo, os efeitos são heterogêneos e 
predominantemente qualitativos. Embora diversos órgãos tenham criado portais, 
Serviços de Informação ao Cidadão (SICs) e regulamentações locais, a simples 
disponibilização de informações não garante transparência efetiva, accountability ou 
redução de irregularidades. O único estudo quantitativo identificado não encontrou 
associação estatisticamente significativa entre as medidas de transparência e a 
redução da corrupção ou da má gestão nos municípios analisados.

articles_hidden.title: The Kia-Hyundai vehicle theft surge: the roles of anti-theft devices and co-occurring offenses
articles_hidden.authors: Graham Farrell; John Roman
articles_hidden.abstract: Between 2019 and 2023, vehicle theft in the United States increased 40 percent. This study addresses this as a natural experiment, using a quasi-experimental design for causal inference to attribute the increase to theft of Kia and Hyundai vehicles manufactured without engine immobilizers. It is conservatively estimated that by the end of 2024 there were over 1.1 million excess vehicle thefts and over three hundred thousand excess co-occurring offenses including homicides, violence and other serious offenses. The evidence indicates that the withdrawal of situational crime prevention measures can increase crime and criminality and that the long-term national crime declines cannot be taken for granted. Additional implications are identified.

articles_hidden.title: How Parties Reshaped Class Participation: The Central Role of Parental Abstention
articles_hidden.authors: Giacomo Melli
articles_hidden.abstract: Labour’s programmatic realignment in the 1990s withdrew a generation of working-class adults from electoral politics. Abstention rose disproportionately in the working class, reshaping the formative environments of subsequent cohorts. This paper traces the lagged intergenerational effects of that shift on class inequalities in turnout. The analysis draws on linked parent-child data from the British Household Panel Survey and Understanding Society (1992-2025), in which parental class position and electoral participation are observed directly during respondents’ formative years, and combines random-effects panel models with parametric and nonparametric decomposition. The association between class origin and adult turnout is stable across cohorts socialised before and after realignment. What differs is the distribution of formative environments: exposure to parental abstention is substantially more unequal across class origins in the later cohort. Parental participation accounts for over forty per cent of the post-realignment class-origin gap, net of class destination and educational attainment, and counterfactual estimates suggest that equalising exposure would return the gap to pre-realignment levels. Class inequalities in turnout are therefore in part the lagged consequence of party strategy, transmitted through households and carried into the electorate by successive cohorts.

articles_hidden.title: How should VAWG be measured in the new UK strategy to halve it in ten years?
articles_hidden.authors: Sylvia Walby; Brian Francis
articles_hidden.abstract:
New metrics to evaluate the UK government’s strategy to halve violence against women and girls in
ten years are proposed. If the strategy to reduce violence against women and girls is to concern the
whole of government and the whole of society, then its measurement needs to mainstreamed not
confined to a separate silo. Three issues in building metrics are identified and resolved: strategic
(mainstreaming rather than a separate silo), conceptual (defining ‘women and girls’ and extending
violence to include non-domestic; distinguishing between different forms of ‘violence’); and
technical (strengths and weaknesses of different data sources and statistical techniques). While the
new government headline metric of a combined measure using a single data source has problems.
Modifying the combined metric and adding five supporting metrics and two additional data sources
would address these, achieving compatibility with the main statistical series on violent crime,
making visible the scale of the gender gap in more serious forms of violence, such as homicide, rape,
and high frequency victims, and making visible specific forms particularly relevant to Black,
minoritised and migrant women. This contribution to the indicators in the UK Strategy engages
global debates while focusing on the English context with its specific epistemic systems that engage
policy and data.

articles_hidden.title: Geographic Diversity and the Strategic Placement of Immigrant Candidates
articles_hidden.authors: Verena Fetscher; Ilayda Yücel
articles_hidden.abstract: Immigrant-background populations remain underrepresented in national legislatures. A common explanation is that parties perceive immigrant-background candidates as electorally costly and therefore place them disproportionately in unwinnable contests. Existing research, however, pays little attention to the geographic concentration of immigrant-background populations, which can create electoral incentives as well as risks. We argue that parties strategically nominate immigrant-background candidates where demographic diversity generates electoral opportunity. Using original data on all candidates in German federal elections from 2002 to 2025, we show that immigrant-background candidates are more likely to be nominated in districts with larger immigrant populations, especially where those districts are electorally competitive. We further show that these nomination patterns can translate into electoral gains, but the effect is limited. The strongest evidence comes from Turkish co-ethnic dynamics, and the electoral benefits are concentrated in the Social Democratic Party, which has historically had the closest ties to Turkish-background voters in Germany.

articles_hidden.title: Converging Across Generations? Intergenerational Integration into Associational Life
articles_hidden.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Anders Bastrup Jørgensen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the extent to which immigrant-native gaps in voluntary association involvement, a key dimension of associational life, narrow across generations. Neo-assimilation theory suggests broad intergenerational progression, whereas segmented assimilation theory points to more heterogeneous trajectories across groups with different civic and religious backgrounds. To test these expectations, we examine intergenerational differences in voluntary association membership, active participation, and volunteering among non-Western immigrant-origin adults aged 18-50, using linked survey and register data from the Danish Citizenship Survey (N = 4,273). Logistic regression analyses reveal substantial intergenerational progression toward native levels of involvement. While first-generation immigrants are markedly less involved than natives, childhood immigrants and second-generation immigrants display involvement levels substantially closer to, and in some cases indistinguishable from, those of natives. Progression occurs broadly across groups with different civic and religious backgrounds, and groups with more distant backgrounds do not consistently exhibit less progression. KHB decomposition analyses further reveal that socioeconomic attainment and, especially, citizenship status account for substantial shares of the observed intergenerational progression, ranging from 40-47% for membership to 80-86% for volunteering. Overall, the findings extend neo-assimilation theory’s expectation of broad intergenerational progression to associational life and highlight the importance of structural and formal incorporation in this process.

articles_hidden.title: The Writing on the Wall: Foreign Coup Success and Preemptive Purges in Autocracies
articles_hidden.authors: Kyosuke Kikuta; Jun Koga Sudduth
articles_hidden.abstract: There is broad scholarly consensus that leaders' perceived vulnerability to removal through coups determines when they act to weaken regime elites' capacity to organize a coup. Existing research, however, primarily examines domestic sources of leaders' perceptions of coup threats and overlooks the influence of foreign events. This study contends that successful foreign coups within the same region increase leaders' perceived vulnerability to coup threats, prompting preemptive purges of potentially threatening regime elites before such threats materialize domestically. We test this argument using novel monthly data on elite purges in autocracies from 1980 to 2010. By leveraging plausibly exogenous variation in foreign coup outcomes and a difference-in-differences approach, we demonstrate that foreign coup success increases the likelihood of authoritarian purges. These findings underscore the important yet frequently neglected role of foreign events in prompting autocrats to shift the leader-elite power balance in their favor.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Questionnaire Notifications on Engagement and Attrition in an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study: Longitudinal Observational Study
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Dvořák; Martin Kreidl; Martin Tancoš
articles_hidden.abstract:
Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies are widely used in mobile health (mHealth) research and interventions. EMA requires participants to repeatedly open short questionnaires announced by smartphone notifications, so notification scheduling is a central design decision. Yet evidence on how repeated prompts shape short-term engagement and long-term attrition remains fragmented.

We examined (a) how notification order within a measurement window relates to the timing and likelihood of questionnaire opening, and (b) whether the number of notifications within a burst relates to permanent disengagement, in a 12-month, multi-burst smartphone EMA study of Czech adolescents.

We analyzed paradata from the FUTURE project, an observational EMA study of 201 adolescents (13–17 years). Four 14-day bursts each contained up to four short questionnaires per day, with up to 10 notifications per questionnaire window. Time from first notification to opening was modeled with Cox survival models with respondent-level frailty. Permanent dropout was modeled with logistic regression at the person-burst level. We tested whether demographics, timing, and the momentary phone context (screen activity, app use) moderated the notification effects. Analyses used Stata 18.

A total of 26,007 questionnaires were notified. Of these, 17,668  (67.9%) were opened. Within a measurement window, among questionnaires still unopened, later reminders were associated with a slightly higher chance of opening (hazard ratio [HR] 1.13, 95% CI 1.06–1.19; P<.001), and this estimate was stable across all models, and we found no sign of within-window reminder fatigue. Gender, age, and socioeconomic status changed this pattern only marginally. The phone context mattered more. When the screen was already on (interaction HR 0.862, 95% CI 0.846–0.878), or social media (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.856–0.913) or messaging (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.844–0.926) was in use (all P<.001), reminders were less efficient. Regarding study dropout, 86 of 201 participants (43%) disengaged permanently. More reminders within a burst were associated with slightly lower odds of study dropout (fully adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.996; P=.01), a small association that was stable across all model specifications (OR 0.978–0.984).

In this adolescent EMA study, engagement was front-loaded: most openings came soon after the first prompt, but even later notifications had a positive effect on questionnaire engagement. So, within each measurement window, more prompts are better. This holds across all socio-demographics. Repeated reminders showed no sign of backfiring on study dropout. In fact, more reminders went with slightly lower study dropout. Responsiveness depended on what the phone was doing just before the first prompt. Context-aware prompting (avoiding prompts especially if a social media or a messaging app are open) is a more efficient design lever than simply adding reminders.

articles_hidden.title: "Fill Out this Survey": Capabilities and Detection of Agentic Browsers
articles_hidden.authors: Renata Topinkova; Carsten Schwemmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers increasingly rely on people to produce data through online interfaces. Agentic browsers create a new challenge for these workflows because they can navigate websites and complete tasks on a user’s behalf with little technical knowledge or effort. We evaluate whether three consumer-facing agentic browsers can complete online surveys and whether recently proposed measures can detect or prevent their use. The agents received only one simple instruction, "Fill out this survey", without detailed prompting or technical optimization. We tested technical screening measures, visible and invisible CAPTCHAs, AI-specific prompt-injection checks, consistency across a longer survey, and the completion of several surveys from a single instruction. The agents completed surveys with little or no user input, maintained assigned demographic profiles, and passed all tested prompt-leaking and jailbreak-style checks. Browser metadata did not reveal automated participation, and invisible reCAPTCHA was consistently passed by some browsers. Visible reCAPTCHA created the strongest barrier, although agents could sometimes solve it or return control to the user. These findings show that widely available AI agents can take over tasks intended for human participants while producing responses that appear coherent and plausible. This raises broader questions about how researchers can verify that supposedly human-generated data were actually produced by humans.

articles_hidden.title: You cannot decompose injustice: interaction, intersection, random effects and simple means in the evolution of MAIHDA
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo
articles_hidden.abstract: Random effects intersectional analysis has promoted the multidimensional study of health inequalities, and the intersectional application of Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) is increasingly used to describe them. Its usual implementation fits an empty random effects model followed by a model adjusting for the variables that define the strata, and reads the remaining between-stratum variance as the intersectional effect. In this essay I trace how that convention grew, including my own contribution to it, and explain why my opinion has changed. Intersectionality, as originally formulated, is not about statistical interaction. The expression "more than the sum of its parts" refers to the uniqueness of a social position, not to an arithmetic operation. Intersectional strata are indivisible analytical units. I propose the term intact strata for strata kept whole in the analysis. I recall that random effects shrinkage describes a modelled population rather than the observed one, and present Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA) as the canonical design for the framework. Each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and the three MAIHDA components, specific contextual effects (SCE), general contextual effects (GCE) and discriminatory accuracy (DA), are obtained on the probability scale. Keeping strata intact does not banish interaction. It relocates it, as effect modification between the intact stratum and the structural axes, such as geography, time or institution, along which the position is lived. You cannot decompose injustice. You can describe it whole, and you can measure what the structures around it do to it.

articles_hidden.title: LLM measurements that agree with human coders overall can still distort specific effects
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander K. Moore; Bingqing Li; Shane Wang; Matt Thomson
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in the social sciences as surrogates for human coders. Standard practice validates them by their correspondence with human measurements of the same stimuli using statistics like correlation. However, overall correspondence can conceal biases that distort specific claims. We demonstrate this with open-weight LLM ratings of 568 food and 1,811 scene photographs. Ratings inflate, attenuate, or reverse effects, and improving overall correspondence with prompts can improve one contrast while worsening another. Rankings also elevate some categories and demote others beyond what random errors of the same size typically produce. Across six prompts, some of these errors are shared, so sampling across prompts may continue to mask biases. We propose validating LLM coders against specific claims they will test rather than the general coding task.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking nature dependencies and nature-related risks: integrated environmental-economic accounting in Australia
articles_hidden.authors: Crystal Bradley; Sarah Taylor; Michael Vardon; Mitchell Lyons; Sarah Clement; Carl Obst
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecosystems and the services they provide underpin economic production and human wellbeing, yet these dependencies are poorly measured and rarely monitored. As a result, conventional economic statistics often fail to show how ecosystem decline may threaten production and wellbeing. The missing information can be supplied by the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA), an international statistical standard for tracking environmental stocks and flows, including ecosystems and their services, which is interoperable with the System of National Accounts (SNA). We assess how a linked system of SEEA and SNA accounts can be used to measure and track nature-economy dependencies, including the transmission of physical risk. We argue that accounting for ecosystem services provides the main connection between nature and the economy. The connection depends upon accounts using consistent classifications and typologies, which we call material join keys, so that information about ecosystems, ecosystem services, industries and economic activities can be reliably linked. Applying the approach to Australia, a gap analysis shows that existing ecosystem service accounts already track several of the dependencies most important and at risk from ecosystem decline, but only partially, and that priority new accounts for water and food security, health, climate resilience and supply chain resilience are needed to close the remaining gaps. Realising the potential of integrated accounting supports the mainstreaming of natural capital considerations into decision-making and public policy, and the proactive management of nature-related risks.

articles_hidden.title: Food Environment Policy Index for the German States: A structured policy analysis with expert consultations
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Wiebke; Peter von Philipsborn; Anette E. Buyken
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Introduction
Subnational governments can play an important role in influencing food environments, particularly in multilevel governance systems such as Germany, where multiple levels can introduce policy and legislation.
