Yet the extent to which subnational governments, including the German States, use this potential remains largely unexplored. To make the scope of subnational food environment policies explicit, comparable and assessable, we developed a state-specific Food Environment Policy Index (Food-EPI), using Germany as an example. 
Methods
The INFORMAS Food-EPI served as the starting point for our analysis. To adapt it to the subnational level, we followed an iterative process drawing on four data sources: i) legal and policy documents and secondary sources; ii) key informant interviews; iii) written feedback from experts; and iv) an online expert workshop. 
Results
The state-specific Food-EPI covers 25 indicators across 12 domains, outlining the substantial scope of subnational governments to influence food environments. The policy domains are food labelling, advertising and marketing, subsidies, provision, retail and food service and waste, combined with six infrastructure support domains. We drew on 128 documents to identify 57 good practice examples from subnational governments and adapted the INFORMAS protocol into a streamlined four-step approach.
Conclusion
We demonstrate that it is feasible to develop a tool to assess food environment policy at the subnational level, that systematically outlines the substantial influence of subnational governments on food environments. Applying the state-specific Food-EPI in practice to German States is an important next step to further corroborate its practical relevance.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Dark Figure: A Causal and Probabilistic Analysis of Crimes Against Women in India
articles_hidden.authors: Rudrani Ghosh
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research on violence against women in India depends on administrative police records. However, this raw data often suffers from severe reporting biases and fails to account for massive population differences between districts. To address these flaws, this study applies causal inference, hierarchical modeling, and machine learning to better understand local crime dynamics. By combining two decades of National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) statistics with 2011 Census demographics, we map both the spatial distribution and the true sociological drivers of this violence. We found no evidence of geographic clustering; a Moran's I analysis shows the violence is distributed randomly across the country. Furthermore, our mixed-effects hierarchical models indicate that broad state-level policies explain less than 1% of the variance in local crime rates. Furthermore, by applying Pearl's do-calculus and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), we isolate the causal effects of the male-female literacy gap and urbanization, proving that urbanization is the dominant driver of reporting rates. A Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) correctly isolates the passage of the 2013 Criminal Law (Amendment) Act as an administrative reporting shock yielding an 88,879 annual case surge rather than a behavioral epidemic. Finally, Bayesian Belief Networks are utilized to model highly nonlinear sociological interactions, providing a mathematical framework for proactive risk assessment.

articles_hidden.title: The Economic Costs of Nepal's Open Border with India: A Case Study on Smuggling
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract:
The border between Nepal and India, which was opened in 1950 by the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, has created unprecedented conditions for developing cultural and social ties between the countries. However, the open border has also led to severe negative consequences for the national economy of Nepal. This research aims to discuss the effects of smuggling through the 1,880 km border and analyse the situation in the context of the foreign trade deficit and the deteriorating economic situation in the country.
Based on the data presented by the study, it is possible to draw the conclusion that smuggling contributes significantly to the trade deficit between Nepal and India. Smuggling of gold, drugs, agricultural products, and people constitutes a substantial part of trade between the countries. It is reported that 42.5% of the officially recorded trade between Nepal and India is smuggling, which results in a loss of 33.5 billion rupees for the Nepalese economy. In addition to the loss from unofficial trade, the state loses 3.58 billion rupees in duty and 3.71 billion rupees in value-added tax. The article also reports that the trade deficit in Nepal this year amounts to NPR 180 billion, of which a considerable part is caused by smuggling.
Thus, the current situation in which Nepal allows free trade between the countries is extremely disadvantageous for the national economy. The study provides multiple examples that prove the severity of the problem, including the cases of Badhaiyatal and Bardibas, where the largest seizures of marijuana, gold, and peas in recent years were registered. According to official data, 30,000 people are trafficked illegally into Nepal every year, resulting in significant losses for the economy. The causes of the problem include the initial policy of open borders, insufficient control mechanisms, corruption, and taxation issues. However, the authors of the article believe that a smart border is necessary to ensure the prosperity of the Nepalese economy through trade with India.

articles_hidden.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles_hidden.authors: John Levi Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field.  Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims.  There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles_hidden.title: Aid Cuts and the Subnational Foundations of Refugee Cooperation
articles_hidden.authors: Mae MacDonald
articles_hidden.abstract: What happens to public support for international cooperation when the transfers that sustain it are withdrawn? I argue that cooperation with the refugee regime rests partly on a subnational bargain: host communities bear concentrated costs of asylum, which foreign aid can offset through jobs, services, and other benefits. These benefits sustain the local support for hosting that can underpin refugee cooperation, which aid withdrawal may erode. I test this argument using the 2025 aid cuts in Kenya. Drawing on two nationwide surveys, a high-frequency panel and vignette experiment near Kakuma refugee camp, and 52 interviews with refugee leaders, I show that support for refugee hosting declined in hosting regions relative to the rest of the country during the height of the cuts. Within the host community, declines were concentrated among households most exposed to the loss of aid-related jobs or services, while national support remained stable. The findings show that host-community support for refugees depends partly on foreign aid, raising concerns about the durability of international refugee cooperation as donor support recedes.

articles_hidden.title: Cities for Seasons - In favor of microclimate diversity as alternative to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours in competitively livable cities in temperate climates
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Ragnhof
articles_hidden.abstract:
Temperate cities compete to rank the world’s most livable, while competing under the same premise: A summer period with relatively abundant life on the streets, and a winter period with relatively sparse life on the streets, owing to cold stress.
Yet these cities – Copenhagen, London, New York, Melbourne, Paris, Vancouver, Vienna – have been implementing strategies that are directly detrimental to the elongation of their streets’ active seasons: Motivated by increasingly frequent and intense heat events, they have set out to mitigate urban heat island effects, aiming to eliminate any time that any surface exceeds the upper limit of the human thermal comfort range. But with no spatial or temporal limit to these strategies and guidelines – the approach is consistently the more heat island mitigation the better – these strategies inadvertently incentivize a
complete, systematic prevention of warm microclimates that, while they may be too hot during the heat waves, can be highly attractive the rest of the year.
Therefore this thesis employs a tri-seasonal rhythmanalysis to explore the dynamic use of places that are subject to urban heat island effects as well as of places which are subject to cooling effects. In the terminology of the author, these places together constitute an area with “high microclimate niche development”, which stands in contrast
to the areas with low niche development that are predictably reproduced when focusing on UHI mitigation, and when optimizing according to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours.
It finds that when the warm niches are accessible – like at south facing ‘soft edges’ of interactive buildings – they significantly extend the local active season: That in early spring, when people first move out of the buildings, they tend to gravitate toward the warm, south facing edges of these buildings, after which a spillover effect happens from these warm niches, into adjacent cooler niches, and back, throughout the days as well as the seasons, whereby the warm niches exhibit a pulsing, gravitational pull.
This descriptive model is synthesized into a prescriptive model and a series of preliminary methods of analysis, which aim to display and thereby enable assessment of microclimate diversity, and of synergy with complementary parameters. As proof of concept, these models are used to formulate re-designs. 
This approach is found to synergize with contemporary approaches for flood mitigation and for biodiversity, but demands one key shift: acknowledging that, in temperate cities, heat islands can play a substantial positive role. It argues that this shift appears as the logical conclusion of the development started by Jan Gehl when he defended the import of the (at the time) uniquely Mediterranean café culture to ‘cold’ northern Europe. It predicts that this shift may transform urban life in temperate cities in a similarly profound way.

articles_hidden.title: kîkway itôtaman ôta Dante? The nine circles of community-engaged Indigenous research hell
articles_hidden.authors: Malcolm Cole Disbrowe
articles_hidden.abstract: Research involving Indigenous Peoples has historically been harmful to Indigenous Peoples and their communities. In recent years, however, growing public awareness of Indigenous Peoples' experiences and histories through national and international initiatives has made research involving Indigenous Peoples much more equitable. However, in this renaissance of change, researchers who work with Indigenous communities and use community-engaged methodologies often rely on terms such as relational, co-designed, collaborative, and community-engaged. This reliance is not a reliable indicator that Indigenous communities themselves have meaningful authority over research that affects them and the knowledges they share. Because of this, I take a satirical, slightly humorous approach, drawing on Dante's Inferno and Neuroskeptic's Nine Circles of Scientific Hell to elucidate recurring issues in research involving Indigenous Peoples, more specifically research that uses, or seems to use, community-engaged methodologies. In the article, I conceptualize the nine circles while identifying problems that recur in community-engaged research involving Indigenous Peoples. These problems encompass tokenistic engagement, late or forced consultation, extractive relationships, pan-Indigenization, having Indigenous advisory bodies without decision-making power, checkbox approaches to Indigenous methodologies/frameworks, possessive relationships to data, poor knowledge return, and helicopter research. This article thus uses satire to make already existing contradictions around authority, accountability, governance, reciprocity, and relationships harder to ignore and to show that “relational” language is not enough, especially if Indigenous communities are not given meaningful authority to shape research projects involving themselves or their knowledges.

articles_hidden.title: ANTHROPOLOGY, COMPLEXITY AND THE LIMITS OF TOP-DOWN CONFLICT ANALYSIS
articles_hidden.authors: Eleonora Zanetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conflict analysis often approaches violence through externally defined categories, scales, and institutional frameworks that simplify complex social relations into identifiable problems and corresponding interventions. Similarly, contemporary localization paradigms seek to bring analysis, decision-making, and intervention closer to affected communities. Yet treating “the local” as a given and bounded site of action can obscure the relations of power through which local social worlds, conflicts, and capacities to act are themselves produced. The problem, I argue, is not only the use of externally defined categories to describe conflict, but also the analytical separation of the local from the wider relations through which it is constituted.
Drawing on long-term ethnographic research among Rendille pastoralists in northern Kenya, I propose an approach that does not treat the community or conflict as a bounded system, but instead reconstructs how actors themselves distinguish forms of violence and the different forms of power through which they are produced and governed, including physical force, symbolic power, and control over information. The ethnographic case shows how resource disputes, ethnic conflict, livestock raiding, political competition, and cross-border processes constitute analytically distinct but increasingly interconnected domains as relationships among socially differentiated actors and their access to different forms of power change across scales. Changes in one domain can alter the conditions through which conflict is interpreted and governed in another, while broader political, economic, ecological, and geopolitical processes are incorporated into local relations and transformed through them.
I argue that complexity emerges not from the simple interconnectedness of everything, or from the number of actors and factors involved, but from changing relationships among systems of order, forms of power, temporalities, and scales. The local is therefore not treated as a pre-existing scale, but as an empirical configuration produced through these relations. Methodologically, I propose an emic, participatory, and multiscalar approach in which ethnographic reconstruction precedes formal modeling. Complexity-science methods, including participatory mapping, System Dynamics, network analysis, and other quantitative approaches, can then formalize and investigate dynamics identified ethnographically, such as feedback, interdependence, emergence, and nonlinearity. This provides a methodological pathway from the emic to the systemic: beginning with local relations to reconstruct how power operates, how processes connect across scales and temporalities, and where change can actually occur.

articles_hidden.title: Missing Victims, Hidden Crimes: Improving Estimates of Honor Killings Using Missing Data Imputation
articles_hidden.authors: Mariel Leonard; Teresa Koenig
articles_hidden.abstract:
Very little accurate data on the incidence and prevalence of honor killings exists. While some countries have made strides to identify and track cases on an ongoing basis, many countries either have no official statistics or rely on outdated data and imprecise methodologies. More accurate and up-to-date statistics are needed to better direct resources, identify cases and behaviors for study and intervention, and reduce biases. Unfortunately, measuring honor killings is methodologically difficult. However, while single lists of honor killings cannot accurately estimate the number of events, two or more lists in combination can, using multi-systems estimation (MSE).
In this paper, we test the application of MSE to honor killings in four countries: Canada, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States by comparing estimates from MSE to counts of cases produced by aggregating multiple lists from each country. We find that MSE produces plausible estimates that demonstrate that even in seemingly complete lists of individuals or cases underestimate the scope of honor killings in these countries.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Employment in Mothers’ Careers After First Birth: A Comparison of South Korea and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Wonjeong Jeong
articles_hidden.abstract: Motherhood can reorganize women’s paid work across wage employment, self-employment, and nonemployment. Yet research on mothers’ employment trajectories has rarely examined self-employment as a distinct arrangement. This paper asks where self-employment appears in mothers’ careers after first birth and how its position differs between South Korea and the United States. Using the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, I follow first-time mothers from the year of first birth through ten years afterward. Descriptive and sequence analyses show that roughly one in five mothers experiences self-employment at least once, although neither country has a continuous self-employment trajectory. In Korea, self-employment more often follows nonemployment and is primarily full-time, appearing within trajectories that lead back into paid work. In the United States, mothers more often enter self-employment from wage work, and part-time self-employment also appears briefly within wage-centered trajectories. These differences show that the same employment status can occupy different positions in mothers’ careers. Self-employment is likely to become increasingly important within workers’ careers as gig and platform work expand and artificial intelligence reshapes occupations and industries. Future research should examine how these changes alter pathways into self-employment and how labor protections, social insurance, and family-support policies can account for its distinctive risks and rewards.

articles_hidden.title: From Getting Ahead to Staying Ahead: Reference Points and Repeated Investment in Status Maintenance
articles_hidden.authors: Hibiki Kamoshita
articles_hidden.abstract: As rapid technological change reshapes the skills employers demand and increases the importance of post-entry human capital accumulation, including reskilling, educational attainment no longer determines a person's position once and for all at labor-market entry. Research on stratification has nonetheless concentrated on who attains advantaged positions, and the repeated investment required to hold a position once attained remains underexplored. This study develops a model that extends the relative risk aversion hypothesis to an infinite-horizon setting, incorporating depreciating status and an endogenously updated reference point, to analyze the decision to invest in maintaining status. The results show that past success does not end the need for further learning: those who have reached higher positions face a larger reference-dependent loss and invest defensively even when resources and costs are identical. Moreover, I identify conditions under which more effective training widens rather than narrows status gaps, and show that individual credential renewals aggregate into a rising credential standard. Wider participation in adult learning is therefore compatible with a stable status order, and the locus of stratification may shift from who gets ahead to who can stay ahead.

articles_hidden.title: University-affiliated sustainability badges: Shared identity, tourist perceptions, and hotel manager receptivity
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Lewin; Danyelle; Anna Kristina Zinn; Sarah MacInnes; Sara Dolnicar
articles_hidden.abstract: Hotel sustainability research shows that pro-environmental behaviour‑change interventions are often effective in field experiments, but widespread adoption by hotels remains limited. One possible explanation is that hotels lack external recognition that would make adopting these measures visible to guests and rewarding to managers. This study investigates whether university-affiliated sustainability badges could serve as a recognition mechanism, testing their effectiveness across two studies drawing on Signalling Theory and Social Identity Theory. In an online experiment (N=975), prospective hotel guests viewed simulated hotel booking pages featuring one of the four badge options, or no badge, across budget, mid-range, and luxury hotel pricing segments. All badge variations increased perceived hotel sustainability and guests’ sense of belonging to a community of environmentally conscious travellers (group identification). Badges did not trigger negative emotions, but the university affiliated logo did not perform better than a generic environmental logo on almost all measures, suggesting these effects are based on the presence of any badge, rather than the university partnership specifically. Semi-structured interviews with ten hotel managers found conditional receptivity to university-affiliated badges, primarily through a sense of shared values and community orientation with the partnering institution (collective values) rather than the badge’s function as a credibility signal. These findings suggest that collective values and shared identities, rather than signalling, may be the more promising mechanism for engaging hotels and guests around sustainability initiatives, and offer an encouraging direction for potential university-hotel partnerships that may translate into the future implementation of pro-environmental behaviour change interventions.

articles_hidden.title: The Latin American Demographic Boom in Spain. Mass Immigration and Ethnic Convergence in a New Country of Immigration
articles_hidden.authors: Miguel González-Leonardo; Guillaume Marois; Elena Ambrosetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Since the late twentieth century, Spain has undergone a rapid transition from emigration to immigration country, receiving around 510,000 immigrants annually between 2000 and 2022, approximately half from Latin America. This transformation has substantially increased population diversity, yet less is known about how diversity develops in relatively new immigration countries compared with established destinations. We combine register data, a retrospective analysis of births by parental background and a multi-state cohort-component model to examine changes in population diversity between 2000 and 2022 and project its potential evolution to 2062. The results show a rapid transformation of Spain’s population composition. Between 2000 and 2022, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background – defined by country of birth and parental origins – increased from 5% to 28%, while 13% had a Latin American background in 2022. Assuming that migration, fertility and ethnic-mixing patterns remain constant, the share of the population under 40 with a foreign background would exceed 65% by 2062, with those of Latin American background reaching 32%. These findings demonstrate that the demographic consequences of immigration extend beyond the growth of the foreign-born population, as births and ethnic mixing progressively reshape the Spanish-born population. The study highlights the importance of incorporating foreign family backgrounds when assessing population diversity and provides new evidence on how diversity may evolve across generations in a recent immigration country.

articles_hidden.title: When is Forgetting an Advantage?: Considering Organizational Amnesia at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency
articles_hidden.authors: Josh Entsminger
articles_hidden.abstract: Organizational amnesia in the public sector is often understood as a pathology and source of capability loss. In response, literature is emerging framing the potential advantages of organizational amnesia; however, the nature and source of potential advantages remain under-developed. In this paper, I argue DARPA provides a counter-intuitive case of organizational design which structurally reinforces organizational amnesia while it is, seemingly paradoxically, perceived as reinforcing capacity for pursuing high-risk, high-reward research & development (R&D) programs. Taking a qualitative perspective, I argue DARPA has evolved an organizational structure which shapes how routinization proceeds, with downstream implications on dynamic capabilities. I frame this work as being driven by memory conditions, oriented around reduced memory formation, reduced memory availability, shaped willingness for memory recall, and shaped utility of memory recall. I pose DARPA as a unique case study in the organization of memory in public sector funding organizations.

articles_hidden.title: Research on Gender Contradictions in Contemporary China: Structural Pressures, the Negativity of Marital Surplus, and the Gender Projection of Class Contradictions
articles_hidden.authors: Yuan Di; ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Against the backdrop of a sustained decline in marriage and birth rates in China and intensifying gender tensions, traditional explanations centered on individual preferences or gender norms are insufficient to account for the structural mechanisms involved. Drawing on the economics of marriage and the family, this paper examines how rising costs of housing, weddings, bride price, childbearing, and education affect men's decisions to enter marriage, as well as how the expansion of higher education, the shortage of standardized professional employment, and the motherhood penalty shape women's opportunity costs associated with marriage. Building on these factors, together with declining expectations of economic growth, changing lifestyle expectations, and the rising utility of singlehood as an alternative, the paper proposes the “Dual Marriage Costs–Expectation Mismatch Integrated Model” (the Di Formula) and uses “marital surplus” to characterize the comprehensive net benefits of marriage relative to singlehood. The paper argues that contemporary gender relations in China involve more than a conflict of values, but separately rising direct marriage costs for men and opportunity costs for women, together with a widening structural mismatch between modernity-based expectations and real resource constraints. When marital surplus declines and eventually becomes negative, individually rational decisions to postpone or forgo marriage may, in aggregate, contribute to declining marriage and birth rates and intensified gender tensions. Marriage is therefore increasingly shifting from a traditional mechanism of family cooperation toward a high-cost, high-risk, long-term economic decision.

articles_hidden.title: apcbound: Bounding Age-Period-Cohort Effects in Stata
articles_hidden.authors: Gordey Yastrebov
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-period-cohort analysis is complicated by the exact linear dependency between age, period, and cohort, which prevents the separate identification of their linear effects without additional assumptions. The bounding approach addresses this problem by replacing arbitrary point-identifying constraints with substantively motivated restrictions on the linear age, period, and cohort components. This article introduces apcbound, a Stata package that implements this approach. The package provides commands for describing age-period-cohort patterns, estimating identified nonlinear components and linear combinations, exploring alternative rotations, deriving bounded and semi-bounded solutions under user-specified assumptions, and visualizing the resulting identification regions. We illustrate the workflow using German data from the European Social Survey on years of education. A substantively plausible restriction that the age effect on educational attainment should be broadly nondecreasing is used to derive bounds on the otherwise unidentified linear components. The package facilitates transparent sensitivity analysis by showing how substantive assumptions translate into alternative admissible decompositions.

articles_hidden.title: Downscaling Industry Employment to European Municipalities from Economic Location Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Boero
articles_hidden.abstract: Fine-scale industry employment is largely unavailable for European municipalities, yet it is required for regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and regional input--output accounts. We present a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates municipal employment while preserving official totals at every geographical level. A reproducible dataset represents settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location using official and remote-sensing sources. Constrained allocation models are trained on data-rich United States geographies and applied to Europe under official Eurostat totals. Independent statistics for Italy, France, Germany, and Spain show that European per-step share error lies within the uncertainty derived from geographically held-out United States data. Full-chain error is neither the sum of per-step uncertainty nor the result implied by independent multiplicative compounding; it remains bounded and grows sub-linearly over four allocation steps. The framework provides open, internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates where sub-national industry data are sparse.

articles_hidden.title: To a neo-patriarchy? How anti-gender backlash shapes the youth gender gap in populist radical right voting in the Netherlands
articles_hidden.authors: Mees Geenen; Anouk Smeekes
articles_hidden.abstract: Why are young European men more likely to vote for populist radical right parties (PRRPs) compared to young European women today? Following the concepts of cultural backlash and gender populism, we argue that anti-gender backlash, in the form of perceived status decline (PSD), opposition to gender diversity (OGD) and support for traditional gender roles (STGR), drives especially young men to PRRPs, in particular those who perceive threat from immigrants. We applied structural equation modelling on an 18–35-year-old subsample of the 2023 Dutch Parliamentary Election Study (N = 1,022). We find that the youth gender gap in PRRP voting can be explained by young men’s higher OGD, STGR, and unexpectedly also perceived threat from immigrants, but not by PSD. We conclude that gender differences in cultural backlash shape today’s youth gender gap in PRRP voting and might shape the future of European liberal democracy.

articles_hidden.title: Settler Colonial Logics: A framework for tracing the ideological currents of European colonisation of the Pacific
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Bedford
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper expands upon Patrick Wolfe’s ‘logic of elimination’ to propose a broader conceptual framework to understand the logics which underpinned European settler colonialism at large. Using the three Pacific voyages of British navigator James Cook between 1768 and 1779 as a case study, the geographic and ideological expansion of empire is positioned as a maritime endeavour which works to draw a singular geographic and political border for Empire. This view of a singular oceanic empire, rather than a collection of diverse and individual nations and peoples is further supported by the integration of the principles of the Doctrine of Discovery. This integration highlights the ways in which settler colonial logics continue to support structures founded on early modern beliefs about race, civilization and faith which, while now condemned by the institutions and cultures which established them, nonetheless continue to shape the lives of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in settler-colonial societies around the Pacific and beyond.

articles_hidden.title: Role of Industry 4.0 Technologies in Enhancing Supply Chain Resilience of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs): A PLSSEM Based Empirical Investigation
articles_hidden.authors: Komal Sharma; Deepika Rathi; Jainish Bhagat; RONAK AJAYKUMAR MEHTA
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines how the adoption of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies – the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data Analytics (BDA), Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), Blockchain (BCT), and Digital Twin (DTW) – influences the supply chain resilience (SCR) of Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), through the mediating roles of supply chain visibility (SCV), supply chain agility (SCA), and supply chain collaboration (SCC), and the moderating role of organizational readiness (ORGREAD).
Design/methodology/approach – A structural model integrating the Resource-Based View and the Dynamic Capabilities View was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) on survey data from 260 supply chain, operations, procurement, and digital-transformation executives in OEM firms across the automotive, electronics/electrical, industrial machinery, aerospace, and consumer-durables sectors. I4.0 technology adoption (I4ADOPT) is modelled as a second-order construct formed by five first-order technology dimensions; supply chain resilience is modelled as a second-order construct reflecting robustness, redundancy, flexibility, and recovery. The structural model was estimated with 2,000-sample nonparametric bootstrapping.
Findings – I4ADOPT significantly and positively predicted SCV (β = 0.487, p < .001), SCA (β = 0.254, p < .001), and SCC (β = 0.193, p < .01), and exerted a significant direct effect on SCR (β = 0.175, p < .01). SCV, SCA, and SCC each significantly predicted SCR (β = 0.237, 0.354, and 0.240 respectively, all p < .001) and significantly, partially mediated the I4ADOPT–SCR relationship. SCV additionally strengthened both SCA (β = 0.335) and SCC (β = 0.308). Organizational readiness had a significant positive direct association with both SCV (β = 0.169) and SCA (β = 0.205), but its hypothesized moderating (interaction) effect on the I4ADOPT–SCV and I4ADOPT–SCA relationships was not statistically supported. The model explained 58.2% of the variance in supply chain resilience, and all measurement-model reliability, validity, and model-fit criteria were satisfied (SRMR = 0.013).
Practical implications – OEM managers should prioritise IoT- and analytics-led visibility investment as the entry point of a digital resilience strategy, since visibility significantly amplifies agility and collaboration in addition to its own direct effect on resilience, and should invest in organizational readiness (leadership commitment, digital skills, process maturity) as a parallel, direct driver of these capabilities rather than solely as a moderating lever.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a sustainable post-pandemic growth
articles_hidden.authors: Ivan Sudibyo
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the long-run relationship between Research and Development (R&D) expenditure, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows, financial market capitalization, population, and Carbon Dioxide (CO2) emissions across five ASEAN economies–Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam– over 2000–2023. Building on the Paramati et al. (2021) framework rooted in the Impact, Population, Affluence, Technology (IPAT) theory of Ehrlich and Holdren (1971), the study applies Pedroni's panel cointegration test, the Pesaran (2007) CIPS unit-root test to address cross-sectional dependence, and Fully Modified OLS (FMOLS) estimation at both the panel and country-level. Results show that (i) population is the most consistently significant driver of CO2 emissions across all five economies, (ii) R&D expenditure carries a negative but statistically insignificant coefficient, a result consistent with the region's structurally low R&D-to-Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratios and lagged green-technology effects (Yang et al., 2025; Mehmood et al., 2022), and (iii) FDI and financial-market effects are heterogeneous, supporting a Malaysia-Singapore green-finance interpretation alongside pollution-haven dynamics elsewhere. The findings highlight the need for ASEAN policymakers to scale R&D intensity, channel financial market deepening toward green sectors, and integrate demographic-driven emission pressures into national climate plans.

articles_hidden.title: From playing computer games to achieving lexical knowledge: Linking attitudes and time allocation with vocabulary acquisition
articles_hidden.authors: Ehsan abbasi
articles_hidden.abstract:
The impact of video games on vocabulary acquisition has not received sufficient attention, despite a growing interest in the influence of digital games on vocabulary learning (i.e., DGVL) in the field of computer-assisted language learning (CALL). Particularly, it is uncertain whether the duration of time spent playing a video game and the attitude of English language learners (ELLs) have significant effects on EFL vocabulary acquisition. The present quasi-experimental study involved 40 male EFL students at a private language institute and examined the link between the students' opinions of a video game as well as the time allocated to it, in terms of vocabulary acquisition. In particular, this research explored the influence of these factors on receptive or productive vocabulary learning. Moreover, the vocabulary learning strategies employed by the participants when playing, along with the features they deemed essential for computer games to be engaging enough to support learning, were addressed in this study. The participants were required to complete a pretest, a posttest, a survey, and a self-reported timetable. The analyses did not reveal meaningful correlation between the participant's perception of the target video game and vocabulary acquisition. Additionally, it was found that the time spent playing the video game, coupled with prior language proficiency, helped to boost English vocabulary learning. Insights regarding the vocabulary learning strategies adopted and the features found appealing were also provided. These outcomes offer important insights for ESL/EFL instructors regarding the most effective approach to employing computer games as a novel vocabulary learning method.  
Keywords: Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL), Game-Enhanced Language Learning, Digital Game-Based Vocabulary Learning (DGVL), Computer games, Video Games, ESL/EFL pedagogy, TESOL, second language acquisition, Vocabulary Acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence of Non-Kin Out-of-Home Placement Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin A Campbell; Elizabeth Wendel
articles_hidden.abstract: This working paper synthesizes peer-reviewed evidence published between 1965 and 2026 on the long-term outcomes of non-kin out-of-home placement for children and describes current child welfare budget allocations in four English-speaking countries. Fourteen peer-reviewed studies using causal, quasi-experimental, or prospective longitudinal designs document elevated risks of premature mortality, adverse mental and physical health, and reduced socioeconomic attainment among placement-exposed populations relative to general-population, adversity-matched, sibling, or instrumental-variable counterfactuals; sibling-comparison and meta-analytic estimates report a roughly doubling of premature mortality risk and a roughly threefold increase in suicide risk associated with childhood out-of-home care experience. Five peer-reviewed studies argue, on methodological grounds, that observational findings have overstated the average effect, that propensity-matched analyses produce smaller estimates, that the instrumental-variable finding does not replicate uniformly across jurisdictions, and that effects are heterogeneous by age, placement type, and outcome. Within the targeted review, no peer-reviewed study was identified that reports non-kin placement producing superior outcomes relative to comparable home or kinship counterfactuals; Section 3.2 sets out the structural features of the literature that bear on how this absence should be read. Evidence on alternative pathways (parental care, intensive family preservation, community-based prevention, and kinship placement) has accumulated over the same interval; the 2018 Cochrane systematic review of 102 quasi-experimental studies finds that kinship-placed children experience fewer behavioral problems, fewer mental health disorders, better well-being, and less placement disruption than non-kin-placed children. Most recently published budget data show placement-related spending accounting for 82 percent (England, 2022/23), 72 percent (United States, SFY 2022), 64 percent (Australia, 2024–25), and 57 percent (New Zealand, 2023/24) of placement-plus-prevention expenditure within each country’s own reporting categories. Cross-national rates of children in out-of-home care, drawn from each country’s national statistics, range from 3.9 to 8.2 per 1,000 aged 0–17 across five high-income systems. The paper closes by identifying limitations and directions for further research.

articles_hidden.title: The Electoral Effects of U.S. Prison Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Ottone; Amanda Weiss
articles_hidden.abstract: From 1980 to 2000, the United States opened over 400 prisons, a rapid expansion of carceral capacity mirroring the punitive turn in public policy and public opinion. Yet few studies have examined the impact of prison construction on nearby residents and their political behavior. We develop a theoretical model tracing how prison openings affect economic, attitudinal, and electoral outcomes in surrounding communities. Using modern difference-in-difference methods and a novel county-level dataset covering forty years of prison openings, we find that prison construction decreases county-level vote share for Republican candidates, especially if Republicans represented the county during prison construction. Drawing on analyses of economic outcomes and prison bond measure support, we argue that voters sanction issue-owning Republican candidates for negative economic externalities and turn against funding for prisons. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about the political economy of prisons and have implications for how we understand contemporary expansions of carceral capacity.

articles_hidden.title: A Multicriteria Multimethod Analysis of Barriers for Green Infrastructure Implementation in Developing Countries: A Case Study of Sri Lanka
articles_hidden.authors: Udya Abeysinghe; Archana Sharma; Jagath Munasinghe
articles_hidden.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Many developed economies are considering the use of Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI) as a tool to enhance the climate resilience of urban areas and align with SDG 11 - Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. Yet, the integration of UGI in developing countries seems to be lagging. Thus, they are missing out on one of the instruments that could facilitate developing nations’ compliance with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. This review examines the current state of UGI knowledge and implementation in Sri Lanka through a comprehensive literature review, an evaluation of UGI-related policies, guidelines, plans, and projects, and an assessment of stakeholder perspectives using the Delphi technique. As a result, the study identifies five significant challenges of mainstreaming UGI in Sri Lanka, such as lack of: clear consensual understanding of UGI- definition, ecosystem service functionality, implementation facilitative classification of UGI, design tool for UGI adaptation in constrained urban context, political willingness to integrate UGI planning principles in urban planning, robust legal framework and well-specified co-governance. Furthermore, the paper identifies concepts and tools as a forward path, such as a clear acknowledgement of current enabling conditions and gaps through known/ unknown diagram, categorization of multifunctional UGI such as with ecosystem service (ES) or place-making (PM) UGI, use of design syntax for adaptable design, and enhancement of regulatory framework. This review aspires to open the conversation on usefulness of UGI as a step towards climate resilience and SDG 11, at all levels of academic institutions to governmental agencies, in Sri Lanka.

KEYWORDS: Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI), Nature-based Solutions (NbS), Climate Resilience, Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11), Urban Planning, Landscape, Design Syntax, Placemaking, Mixed method, Multimethod, Multicriteria, Analysis

articles_hidden.title: Minimum Attainment Cost: National Benchmark Framework for Measuring Healthcare Accessibility in Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias-Related Services
articles_hidden.authors: Kyusik Kim; Amber DeJohn; Weining Kan
articles_hidden.abstract: A threshold represented as travel time or distance is a key concept for determining catchment areas in cumulative opportunity and Two-Step Floating Catchment Area methods. As destinations included in a catchment area are determined by the threshold, it is a primary factor affecting spatial accessibility. In many cases, thresholds are arbitrarily determined or fixed values are used. The resulting accessibility based on these arbitrary or fixed thresholds makes it challenging to compare accessibility scores across heterogeneous geographic contexts (e.g., urban and rural areas). In this paper, we propose the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC) as a context-sensitive spatial accessibility measure using the national average facility-to-population ratio as a benchmark and explore how fixed thresholds can over- or underestimate accessibility compared with MAC in a nationwide U.S. analysis. Using the national benchmark, MAC measures the minimum travel time required to reach the national average level of a given resource in each zone, accounting for the geographic distributions of demand and resources. By comparing MAC with multiple fixed thresholds (i.e., 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes), we find that MAC is sensitive to geographic contexts in terms of the distributions of demand and resources. This approach enables direct geographic comparisons of spatial accessibility to different resources and provides evidence to support effective policy interventions by providing more context-sensitive accessibility estimates.

articles_hidden.title: The Changing Gender Training Gap - A Systematic Review of Evidence from Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Marco Seegers
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on gender differences in non-formal job-related further training in Germany has produced inconsistent findings, leaving unclear how gender inequalities in training have developed and whether divergent findings reflect training forms or conceptual and meth-odological differences. This systematic review synthesised quantitative evidence from studies published between 1990 and 2026. Web of Science, Scopus, and FIS Bildung were searched in June 2026 and supplemented by backward citation searching. Forty-two stud-ies yielded 160 finding-level records, which were integrated using a structured narrative synthesis. The evidence indicates a weakening of the earlier male advantage in overall training participation, with later evidence increasingly showing no statistically detectable gender difference or higher participation among women. This convergence was weaker for employer-supported training, while population-level convergence coexisted with life-course-specific inequalities. Conceptual and methodological differences shaped the com-parability and empirical visibility of gender inequalities but did not systematically ac-count for the broader historical pattern, which remained visible under more restrictive comparisons. Overall, gender inequality in further training appears to have been recon-figured rather than eliminated or simply reversed, with inequalities remaining conditional on institutional and life-course contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Modeling Network Dynamics with Overlapping Cohesive Subgroups
articles_hidden.authors: Stepan Zaretckii; Tom A.B. Snijders; Marijtje A.J. van Duijn; Christian Steglich
articles_hidden.abstract: We introduce a longitudinal extension of the latent membership stochastic actor-oriented model (LM-SAOM) for analyzing the co-evolution of network ties and actors’ memberships in overlapping cohesive subgroups. The model treats group memberships as latent and time-evolving, giving actors frequent opportunities to update their memberships while a strong \emph{membership cohesion} effect favors membership choices that place actors in the same groups as their network contacts, thereby keeping the inferred cohesive subgroups aligned with the evolving network. In an application to a friendship network, we find evidence that students are more likely to have ties with peers with whom they share cohesive subgroup membership, beyond what is captured by dyadic and triadic effects. Goodness-of-fit assessments indicate that incorporating group-level dependence improves the representation of selected meso-level network configurations.

articles_hidden.title: Uncovering the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth:  an interdisciplinary review and research agenda
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Cooiman; Julia de Groote; Isabell Stamm; Jan Ole Krieg
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the centrality of entrepreneurial activity to the accumulation, reproduction, and legitimization of wealth – and conversely, of wealth in the form of capital to foster entrepreneurship – it might be reasonable to expect a plethora of research on the relationship between entrepreneurship and wealth. However, as we demonstrate in our interdisciplinary literature review, a surprising lack of engagement exists with regard to this relationship. Sociological studies of wealth inequality rarely address entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship research rarely addresses wealth. We systematically review, discuss, and synthesize the discourse in the leading journals of both fields. In the sociological discourse on wealth, we find that entrepreneurship is seen as one of many sources of income and wealth, and as a means of legitimizing its accumulation. However, the social practices, actors, and institutions that mediate the concentration of wealth through entrepreneurship, as well as the structural power of wealth in entrepreneurial activity, are rarely addressed. Similarly, in entrepreneurship research, we show that considerable attention is paid to the role of family businesses, transgenerational wealth, and non-financial wealth (“socioemotional wealth”), whilst the fundamental role of these factors in fostering wealth concentration more broadly remains largely unremarked upon in the literature. We therefore suggest future research that systematically engages with how entrepreneurial activity shapes wealth accumulation, and how wealth, in turn, structures entrepreneurial opportunities and outcomes. With this review, we contribute to advancing debates on inequality, social mobility, and economic development.

articles_hidden.title: Global Trends in Widowhood Prevalence, 1970–2020: The Role of Population Ageing, Mortality, and Union Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Elder Lara-Castaneda; Zachary Van Winkle
articles_hidden.abstract: Widowhood is the predominant marital status at older ages, especially among women. Although population ageing is expected to increase widowhood, evidence on this trend remains scarce or fragmented across countries. This study contributes to the global understanding of widowhood by addressing two questions. First, how has widowhood prevalence changed among women and men across countries and world regions between 1970 and 2020? Second, to what extent are changes in overall widowhood prevalence attributable to changes in population age structure rather than to changes in age-specific widowhood prevalence, i.e. mortality and union dynamics. We gathered marital-status tabulations from censuses, registers, and nationally representative surveys covering 222 countries and territories, and trace crude and age-standardized widowhood prevalence from 1970 to 2020. A Kitagawa decomposition separates change between 1980 and 2010 in 135 populations into age-structure and age-specific-prevalence components. Widowhood prevalence declined globally and in most regions, especially among women. Although population ageing contributed to increasing widowhood prevalence, changes in age-specific prevalence more than offset this effect. An ageing world is not necessarily one in which an increasing share of people are widowed, but it may still be one in which large, socially vulnerable populations live with the consequences of spousal loss.

articles_hidden.title: Políticas industriais regionalizadas e estado desenvolvimentista em rede como orientadores do desenvolvimento policêntrico no Brasil
articles_hidden.authors: Isaias Albertin de Moraes; Humberto Martins
articles_hidden.abstract: O artigo trata da trajetória da indústria de transformação brasileira no período recente, observando a evolução de seu peso na estrutura produtiva, bem como sua dinâmica regional nas escalas macro e microrregional. Diante da identificação de um processo de desindustrialização (1985-2024) simultâneo a uma tendência de desconcentração regional limitada, ressalta-se a importância da dimensão regional das políticas industriais. Nessa perspectiva, discute-se o potencial de um Estado Desenvolvimentista em Rede (EDR) para estabelecer políticas industriais regionalizadas no Brasil com vistas a favorecer a ampliação, integração e a sofisticação da estrutura produtiva, bem como a reduzir as desigualdades regionais e estimular o desenvolvimento policêntrico do país.

articles_hidden.title: Unbundling Support for Political Violence
articles_hidden.authors: Sam Fuller; Jack T. Rametta; Alexa Federice
articles_hidden.abstract: Measures of support for political violence (SPV) vary drastically across what violence they describe, who performs it, against whom, and the stated justification. We argue that these measures are not interchangeable operationalizations of a single latent attitude but rather represent correlated, distinct subdimensions of SPV. Across three studies, we iteratively develop and validate concise batteries that 1) differentiate between actor-target combinations and reactive versus proactive violence and 2) vary across justification and the response's severity. We find that SPV is a multidimensional concept: levels of reactive support are remarkably higher than proactive; support for state-on-mass and mass-on-state violence are only weakly correlated, with Republicans supporting state-on-mass and Democrats supporting mass-on-state violence at significantly higher rates; common SPV measures correlate with proactive more than reactive; and we find mixed evidence that survey disengagement influences SPV. Our findings contextualize disparate and conflicting literatures, offering measurement strategies tailored to specific research questions.

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Health Financing in Chile: A Historical Analysis of the Segmented System, 1981–2024
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Camilo Cid Pedraza
articles_hidden.abstract: The objective of this article is to present the results of reconstructing the historical series of health expenditure in Chile from the creation of the segmented model in 1981 to 2024, and to briefly analyze its evolution in historical context. To this end, data were collected and digitized from primary sources: the Statistical Bulletins and Public Accounts of FONASA (1989–2016; 2020–2024), the Statistical Series of the Isapre System (SUPER, 1990–2024), and the Public Finance Statistics of DIPRES (2004–2025). The results show accelerated growth in private spending until the 1990s, followed by a sustained increase in public health expenditure associated with higher fiscal contributions and mandatory contributions. However, the long-term analysis reveals periods of slowdown in public spending coinciding with the expansion of private infrastructure, revealing the persistence of a segmented and unequal financing system. The trajectory of Chilean health expenditure shows significant variation in proportions and pace, conditioned by political and economic contexts. Alongside this analysis, we make the complete series used available to researchers in open access.

articles_hidden.title: Specific Support, Diffuse Trust: Central Banks and the Mass Politics of Unconventional Monetary Policy
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth
articles_hidden.abstract: Central banks relied for a decade on unconventional monetary policies (negative interest rates, large-scale asset purchases, and forward guidance) that carry significant distributive consequences and became intensely politicized. Yet little is known about the mass politics of central banking, or whether contestation over specific instruments threatens central banks' broader legitimacy. We provide evidence from two pre-registered survey experiments in Germany and the Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that citizens strongly oppose negative interest rates, the most penalized levels in the design, and are skeptical of unconditional asset purchases. A framing experiment shows support for negative rates responds to both egotropic and sociotropic arguments, with pocketbook concerns resonating most strongly. Exploiting a within-respondent measure of trust in the European Central Bank (ECB), we show that these same frames shift citizens' specific support for the policy without eroding their diffuse trust in the ECB, a highly insulated, technocratic, non-elected institution.

articles_hidden.title: How Intergenerational Closure Shapes Parental Aspirations in a Highly Differentiated Educational System: Evidence from Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Monja Schmitt; Kerstin Schörner; Felix Bittmann
articles_hidden.abstract: According to James Coleman's theoretical considerations, intergenerational closure, defined as social ties among the parents of children's peers, is a crucial factor in the formation of educational inequalities. Empirical studies report positive associations between intergenerational closure and academic success, while indicating that these associations cannot be understood in isolation from the social contexts in which closure is embedded. Nothing is known about its impact on parental aspirations that precede the children's educational success. From the perspective of the Wisconsin Model, aspirations are not only precursors of educational attainment but are themselves shaped through social interactions with significant others. Educational systems structure the social contexts in which children and parents form networks and become significant to each other, and the extent to which educational outcomes, including educational aspirations, are shaped by the degree of educational stratification. Germany represents a highly differentiated educational system with secondary school tracks that differ in their student composition and educational opportunities. No study has examined whether parents of classmates function as significant others for parental educational aspirations, nor whether this role varies across school tracks. Using unique data from a National Educational Panel Study (n = 6,162), we examine whether intergenerational closure is associated with parents’ realistic and idealistic aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. Results from linear probability models indicate that intergenerational closure significantly increases realistic aspirations only among parents with children in intermediate educational tracks, suggesting that significant others shape realistic aspirations primarily as models providing information and resources, rather than through normative mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: What’s Worth Dreaming of? The Gendered and Classed Logics Behind Occupational Aspirations
articles_hidden.authors: Diego Strassmann Rocha; Marie Labussière
articles_hidden.abstract:
Even though occupations have multiple characteristics that make them more or less likely to
be aspired to, research has yet to capture which characteristics matter most for which
adolescents. This limits our understanding of inequalities in aspirations because different
theories emphasize the role of certain occupational characteristics over others. This article
examines whether and how evaluations of multiple characteristics combine into distinct logics
of aspirations based on adolescents’ gender, class, and gender-class intersection. We combine
Swiss data from the DAB Panel Study on adolescents’ aspirations with O*NET data on
occupational characteristics. Using conditional logit models, we estimate the relationships
between occupational characteristics and the choice of aspired occupation. Results show that
girls prioritize occupations satisfying female-typed interests and those requiring higher
education levels, while boys avoid occupations with high shares of women and high
educational requirements. High-class adolescents favour artistic and investigative occupations,
whereas low-class adolescents are averse to highly educated and high-income occupations.
Intersectional analyses reveal that low-class boys are particularly disadvantaged, exhibiting the
strongest aversion to highly educated occupations. Overall, findings highlight that aspirations
are shaped by multiple occupational characteristics rather than a single dimension,
underscoring the importance of a multidimensional perspective to better understand
inequalities in adolescent aspirations.

articles_hidden.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
articles_hidden.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro di Molfetta; Valeria Notarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles_hidden.abstract: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3,225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2,991 priced capital increases on 1,330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

articles_hidden.title: From Working Life to Retirement: Changing Educational Inequalities in Income Trajectories in Germany
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Ordemann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Previous literature has mainly focussed on either income trajectories of higher education graduates in working life or in retirement. This paper advances this literature by investigates the inequalities of income trajectories at the transition into retirement and compare the trajectories to other educational graduates for the case of Germany. While cumulative advantage theory suggests that education-based income inequalities widen throughout working life, the institutional design of the German pension system fundamentally alters these trajectories. 
Using data from 1,741 (11,740 observations) baby boomers from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study (SOEP) I combine descriptive income trajectories with fixed effects regression and replacement rate analysis. find a stratified pattern by educational degree in pre- and post-retirement income. However, income inequality by education degree is more pronounced during work life than in retirement: At the transition into retirement income differences are compressed relative to pre-retirement disparities. This compression operates through heterogeneous replacement rates. Higher educated individuals have lower replacement rates than the rest of the educational groups. Germany’s contribution-capped statutory pension system therefore constitutes a structurally induced erosion of the income advantage that higher education generates over a working lifetime.
